He even wanted to propagate Yoga-vāśiṣṭha—Māyāvāda philosophy—in order to be punished by Lord Caitanya, which would prove that He was recognized as a servant of the Lord. Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura, Gadādhara Paṇḍita, and Nityānanda were also completely absorbed in rendering service to Lord Caitanya. The associates of the Lord are all absorbed in the meditation of service to Lord Caitanya, and therefore they have the power to make others servants of the Lord. Their hearts are free from pride, they have no personal ambitions whatsoever, and they offer respect to everyone.

Lord Nityānanda was so tolerant that even though He was struck on the head with a clay pot, still He prayed for the deliverance of Jagāi and Mādhāi. He begged Lord Caitanya, “Please, deliver them!” How can the Lord ever refuse His servants? It is therefore our great fortune to come in contact with the servants of Lord Caitanya. Only by their mercy can we someday hope to obtain the greatest benediction—the service of Lord Caitanya—and become recognized as His servants. There is no other way to become recognized.

Our attitude should be that whatever happens to us, we see how Kṛṣṇa’s hand is involved in it. Kṛṣṇa may put us in a difficult situation or in a very happy situation, but we should always pray, “Whatever situation I am put in, as long as You are involved in it, Kṛṣṇa, I know I am safe. I do not want to be put into any situation in which You are not personally involved.” Kṛṣṇa is all good, He is Absolute, He has no friends and no enemies, and He is equal to everyone.

Kṛṣṇa says, “I have no enemies, nor have I friends.” Na me dveṣyo ’sti na priyaḥ. The word dveṣya means “enemy.” We are envious of our enemies and friendly toward our friends, but because Kṛṣṇa is absolute, even when He appears to be inimical toward some demon He is actually a friend. When Kṛṣṇa kills a demon, the demon’s demoniac activities are killed, and he immediately becomes a saint and merges into the supreme impersonal effulgence, the brahma-jyotir. (Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Chapter 11)

If Kṛṣṇa punishes somebody or kills a demon, it is for their benefit. When Kṛṣṇa appeared, He carried weapons. Sometimes He invoked His Sudarśana cakra and cut off the heads of demons like Śiśupāla. Lord Caitanya, however, is so merciful that when He appeared in this Age of Kali-yuga, He did not carry any weapon to kill the demons. Instead, He appeared to destroy within us the demoniac mentality for engaging in sinful activities. However the Lord deals with us, we benefit.

Lord Kapiladeva states:

*mad-āśrayāḥ kathā mṛṣṭāḥ*  
*śṛṇvanti kathayanti ca*  
*tapanti vividhās tāpā*  
*naitān mad-gata-cetasaḥ*

**“Engaged constantly in hearing and chanting about me My devotees never suffer from material miseries because they are always filled with thoughts of My activities and pastimes.” (Bhāg. 3.25.23)**

A pure devotee prays to always remember the Lord. We may not be so advanced to say to Kṛṣṇa, “Do whatever You have to do to make me Your devotee.” However, we can pray, “Please, let me always remember You. That is the greatest benediction.” Nobody wants to ask for suffering, except for someone like Queen Kuntī:

*vipadaḥ santu tāḥ śaśvat*  
*tatra tatra jagad-guro*  
*bhavato darśanaṁ yat syād*  
*apunar bhava-darśanam*

**“I wish that all those calamities would happen again and again so that we could see You again and again, for seeing You means that we will no longer see repeated births and deaths.” (Bhāg. 1.8.25)**

When we hear this prayer, we can understand how elevated a devotee Queen Kuntī must be. She is saying that when she is in difficulty, she remembers always remembers the Lord.” By remembering Kṛṣṇa, the difficulties become so insignificant that she does not even see them. The devotee can transcend them by his constant remembrance of the Lord.

Since it is not such an easy thing to be recognized as the servant of the Lord, we should pray for it, and associate with and faithfully serve those devotees who are servants of the Lord. They can help us to clean all these impurities within our heart, which are obstacles for becoming recognized as the servants of the Lord. By the mercy of the servants of Lord Caitanya, even a proud person can become free from pride.

We should all aspire to become servants of Lord Caitanya. Lord Caitanya and Lord Nityānanda have very mercifully appeared together to engage us in Their service for our benefit. There are so many ways we can render service unto Them, which will allow our hearts to become clean. Śrīla Prabhupāda would often say that purification comes in the fire of ordeal. In other words, purification will come when we are put in a difficult situation. However, such purification is the cleansing of the heart, and when the heart becomes clean, then we can be recognized as servants of Lord Caitanya.

Lord Caitanya and Lord Nityānanda work so nicely together. They are very close associates and perfectly know each other’s heart. We should approach the servants of Lord Caitanya by approaching His greatest servant, Lord Nityānanda, who is the original spiritual master. We should also pray to those Vaiṣṇavas who are representatives of Lord Nityānanda to help us clean our hearts and become free from all of the impediments that are keeping us away from serving Lord Caitanya purely. We should pray for their association, instructions and even their punishment. Only by the association of the servants of the Lord can we become servants of the Lord.

Not only should we give our bodies to Lord Caitanya and Lord Nityānanda, but we should also give Them our minds and words. We should place our hearts on the sacrificial altar and beg Them to clean our heart, and not only take our mind, body and words, but our very life itself. This will make us a dedicated servant birth after birth after birth. This should be our fervent prayer to Their Lordships.

## Qualification to Come Closer to the Lord

*nityo nityānāṁ cetanaś cetanānām*  
*eko bahūnāṁ yo vidadhāti kāmān*

**He is the supreme eternally conscious person who maintains all other living entities. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.13)**

How Kṛṣṇa maintains all the living entities in the material world is very different from the way He maintains His devotees in the spiritual world. In the material world, material nature takes care of the living entities and the Lord accompanies them as the Supersoul. The relationship that the living entities have with the Supersoul in the material world is not exactly the same as the relationship the devotees have with the Lord in the spiritual world. In the material world, Kṛṣṇa is simply seated within everyone’s heart as the witness. He gives sanction to everyone’s activities, but there is no līlā. There is no līlā when there is no bhakti in the heart, although it is lying dormant. When bhakti is awakened within the heart, līlā begins and there is a reciprocal relationship between the Lord within the heart and the living entity. When bhakti is lying dormant within the heart and the living entity is turning away from Kṛṣṇa, the Supersoul simply witnesses and gives sanction. It is not a very relishable or intimate relationship.

When the living entity goes on to the next birth, the Lord reminds him about all of his desires, and fashions a suitable body for his next life. Although He gives sanction to the desires of the living entity, He says, “When the living entity turns to Me, then I give him the understanding by which he can come to Me.” Kṛṣṇa smiles and says, “Now I am ready to help you.”

Prabhupāda says that the Lord is protecting all living entities just as a king is protecting all of his citizens. Without His protection, no one can live for a single moment. Although Kṛṣṇa is giving His protection, the intimacy is not there until bhakti is awakened. For the pure devotees, it is certainly a very intimate connection. Because the pure devotees only think of Kṛṣṇa, He says, “My devotee is in My heart and I am in the heart of the devotee. My devotee doesn’t think of anybody but Me and I don’t think of anyone but him.”

This is the natural relationship that exists between the devotee and the Lord. The relationship becomes increasingly intimate and the Lord becomes inclined to give more of Himself to His devotee.

*ye yathā māṁ prapadyante*  
*tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham*

**“As they surrender unto Me I will reward them accordingly.” (Bg. 4.11)**

*mayy āsakta-manāḥ pārtha*  
*yogaṁ yuñjan mad-āśrayaḥ*  
*asaṁśayaṁ samagraṁ māṁ*  
*yathā jñāsyasi tac chṛṇu*

**“Now hear, O son of Pṛthā, how by practicing yoga in full consciousness of Me, with mind attached to Me, you can know Me in full, free from doubt.” (Bg. 7.1)**

Kṛṣṇa gives more confidential knowledge to the devotee to the degree that he is eager to come to Him. If we want an intimate connection and confidentiality, then we have to be consistent in our desires to go to Kṛṣṇa. Being in our heart, He knows the degree to which we want to go to Him. When He sees the devotee making an endeavor to come closer to Him, to please Him and to serve Him, then He reveals more about Himself. When Kṛṣṇa says, “I give them the understanding by which they come to Me,” it means “so that they can come closer to Me.” The closer one comes to somebody, the more they will know about him.

Similarly, a confidential friend may tell you something very private within their heart that they do not speak openly about to everybody. They only speak about it to those who are close to them. Thus, Kṛṣṇa says that to those who are always endeavoring to come to Him, He gives them a more confidential understanding of Himself.

Sometimes devotees are very eager to jump immediately into the confidential subject matters, but if the adhikāra (qualification) is not there, they will not be able to come closer to Kṛṣṇa.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says that it is like the person who tries to get the ripest fruit on the top of the tree by jumping. You can jump as much as you want, but the fruit is out of reach at the top of the tree. If you want to get to that ripe fruit, you have to climb the tree. Similarly, sometimes people want to get the confidential subject matter, but they do not want to climb the tree. As Prabhupāda said, one must first deserve and then desire. We have to show Kṛṣṇa that we really want confidential knowledge of Him. We have to hanker for it and qualify ourselves. That should be our bhajana and sādhana.

When Kṛṣṇa in our heart sees that we have a sincere desire to come closer to Him and that we have the adhikāra, then He will speak to us through the mouths of Vaiṣṇavas. When we hear the confidential subject matter through the mouths of Vaiṣṇavas, then we will see how close we can come to Kṛṣṇa. We will want to serve Kṛṣṇa more intimately. Such an intimate relationship can be achieved between Kṛṣṇa and His devotee. Prabhupāda says:

Kṛṣṇa always sees to the comforts of His devotees, and the devotees are always busy seeing that Kṛṣṇa is satisfied. The devotees dress Kṛṣṇa, supply Him food, and always engage in serving Him, and similarly Kṛṣṇa always sees to the happiness of His devotees. This is the intimate relationship between the devotee and Kṛṣṇa. Every living entity has a relationship with Kṛṣṇa, but when one becomes a devotee the relationship becomes intimate. (Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Chapter 20)

Kṛṣṇa is very eager for that relationship with His devotees. He is reciprocating with them, maintaining them, and taking care of them. That is His līlā. The Lord always thinks of His devotees as His most precious possessions, and never considers them a burden.

Just as a person who has a very valuable jewel holds it very tightly, in the same way, Kṛṣṇa always holds His devotees very tightly, because they are so dear to Him. He says, “I will do anything for you. Please ask Me what you want.”

The devotee will say, “I do not want anything.”

Kṛṣṇa will insist, “Ask Me anything, please! Let Me do something for you.”

The devotee always says, “Please let me remember You! Please do not let me ever forget You even for a moment! Please let me serve You!”

It is explained in the Bhāgavatam by Nārada Muni that the Supreme Lord is very dear to those devotees who have no material possessions and who desire to possess only devotional service to the Supreme Lord. Indeed the Lord relishes the activities of those devotees.

When Lord Caitanya wanted to give Haridāsa Ṭhākura a benediction, he said, “I beg You Lord, please just let me have the remnants of foodstuff from Your devotees. That is all I ask!” Then, becoming embarrassed, he said, “Please, forgive me! I realize that I have asked for something that I am not qualified for. I have asked for something so great! I should not have asked for something like that!” Feeling unqualified, he begged the Lord for forgiveness.

There are many prayers of devotees mentioned in the Bhāgavatam to which the Lord says, “Please ask any benediction you would like,” and the devotee says, “Please just let me be in the association of Your devotees, because Your devotees are always speaking about You! If I can always be in the association of Your devotees, then certainly I will be able to remember You! Please, give me this benediction.” Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura even prayed, “Let me take birth as an insect in the house of Your devotee so that I can hear Your glories. That is much better than taking birth as a Lord Brahmā.”

Therefore, devotees do ask something from the Lord, but He is so grateful and loves them so much that He will give them much more than they asked, by giving them the most intimate connection with Himself.

## Full Surrender

*apy adya nas tvaṁ sva-kṛtehita prabho*  
*jihāsasi svit suhṛdo ’nujīvinaḥ*  
*yeṣāṁ na cānyad bhavataḥ padāmbujāt*  
*parāyaṇaṁ rājasu yojitāṁhasām*

**“O my Lord, You have executed all duties Yourself. Are You leaving us today, though we are completely dependent on Your mercy and have no one else to protect us, now when all kings are at enmity with us?” (Bhāg. 1.8.37)**

PURPORT

The Pāṇḍavas are most fortunate because with all good luck they were entirely dependent on the mercy of the Lord. In the material world, to be dependent on the mercy of someone else is the utmost sign of misfortune, but in the case of our transcendental relation with the Lord, it is the most fortunate case when we can live completely dependent on Him. The material disease is due to thinking of becoming independent of everything. But the cruel material nature does not allow us to become independent. The false attempt to become independent of the stringent laws of nature is known as material advancement of experimental knowledge. The whole material world is moving on this false attempt of becoming independent of the laws of nature. Beginning from Rāvaṇa, who wanted to prepare a direct staircase to the planets of heaven, down to the present age, they are trying to overcome the laws of nature. They are trying now to approach distant planetary systems by electronic mechanical power. But the highest goal of human civilization is to work hard under the guidance of the Lord and become completely dependent on Him. The highest achievement of perfect civilization is to work with valor but at the same time depend completely on the Lord. The Pāṇḍavas were the ideal executors of this standard of civilization. Undoubtedly they were completely dependent on the good will of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, but they were not idle parasites of the Lord. They were all highly qualified both by personal character and by physical activities. Still they always looked for the mercy of the Lord because they knew that every living being is dependent by constitutional position. The perfection of life is, therefore, to become dependent on the will of the Lord, instead of becoming falsely independent in the material world. Those who try to become falsely independent of the Lord are called anātha, or without any guardian, whereas those who are completely dependent on the will of the Lord are called sanātha, or those having someone to protect them. Therefore we must try to become sanātha so that we can always be protected from the unfavorable condition of material existence. By the deluding power of the external material nature we forget that the material condition of life is the most undesirable perplexity. The Bhagavad-gītā therefore directs us (7.19) that after many, many births one fortunate person becomes aware of the fact that Vāsudeva is all in all and that the best way of leading one’s life is to surrender unto Him completely. That is the sign of a mahātmā. All the members of the Pāṇḍava family were mahātmās in household life. Mahārāja Yudhiṣṭhira was the head of these mahātmās, and Queen Kuntīdevī was the mother. The lessons of the Bhagavad-gītā and all the Purāṇas, specifically the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, are therefore inevitably connected with the history of the Pāṇḍava mahātmās. For them, separation from the Lord was just like the separation of a fish from water. Śrīmatī Kuntīdevī, therefore, felt such separation like a thunderbolt, and the whole prayer of the Queen is to try to persuade the Lord to stay with them. After the Battle of Kurukṣetra, although the inimical kings were killed, their sons and grandsons were still there to deal with the Pāṇḍavas. It is not only the Pāṇḍavas who were put into the condition of enmity, but all of us are always in such a condition, and the best way of living is to become completely dependent on the will of the Lord and thereby overcome all difficulties of material existence. (Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Chapter 20)

Teachings of Queen Kuntī is not only deep philosophy, but it teaches us how to apply it. Śrīla Prabhupāda has a way of presenting his commentaries to prevent us from eluding application of his teachings. Śrīla Prabhupāda is talking about the very elevated subject of full surrender, and he is giving us an indication of the necessity of doing so. He describes the Pāṇḍavas as an ideal example, especially as they were mahātmās in household life. The Pāṇḍavas were an ideal and exemplary family.

In the purport, it says that in the material world, to be dependent on the mercy of someone else is the utmost sign of misfortune. This is because it means that we have to give up our independence and do whatever they tell us to do, so that we can get what we need from them. Nobody likes that. In fact, that is the cause of so many wars in the material world. People do not want to be dictated by someone else. They do not want to be controlled by someone else.

For example, when the British took control of India, Mahatma Gandhi wanted to free the Indians from the influence of British rule, not wanting to be controlled by them and dependent upon them.

When one works for somebody else, he may realize that in order to get his salary, he has to do everything he is told to do, being completely dependent upon the other person. Sometimes the employer has to give certain concessions to his workers so that they will continue to work for him, and then there are always negotiations between the employers and the workers. The workers want to get as much as they can with the least amount of work as possible, and employers want to get as much work as they can with the least amount of salary as possible. They are always struggling. Unless a person has unlimited assets at his disposal to continue accepting more and more dependents, it is actually a burden for him.

In the case of a transcendental relationship with the Lord, however, it is the most fortunate case when we can live in complete dependence upon Him. The difference is obviously that the Lord does not consider His dependent to be a burden upon Him. Prabhupāda says in his commentary that Kṛṣṇa is always eager to see to the comforts of His devotees.

Of course, this is not referring to being dependent upon a devotee. If we are dependent upon a devotee, we are dependent upon him for something else besides material things. Prabhupāda always spoke very strongly against going to a Vaiṣṇava simply to beg for some material boon or benediction. A devotee has something much more valuable to give than material assets. He possesses the Supreme Lord and is very eager to give Kṛṣṇa to others. It is not a burden for him to maintain others by giving them what he has in his possession. It is the source of his happiness, because it is the source of the Lord’s pleasure. Kṛṣṇa says:

*ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ*  
*mad-bhakteṣv abhidhāsyati*  
*bhaktiṁ mayi parāṁ kṛtvā*  
*mām evaiṣyaty asaṁśayaḥ*

**“For one who explains the supreme secret to the devotees, devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me. There is no servant in this world more dear to Me than he, nor will there ever be one more dear.” (Bg. 18.68-69)**

*mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat*  
*kiñcid asti dhanañjaya*  
*mayi sarvam idaṁ protaṁ*  
*sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva*

**“There is no Truth superior to Me. Everything rests upon Me, as pearls are strung on a thread.” (Bg. 7.7)**

Everything is resting upon Kṛṣṇa and everyone is depending upon Him. However, the devotees depend upon Kṛṣṇa exclusively, under all circumstances, for the opportunity to be able to remember Him. The symptoms of a really Kṛṣṇa conscious person are that he knows that Kṛṣṇa is the supreme master, he always thinks himself in danger without Kṛṣṇa, and by taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, he always feels safe.

Prabhupāda’s tells the story of his son on the train. He was in great distress when the conductor told him, “You don’t have a ticket? Get off the train!” But as soon as he remembered that his father was there, all his anxiety went away. The child feels so dependent upon the father, and remembrance of the father is a source of strength and the feeling of protection.

Similarly, the devotee can be satisfied in any condition of life by remembering the Lord, and therefore feels so protected. There is no greater protection that one can possibly have. In such a condition, he has no fear and no anxiety. This is Vaikuṇṭha, and is what the devotees experience in the spiritual world. When there is danger, they simply remember their friend and call out, “Kṛṣṇa!”

When the cowherd boys were entering into the mouth of the Aghāsura demon, they thought, “It is okay because Kṛṣṇa is here!” They did not experience any anxiety at potentially being swallowed up by the fiery demon.

Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure is in hearing devotees who are calling out His names, and in taking care of all of their needs.

*nityo nityānāṁ cetanaś cetanānām*  
*eko bahūnāṁ yo vidadhāti kāmān*

(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.13)

Kṛṣṇa is the supreme eternal living being, maintaining all other living beings. He maintains His devotees by giving His devotee what is most important for him. However, in the material world, the most important thing for the materialist is that which maintains and gives pleasure to his body. Kṛṣṇa therefore says, “Why do I have to get involved in that? If that is all they want from Me, let somebody else take care of them.” Prahlāda Mahārāja describes that in his prayer to Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva in the Bhāgavatam:

*bālasya neha śaraṇaṁ pitarau nṛsiṁha*  
*nārtasya cāgadam udanvati majjato nauḥ*  
*taptasya tat-pratividhir ya ihāñjaseṣṭas*  
*tāvad vibho tanu-bhṛtāṁ tvad-upekṣitānām*

**“My Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva, O Supreme, because of a bodily conception of life, embodied souls neglected and not cared for by You cannot do anything for their betterment. Whatever remedies they accept, although perhaps temporarily beneficial, are certainly impermanent.” (Bhāg. 7.9.19)**

Because of their bodily conception of life and because they only want something material to give them pleasure and maintain the body, they are neglected by the Lord and He does not personally take care of them. The material nature has already been perfectly set up in such a way to give them what they deserve. Śrīla Prabhupāda says that those who try to become falsely independent of the Lord are called anātha, or without any guardian. On the other hand, that which is most important for the devotee is the opportunity to serve the Lord. Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura offers a very nice prayer in his Gītā-mālā (2.26):

*anatha-batsala tumi, adhama anatha ami,*  
*twadiya saksat-dasya magi*  
*e prasāda koro dan, rakho anather pran,*  
*chadi’ sab taba dasya magi*

**“I know that You are most kind and affectionate to those who are helpless without their master. I am actually such a fallen soul who is also bereft of my Master, and feeling so helpless. Therefore I am now begging for Your personal service. Please grant this favor just to save the life of this helpless orphan. Giving up everything else, I am now begging only for Your service.”**

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura is asking for the gift of service to the Lord. That is what is most important for a devotee. When a devotee takes that position of desiring the opportunity to serve the Lord, the Lord maintains him by giving him service. Everything else he needs is automatically there, because the Lord is very eager to take care of His devotee. Mixed devotees, however, do not realize that. They think that they have to take care of all their material needs first before they can do some service, but the Lord is very much inclined to those devotees who are fully dependent upon Him.

The Lord had told Śrīvāsa Paṇḍita, “Even if the Goddess of Fortune becomes impoverished, I will personally carry on My head everything that you need directly to your doorstep. You will never be in want. You will never be in need.”

We must not think that only if Kṛṣṇa brings everything to our doorstep, then we will serve Him. By making such a condition, the devotee actually expresses to Kṛṣṇa that more important than the service are his necessities, and that is his condition for Kṛṣṇa’s service. Kṛṣṇa is very much inclined to those devotees who only want to serve Him. Nārada Muni states this in the Fourth Canto of the Bhāgavatam (4.31.21): “The Supreme Lord is very dear to those devotees who have no material possessions and who are fully satisfied in possessing devotional service to the Lord. Indeed, the Lord relishes the activities of such devotees.”

We should never think that our dependence upon Kṛṣṇa is a burden to Him. Kṛṣṇa is ready to accept all of His devotees and to serve them. He wants to do that. He is anātha-vatsala—very kind and affectionate to those who have no shelter. He is also glorified as bhakta-vatsala—very kind and affectionate to those who have devotion, and He is very much inclined to give them everything they need. A devotee needs an opportunity to serve Kṛṣṇa, and if he has the opportunity to do so, he is so satisfied by that service in any condition of life. A devotee is happy to let Kṛṣṇa do with him whatever He would like. That is the difference between a devotee and a non-devotee.

**Question: It may be very difficult to pray to Kṛṣṇa like this if we are afraid to say, “Do with me whatever You like,” because Kṛṣṇa may do it in such a way that we will have to suffer. How should we pray to Kṛṣṇa?**

This is a very honest question. We are afraid to fully surrender because we are afraid of how Kṛṣṇa might do it. Queen Kuntī prayed to Kṛṣṇa, “Just let me remember You.” She said:

*vipadaḥ santu tāḥ śaśvat*  
*tatra tatra jagad-guro*  
*bhavato darśanaṁ yat syād*  
*apunar bhava-darśanam*

**“I wish that all those calamities would happen again and again so that we could see You again and again, for seeing You means that we will no longer see repeated births and deaths.” (Bhāg. 1.8.25)**

A devotee should pray like this and should not be afraid. The goal is to always remember the Lord, and by so doing the devotee feels safe.

*smartavyaḥ satataṁ viṣṇur vismartavyo na jātucit*  
*sarve vidhi-niṣedhāḥ syur etayor eva kiṅkarāḥ*

**Kṛṣṇa is the origin of Lord Viṣṇu. He should always be remembered and never forgotten at any time. All the rules and prohibitions mentioned in the śāstras should be the servants of these two principles. (Padma Purāṇa, as quoted in Cc. Madhya 22.113)**

If we are too afraid, we do not have to say to the Lord, “Do with me as You like.” We can just pray, “Let me remember You under all circumstances.” Remembrance of the Lord is the safest place for us. If we can remember the Lord, then we can see the Lord in everything, and thus we will feel sheltered, safe and protected. The Lord will never do anything that will not help His devotee. Everything He does for His devotee is always for their benefit. We must practice cultivating that faith in the Lord. With that faith, we can be satisfied.

The Pāṇḍavas are such ideal examples, because in all circumstances they were fully dependent upon the Lord. Śrīla Prabhupāda describes that to be fully dependent upon the Lord does not mean that they would simply let the Lord do everything for them. Śrīla Prabhupāda says:

The highest goal of human civilization is to work hard under the guidance of the Lord and become completely dependent on Him. The highest achievement of perfect civilization is to work with valor, but at the same time depend completely on the Lord. The Pāṇḍavas were the ideal executors of this standard of civilization. Undoubtedly they were completely dependent on the good will of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, but they were not idle parasites of the Lord. (Purport to Bhāg. 1.8.37)

Sometimes people misunderstand, thinking that to live completely dependent upon the Lord means to not do anything themselves, and just wait for the Lord to provide. However, as Prabhupāda says, the Pāṇḍavas were not idle parasites. They worked very hard, but always depended upon the Lord for the results. A parasite is something that depends upon somebody else’s mercy. It lives off the work and efforts of others, but does not contribute anything itself.

Prabhupāda further explains in the Third Chapter of the Bhagavad-gītā that devotees are not idle parasites. Everybody has some work to perform, and those who do not perform their work are a disturbance to society. Thus, we must perform our duties, but the perfection of our duties is to do it for the satisfaction of the Lord. This is what distinguishes the devotee from the non-devotee.

Kṛṣṇa also states in the Eighteenth Chapter of the Bhagavad-gītā (18.57-58): “In all activities just depend upon Me and work always under My protection. In such devotional service, be fully conscious of Me. If you become conscious of Me, you will pass over all the obstacles of conditioned life by My grace. If, however, you do not work in such consciousness but act through false ego, not hearing Me, you will be lost.” Thus, all activities should be connected to Kṛṣṇa. Every devotee should see how the duties that have been given to him have been given to him by Kṛṣṇa. If he cannot see the connection between his duties and Kṛṣṇa, then how can he depend on the Lord? The goal of all our efforts is to be conscious that we are subordinate to the will of the Lord.

Śrīla Prabhupāda named our society the International Society for Krishna Consciousness for a reason—he wanted to see every one of its members become Kṛṣṇa conscious. The highest stage is to be able to always remember Kṛṣṇa. The paramahaṁsas, who are on the topmost platform, have no duties to perform, because they are always fixed in remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, and are always satisfied in any condition of life.

Thus, the Pāṇḍavas were always endeavoring to satisfy the Lord, and they worked with courage because they had firm faith. This is how to live a life of dependence—by learning how to see Kṛṣṇa’s presence in everything, and by being dependent upon Him in all circumstances—whether in happiness or distress and whether in difficult times or easy times. In fact, the devotee is even afraid of easy times, because in the easy times it is easier to forget the Lord. Knowing that, the Lord helps His devotees accordingly. Kṛṣṇa knows the best way to help His devotees. He will therefore put His devotees into a difficult situation so that they can remember Him. It is for our benefit. He knows exactly what His devotee needs to advance in spiritual life, and if Kṛṣṇa does it, we should accept it.

In the material world, we are always trying to prove that somebody else is to blame for our suffering. Somebody who lives in this kind of consciousness lives in hell because he can never think of Kṛṣṇa. He is always trying to do different things to change the situations externally, but this only creates more problems for himself. He is creating his own suffering because he refuses to see Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇa’s hand. Therefore, Kṛṣṇa consciousness means changing this consciousness. When we change our consciousness from mundane consciousness to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, Kṛṣṇa helps. He says in Bhagavad-gītā (10.10):

*teṣāṁ satata-yuktānāṁ*  
*bhajatāṁ prīti-pūrvakam*  
*dadāmi buddhi-yogaṁ taṁ*  
*yena mām upayānti te*

**“To those who are always endeavoring, worshipping Me with love, I give them the understanding by which they can come to Me.”**

## Real Dependence

*apy adya nas tvaṁ sva-kṛtehita prabho*  
*jihāsasi svit suhṛdo ’nujīvinaḥ*  
*yeṣāṁ na cānyad bhavataḥ padāmbujāt*  
*parāyaṇaṁ rājasu yojitāṁhasām*

**“O my Lord, You have executed all duties Yourself. Are You leaving us today, though we are completely dependent on Your mercy and have no one else to protect us, now when all kings are in enmity with us?” (Bhāg. 1.8.37)**

PURPORT

The symptoms of a really Kṛṣṇa conscious person are that he knows that Kṛṣṇa is the supreme master, he always thinks himself in danger without Kṛṣṇa, and by taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet he always feels safe. Kṛṣṇa says, kaunteya pratijānīhi na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati: “You may declare to the world that My devotee is never vanquished.” (Bg. 9.31) If one becomes a pure devotee of Kṛṣṇa, there is no question of danger. Of course, Kṛṣṇa gives protection to everyone, for without His protection no one can live even for a single moment. But one should not think, “If Kṛṣṇa is giving protection to everyone, what is the use of becoming a devotee?” A king gives protection to every one of his citizens, for that is his duty, but he especially protects his own circle of men. This is not unnatural. If one directly engages in the service of the President, when one is in some difficulty he is especially protected. Although the President gives protection to all the citizens, those who personally associate with him, giving him service, receive special consideration. That is not actually partiality. That is natural. When a gentleman loves all children but has special love for his own children, no one will say, “Oh, why do you love your own children more than others?” No, that is natural. Similarly, Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā, samo ‘haṁ sarva-bhūteṣu: (Bg. 9.29) “I am equal to everyone.” Kṛṣṇa, being God, loves everyone because everyone is part of Him. Nonetheless, He takes special care of His devotees. Therefore He says, kaunteya pratijānīhi na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati: (Bg. 9.31) “My devotee will never be vanquished.”

Kṛṣṇa always sees to the comforts of His devotees, and the devotees are always busy seeing that Kṛṣṇa is satisfied. The devotees dress Kṛṣṇa, supply Him food, and always engage in serving Him, and similarly Kṛṣṇa always sees to the happiness of His devotees. This is the intimate relationship between the devotee and Kṛṣṇa. Every living entity has a relationship with Kṛṣṇa, but when one becomes a devotee the relationship becomes intimate. Therefore Kuntīdevī says to Kṛṣṇa, “How can You leave us? We are Your intimate friends. We are simply living by Your care, by Your mercy. Don’t think that we are safe and that You can therefore leave us. Our life is always under Your mercy, for we have no shelter other than Your lotus feet. Kindly don’t leave us.” This is Kuntī’s prayer. (Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Chapter 20)

In this verse, Queen Kuntī is appealing to the Lord, “Please don’t leave us! Don’t think we are safe. Without You we can never be safe.” This is the mentality of a devotee. He always thinks himself in danger without Kṛṣṇa. By taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, he always feels safe.

It is very natural for the Lord to feel very intimately connected to His devotees, because His devotees are very intimately connected to Him. Therefore a devotee is one who sees Kṛṣṇa’s presence in everything and always depends on the Lord. No matter what situation he is in, the devotee always feels protected.

In an earlier part of his commentary, Śrīla Prabhupāda says that if one becomes fully dependent upon somebody in the material world, generally it is a sign of great misfortune and we feel that we have to give up our individuality and are a slave. It is virtually impossible for the living entity to be independent from everything because by nature, we are dependent beings meant to be dependent upon the Lord. Because we are not dependent upon the Lord, we have to become dependent upon so many other things for our maintenance in this world. We are dependent upon family members, friends, work, the demigods, etc.

*devarṣi-bhūtāpta-nṛṇāṁ pitṝṇāṁ*  
*na kiṅkaro nāyam ṛṇī ca rājan*

(Bhāg. 11.5.41)

Anyone who is completely surrendered to Kṛṣṇa is no longer obliged to anyone else—the demigods, sages, forefathers, humanity, or people in general. By placing oneself in a fully dependent relationship with the Lord, all his obligations are automatically fulfilled.

Having lost our dependence on the Supreme Lord by our artificial attempts to be independent in the material world, we feel cheated and we suffer. Therefore, in the material world, we do not want to be dependent upon anyone else, and our desire to become independent simply increases. A wealthy person thinks, “If I accumulate wealth, I can be independent. I don’t need anybody else for my maintenance.” Everyone is trying to become fully self-sufficient.

In Caitanya-bhāgavata, Lord Caitanya gave the example that a person may have so much food in his house, but it does not mean that he will be able to eat it. If he gets one bacterial germ in his stomach, he will not be able to eat it. Similarly, we may have so much wealth or power, but it does not mean that we are independent. We are always dependent upon the Lord, although we may temporarily think ourselves to be independent. When a person thinks that he has so much wealth, forgetting that everything is coming from Kṛṣṇa, then he simply wants to enjoy it. If we are not careful, using that which has been given to us by the Lord for our own desires, in due course of time, we will be punished by the laws of nature.

In the Seventh Canto of the Bhāgavatam there is a verse in the chapter, Ideal Family Life, which says that one may desire as much wealth as necessary to maintain body and soul together, but one who desires more than that is considered to be a thief and deserves to be punished by the laws of nature. These are the stringent laws of nature that the materialists are blind to, thinking that they are independent from God’s laws.

*prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni*  
*guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ*  
*ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā*  
*kartāham iti manyate*

**The spirit soul bewildered by the influence of false ego thinks himself the doer of activities that are in actuality carried out by the three modes of material nature. (Bg. 3.27)**

Although it is impossible, the living entity tries very hard to be independent from the laws of God. He therefore has to accept so much repeated suffering in the material world. It is therefore good fortune that a devotee is dependent upon the Lord.

*nārāyaṇa-parāḥ sarve*  
*na kutaścana bibhyati*  
*svargāpavarga-narakeṣv*  
*api tulyārtha-darśinaḥ*

**Devotees solely engaged in the devotional service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Nārāyaṇa, never fear any condition of life. For them the heavenly planets, liberation and the hellish planets are all the same, for such devotees are interested only in the service of the Lord. (Bhāg. 6.17.28)**

Thus paramahaṁsas being always fixed in remembrance of the Lord, cannot forget Kṛṣṇa for a moment. The Lord always takes care of such devotees, protects them, and maintains them by providing all their necessities.

We tend to think the necessities of life are food, air, water and shelter, but they are not. Those may be necessities for maintaining life within the body, but life itself, which is not dependent upon the body, also has its necessities.

Govinda dāsa explains in his song, Bhajahū re mana:

*e dhana, yaubana, putra, parijana*  
*ithe ki āche paratīti re*  
*kamala-dala-jala, jīvana ṭalamala*  
*bhajahū hari-pada nīti re*

**What assurance of real happiness is there in all of one’s wealth, youthfulness, sons, and family members? This life is tottering like a drop of water on a lotus petal; therefore you should always serve and worship the divine feet of Lord Hari.**

Because Govinda dāsa considered his worship of the Lord as his only necessity, the Lord took care of all of his material necessities. Teṣāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ, yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham, as Kṛṣṇa says in the Bhagavad-gītā (9.22)—“For those who are always depending upon Me and meditating on My transcendental form, I carry what they lack, and I preserve what they have.” Kṛṣṇa enjoys by serving His devotees who want to come to Him only for service.

The Ninth Canto of the Bhāgavatam describes the story of Durvāsā Muni. When Durvāsā Muni had offended Mahārāja Ambarīṣa, Lord Viṣṇu invoked His Sudarśana cakra to punish him for committing an offense to His fully dependent devotee. As the chakra was chasing Durvāsā Muni, he was seeking shelter from Lord Brahmā and Lord Śiva. When he came to Lord Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha, he begged, “Please protect me. I have gone to Lord Brahmā and Lord Śiva. They can’t give me protection. Please protect me!”

The Lord told Durvāsā Muni, “I am not independent. I am completely under the control of My devotee. Because My devotees have no fruitive desires within the core of their hearts, I am seated there. Those who are servants of My devotees are also very dear to Me. My devotee is in My heart and I am in the heart of My devotee. A devotee does not think of anyone but Me and I do not think of anyone but him.”

Durvāsā Muni said to the Lord, “But You are the Supreme Lord! Certainly You are independent! How can You say You are not independent?”

The Lord said, “But it is My svabhāva (nature) to be dependent upon My devotees.”

“But surely when You see somebody suffering and they are coming to You, You feel compassion for them?”

“Yes, I could, but I don’t have a mind or a heart to think about their suffering, because I don’t even belong to Myself. My devotees take Me into their hearts and serve Me very nicely. Because they are always anxious to serve Me, I want to give them something. But every time I ask My devotee, ‘Please let Me give you something out of gratitude,’ My devotee says, ‘No, I don’t want anything! I just simply want to serve You.’ Therefore even though My devotee doesn’t ask for something, I still want to give him something, which is most valuable, because I am always grateful to those who simply want to serve Me. I therefore give him My most valuable possession—My heart. You are coming to Me for My compassion, but I can’t even think of your need for compassion, because My heart is with My devotee. Therefore, you have to go to My devotee and get My compassion from him, because he has My mind and My heart.”

When the Lord gives His heart, He gives Himself. If one has the Lord, he has everything. All the necessities of life are automatically fulfilled for such a devotee. There will never be any lack in that devotee’s life. Whether he is in poverty or in wealth, he is always satisfied, as Kṛṣṇa is with him constantly and satisfies all his desires much better than he could possibly satisfy himself.

This is also exemplified in the story of Śuklāmbhara Brahmacārī in the Caitanya-bhāgavata. Śuklāmbhara Brahmacārī lived by begging at the homes of the poorest householders. He would get a few broken grains of rice from each home. After accumulating enough broken grains of rice, he would offer it to the Lord, and would be fully satisfied accepting it as prasāda.

Śrīla Vṛndāvana dāsa Ṭhākura describes that although Śuklāmbhara Brahmacārī lived like this, he never knew the meaning of the word poverty because he was satisfied in any condition of life. Śuklāmbhara Brahmacārī was satisfied to do whatever was necessary to maintain body and soul together. Thus, the Lord provided whatever he needed, and Śuklāmbhara did not have to endeavor for anything else. The Lord was so pleased by his devotion that He personally came and took the rice out of his hands.

One time, the Lord asked Śuklāmbhara, “Today I want you to cook something for Me.”

Śuklāmbhara said, “Lord, please don’t test me like this! How could You want something from me? I am just a poor, insignificant beggar. Why would You want anything from my hands?”

The Lord responded, “I do want it. Please cook something for Me today.”

Śuklāmbhara was so bewildered. He started asking all the Vaiṣṇavas, “What should I do? The Lord wants me to cook for Him today!”

The devotees told him, “This is the Lord’s nature. He is always eager to take something from the hands of His devotees.” Similarly, Vidura, in his ecstasy, offered banana peels instead of bananas to the Lord, but the Lord gladly ate the banana peels. Thus the Lord is very anxious to take from His devotees.

Śuklāmbhara said, “How am I going to do this? How can I cook something for the Lord?” He felt unqualified to offer anything to the Lord that was prepared by his own hands.

The Vaiṣṇavas therefore told him, “Go back home and prepare something for the Lord, but just do not touch any of the ingredients with your hands.”

In ecstasy, Śuklāmbhara agreed to do so. He went home and began preparing some nice ghee and the finest rice. While cooking, he was meditating on the Lord’s pleasure. It is described that the Goddess of Fortune personally entered into that kitchen and made everything taste so wonderful.

Lord Caitanya went to perform His midday duty of going down to the Gaṅgā to take His bath. After His bath, He stopped at the house of Śuklāmbhara who lived near the banks of the Gaṅgā. When He came into the house, the Lord stood there and smiled at all the devotees who were present. Then He sat down to take the food from Śuklāmbhara’s hands. Śuklāmbhara very carefully took all the cooked ingredients he prepared, put them on a plate and brought it to the Lord. The Lord began eating the rice. He then looked at Śuklāmbhara in the eyes and said, “Śuklāmbhara, how have you cooked such wonderful rice without touching it with your hands? Such rice I have never tasted before. Friends like you are the root from which I grow.” He was so satisfied by this devotional offering by Śuklāmbhara.

On another occasion, in the middle of kīrtana, Lord Caitanya came over to Śuklāmbhara who used to keep a pouch on his shoulder with all the broken rice he would collect. The Lord grabbed the pouch of rice. However, Śuklāmbhara took back the rice, saying, “No! This is not fit for You! Please do not eat this!”

The Lord said, “What do you mean this is not fit for Me? Don’t you know I relish food from My devotees?” The Lord took that rice back and immediately began to eat it. He said, “I always accept rice from your hands! Previously you, as Sudāmā Brāhmaṇa, came to Me with some broken rice that you had collected. I took that from you at that time and I am taking it from you again! I am always eager to accept from the hands of My devotees.”

Vṛndāvana dāsa Ṭhākura explains that the Lord is so eager to accept from the hands of His devotees that sometimes He will take from His devotees even before the devotee offers it. Ordinarily if one wants the Lord to accept his offering, he must offer it with the appropriate mantras and mudrās. However, when the Lord’s pure devotee is involved, the Lord takes these mantras and mudrās and smashes them into powder! He considers them to be insignificant and He immediately takes directly from the hands of His devotees. This is the relationship the Lord has with His devotees. He is always eager to accept from them, and He is always eager to maintain them by giving them devotional service.

Those who are puffed up with material opulence, great heritage and bodily beauty are generally proud of possessing such things, and will oftentimes deride those who are devotees of the Lord. Even if such persons offer the Lord worship, He will never accept it, as He will not accept anything from the hands of a non-devotee. The Lord is only interested in accepting from the hands of His devotees. That is the perfection of the devotee’s life, because the Lord is maintaining that devotee by giving him devotional service.

The most wonderful characteristic of the Lord is that He is bhakta-vātsalya, which means that He wants to satisfy His devotees. He becomes subordinate and subservient to the desires of His devotees. Any desire that the devotee keeps within the core of the heart, the Lord is always very eager to fulfill.

*smartavyaḥ satataṁ viṣṇur vismartavyo na jātucit*  
*sarve vidhi-niṣedhāḥ syur etayor eva kiṅkarāḥ*

(Padma Purāna)

In his commentary to this verse, Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura explains that Kṛṣṇa must always be remembered and must never be forgotten. This is the constitutional nature, and the primary duty of the living entity. We must become Kṛṣṇa conscious in this life, otherwise it is wasted. He says that all the rules and prohibitions given in the scriptures are meant to serve these two principles—to always remember Kṛṣṇa and to never forget Him. If somebody needs to follow rules and prohibitions, it is because he is unable to always remember Kṛṣṇa.

There are certain favorable things that help us to remember Kṛṣṇa and there are certain unfavorable things that we are supposed to avoid. However, if a person is always thinking of Kṛṣṇa, why does he have to worry about unfavorable things that make one forget Kṛṣṇa?

In this verse, the word satataṁ is used. Generally it means always, but in this verse it means every day. Thus, every day, one has to remember Kṛṣṇa. One has to have some sādhana to do this. That is the devotee’s most important duty in life. Everything else he does is subordinate. Whether he is worshipping the deities, distributing books, working, or taking care of family members, all these activities are part and parcel of remembering Kṛṣṇa and never forgetting Him. They are all meant to support our hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa.

If one sees the activities in his life in this way, he can remember Kṛṣṇa. Otherwise it is very difficult to become Kṛṣṇa conscious. Just as the Pāṇḍavas did, the highest achievement of perfect civilization is to work with valor, but at the same time depend on the Lord. The more we depend on the Lord, the more we will begin to experience internal satisfaction. The more we experience internal satisfaction, the less we need to externally satisfy the demands of the body. We will then have more time to remember the Lord, giving us increasing internal satisfaction. If you are getting spiritual satisfaction, if you are experiencing your devotion increasing, if you are experiencing Kṛṣṇa’s presence in your life, and if you are seeing that your attachment to material things is diminishing, then you know you are engaged in devotional service. It is just like a person who knows that his hunger is being satiated by eating.

If one does not depend on Kṛṣṇa, then Māyā takes care of all of their dealings. Daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī, mama māyā duratyayā. (Bg. 7.14) Kṛṣṇa says, “Māyā is very difficult to overcome. But one who surrenders unto Me can easily overcome it.” Kṛṣṇa will tell Māyā, “Live him alone!” If we try to fight Māyā by our own efforts, we will be subject to more of her efforts. She is much stronger than we are. However, Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (18.66): sarva-dharmān parityajya, mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja—“Abandon all varieties of religion and surrender unto Me. I will deliver you from all sinful reactions.” Kṛṣṇa also explains that we should surrender unto Him by always thinking of Him, always worshipping Him, always offering our obeisances unto Him. By so doing, surely we will return to Him.

We should try to increase our surrender to Kṛṣṇa by utilizing the valuable human form of life every day by performing those activities that help us to remember Him. If we mold our life in that way, then Kṛṣṇa will take care of us by providing whatever we need to return to Him.

**Question: Our material external duties are supposed to support us in coming closer to Kṛṣṇa, but in our practical material life we see that in most cases, they just separate us even more from Kṛṣṇa. Why does this happen?**

It is because of our association. Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains this in great detail in Śrī Bhaktyāloka. By nature, all of us are dependent upon association. If we associate with devotees who are hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa and we develop our affection to associate with those devotees who help us to remember Kṛṣṇa, then because of those affectionate relationships, although we may be in the physical presence of non-devotees in the course of our work, we will not be affected by their association.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says, “Association begins when there is affection.” When there is no affection, one simply deals with non-devotees as a matter of duty, and he is detached: “If have to deal with this non-devotee, I will deal with him as much as is necessary to fulfill my duty.” In his heart, his affection is for devotees, and because he has an attraction for this kind of relationship with devotees, he does not become attracted to the affairs of the materialistic people. He therefore minimizes his time as much as possible in engaging in those affairs, and in his heart he is always thinking of how he can get back into the association of devotees who are increasing his attraction for Kṛṣṇa.

We must know how to associate with devotees. Association does not mean physical proximity or simply working with devotees. Devotees will not have any affection to work together, unless they have affection for hearing and chanting together. If they simply work together, they will see the other devotees in terms of their role in their work. Because they have no other relationship than the role they are playing at work, they will start to find faults in one another, not having any other basis for association. Physical proximity is not association. Association is coming together to increase our Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

Rūpa Gosvāmī describes how devotees should associate with each other with love: “Inquire confidentially and reveal your mind in confidence. Give some gift and accept gifts. Give prasādam and accept prasādam.” When done with love, this is association because we are giving out of affection and because we want nothing in return. By hearing and chanting together, this affection will develop. When we have affection for those kinds of relationships, we will not have affection for materialistic people, we will not become contaminated, and we will remember Kṛṣṇa.

## The Lord’s Protection

**Question: How can we come under the protection of the Lord’s internal potency instead of his external potency?**

Prabhupāda says in his purport in Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Chapter 20:

Those who try to become falsely independent of the Lord are called anātha, or without any guardian, whereas those who are completely dependent on the will of the Lord are called sanātha, or those having someone to protect them. Therefore we must try to be sanātha, so that we can always be protected from the unfavorable condition of material existence. By the deluding power of the external, material nature we forget that the material condition of life is the most undesirable perplexity. The Bhagavad-gītā (7.19) therefore directs us that after many, many births one fortunate person becomes aware of the fact that Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, is all in all and that the best way of leading one’s life is to surrender unto Him completely. That is the sign of a mahātmā. All the members of the Pāṇḍava family were mahātmās in household life. Mahārāja Yudhiṣṭhira was the head of these mahātmās, and Queen Kuntīdevī was the mother. The lessons of the Bhagavad-gītā and all the Purāṇas, specifically the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, are therefore inevitably connected with the history of the Pāṇḍava mahātmās. For them, separation from the Lord was just like the separation of a fish from water. Śrīmatī Kuntīdevī, therefore, felt such separation like a thunderbolt, and the whole prayer of the Queen is to try to persuade the Lord to stay with them. After the Battle of Kurukṣetra, although the inimical kings were killed, their sons and grandsons were still there to deal with the Pāṇḍavas. It is not only the Pāṇḍavas who were put into the condition of enmity; all of us are always in such a condition, and the best way of living is to become completely dependent on the will of the Lord and thereby overcome all difficulties of material existence.

After the Battle of Kurukṣetra ended and the Pāṇḍavas were established in their kingdom, Kṛṣṇa, before going back home to Dvārakā, was taking leave of His aunt and bidding her farewell. It was at that time that Kuntī offered this prayer. Now she directly asks, “Is it a fact that after finishing Your duty You are going away and leaving us alone?” This is the devotee’s position. Kuntīdevī says, yeṣāṁ na cānyad bha vataḥ padāmbujāt: “We have no means of protection other than Your lotus feet.” This is full surrender.

In the process of surrender (śaraṇāgati) there are six items. The first is that one should completely depend on Kṛṣṇa, and the next is that one should accept everything favorable for Kṛṣṇa’s service (ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ). Ānukūlyena kṛṣṇānuśīlanaṁ bhaktir uttamā: \[Cc. Madhya 19.167\] a symptom of first-class bhakti, devotional service, is that one accepts everything favorable for that service. Another item of surrender is prātikūlyasya-vivarjanam, rejecting everything unfavorable to the procedures of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Sometimes the spiritual master says, “Don’t do this,” forbidding something unfavorable, and he also recommends that which is favorable: “Do this. Chant Hare Kṛṣṇa.” Full surrender, therefore, entails giving up unfavorable things and accepting that which is favorable (ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ prātikūlyayasya-vivarjanam). Furthermore, one should believe with full faith, “Kṛṣṇa will give me protection,” and one should count oneself as one of the servants of Kṛṣṇa. These are some of the items of śaraṇāgati, full surrender.

Those who try to become falsely independent are called anātha—those who have no guardian. Śrīla Prabhupāda gives the example that a devotee is like the son of the king, whereas the non-devotee is like an orphan. Even though the son of the king may leave his kingdom, his father always keeps his watchful eye out for him. But the orphan has nobody to look after him. Thus, a devotee is one who has captured Kṛṣṇa’s attention. Kṛṣṇa is ready to offer him protection and to help him to overcome the obstacles of conditional life. However, to come under the complete protection of the Lord through full surrender, one has to come under the protection of the Lord’s internal potency.

Mahātmānas tu māṁ pārtha, daivīṁ prakṛtim āśritāḥ, as Kṛṣṇa describes (Bg. 9.13)—those who are mahātmās, great souls, are under the protection of the daivīṁ prakṛtim (the Lord’s internal potency). One who comes under the protection of this internal potency cannot fall from this position. Kṛṣṇa gives so many indications in Bhagavad-gītā that one who returns to the spiritual world never again has to take his birth in the material world.

In the spiritual world, the Lord’s internal potency, Yogamāyā, is manifest, and she is covering the Lord’s pāriṣads (eternal associates), so that they forget about the Lord’s divinity and simply think of Him in terms of their relationship with Him. The nature of their love is that they only know Kṛṣṇa; they do not know of anything else. In fact, because they are on the topmost platform of devotion, they do not even know that they are the greatest devotees throughout all of creation. This is the nature of the highest platform of knowledge—jñāna-śūnyā bhakti, which means that they are not aware of the Lord’s divinity, of the Lord’s majestic features, of their own greatness, and of the external energy, māyā. They are under the protection of the Lord’s divine internal potency. Therefore their primary activity is giving pleasure to the Lord, and the Lord’s primary activity is giving pleasure to His devotees by keeping them eternally engaged in His loving devotional service. The Lord therefore personally gives Himself to His devotees who love Him, and He submits Himself according to their desires. Such is the nature of bhakti. This is all arranged by the Lord’s internal potency.

Kṛṣṇa says (Bg. 7.25):

*nāhaṁ prakāśaḥ sarvasya*  
*yoga-māyā-samāvṛtaḥ*  
*mūḍho ’yaṁ nābhijānāti*  
*loko mām ajam avyayam*

**“I am never manifest to the foolish and unintelligent. For them I am covered by My internal potency, and therefore they do not know that I am unborn and infallible.”**

That is the potency of the Supreme Lord, Yogamāyā, expanded into the form of Mahāmāyā in the material world. Within the four verses of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam that were revealed within Brahmā’s heart, the Supreme Lord told him, “Whatever you see of any value, if it has no connection with Me, you should know it to be My material energy, or a reflection, which is the projection of light in the darkness.” Thus, anything that may appear to have value, but is not connected to Kṛṣṇa, is His illusory energy.” Therefore in many places, it is described how anyone who conceives anything that is not connected to Kṛṣṇa is under the influence of the illusory energy.

The Eleventh Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam describes the nature of the dualities of the material world:

Although the duality of the material world does not ultimately exist, the conditioned soul experiences it as real under the influence of his own conditioned intelligence. This imaginary experience of a world separate from Kṛṣṇa can be compared to the acts of dreaming and desiring. When the conditioned soul dreams at night of something desirable or horrible, or when he daydreams of what he would like to have or avoid, he creates a reality that has no existence beyond his own imagination. (Bhāg. 11.2.38)

This is the imaginary experience of a world separate from Kṛṣṇa. Just as the conditioned soul who dreams of something very wonderful enjoys his dream, but when he finally wakes up, he realizes that it was just a dream and then suffers. Similarly, when he has a terrible dream, he is in great anxiety, but when he wakes up, he is in ecstasy. However, his ecstasy and suffering are connected to only a dream; they have no connection with reality. Therefore, all that happiness and distress are simply an illusory conception. Thus, the verse describes that he creates a reality which has no existence beyond his own imagination. He imagines that it is very good or very bad, but it has no connection with reality.

Similarly, just as there are night dreams, there are also day dreams, during which one dreams of something he would like to have or something he would like to avoid. The day dream is no different from the night dream, because in the day dream, one is also creating a reality that has no existence beyond his imagination. It is an illusion because that anticipation of happiness does not last. When one gets the fulfillment of his material desire, then there are so many other problems that come with the maintenance of that desire.

Prabhupāda gives the example that happiness in the material world is just like sweet rice mixed with sand. There is some pleasure, but with the sand mixed in, it is really hard to fully appreciate it. Similarly, we cannot fully appreciate happiness that is separate from Kṛṣṇa.

Lord Caitanya says: jīv jāgo, jīv jāgo, gauracānda bole, kota nidrā jāo māyā-piśācīra kole—“How long will you sleep on the lap of the witch called Māyā?” Prabhupāda describes how the conditioned souls are sleeping on Māyā’s lap, and Māyā gently strokes the head of the conditioned soul. However, when the conditioned soul is feeling such comfort on the lap of Māyā, she cuts his throat. That is Māyā’s business. When we are under her shelter, she is doing her service. She is creating a situation where the living entity gets the fulfillment of his material desires.

As soon as he thinks, “Now I am enjoying the fulfillment of my desires!” Māyā always pulls out a very revealing blade to show that this is an illusion. Māyā says, “How long will you be able to enjoy this illusion? Something is going to have to happen. Now that you have enjoyed it enough, it is time for me to reveal the temporary nature of this material world and show you that all of your pleasure is only going to result in your suffering.”

Therefore, a devotee is always praying, “Whatever happens to me, please, Kṛṣṇa, You make it happen! If You do it, I know it has to be for my benefit, because You don’t do anything that is unbeneficial to anyone! You don’t have any friends or enemies! You are equal to everyone! Even if You kill somebody, Your killing makes that person saintly and he gets liberation! Whether You bestow benedictions or You kill, it is always for the benefit of the recipient!”

A devotee is one who has this firm faith in Kṛṣṇa’s protection: “If I always remember Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa will always act for my best interest.” Why would He ever want to put a devotee in a situation to cause him to suffer? Our suffering is only due to forgetfulness of Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, although the Lord may put His devotee in an apparently suffering situation, the Lord does that only to bring His devotee closer to Him so that he can become fully freed from all suffering. Yasyāham anugṛhṇāmi, hariṣye tad-dhanaṁ śanaiḥ—when the Lord is particularly disposed towards His devotee, He takes everything away from him so that he has nothing except Kṛṣṇa and thus comes closer to Him. Kṛṣṇa is a thief who steals the garments of the gopīs, but He also steals the reactions of sinful life from those who surrender unto Him. Kṛṣṇa says, “Abandon all varieties of religion and surrender unto Me. I will steal all your reactions away from you.”

There is a very wonderful prayer wherein a devotee is praying to the Supreme Lord as the Supreme Thief. The devotee prays to the Lord, “O Supreme Thief, You have taken away my family; You have taken away my position; You have taken away my wealth; You have taken away my home; You have taken everything away from me. You are a Supreme Thief. You have taken away all sinful reactions. A thief deserves to be punished. Therefore, now I will punish You. My punishment is that I will bind You with a rope. I will tie You up and will lock You in the prison of my heart. You will have to stay there forever. I will never let You out. Hundreds of millions of pralayas may come and go, but this is the fit punishment for such a thief as You.”

A devotee prays to the Lord in this way, seeing the Lord as the Supreme Thief who has taken everything away. The Lord allows Himself to be tied up and locked in the heart of His devotee as a prisoner.

Lord Caitanya said to Haridāsa Ṭhākura, “You have purchased Me with your love. You have locked Me up in your heart. Because you have purchased me with your love and I belong to you, you can sell Me to whomever you like.” Only a person who owns something can sell it to whomever he wants.

If you walk out on the street and you call a gentleman over and say, “I would like to sell you this Mercedes Benz. I’ll sell it to you for one thousand dollars.”

“I can have this Mercedes Benz for one thousand dollars?!!”

“Yes, that’s all.”

“Where are the papers?”

“I have no documents.”

However, without the ownership documents, no one will buy it—even at a reduced price. Only the possessor of the car can sell it to whomever he likes.

Lord Caitanya tells Haridāsa Ṭhākura, “You have purchased Me with your love. You have made Me a prisoner in your heart. Now you can sell Me wherever you like.” Such is the power of the Lord’s devotees. The Lord helps His devotee and protects them. Therefore, the devotee simply prays, “Let me remember You. Whatever has to come in the course of making me remember You, it will have to come. But let me always remember You.”

This is exemplified in the story of the brāhmaṇa, Arjunācārya, who lived in poverty. He was sitting and studying Bhagavad-gītā and writing his commentaries. He came to the following verse (Bg. 9.22):

*ananyāś cintayanto māṁ*  
*ye janāḥ paryupāsate*  
*teṣāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ*  
*yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham*

He saw the word vahāmy, which meant that Kṛṣṇa was saying, “I will carry whatever you lack.”

Arjunācārya thought, “This must be some misinterpretation of this word in this verse. I am a very poor brāhmaṇa. Kṛṣṇa is not giving to me, and why should Kṛṣṇa give to me? This word vahāmy is a mistake. It must be karomi.” Karomi means that the Lord makes arrangements, whereas vahāmy means that the Lord personally acts. He therefore took a red pen and struck out the word vahāmy three times and wrote in the word karomi.

This brāhmaṇa and his wife lived in extreme poverty, but they were always satisfied. That is one of the characteristics of Kṛṣṇa’s devotees—to always be satisfied with whatever Kṛṣṇa provides. It is described that all the brāhmaṇa and his wife had between them was one good cloth. So if the wife had to go out, she would wear that cloth and he would stay inside with the torn cloth. If he went out, she would wear the torn cloth.

When Arjunācārya finished making this correction in his work on the verse, he went out to beg for the day, taking the one good cloth for begging. His wife stayed at home, wearing the old, torn cloth. It just so happened that wherever he went that day, he could not get anything. He did not know why no one was giving anything.

Back at his home, there was a knock at their door. Since his wife was in the torn cloth, she could not come to the door. The person kept persistently knocking. She was sitting and thinking, “Oh, what can I do? I can’t answer the door like this! Maybe he’ll go away…” However, he did not go away. He kept on knocking at the door. Then, embarrassed, she covered herself as best as she could and answered the door. There she saw two young boys.

One boy said, “Please, take this quickly!” handing her a huge basket of food—more food than this woman had seen for such a long time!

When she saw this food, she thought, “This is enough for us to live for a year!”

The boy was saying, “Here! Quickly! Please take, take!! We have to go quickly before your husband strikes me again!”

“What?”

“Yes! Your husband struck me!”

“My husband would not do that!”

“You think your husband would not do that? Look at these marks on my body! This is proof!”

She was so amazed and said, “My husband is such a passive brāhmaṇa! He would never do something like this!” The boys quickly left and the wife took all the food and began preparing it.

Meanwhile, Arjunācārya could not get anything from begging that day. After making some attempts to beg, he returned home. He saw the food in their home and asked his wife where it all came from?

His wife said, “Before you ask me that question, please answer my one question. What are you doing beating young boys?!”

“What are you talking about?”

“A young boy came here and brought this huge basket of food. He said you struck him three times! He showed me the marks on his body.”

Arjunācārya asked his wife, “What did you say?” Then he began to think, “Three times?” He went over and looked at his book. He saw in that place where he had struck the word vahāmy—those lines were now gone. He remembered that he had struck it with three lines.

He understood and told his wife, “Do you know who that boy was? You are so fortunate! You are the most fortunate person in all the three worlds! The Supreme Lord has come and He has brought this food to your home! He has personally given it to you with His own hands!”

He began crying, realizing how merciful and kind the Lord is. The Lord wanted to prove that He will always take care of His devotees. He relishes it. For Him, that is His pleasure pastime. The Lord never considers the devotee’s dependence upon Him as some burden. Similarly, the devotee never considers himself to be a burden on the Lord. The devotee just naturally always remembers the Lord and prays for the opportunity to be in such a place that he can always remember the Lord. That is the most valuable protection for the devotee in this world. When the devotees have firm faith in the Lord and depend upon Him utterly, then Kṛṣṇa says, “I will help them! I will bring them to a more intimate relationship with Me! I will reveal everything they need to come to Me.”

This is intimacy, and it is awakened within the heart of the devotee by hearing about these pastimes from the mouth of the Lord’s devotees. Once that intimacy is awakened within the heart and one has faith in what he has heard, he obtains the eligibility for pure devotional service. Therefore, he always prays to be in the association of devotees and to always hear the glories of the Lord. He always endeavors to increase his remembrance of the Lord, and he depends upon the Lord in all circumstances. The more endeavors we make in this direction, the closer we will feel ourselves coming to Kṛṣṇa.

This is how Kṛṣṇa protects His devotees—by helping His devotee to remember Him. Kṛṣṇa is always very eager to give this remembrance of Him to others, in the same way as the devotees of the Lord are always very eager to distribute Kṛṣṇa’s kindness and mercy to others. To be dependent upon the Lord and His devotees is our most fortunate position. If we become fully dependent upon this type of association, then everything else will become much less significant. It will protect us from having to be fully dependent upon the mercy of materialistic people. We will find ourselves not being so dependent upon them, but will simply deal with them as a matter of duty. We are dependent upon Kṛṣṇa. If Kṛṣṇa gives or does not give, the devotee is detached, because he depends only on Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa says that He will never let such a devotee be vanquished. He will always protect him.

The best prayer we can offer to the Lord is to be able to remember Him in any condition of life. Often it is more difficult to remember the Lord when we are experiencing material happiness. Whereas when we are enjoying, it is easy to think that we do not need to depend on the Lord. However, Queen Kuntī says (Bhāg. 1.8.26):

*janmaiśvarya-śruta-śrībhir*  
*edhamāna-madaḥ pumān*  
*naivārhaty abhidhātuṁ vai*  
*tvām akiñcana-gocaram*

**“My Lord, Your Lordship can easily be approached, but only by those who are materially exhausted. One who is on the path of \[material\] progress, trying to improve himself with respectable parentage, great opulence, high education and bodily beauty, cannot approach You with sincere feeling.”**

Prabhupāda explains in the purport to this verse that a person who is experiencing material satisfaction cannot sincerely call out the name of the Lord because he is not depending upon the Lord for his happiness. He is depending upon his wealth, high position, bodily beauty, etc. Therefore, even to be happy is dangerous, especially in the material world, because it is a false conception. We think we are happy, because we are not suffering, but there is so much suffering that still has to come. The devotee therefore prays to the Lord, “Whether I am in happiness or in distress, let me remember You, because then I can see the connection of the happiness and distress in relationship to You. That is my platform of fearlessness in the material world; I simply want to come under Your protection. Don’t let me stay under the protection of Your illusory energy.” A devotee should pray like this every day when he is chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. Pray to the Lord’s internal energy, “Please accept me under Your protection. Please engage me in Kṛṣṇa’s service.” That is the safest place to be. However, we cannot get there by some material formula.

In one lecture, Prabhupāda says that if one wants to go to the spiritual world, he has to be spiritual. By material formulas, we cannot enter into the spiritual world. Just like if one wants to enter into water, he has to have a body suitable for doing so, or else he will drown. If one wants to enter into fire, he has to have a body suitable for entering into fire, or else he will burn. If one wants to enter into the spiritual world, he must be Kṛṣṇa-ised, with no material desires. No one can try to force his way into the spiritual world. Prauḍhā-māyā, the protector of the holy dhāma, protects the Lord from being disturbed by deceitful people whose hearts are full of pride and who think they are qualified to serve the Lord. Such deceitful people can never enter the dhāma.

We should follow in the footsteps of the previous ācāryas and learn from their examples about how to face death and come under the protection of the Lord. If we practice this throughout this life, then certainly Kṛṣṇa will help us at the time of death. Kṛṣṇa says that if we simply go on practicing and endeavoring in this life, whatever assets of devotional service we have, He will preserve for us, and anything that we are lacking, He will give to us. We should cultivate this attitude and learn from Śrīla Prabhupāda’s teachings and his examples given here on how to come under the protection of the Lord’s internal potency.

**Question: By sincere prayers, Kṛṣṇa may remove many undesirable things from the heart, but it may be painful for us. How can we overcome the fear of sincere prayer?**

Purification comes in the fire of ordeal. On a morning walk in Tehran, Prabhupāda was with a group of devotees and was talking about being tested by Kṛṣṇa. Prabhupāda stopped, put his cane down, and looked at the devotees. He said, “Nobody can be recognized as a great devotee of the Lord until he has been severely tested by Kṛṣṇa.” He gave different examples of devotees who had been placed in severe tests, such as Prahlāda Mahārāja and Bali Mahārāja. Prabhupāda explained that there is a price to pay if we want to go back to Godhead, and Kṛṣṇa always helps His devotee who is willing to pay that price. That will give us the strength to go on to the next test. If we are genuinely sincere in our prayers, we will experience how Kṛṣṇa helps us to come closer to Him. Bhaktiḥ pareśānubhavo viraktir, anyatra caiṣa trika eka-kālaḥ (Bhāg. 11.2.42)—devotion, direct experience of Kṛṣṇa and detachment from material things are the three things that come simultaneously for a person who is engaged in devotional service.

If we offer sincere prayers, even though we may be put into difficulty, we will experience Kṛṣṇa’s direct participation in our life and how He helps us to overcome such a difficult situation. Even that which is painful still becomes a source of relief when we remember Kṛṣṇa. This will increase our faith. If our faith remains very weak, it is very difficult to advance. The more our faith increases, however, the more we are capable of dealing with the next test that Kṛṣṇa will give us.

Prabhupāda tells a story of a feather weight fighter, which is one of the lightest weight categories.
