The fighter has a championship match coming up, and he thinks that because this is the most important fight he has ever had, he will work hard, eat more, get more protein, and prepare himself for the fight. However, after many long months of hard work, he steps into the ring and sees that his opponent is a middle weight class! He is no longer in the feather weight class because of all of his work.

Similarly, when we are advancing in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, we become more prepared to deal with the higher opponent by having defeated the previous opponents. Kṛṣṇa helps us. We just have to increase our faith. If we do not step forward and take some risks, then we will not advance. It is a risk, but so is the material world. Which risk would we rather have? Take risks to have to come back again in the material world and go through it all over again, and again, and again? Or take a risk for Kṛṣṇa, and make this our last life and go back to Kṛṣṇa? Either way, we have to give up this body. The death rate is the same as it was thousands of years ago—it is one hundred percent. Therefore, we should put ourselves under Kṛṣṇa’s protection and make this our last life in the material world.

Kṛṣṇa says (Bg. 18.68): ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ, mad-bhakteṣv abhidhāsyati—“For one who explains this supreme secret to the devotees, pure devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me.” It is therefore risk-free. When Kṛṣṇa gives His guarantee, nobody can stop it. Even though we think we are taking a risk, it is insignificant in comparison to the risk of staying in the material world.

**Question: Does Kṛṣṇa only protect His devotee?**

Kṛṣṇa is protecting all living entities, as He is situated within everyone’s heart. No one can live even for a moment without Kṛṣṇa. He is the support and maintenance of all living beings. He is maintaining the entire material and spiritual worlds. Everyone is resting upon Him, just as pearls are resting on a thread. As explained earlier in this chapter, the maintenance of the Lord’s devotees and the maintenance of non-devotees is different. The Lord personally maintains His devotees, whereas living entities in the material world are being maintained by the agency of the Lord’s energies, and the Lord is simply situated within their hearts as Supersoul.

Similarly, although a king protects all his citizens, he naturally protects his intimate circle of men. It is not that it is due to partiality. Rather, it is natural. A gentleman loves all children, but no one will question him of loving his own children more than other children, because it is natural for him to do so. The Supersoul is there within the heart of all living entities, watching over them. He is acting as a witness and a giver of sanction. Thus everyone is being protected by the Lord.

When Prahlāda Mahārāja says that those who are in the bodily conception of life are neglected and not cared for by the Lord, it means that there is no intimacy, but the Supersoul is protecting by giving sanction according to the living entity’s desire, which may be separate from the desire of serving the Lord. The Lord has not forgotten the living entity, but the living entity has turned away from the Lord, and therefore the intimacy and reciprocation is not there. What kind of reciprocation is there if your relationship with somebody is just to have them sanction what you want? You basically do not care about them except that they can sanction what you want. The living entity does not understand his relationship with the Lord, because all he can think about is the fulfillment of his own desires. He therefore does not feel cared for by the Lord, even though the Lord cares for him and protects him, being within the heart witnessing and fulfilling his desires.

Prabhupāda says that every living entity has a relationship with Kṛṣṇa, but when one becomes a devotee, the relationship becomes intimate. When the intimacy is there, then there is līlā—the Lord’s dealings with His devotees. Kṛṣṇa always sees to the comforts of His devotees.

Someone will say, “Kṛṣṇa is not seeing to my comforts! Why is He not taking care of my comforts?” However, intimacy is not there, because there is no loving relationship.

The analogy of two birds is given to describe the Supersoul and living entity. One bird is simply witnessing and the other bird is enjoying the fruits. When the bird who is enjoying the fruits gives up doing so and turns to the other bird, then a relationship is established. Similarly the Lord is in our heart, but we are not turning to Him.

In any situation, whether it is in happiness or distress, we should always be attempting to turn our attention to Kṛṣṇa, because, by so doing, we will actually feel comfortable. A devotee feels satisfied in any situation because he sees how Kṛṣṇa is taking care of him.

Prabhupāda says that the symptoms of a really Kṛṣṇa conscious person are that he knows that Kṛṣṇa is the supreme master, he always thinks himself in danger without Kṛṣṇa, and by taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, he always feels safe. Even in the midst of so many difficulties or calamities, a devotee feels safe if he remembers Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, we must seek out the association of those who will help us to remember Kṛṣṇa.

**Question: Sometimes a devotee is put in a situation where it appears that Kṛṣṇa is not protecting him. How can this be explained?**

The daughter of one godsister of mine recently had a very serious accident in India. She was about twenty-three years old. She and her sister were walking on a street, when her sister stopped to pet a cow. A car was coming and was about to hit her sister. She pushed her sister out of the way, but lost her balance and got hit by the car. Her leg was run over by the car. The very next morning she was supposed to begin dancing school, and had been meditating her whole life on going to India to learn to dance.

She was rushed the hospital, but the hospital would not do the surgery unless they got paid, and the family did not have any money. They were in such a difficult situation. There was an appeal for help. I contacted some devotees and arrangements were made to help. After that, I spoke to her mother twice. The first time, her mother called me to thank me. I asked her how her daughter was doing. She told me that right now her daughter hates Kṛṣṇa, not understanding why He did this to her. But later when I spoke to her mother again, she said that now her daughter is starting to understand how Kṛṣṇa still cares for her. When she felt that other devotees were caring for her, she was starting to see Kṛṣṇa’s hand a little more involved.

Sometimes we may not understand or we may forget what protection Kṛṣṇa gives His devotees. When He says that He always protects His devotees, it does not mean that He is going to always protect them from physical injury or pain. The real protection that He gives is by helping the devotees to always remember Him. That is protection! Therefore, sometimes He will put His devotee in a difficult situation. We want to see that Kṛṣṇa’s hand is there, but often we do not remember. We blame so many other causes for our difficulties, but if we can see Kṛṣṇa’s hand, then we will understand that Kṛṣṇa is helping us to remember Him. Remembering Kṛṣṇa is the greatest source of shelter. The greatest aspiration of our lives is to always remember Kṛṣṇa and to never forget Him.

Whoever helps us remember Kṛṣṇa cares for us. If we have that care, we will be able to tolerate many difficulties, which will always be there. If we think there will be no difficulties in the material world, we are in a very deep illusion. Duḥkhālayam aśāśvatam—this material world is temporary and full of miseries. It is kuṇṭha—a place of anxiety. We should not be so illusioned to think that there is a perfect situation in the material world where there is no anxiety. A devotee expects difficulties because he knows the nature of the material world. But Kṛṣṇa says, “If you remember Me, then you can easily cross beyond these difficulties.”

*daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī*  
*mama māyā duratyayā*  
*mām eva ye prapadyante*  
*māyām etāṁ taranti te*

**“This divine energy of Mine, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is difficult to overcome. But those who have surrendered unto Me can easily cross beyond it.” (Bg. 7.14)**

## Chapter 3 – Proper Cultivation of Knowledge

## Purifying Our Intelligence

*buddhir jñānam asammohaḥ*  
*kṣamā satyaṁ damaḥ śamaḥ*  
*sukhaṁ duḥkhaṁ bhavo ’bhāvo*  
*bhayaṁ cābhayam eva ca*  
*ahiṁsā samatā tuṣṭis*  
*tapo dānaṁ yaśo ’yaśaḥ*  
*bhavanti bhāvā bhūtānāṁ*  
*matta eva pṛthag-vidhāḥ*

**“Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from doubt and delusion, forgiveness, truthfulness, control of the senses, control of the mind, happiness and distress, birth, death, fear, fearlessness, nonviolence, equanimity, satisfaction, austerity, charity, fame and infamy—all these various qualities of living beings are created by Me alone.” (Bg. 10.4-5)**

PURPORT

The different qualities of living entities, be they good or bad, are all created by Kṛṣṇa, and they are described here. Intelligence refers to the power to analyze things in their proper perspective, and knowledge refers to understanding what is spirit and what is matter. Ordinary knowledge obtained by a university education pertains only to matter, and it is not accepted here as knowledge. Knowledge means knowing the distinction between spirit and matter. In modern education there is no knowledge about spirit; they are simply taking care of the material elements and bodily needs. Therefore academic knowledge is not complete.

Asammoha, freedom from doubt and delusion, can be achieved when one is not hesitant and when he understands the transcendental philosophy. Slowly but surely he becomes free from bewilderment. Nothing should be accepted blindly; everything should be accepted with care and with caution. Kṣamā, tolerance and forgiveness, should be practiced; one should be tolerant and excuse the minor offenses of others. Satyam, truthfulness, means that facts should be presented as they are, for the benefit of others. Facts should not be misrepresented. According to social conventions, it is said that one can speak the truth only when it is palatable to others. But that is not truthfulness. The truth should be spoken in a straightforward way, so that others will understand actually what the facts are. If a man is a thief and if people are warned that he is a thief, that is truth. Although sometimes the truth is unpalatable, one should not refrain from speaking it. Truthfulness demands that the facts be presented as they are for the benefit of others. That is the definition of truth.

The first quality spoken of in this verse is intelligence. Śrīla Prabhupāda explains that intelligence refers to the power to analyze things in their proper perspective. Therefore, intelligence and knowledge must be put together.

Knowledge refers to understanding what is spirit and what is matter. There is an example in which the body is compared to be like a chariot: the senses are like five horses which pull the chariot, the mind is like the reins that are connected to the horses and control them, the intelligence is like the driver who holds the reins, and the spirit soul (the self) is like the passenger who instructs the driver. If the intelligence is discriminating, then the mind can be controlled.

Kṛṣṇa explains in the Bhagavad-gītā (3.42): “The working senses are superior to dull matter; mind is higher than the senses; intelligence is still higher than the mind; and he \[the soul\] is even higher than the intelligence.” If the reins are properly guided by the driver of the chariot, then the horses can be properly controlled. Similarly, if the mind is properly controlled, then the senses can come under control. If the horses remain unbridled and are free to go in any direction they wish, then it will be a very difficult ride for the passenger. Similarly, if the mind and senses are not controlled, then the soul suffers the circumstances. Thus the intelligence refers to the power to analyze things in their proper perspective, and to discriminate between what is right and what is wrong.

Elsewhere, Śrīla Prabhupāda describes the mind to be like a reservoir of all ideas for sense enjoyment. A yogī must attempt to control his mind. As Kṛṣṇa says in the Bhagavad-gītā (6.6), “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his mind will remain the greatest enemy.” Therefore one has to learn to make a distinction between the desires that are coming from the uncontrolled mind and that which is for our best interest.

Another word for this is religion. Religion is when one is distinguishing between what is right and wrong. Śrīla Prabhupāda often uses the example of the animals—they do not have the ability or capacity to practice religion. Thus, because the human being has higher intelligence, he is able to discriminate between what is right and what is wrong.

Śrīla Prabhupāda gives the example of a man knows that he is supposed to drive the car on the right side of the road, but he drives the car on the left side of the road. The man is stopped by a police officer who says to him, “You are driving on the left side of the road. You could create a disaster. You should drive on the right side of the road.”

The man responds, “Sir, I am sorry. I am like a dog.”

However, he will still be held responsible, because he is not a dog. He is a human being and he must drive on the right side of the road. While animals act according to their instincts or senses, the human being is supposed to have a different standard for behavior. He should know that if he engages in certain activities, there will be consequences. Therefore the ability to discriminate between what is wrong and what is right is spiritual intelligence.

Although the duality of the material world does not ultimately exist, the conditioned soul experiences it as real under the influence of his own conditioned intelligence. This imaginary experience of a world separate from Kṛṣṇa can be compared to the acts of dreaming and desiring. When the conditioned soul dreams at night of something desirable or horrible, or when he daydreams of what he would like to have or avoid, he creates a reality that has no existence beyond his own imagination. The tendency of the mind is to accept and reject various activities based on sense gratification. Therefore an intelligent person should control the mind, restricting it from the illusion of seeing things separate from Kṛṣṇa, and when the mind is thus controlled he will experience actual fearlessness. (Bhāg. 11.2.38)

This verse is about conditioned intelligence. Conditioned intelligence means māyayāpahṛta-jñānā—one whose intelligence has been stolen by māyā or illusion. In the first case, this verse gives an example of a person dreaming at night. It says that if a person has a desirable dream or a horrible dream, he may have different experiences in relationship to the dream. We may dream of ourselves being in some very enjoyable situation, or being very wealthy or positioned like a king surrounded by maidservants. When we wake up, we feel terrible because we realize it was only a dream. Conversely, we may have a terrible dream, such as being devoured by a tiger. When we wake up, we feel good after realizing that it was only a dream. In the same way, a person who has conditioned intelligence creates a reality which has no existence beyond his imagination.

Not only is this verse about dreams at night, but it is also about dreams during the day. In daydreams, we contemplate things that we very much desire. We also contemplate distresses that we really want to avoid. Our whole life during the day becomes obsessed with fulfilling these dreams. We may actually get them fulfilled, but the happiness we derive from their fulfillment is not always what we expected, as we did not anticipate the problems that would come as well. We always dream about some state of perfect happiness, but when we achieve it, we see that there are other underlying problems that we never anticipated would come. Then trying to maintain the happiness we wanted to obtain also creates anxiety.

We must remember that everything is meant to be directed for the pleasure of the Lord. What makes something genuinely valuable is when it is properly connected to the Lord. We should therefore have the intelligence to know how to be connected to the Lord. If we do not know how to connect things properly to the Lord, then we have to take shelter of somebody who can guide and direct us.

In the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Yudhiṣṭhira Mahārāja says to Nārada Muni, “You are brahmacārī; you are renounced. I am gṛha-mūḍha-dhīḥ, one who is forgetful about the goal of life. Therefore, I beg you to please instruct me how I can properly direct my activities according to the prescriptions given in the Vedic literature and achieve the ultimate goal of life.”

Nārada Muni responds (Bhāg. 7.14.2), “My dear King, those who stay at home as householders must act to earn their livelihood, and instead of trying to enjoy the results of their work themselves, they should offer these results to Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva. How to satisfy Vāsudeva in this life can be perfectly understood through the association of great devotees of the Lord.” In other words, one has to learn how to connect his activities to the pleasure of the Supreme Lord.

Prahlāda Mahārāja says in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (Bhāg. 7.7.42): “In this material world, every materialist desires to achieve happiness and diminish his distress, and therefore he acts accordingly. Actually, however, one is happy as long as one does not endeavor for happiness; as soon as one begins his activities for happiness, his conditions of distress begin.”

Everyone is trying to obtain happiness, as it is our natural constitutional position to be happy. However, when we endeavor for our happiness separate from Kṛṣṇa, we simply create our conditions for distress. Although we cannot make the connection between our present distress and our previous attempts for happiness, any distress that we experience now is due to misuse of our independence in the past. Distress comes of its own accord; nobody endeavors for it. When we make plans to try to avoid distress, we do so simply to be happy. However, Bhāgavatam says:

*tasyaiva hetoḥ prayateta kovido*  
*na labhyate yad bhramatām upary adhaḥ*  
*tal labhyate duḥkhavad anyataḥ sukhaṁ*  
*kālena sarvatra gabhīra-raṁhasā*

**Persons who are actually intelligent and philosophically inclined should endeavor only for that purposeful end which is not obtainable even by wandering from the topmost planet \[Brahmaloka\] down to the lowest planet \[Pātāla\]. As far as happiness derived from sense enjoyment is concerned, it can be obtained automatically in course of time, just as in course of time we obtain miseries even though we do not desire them. (Bhāg. 1.5.18)**

The intelligent person endeavors for neither temporary happiness not distress, because he knows that both will come automatically in due course of time as a result of our previous activities.

Spiritual intelligence is to know what is right and what is wrong, and it is strengthened by the instructions of higher authorities. While there are scriptures and instructions of saintly personalities, there are also higher instructions in the form of dictations of the Lord coming from within the heart.

“For one who has conquered the mind, the Supersoul is already reached, for he has attained tranquility. To such a man happiness and distress, heat and cold, honor and dishonor are all the same.” (Bg. 6.7) Therefore, the intelligent person is one who follows the higher dictation coming from the higher authority. Kṛṣṇa is in the heart and He can also dictate to the living entity, but will do so according to the living entity’s desires.

The intelligent person should therefore restrict the mind from the illusion of seeing things separate from Kṛṣṇa. When his mind is thus controlled, he experiences real fearlessness in this world. This is the intelligent person. Lord Caitanya says:

**“Anything not conceived in relationship to Kṛṣṇa should be understood to be illusion \[māyā\]. None of the illusions uttered by words or conceived in the mind are factual. Because illusion is not factual, there is no distinction between what we think is good and what we think is bad. When we speak of the Absolute Truth, such speculations do not apply.” (Cc. Antya, 4.175)**

*‘dvaite’ bhadrābhadra-jñāna, saba—‘manodharma’*  
*‘ei bhāla, ei manda’,—ei saba ‘bhrama’*

**“In the material world, conceptions of good and bad are all mental speculations. Therefore, saying ‘This is good’ and ‘This is bad’ is all a mistake.” (Cc. Antya 4.176)**

In this verse, Lord Caitanya says manodharma. Manaḥ means mind, and dharma means religion. Manodharma is thus the religion of the mind, where we always have dualities, such as “this is good, this is bad; this will make me happy, this will make me sad; this will make me famous, this will make me infamous; this will give me a good reputation, and this will give me a bad reputation.”

Real religion, however is that which is eternal—sanātana-dharma—which is separate from the acceptance and rejection based upon the mundane mind. That dharma which is eternal is that which is coming from Kṛṣṇa in the form of spiritual instructions. As explained in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, real religious principles are coming from Kṛṣṇa Himself (Bhāg. 6.3.19): dharmaṁ tu sākṣād bhagavat-praṇītaṁ—one must become obedient to the instructions given by the Lord. This is real dharma, and this is real applied intelligence.

Śrīla Prabhupāda said to his disciples, “Intelligence means to follow the instructions of the spiritual master. This is spiritual intelligence.” In other words, whenever we are about to engage in some activity, we should think, “Is this what my spiritual master might want me to do?” We need a gauge (standard) of how to apply our decisions in life.

*yasyāsti bhaktir bhagavaty akiñcanā*  
*sarvair guṇais tatra samāsate surāḥ*  
*harāv abhaktasya kuto mahad-guṇā*  
*manorathenāsati dhāvato bahiḥ*

**All the demigods and their exalted qualities, such as religion, knowledge and renunciation, become manifest in the body of one who has developed unalloyed devotion for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vāsudeva. On the other hand, a person devoid of devotional service and engaged in material activities has no good qualities. Even if he is adept at the practice of mystic yoga or the honest endeavor of maintaining his family and relatives, he must be driven by his own mental speculations and must engage in the service of the Lord’s external energy. How can there be any good qualities in such a man? (Bhāg. 5.18.12)**

All the good qualities automatically manifest in a devotee who is engaged in devotional service to Kṛṣṇa. One will not have to make extra endeavors to develop good qualities, as all of these good qualities are the natural characteristic of the soul. If one knows how to direct his intelligence towards Kṛṣṇa, then it is like facing the sun—everything is bright. With purified intelligence, one will make progress towards the ultimate goal of life by getting directions both from within the heart (from Supersoul) and from without (from the scriptures and Vaiṣṇavas). If one simply rides in the chariot of the mind (manorathena), then at some point in time he will have to meet up with distress.

When one is very happy, he thinks there is no cause for worry. Everything is good as long as there are no problems. However, Śrīla Prabhupāda gives the analogy of the dunking stool: You tie a person to a chair and put him under water. Then you hold him there until he cannot breathe anymore, at which point you bring him back up. He thinks, “Oh this is wonderful,” but then you dunk him back under the water again. Thus we think it is wonderful only when we are pulled out of the water. We define our happiness by the absence of distress. Material happiness is only a temporary mitigation of distress.

Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī has analyzed the different sources of happiness, dividing them into three categories: (1) happiness derived from material enjoyment, (2) happiness derived by identifying oneself with the Supreme Brahman and (3) happiness derived from Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

Liberation is when you are no longer identifying with false temporary pleasures of this material world (i.e. lack of suffering). The third type of happiness, however, is much higher and far more pleasurable. That happiness is superior because Kṛṣṇa personally gives it. He is Govinda, the giver of that pleasure or happiness, for which there is no other superior pleasure. Kṛṣṇa says (Bg. 9.22), “But those who always worship Me with exclusive devotion, meditating on My transcendental form—to them I carry what they lack, and I preserve what they have.” He says:

*man-manā bhava mad-bhakto*  
*mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru*  
*mām evaiṣyasi satyaṁ te*  
*pratijāne priyo ’si me*

**“Always think of Me, become My devotee, worship Me and offer your homage unto Me. Thus you will come to Me without fail. I promise you this because you are My very dear friend.” (Bg. 18.65)**

We should make some endeavor in this life to utilize our body, mind and words for the pleasure of the Lord. Even if it apparently appears to bring us unhappiness, it will be the source of greatest happiness, because the Lord is pleased by the devotee who is determined to satisfy Him by his endeavors and will not allow him to remain unhappy. He will help that devotee both from within and from without. This is śraddhā. This type of faith is required if one wants to advance in devotional service.

*‘śraddhā’-śabde—viśvāsa kahe sudṛḍha niścaya*  
*kṛṣṇe bhakti kaile sarva-karma kṛta haya*

**Śraddhā is confident, firm faith that by rendering transcendental loving service to Kṛṣṇa one automatically performs all subsidiary activities. Such faith is favorable to the discharge of devotional service. (Cc. Madhya, 22.62)**

To have this faith does not mean we neglect all other duties, but rather, we perform them in the proper perspective in relationship to chanting and hearing about Kṛṣṇa.

*kāmasya nendriya-prītir*  
*lābho jīveta yāvatā*  
*jīvasya tattva-jijñāsā*  
*nārtho yaś ceha karmabhiḥ*

**Life’s desires should never be directed toward sense gratification. One should desire only a healthy life, or self-preservation, since a human being is meant for inquiry about the Absolute Truth. Nothing else should be the goal of one’s works. (Bhāg. 1.2.10)**

This is spiritual intelligence and spiritual knowledge. Asammoha, freedom from doubt and delusion, can be achieved when one is not hesitant and when he understands the transcendental philosophy. Slowly but surely he becomes free from bewilderment. Nothing should be accepted blindly; everything should be accepted with care and caution.

## Receiving Knowledge

**Question: What are the conditions for reading the books of the previous ācāryas, such as Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura and Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura?**

In his books, Śrīla Prabhupāda’s says that we should read the books of the previous ācāryas, including the Gosvāmīs. We should read Bhakti-sandarbha by Jīva Gosvāmī. He also talks about Jaiva Dharma by Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura and how it contains all the conclusive truths about Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava philosophy. Therefore, there is nothing wrong with reading these books. However, Prabhupāda also said that if we read Nectar of Devotion, Caitanya-caritāmṛta, Bhagavad-gītā, Śrī Īśopaniṣad and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, it is all we need. He said, “Everything is here in my books.” Thus unless one has read all of Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books, he should never think that he is taking a shortcut by going to the works of the previous ācāryas and bypassing Prabhupāda’s books. It is only by reading and understanding Prabhupāda’s books that one can get the blessings and adhikāra (qualification) to read and understand the books of the previous ācāryas. In addition, the works of the previous ācāryas require commentaries for us to understand them.

We should also be careful with the proliferation of books that are being produced now. Devotees are translating books, but many of the translations are not even right. Furthermore, there are so many books that nobody knows which ones to read. They decorate their bookshelves and pick and choose pieces from various books.

Lord Caitanya, in speaking to Devānanda Paṇḍita in Caitanya-bhāgavata, says that such a person is just like an ass. He simply collects so many books, filling his mind with so much knowledge, but devotion is still not manifest. Therefore the qualification to understand the books is not there either. Such a person is like an ass who carries a heavy burden.

Prabhupāda mentions this point about reading too many books in Nectar of Devotion. He also gives an elaborate commentary in Caitanya-caritāmṛta about how devotees are reading so many books that are proliferating throughout the movement, but for the most part, they have no qualification to read them. Such devotees then ask ridiculous questions, trying to learn about prayojana-tattva, when they have not even understood sambandha-jñāna. They are reading books that they are not qualified to read, and they do not understand them with the proper conclusion according to our Gauḍīya-siddhānta.

Therefore everyone should first read Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books. After reading all of his books, one should seek blessings to read other books. One will find that the teachings of many of these other books are given in Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books with the proper conclusion.

**Question: Can we quote ācāryas like Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura, or should we only quote Śrīla Prabhupāda?**

We can quote Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura as long as the siddhānta (conclusion) is not different than Prabhupāda’s. Śrīla Prabhupāda is in line with Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura and he represents the disciplic succession. He quotes Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura, Rūpa Gosvāmī, Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura, etc. Prabhupāda’s Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam was written by quoting Sanātana Gosvāmī, Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura and Śrīdhara Svāmī. We should see other commentaries or quotations according to our Gauḍīya-siddhānta. Thus we can quote the previous ācāryas, but we should ensure it is not different from the siddhānta that was given to us by Śrīla Prabhupāda.

Sometimes the previous ācāryas give us more detail, but we will see that everything is in Prabhupāda’s books. If we have read all of his books, we will see that Prabhupāda has given us everything, although some is still in the form of a seed. When we understand the commentaries of the previous ācāryas in relationship to these seeds that Prabhupāda has given in his books, then we will see that everything is right there in Caitanya-caritāmṛta—sambandha, abhideya and prayojana.

**Question: In Caitanya-caritāmṛta, in the discussion between Lord Caitanya and Chand Kazi, there is reference to Christian and Muslim scriptures. Śrīla Prabhupāda says sharp words about those scriptures. What should be our attitude towards the Bible and the Koran?**

In a commentary in the Third Canto of the Bhāgavatam, Prabhupāda explains what our attitude should be towards other religions. We should be tolerant of other religions. In other words, we should try to understand that other people are following different paths. We are not against following these other paths. What we are against is the misinterpretation of the paths, or the misinterpretation of Lord Jesus Christ’s instructions. Wherever there is an interpretation, we must expose the misinterpretation.

Prabhupāda gives the example that the Bible is like the pocket dictionary and the Bhāgavatam is like a big Oxford Dictionary. Therefore we should respect other religions, but we should try to make others go deeper into their own traditions and understand the goal. Prabhupāda often said that any system of religion that teaches its followers to love God is a bona fide system of religion. However, we should not compromise. We should be prepared to show others where they are misinterpreting those scriptures, just as we should be prepared to show others who may be misinterpreting Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books.

Even in ISKCON there are so many interpretations of what Śrīla Prabhupāda said. Some people say “This is the essence,” while others say that something else is the essence. Some say that we must establish varṇāśrama-dharma. Varṇāśrama-dharma is mentioned in Prabhupāda’s books, but is it the essence? Lord Caitanya rejected varṇāśrama-dharma. He said that it is insufficient. In so many places, Prabhupāda says that varṇāśrama-dharma is impossible in the Age of Kali.

People often take certain quotations and hold it as the highest ideal, but wherever there is misinterpretation, we should not compromise. We should neither criticize another’s religion. However, we should show them how they misinterpret it. That was Prabhupāda’s position, and that is what he would do with other bogus gurus.

Someone asked Śrīla Prabhupāda, “What is your opinion about Krishnamurti?”

Prabhupāda responded, “What’s his philosophy?”

The person then explained his philosophy. Prabhupāda did not criticize Krishnamurti, but he picked apart the philosophy and showed how it was compromised and misinterpreted. He did this with the book Dialectic Spiritualism and with the philosophy of different philosophers.

It is noted that Prabhupāda never criticized Jesus Christ. He said, “He is our guru.”

## Chapter 4 – Freedom from the Material World

## Proper Use of this Life

*anta-kāle ca mām eva*  
*smaran muktvā kalevaram*  
*yaḥ prayāti sa mad-bhāvaṁ*  
*yāti nāsty atra saṁśayaḥ*

**“And whoever, at the end of his life, quits his body remembering Me alone at once attains My nature. Of this there is no doubt.” (Bg. 8.5)**

PURPORT

In this verse the importance of Kṛṣṇa consciousness is stressed. Anyone who quits his body in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is at once transferred to the transcendental nature of the Supreme Lord. The Supreme Lord is the purest of the pure. Therefore anyone who is constantly Kṛṣṇa conscious is also the purest of the pure. The word smaran (“remembering”) is important. Remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is not possible for the impure soul who has not practiced Kṛṣṇa consciousness in devotional service. Therefore one should practice Kṛṣṇa consciousness from the very beginning of life. If one wants to achieve success at the end of his life, the process of remembering Kṛṣṇa is essential. Therefore one should constantly, incessantly chant the mahā-mantra—Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare/ Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma, Hare Hare. Lord Caitanya has advised that one be as tolerant as a tree (taror iva sahiṣṇunā). There may be so many impediments for a person who is chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. Nonetheless, tolerating all these impediments, one should continue to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare/ Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma, Hare Hare, so that at the end of one’s life one can have the full benefit of Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

This lecture is given in remembrance of a departed godbrother of mine named Nirguṇa dāsa. What is said about him herein is an example for all of us, because we must all face the same circumstance sooner or later.

Parīkṣit Mahārāja asked Śukadeva Gosvāmī, “What is the duty of a man who is about to die?”

Śukadeva Gosvāmī said, “His duty is to hear about, glorify, and remember Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the Supersoul and the savior from all miseries.”

The ultimate duty of a person who is about to die is also described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

*etāvān sāṅkhya-yogābhyāṁ*  
*sva-dharma-pariniṣṭhayā*  
*janma-lābhaḥ paraḥ puṁsām*  
*ante nārāyaṇa-smṛtiḥ*

**The highest perfection of human life, achieved either by complete knowledge of matter and spirit, by practice of mystic powers, or by perfect discharge of occupational duty, is to remember the Personality of Godhead at the end of life. (Bhāg. 2.1.6)**

Śukadeva Gosvāmī tells Mahārāja Parīkṣit in the Twelfth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, “My dear King, the Supreme Personality of Godhead is the ultimate controller of all living entities. He is the Supreme Soul and He is the supreme shelter for all living beings. When meditated upon, especially by those who are about to die, He reveals to them their eternal transcendental spiritual identity.”

*etan nirvidyamānānām*  
*icchatām akuto-bhayam*  
*yogināṁ nṛpa nirṇītaṁ*  
*harer nāmānukīrtanam*

**“O King, constant chanting of the holy name of the Lord after the ways of the great authorities is the doubtless and fearless way of success for all, including those who are free from all material desires, those who are desirous of all material enjoyment, and also those who are self-satisfied by dint of transcendental knowledge.”(Bhāg. 2.1.11)**

Śrīla Prabhupāda explains that it is very difficult for the impure soul who has not practiced Kṛṣṇa consciousness in devotional service to remember Kṛṣṇa at the time of death. However, he emphasizes that remembrance of the Lord is achieved by chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa.

The example shown by Vaiṣṇavas at the time of death is that perfection is to be able to remember the Supreme Lord. The Lord is very merciful upon the conditioned soul. Even though one may not be fully situated in complete Kṛṣṇa consciousness at the time of death, if the devotee is endeavoring to meditate on the Lord, then whatever lack there is, the Lord will give to that devotee.

Prabhupāda always said that if we take one step towards Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa will take one hundred steps towards us. Kṛṣṇa will appear in our minds even if we cannot fully remember Him. The secret is constant endeavor. Kṛṣṇa says:

*teṣāṁ satata-yuktānāṁ*  
*bhajatāṁ prīti-pūrvakam*  
*dadāmi buddhi-yogaṁ taṁ*  
*yena mām upayānti te*

**“To those who are constantly devoted to serving Me with love, I give the understanding by which they can come to Me.” (Bg. 10.10)**

Therefore, even when the time of death comes for one who has practiced Kṛṣṇa consciousness and simply endeavors to remember Him, even though he may not be perfected in his practice of spiritual life, the Lord will take care of him and will make arrangements for him.

My godbrother, Nirguṇa dāsa, was a book distributor for approximately 35 years. He was very steady, always going out and distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books. Even up until recently, he would from time to time go out and distribute books. I say from time to time because he was a householder and had many other arrangements to attend to in family life. He had a very difficult family life.

The source of Nirguṇa Prabhu’s troublesome household life was that he was Kṛṣṇa conscious, and determined to remain so. He was also very determined to distribute Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books, and was very absorbed in Śrīla Prabhupāda’s preaching mission.

More than ten years ago, Nirguṇa Prabhu was distributing books in America with a group of three other devotees. It was nighttime when they were coming back from where they were distributing books. They were walking across a very wide road. There was a car coming, and it was traveling 35 to 40 miles per hour, and it was about to hit the three devotees that were with him. Then with all his strength (and he is not a big or tall person), Nirguṇa Prabhu ran, pushed them all out of the way, and got hit. He was thrown 20 feet into the air and landed on the asphalt road. He was immediately taken to the hospital.

I happened to be in a town approximately 15 miles away with another godbrother, Madhuhā. Somebody called and described what had happened and said that Nirguṇa Prabhu was in the hospital. We said, “Let’s go immediately and see what kind of condition he’s in.” The devotee on the phone said, “He’s in a very serious condition; there are a lot of broken bones in his body.”

When we got to the hospital and asked if we could see him, we were told: “He’s still in surgery. He cannot be seen. If you want to wait, the doctors may allow you to see him after the surgery.”

Because many bones had been broken in his body, they had to use nails to hold the pieces of bones together. We waited several hours for the surgery to be completed and for him to regain consciousness after having been under general anesthesia. We begged the doctors, “He is a very close friend of ours. Please let us see him for a little time.” The doctors agreed and let us go in.

His body from neck to toe was bandaged up. He was in a contraption such that his body was suspended so that he could not move. He could not even turn his head to see who was coming into the room.

When I walked into the room, I stood in front of him and said, “Haribol, Nirguṇa Prabhu.”

He said, “Nirañjana Mahārāja, Hare Kṛṣṇa. How is the preaching in the Soviet Union?”

I thought, “What kind of yogī is this?”

He continued, “Mahārāja, what is happening in the Soviet Union? Did you just get back? How are the devotees doing there? Is book distribution going nicely?” He kept asking all these questions and talking about preaching, not allowing me to ask a question about his body. He did not even want to talk about it. I had to sit down in the chair in front of him and tell him about all the preaching in the Soviet Union.

He said, “This is nectar. Keep on going, Mahārāja.”

The doctors let us stay for about a half hour, and we continued to speak. Before leaving, Nirguṇa Prabhu said, “Mahārāja, I beg you… I can’t fold my hands, but I plead with you, could you please bless me? Whatever happens to me is in Kṛṣṇa’s hands, but please bless me so that I can distribute Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books for the rest of my life.”

This gives you a little idea of what kind of a devotee Nirguṇa Prabhu was. He was just absorbed in preaching. He was not thinking of himself; he was thinking about Prabhupāda’s mission.

I had gotten close to him over the last few years, because when his marriage fell apart, he wanted to preach. I therefore made arrangements for him to go to Ukraine and give seminars on book distribution to inspire the book distributors in Ukraine and Russia. He tried to see everything as a sign from Kṛṣṇa for him to dedicate his life to preaching.

A few months ago, Nirguṇa Prabhu called me when I was in America to tell me that the doctors had found some tumor in his body. It took them months to identify it and they still did not really know what it was. The medical system in America is terrible. It is very commercial and it costs a lot of money. If you do not have enough money, they put you through a very slow procedure for getting treatment. It took them two months to find that there was a tumor that was strangling his heart and other organs in his body. He called me and asked if I thought the treatment could happen a little faster if he went to the Bhaktivedanta hospital. I therefore tried to make an arrangement for him at the Bhaktivedanta hospital.

When he went to the Bhaktivedanta hospital, the doctors recommended that he simply go to hospice care. They did not think that anything could be done. They tried chemotherapy, but it was not working.

The following is a portion of a letter that he sent me:

After my first day of chemotherapy I felt better than I have for two months. On May 31, even before my first chemotherapy treatment, I was granted some realizations. Previously I have realized that anything can happen to anyone at any time. Now I am aiming to live as fully in the present as much as possible, utilizing each moment to its fullest potential \[meaning spiritual potential\] as much as I can, and being forever and always grateful for everything. Since I am eternal and on the spiritual path, anything that comes to be is all auspicious. I don’t have to worry or care about that; it’s given. So \[I have the means to\] experience perfect satisfaction at all times, \[and even\] at every moment.

As soon as I accepted these granted realizations, the monsoon rains began. I felt this as an auspicious omen and it was comforting, soothing and reaffirming. Whatever happens, I accept. Just as a doctor told me two months ago that I have a large mass in my chest. OK. That’s what is, now what’s next? I’m ready to be detached from this world and all it offers. In fact, I’ve already processed it, and I was OK with it. Ultimately Kṛṣṇa is in charge and the ride He is taking me on is what I need for my purification. I wish to serve Him and He wishes that I do so, and He loves and even serves me. So we don’t know what will come. But although I’m trying to be accepting and grateful for whatever, I’m going for disease eradicated and serving fully for more years to come. \[In other words he is going to try to eradicate his disease and continue his service for years.\] I’m grateful for being surrounded by so many caring devotees serving my many needs. I’m also grateful for you for sending your concern and love and praying to Kṛṣṇa on my behalf. I’m truly extremely fortunate and grateful.

Thank you very much,

Your servant,

Nirguṇa dāsa

He was very much accepting of his condition. I spoke to Nirguṇa dāsa about two weeks ago and he told me he was experiencing a lot of pain. He was always trying to find the right balance between trying to stay in clear consciousness and dealing with his pain. He did not want to take too much drugs so that he could be in clear consciousness to remember the Lord at the time of death. Although he was experiencing a lot of pain, he was very positive and he kept on using the word grateful so many times during our conversation.

It made me think of another recent experience I had with another godbrother of mine in America who had a heart attack earlier this year (2007). He is a very simple and hard-working devotee. He works by selling flowers and he donates practically all his money to the temple or to the devotees. He lives in some corner of the basement of the temple room. He does not even have any furniture; he just sleeps in a little sleeping bag. He works all day, every day, making money and using it all for Kṛṣṇa’s service.

One day when he was going to work, he felt some pain, and it got very severe. He did not know what to do. His mechanic lived nearby, so he drove to his house and knocked on the door. It was approximately 4:30 in the morning. He woke up the mechanic who asked him, “Why are you coming so early to get your car fixed?”

My godbrother said, “Well, I don’t think it’s my car this time. I think it’s something else that needs to be fixed.”

The mechanic asked, “What’s the matter?”

My godbrother said, “I can’t do anything anymore. I can’t move.”

The mechanic understood that something serious was happening to him. He immediately put him in a car and took him to the hospital. At that hospital, they could not treat him, so they had to bring in a helicopter to airlift him to another hospital where they had to perform an operation to open up the blocked valve in his heart. If he did not have this operation, he would have left his body.

I spent a lot of time with him after the operation. He was healing, and getting a little bit better. I asked him, “Why don’t you come and share your realizations at the Sunday program and give a little talk about your realizations you had with your heart attack?” This devotee, as I said, is very simple. He is not a big preacher, but he is giving everything. He is giving his life to serving Śrīla Prabhupāda’s mission. He agreed and gave a very simple lecture about gratitude.

People asked him: “What were you thinking about when you were being lifted in the helicopter?”

He said, “You just have to remember Śrīla Prabhupāda and Kṛṣṇa, and then gratitude takes over.” It is a very simple statement, but very profound. Gratitude is a very important principle in spiritual life. He made it sound so simple. He said, “Just remember Prabhupāda and Kṛṣṇa, and then everything will be taken over by gratitude.” When he gave this simple talk at the Sunday feast, everybody applauded, appreciating his talk because it was so heartfelt.

When I was speaking with Nirguṇa, I was remembering this devotee and his feeling of gratitude, because Nirguṇa was saying the same thing: “I’m so grateful.” It takes some realization to be in a situation like that—lying on one’s deathbed and being joyful and grateful for what Kṛṣṇa is doing to him.

Despite the intense pain he was feeling, he kept speaking of his gratitude: “I’m so grateful to devotees. I’m so grateful to my godbrothers. I’m so grateful to Kṛṣṇa for putting me in this situation in Māyāpura-dhāma \[where he had been brought to leave his body\].”

Two days before he left his body, he had a dream in which Rādhārāṇī and the gopīs appeared to him. When he woke up the following morning, he said, “Rādhārāṇī and the gopīs came to me in a dream. They invited me to come with them.” Two days later, he left his body, holding a govardhana-śilā. He had two śilās—one śilā was in his hand and the other was next to his hand. A hundred devotees were present, chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. He received so much mercy.

Śukadeva Gosvāmī says in the Twelfth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam that the Supreme Lord is the ultimate controller. He is the supreme shelter for all living beings. When meditated upon at the time of death, the Supreme Lord will reveal one’s eternal spiritual form.

Śrīla Prabhupāda says that to remember Kṛṣṇa at the time of death is not possible for the impure soul. We can understand how purifying it is to take part in the saṅkīrtana movement. Prabhupāda said that there may be so many impediments for a person who is chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. Nonetheless, tolerating all these impediments, one should continue to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa.

*tat te ’nukampāṁ su-samīkṣamāṇo*  
*bhuñjāna evātma-kṛtaṁ vipākam*  
*hṛd-vāg-vapurbhir vidadhan namas te*  
*jīveta yo mukti-pade sa dāya-bhāk*

**“My dear Lord, one who earnestly waits for You to bestow Your causeless mercy upon him, all the while patiently suffering the reactions of his past misdeeds and offering You respectful obeisances with his heart, words and body, is surely eligible for liberation, for it has become his rightful claim.” (Bhāg. 10.14.8)**

Prabhupāda says, in reference to the verse, mukti-pade sa dāya-bhāk, that dāya-bhāk means inheritance. Just as when one’s parents die, they receive an inheritance. All they have to do is live and the inheritance will come. Nothing else is required.

Similarly, for a devotee, mukti-pade sa dāya-bhāk means he inherits his rightful claim, which is liberation to be engaged in pure devotional service to the Supreme Lord, by having simply tolerated all inconveniences and continuing to chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa.

We have so many examples, even in contemporary times, of devotees who have become Kṛṣṇa conscious at the time of death. We should try to take advantage of these examples, because it is something that each and every one of us is going to have to face at one time or another. We should simply try to be grateful for whatever situation Kṛṣṇa has put us in, and tolerate it.

The very first verse I learned in the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement was mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya (Bg. 2.14). I memorized this verse, because for me, book distribution in the earlier years was very difficult. Sometimes I would cry because it was so hard for me. I was approaching people with tears in my eyes, but they were neither tears of ecstasy nor tears of compassion. I needed to find some shelter, and I looked for it in this verse:

*mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya*  
*śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ*  
*āgamāpāyino ’nityās*  
*tāṁs titikṣasva bhārata*

**“(…) The nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.” (Bg. 2.14)**

We must learn to tolerate these impediments and to continue to remain grateful for whatever situation Kṛṣṇa has put us in. If we live in this way, then we will get our inheritance as our rightful claim. If we somehow or other remain fortunate to take part in the saṅkīrtana mission of Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, then our destination is guaranteed. In many places Kṛṣṇa gives this guarantee. One such example is given in the Bhagavad-gītā (18.68-69): “For one who explains this supreme secret to the devotees, pure devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me. There is no servant in this world more dear to Me than he, nor will there ever be one more dear.” If we cannot accept Kṛṣṇa’s words, whose can we accept? Thus we must accept Kṛṣṇa’s words with faith.

We are very fortunate to have living examples of devotees who have perfected their lives in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, because they have dedicated their lives to serving Śrīla Prabhupāda’s movement and his mission for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness for the welfare of others. We should be grateful to them for giving us their association, and if we can always remain grateful in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, we can be assured of the same success.

## Overcoming Māyā’s Tests

*sa uttama-śloka-padāravindayor*  
*niṣevayākiñcana-saṅga-labdhayā*  
*tanvan parāṁ nirvṛtim ātmano muhur*  
*duḥsaṅga-dīnasya manaḥ śamaṁ vyadhāt*

**Because of his association with perfect, unalloyed devotees who had nothing to do with anything material, Prahlāda Mahārāja constantly engaged in the service of the Lord’s lotus feet. By seeing his bodily features when he was in perfect ecstasy, persons very poor in spiritual understanding became purified. In other words, Prahlāda Mahārāja bestowed upon them transcendental bliss. (Bhāg. 7.4.42)**

PURPORT:

Apparently Prahlāda Mahārāja was placed in circumstances in which he was always tortured by his father. In such material conditions, one cannot have an undisturbed mind, but since bhakti is unconditional (ahaituky apratihatā), Prahlāda Mahārāja was never disturbed by the chastisements of Hiraṇyakaśipu. On the contrary, the bodily symptoms of his ecstatic love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead turned the minds of his friends, who had also been born in atheistic families. Instead of being disturbed by the torments of his father, Prahlāda influenced these friends and cleansed their minds. A devotee is never contaminated by material conditions, but persons subjected to material conditions can become spiritually advanced and blissful upon seeing the behavior of a pure devotee.

In this verse we see how Prahlāda Mahārāja’s rigid devotional service has protected him from external disturbances. Even others who were poor in spiritual understanding turned their minds towards devotional service, and became spiritually advanced and blissful upon seeing the behavior of the pure devotee, Prahlāda Mahārāja.

This example of Prahlāda Mahārāja is an important principle for every devotee aspiring to advance in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. We all need to see examples of others who are overcoming obstacles. Everyone in the material world is faced with obstacles. In due course of time, the upheavals that come without any invitation will manifest—even in the life of a devotee.

We should not foolishly think that when one comes to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, then immediately upon taking to devotional service, automatically everything is going to be enjoyable and disturbances will cease to exist. Actually, when one comes to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, there will be so many disturbances and upheavals.

Many years ago, after having come in contact with the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, I had been visiting the temple in Boston for some time. One of the devotees had given me an audio cassette tape of Śrīla Prabhupāda’s lecture on the Teachings of Queen Kuntī. It was the only tape I had, and I used to listen to it frequently—almost every day—since having Prabhupāda’s books and lectures was not so easy during those days. On this tape, Prabhupāda was saying that when one comes to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, Māyā will test the devotee to see if he is coming to serve Kṛṣṇa or to disturb Kṛṣṇa.

In the beginning, it is described like being in the ocean. When one is in the ocean, there will be many disturbances. Thus one should not expect an easy journey, having to traverse a massive ocean. In the same way, we are in the middle of the ocean, and Māyā will test us to see if we are coming to serve Kṛṣṇa or to disturb Him.

When I moved into the temple, I was always thinking of these words—that Māyā would test us. I remember going to maṅgala-ārati, and doing all the simple jobs in the temple, such as washing pots. I was blissful, and I was starting to wonder why Prabhupāda said that in the beginning there would be many disturbances.

This went on for a few weeks. Then one morning, it was a little difficult to get up for maṅgala-ārati. I was struggling a little bit. In those days, the temple commander’s duty was to get everybody up in the morning, and sometimes he would use strong techniques such as lifting up the end of the sleeping bag where your feet are and shaking you out. If that did not work, they poured a glass of water on your face. You simply had to get up for maṅgala-ārati. However, all of a sudden, getting up for maṅgala-ārati became increasingly difficult for me. I was tired and would think, “I worked so hard yesterday.” My mind would find so many excuses. The temple commander persisted. Finally, one morning, I took my fist and I slammed it on the floor. I said, “That’s it! I can’t do it! I have to leave!”

Then, all of a sudden, Prabhupāda’s words started reverberating in my mind: “When one comes to devotional service, in the beginning there will be so many difficulties, and Māyā will be testing if one is coming to serve Kṛṣṇa or to disturb Kṛṣṇa.”

These words, resonating in my mind, really gave me strength to get up that day, and then the next day, and then the next day. That was my first test in Kṛṣṇa consciousness—dealing with my fatigue, and especially then staying awake for the rest of the morning program. However, Prabhupāda saved me. I knew there was no other reason for me to have that cassette and to listen to that little section, except that Kṛṣṇa and Śrīla Prabhupāda knew exactly what was going to happen to me and knew that I needed to be rescued from my delirium of thinking that I should leave for such a foolish reason as finding it difficult to get up for maṅgala-ārati. This was a minor test, but to the degree that we make advancement in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, Māyā will have a test (anarthas) proportionate to our advancement which is even more difficult to overcome. We therefore need strength. There is a verse that says (Cc. Antya 1.2): “My path is very difficult. I am blind, and my feet are slipping again and again. Therefore, may the saints help me by granting me the stick of their mercy as my support.” In my case, Prabhupāda’s words were like a stick of mercy for extra support for my little test in the beginning.

As a devotee advances in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, there will be many obstacles, adversities, and even sometimes major upheavals in his life. By seeing others overcome upheavals by their rigid determination to be engaged in the service of the Lord, it gives us strength to go on.

This reminds me of the example of Śrīdhara Mahārāja, whom I was with in Māyāpura when he was preparing to leave this world. He was having kīrtana every night in his room, and I was going at his request to lead kīrtana for him. It became a routine during that time.

Śrīdhara Mahārāja was so sick. His stomach was bloated because it was filled with liquid, and it had to be drained regularly with a big needle. Sometimes he could not even get up. During kīrtana, he would raise his hands in the air while lying down in the bed and chanting.

One night, after being with him for a substantial amount of time, the kīrtana ended and Śrīdhara Mahārāja sat up and gave a lecture about how we are not these bodies. It was such a simple but profound talk. It was not very long, but the substance was realized.

In a situation like that, the tendency is to think, “Everybody knows I’m sick. Why should I get up and speak?” Instead, he sat up and spoke to everyone about how these bodies are meant to be engaged in Kṛṣṇa’s service. We are not these bodies. We are transcendental to the material body. The body will die, but the soul will live on. This was the simple truth from Bhagavad-gītā, spoken with such conviction. This left an indelible impression in my mind, and I was speaking about it for days. Such examples give us faith. When looking at our own difficulties in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, such examples remind us of how we should try to overcome them by faith.

*‘śraddhā’-śabde—viśvāsa kahe sudṛḍha niścaya*  
*kṛṣṇe bhakti kaile sarva-karma kṛta haya*

**Śraddhā is confident, firm faith that by rendering transcendental loving service to Kṛṣṇa one automatically performs all subsidiary activities. Such faith is favorable to the discharge of devotional service. (Cc. Madhya 22.62)**

Prahlāda Mahārāja embodied that type of example, but his example was constant because he was a perfect, unalloyed devotee who had nothing to do with anything material. He was constantly engaged in the service of the Lord’s lotus feet. By seeing not only his constant engagement, but also his symptoms of ecstasy, it has such an impression.

## Fearlessness of the Devotee

*nāhaṁ bibhemy ajita te ’tibhayānakāsya-*  
*jihvārka-netra-bhrukuṭī-rabhasogra-daṁṣṭrāt*  
*āntra-srajaḥ-kṣataja-keśara-śaṅku-karṇān*  
*nirhrāda-bhīta-digibhād ari-bhin-nakhāgrāt*

**“My Lord, who are never conquered by anyone, I am certainly not afraid of Your ferocious mouth and tongue, Your eyes bright like the sun or Your frowning eyebrows. I do not fear Your sharp, pinching teeth, Your garland of intestines, Your mane soaked with blood, or Your high, wedgelike ears. Nor do I fear Your tumultuous roaring, which makes elephants flee to distant places, or Your nails, which are meant to kill Your enemies.” (Bhāg. 7.9.15)**

PURPORT:

Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva’s fierce appearance was certainly most dangerous for the nondevotees, but for Prahlāda Mahārāja such a fearful appearance was not at all disturbing. The lion is very fearsome for other animals, but its cubs are not at all afraid of the lion. The water of the sea is certainly dreadful for all living entities on the land, but within the sea even the small fish is unafraid. Why? Because the small fish has taken shelter of the big ocean. It is said that although great elephants are taken away by the flooding waters of the river, the small fish swim opposite the current. Therefore although the Lord sometimes assumes a fierce appearance to kill the duṣkṛtīs, the devotees worship Him. Keśava dhṛta-nara-hari-rūpa jaya jagadīśa hare. The devotee always takes pleasure in worshiping the Lord and glorifying the Lord in any form, either pleasing or fierce.

These prayers, offered by Prahlāda Mahārāja, completely pacified the Lord from His anger. In this verse, Prahlāda Mahārāja is describing his position of fearlessness in the presence of such a ferocious form. Prahlāda Mahārāja is fearless, whereas others who perceive such a form are fearful—especially a nondevotee. Such a form for the nondevotees certainly represents a cause for fear because it represents death.

However, Śrīla Prabhupāda has described here in his purport that the devotee who has taken shelter of the Lord is not fearful of this form nor of any other form of the Lord. Kṛṣṇa states in the Bhagavad-gītā that He is immortality and death personified. Therefore, such a ferocious form is certainly a cause for fear for those who have not taken shelter of the Lord.

It reminds me of an incident in Boston when I was a witness in a court case against our temple by a previous member of the temple who was suing for damages. She claimed that her life was destroyed as a result of coming in contact with Kṛṣṇa consciousness. I was called as a witness to the case because I was living at the temple at the time when she was in the temple. The prosecuting attorney was cross-examining me. In the middle of his cross-examination, he pulled out a photo of Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva. The following is the conversation between me and the lawyer, which happened in front of a ten-person jury:

Lawyer: (He pulls out a picture of Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva and shows it to me.) Mr. Swami, could you please tell me who this is?

Me: That is Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva.

Lawyer: And who is Nṛsiṁhadeva?

Me: He is an incarnation of the Supreme Lord.

Lawyer: Uh huh! And could you please tell me, Mr. Swami, what is this around His neck?

Me: Those are intestines.

Lawyer: Whose intestines are these, Mr. Swami?

This is exactly how he was asking his questions. I was told that I had to answer the questions, but I was certainly getting a little bit disturbed at this point.

Me: They are Hiraṇyakaśipu’s.

Lawyer: Who is Hiraṇyakaśipu?

Me: He is a demon.

Lawyer: Tell me, Mr. Swami, who is this boy?

Me: He is Prahlāda.

Lawyer: And what is his relationship with Hiraṇyakaśipu?

Me: He is his son.

Lawyer: Why is he smiling?

Me: Because he is happy to see his Lord.

Lawyer: But this is his father. Why is he smiling? Why is he so happy to see his father dead?

They were trying to establish that our movement was a very dangerous cult. The lawyer then took the photo and said to the judge, “Your honor, I would like to show this picture of their God to all the people of the jury. May I show it to them?”

The judge said, “Yes, you may show them.” The lawyer then handed the picture to the people of the jury.

His last question was, “Mr. Swami, where do you keep this picture? Is it true that this picture is on your altar in your temple?”

I said, “Yes, it is.”

We lost the court case in front of the jury. When the court case was taken to the state appeals court and the judges examined what had happened in the previous court room, they said, “We will not allow such heresy in a trial in our state. We will not allow religion to be put on trial.” Seeing what the judge allowed in the other court room, the judges in the higher court threw out all the charges. Fortunately, this was in our favor and Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva protected us.

Thus when the nondevotees see this fierce form with garlands of intestines and a blood-soaked mane, and they hear that He is our worshipable God, they cannot understand. For them, it is such a fearsome form. However, this is exactly the point that Śrīla Prabhupāda is making in the purport—the devotee always takes pleasure in worshiping the Lord and glorifying the Lord in any form—either pleasing or fierce. The devotee understands the Lord’s purpose. Even when the Lord kills the demons, it is the Lord’s benediction upon them. As Śrīla Prabhupāda explains in the Teachings of Queen Kuntī, even when the Lord kills demons, the demons become saintly.

The devotee who understands the Lord worships the Lord in any form. The nondevotee is very fearful, especially of this form of Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva, because to them it represents death, which is something that is very fearful for anyone who does not understand the Lord.

Kṛṣṇa says, “I am all-devouring death, I am death personified and I am immortality.” Therefore, anyone who comes face-to-face with death actually comes face-to-face with Kṛṣṇa.

Prabhupāda also gives the example that when Dhruva Mahārāja was entering into the flower airplane and death personified appeared before him, he simply stepped on the head of death personified and used it as a step for entering into the airplane. He did not see death as something fearful, but rather as a step to get to the place where he really wanted to go.

Another example that Prabhupāda gives in the purport is that of the mother cat. When she opens up her mouth to the kitten, the kitten thinks, “She is my mother and is coming to take me home.” However, when the cat opens her mouth and shows her fierce teeth to the rat, the rat sees it from a different perspective. They are the same teeth, mouth, and cat, and both the kitten and the rat are seeing the same thing. Yet the rat is thinking, “This is the termination of all of my plans.” Therefore, when a devotee has taken shelter of the Supreme Lord, he actually comes to this platform of fearlessness. For him, death is no longer a cause of fear. Death is simply a change of dress.

Kṛṣṇa instructs Arjuna about this in the Bhagavad-gītā, thus helping him to understand that the body is simply clothing that one takes off at the end of life, and puts on a new set. It is due to attachment to enjoying within the body that death becomes really fearful. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura describes it as abhiniveśa, which means to instinctively cling to the conception that enjoyment is meant to be done with this body, and death means the termination of all enjoyment. This notion is actually described as ignorance and is the binding force that keeps the living entity attached to the material world.

One who has never experienced something higher certainly thinks that pleasure refers to this body. By nature, the living entity is ānanda-mayo ’bhyāsāt—a pleasure seeking being. Thus it is easy to understand how it can be fearful to have to face death without having taken shelter of Kṛṣṇa. The devotee takes shelter of the Supreme Lord by his constant remembrance of the Lord, and thus when faced with difficulties in life, he can remain equipoised.

Death is the final examination, but there are many preliminary examinations that one must take as well. All these preliminary examinations invoke fear in the heart of those who are not prepared to pass them. Prabhupāda explains that fear comes from uncertainty about one’s future. For a devotee who has taken shelter of the Lord, he knows that his future is always bright. Even in the face of adversity, because he has taken shelter of the Lord and he has experienced devotion to the Lord, he gets direct perception of the self.

*bhaktiḥ pareśānubhavo viraktir*  
*anyatra caiṣa trika eka-kālaḥ*  
*prapadyamānasya yathāśnataḥ syus*  
*tuṣṭiḥ puṣṭiḥ kṣud-apāyo ’nu-ghāsam*

**Devotion, direct experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment from other things—these three occur simultaneously for one who has taken shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in the same way that pleasure, nourishment and relief from hunger come simultaneously and increasingly, with each bite, for a person engaged in eating. (Bhāg. 11.2.42)**

How does a person know he is eating? He knows by each bite he experiences. All these experiences—taste, strength, and relief from hunger—come simultaneously and increasingly with each bite. A person who is engaged in devotional service experiences that his detachment from the material world is manifesting, he directly perceives Kṛṣṇa in his life, and he sees that his devotion increases. Thus he knows that he is engaged in devotional service. As he directly perceives the presence of the Lord, he feels the protection of the Lord. It is described in Śaraṇāgati that one of the characteristics of full surrender is to have firm faith that the Lord will always give full protection.

Prabhupāda describes in the Bhāgavatam that when Durvāsā Muni invoked the demon to kill Ambarīṣa Mahārāja, Ambarīṣa Mahārāja did not think of the Supreme Lord for protection. He simply thought of the Supreme Lord out of duty. Prabhupāda explains that for the devotee, protection is guaranteed even before the devotee asks for it. As soon as one begins devotional service, the Lord guarantees his protection to that devotee. Thus Ambarīṣa Mahārāja was remembering the Lord because it is natural for him to always remember the Lord in all circumstances—whether in happiness or distress, or whether he is in the face of adversity or in the most protected environment. Ambarīṣa Mahārāja simply remembered the Lord and the Lord gave His protection to that devotee.

Prabhupāda also gives the example that when all the creatures see the snake in the forest, they become fearful. However, when a forest fire comes to consume the forest, the snakes become completely helpless. They will be consumed by the fire as they cannot flee very fast. Similarly, the enemy of a devotee may appear to be strong and can be compared to the snake in the forest. However, in the presence of the devotee’s constant remembrance of the Supreme Lord, or the fire of devotional service, the enemy is rendered helpless and the devotee experiences no fear.

If a devotee is always endeavoring to meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, especially in the face of adversity, Kṛṣṇa will certainly give His protection and help that devotee. Kṛṣṇa will give to him whatever he lacks. Even if it is very difficult for the devotee to remember Kṛṣṇa, if he simply endeavors to do so, then Kṛṣṇa can very easily force Himself into that devotee’s mind and give him whatever he lacks at the time of death.

That reciprocation of the Lord comes by the efforts that we make throughout this life. The biggest endeavor that we have to make throughout this life is to remember Kṛṣṇa. It is very difficult to always remember Kṛṣṇa. Thus He said to Arjuna in the Bhagavad-gītā, “If you cannot always fix your mind upon Me, then follow the regulative principles of bhakti-yoga.” By following regulative principles of bhakti-yoga, we will develop a desire to come to Kṛṣṇa. To follow the regulative principles of bhakti-yoga means that each day we must be engaged in those activities that help us remember Kṛṣṇa.

*smartavyaḥ satataṁ viṣṇur*  
*vismartavyo na jātucit*  
*sarve vidhi-niṣedhāḥ syur*  
*etayor eva kiṅkarāḥ*

**Kṛṣṇa is the origin of Lord Viṣṇu. He should always be remembered and never forgotten at any time. All the rules and prohibitions mentioned in the śāstras should be the servants of these two principles. (Cc. Madhya, 22.13)**

In the commentary to this verse, it is described that the word satataṁ, although it normally means always, actually means every day in this verse. If a person can always remember Kṛṣṇa, there will be no need for him to follow vidhis and niṣedhas (prescribed activities and prohibited activities), which are for those persons who cannot always remember Kṛṣṇa. Thus every devotee must practice remembering the Lord. A devotee must mold or regulate his life in a way that he can remember Kṛṣṇa every day. If we take shelter of Kṛṣṇa, He will help.

Lord Brahma describes that those devotees who always hear the topics of the Supreme Lord (which are vibrated by the Lord personally and by His devotees) can certainly conquer the Lord. When the Lord sees that the devotee is making this effort to remember Him, He will help that devotee. He will protect him from the most fearful state of existence—the fear of having to give up this body. Thus Śrīla Prabhupāda says that the nondevotees have no hope for protection, because they have not taken shelter of the Lord. The devotee can always be assured of protection.

*ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ*  
*mad-bhakteṣv abhidhāsyati*  
*bhaktiṁ mayi parāṁ kṛtvā*  
*mām evaiṣyaty asaṁśayaḥ*

**“For one who explains this supreme secret to the devotees, pure devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me.” (Bg. 18.68)**

When Kṛṣṇa gives His guarantee, the devotee can rest assured. Nobody can impede the Lord’s guarantee that He makes to His devotees.

Let us use these examples to help us remember the importance of taking shelter of the Lord. We should learn how to depend upon Him in all of our activities, and directly perceive His presence in our life, day after day. The devotee is thus prepared for anything.

*ahany ahani bhūtāni*  
*gacchantīha yamālayam*  
*śeṣāḥ sthāvaram icchanti*  
*kim āścaryam ataḥ param*

(Mahābhārata, Vana-parva 313.116)

It is described by Yudhiṣṭhira Mahārāja that the most amazing thing in the world is that every day hundreds and millions of living entities are being sent to the kingdom of death, but still those who are remaining are making preparations to stay here forever. What can be more amazing than this?

Prahlāda Mahārāja also says in his prayers:

*bālasya neha śaraṇaṁ pitarau nṛsiṁha*  
*nārtasya cāgadam udanvati majjato nauḥ*  
*taptasya tat-pratividhir ya ihāñjaseṣṭas*  
*tāvad vibho tanu-bhṛtāṁ tvad-upekṣitānām*

**“My Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva, O Supreme, because of a bodily conception of life, embodied souls neglected and not cared for by You cannot do anything for their betterment. Whatever remedies they accept, although perhaps temporarily beneficial, are certainly impermanent. For example, a father and mother cannot protect their child, a physician and medicine cannot relieve a suffering patient, and a boat on the ocean cannot protect a drowning man.” (Bhāg. 7.9.19)**

Those in the bodily conception of life are not protected or cared for by the Lord, but those who take shelter of the Lord—utilizing the tongue, ears and all other senses for the service of the Lord—can transcend the bodily conception of life. They understand that real pleasure comes from something different than this body. They can enjoy without this body even when Kṛṣṇa takes it away at the time of death.

We should therefore aspire for this taste in taking shelter in hearing and chanting. This is the safest position to be in, and the best guarantee to be protected by the Lord. For those who are taking shelter of this process, they will be able to face even the most dangerous situation, just as a small fish having taken shelter of the ocean can face a big tsunami. Everybody is fearful of tsunamis, but the fish do not fear them because they have taken shelter of the ocean. In this way we must take shelter of the Lord and overcome fear.

We can see that Prahlāda Mahārāja was not fearful. One who knows the Lord’s purpose is always sheltered by Him. Prahlāda Mahārāja, knowing the Lord’s purpose, was able to pacify the Lord with his prayers, and the Lord gave up His anger.

## Spiritual Strength

*apy adya nas tvaṁ sva-kṛtehita prabho*  
*jihāsasi svit suhṛdo ’nujīvinaḥ*  
*yeṣāṁ na cānyad bhavataḥ padāmbujāt*  
*parāyaṇaṁ rājasu yojitāṁhasām*

**“O my Lord, You have executed all duties Yourself. Are You leaving us today, though we are completely dependent on Your mercy and have no one else to protect us, now when all kings are in enmity with us?” (Bhāg. 1.8.37)**

PURPORT

After the Battle of Kurukṣetra ended and the Pāṇḍavas were established in their kingdom, Kṛṣṇa, before going back home to Dvārakā, was taking leave of His aunt and bidding her farewell. It was at that time that Kuntī offered this prayer. Now she directly asks, “Is it a fact that after finishing Your duty You are going away and leaving us alone?” This is the devotee’s position. Kuntīdevī says, yeṣāṁna cānyad bha vataḥ padāmbujāt: “We have no means of protection other than Your lotus feet.” This is full surrender.

In the process of surrender (śaraṇāgati) there are six items. The first is that one should completely depend on Kṛṣṇa, and the next is that one should accept everything favorable for Kṛṣṇa’s service (ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ). Ānukūlyena kṛṣṇānuśīlanaṁ bhaktir uttamā: \[Cc. Madhya 19.167\] a symptom of first-class bhakti, devotional service, is that one accepts everything favorable for that service. Another item of surrender is prātikūlyasya-vivarjanam, rejecting everything unfavorable to the procedures of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Sometimes the spiritual master says, “Don’t do this,” forbidding something unfavorable, and he also recommends that which is favorable: “Do this.
