Chant Hare Kṛṣṇa.” Full surrender, therefore, entails giving up unfavorable things and accepting that which is favorable (ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ prātikūlyayasya-vivarjanam). Furthermore, one should believe with full faith, “Kṛṣṇa will give me protection,” and one should count oneself as one of the servants of Kṛṣṇa. These are some of the items of śaraṇāgati, full surrender.

Now Kuntīdevī says, “My dear Kṛṣṇa, if You think that we are well established now that we have our kingdom back, and if You therefore want to leave us, that is not a very good proposal. We are not free yet. Because we have killed so many kings, all their friends and relatives are planning to come fight with us again. So don’t think that we are free from all dangers. We are not. And we have no protection other than Your lotus feet. That is our position.” Thus she indirectly says to Kṛṣṇa, “Do not leave us. Don’t think that we are now safe. Without Your protection, we are always unsafe.”

This should be the position of a devotee. We should know that we are actually in danger in this material world. Māyā, illusion, may catch us at any time, as soon as we are a little inattentive, thinking, “Now I have done my duty. Let me take a little rest.” No, there is no rest. We must be always alert. (Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Chapter 20)

Kuntī-devi prays to Kṛṣṇa, “We are completely dependent on Your mercy.” This is the position of a devotee—to be always dependent on the mercy of Kṛṣṇa. This is one of the items of śaraṇāgati or full surrender.

*ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ*  
*prātikūlyasya varjanam*  
*rakṣiṣyatīti viśvāso*  
*goptṛtve varaṇaṁ tathā*  
*ātma-nikṣepa-kārpaṇye*  
*ṣaḍ-vidhā śaraṇāgatiḥ*

**The six divisions of surrender are the acceptance of those things favorable to devotional service, the rejection of unfavorable things, the conviction that Kṛṣṇa will give protection, the acceptance of the Lord as one’s guardian or master, full self-surrender, and humility. (Cc. Madhya, 22.100)**

These are the six items given in Caitanya-caritāmṛta for the process of surrender. Prabhupāda explains the two items, ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ prātikūlyasya varjanam—one should accept everything favorable and reject everything unfavorable. He gives the example that sometimes the spiritual master may say, “Don’t do this,” forbidding something that is unfavorable, and sometimes he may say, “Do this—chant Hare Kṛṣṇa.”

To do what is proper and to avoid that which is improper, one must have the ability to discriminate between what is right and what is wrong. This power of discrimination comes by the mercy of a spiritual master. Accepting and rejecting is the process of the mind, but this is not the type of accepting and rejecting that is being mentioned here in this verse. The mind also accepts and rejects on the basis of sense enjoyment. It will accept that which is anticipated to bring one some pleasure or some satisfaction. Then after it fails to satisfy him, a person rejects it to look for something else.

However, śaraṇāgati requires a higher power of discrimination, based on the spiritual platform. We should know what is favorable for devotional service, and that which is unfavorable should be rejected. However, even if we know, still we cannot fully reject it. Arjuna asked Kṛṣṇa, “What compels a person to act even if he knows that it is not right?”

The Supreme Personality of Godhead said (Bg. 3.37): “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.” Therefore, to be able to properly discriminate between right and wrong, one requires spiritual strength because lust is very powerful. A person who is driven by lust cannot discriminate. Although in the back of his mind, he may think: “This is wrong,” still lust drives him to do something that he knows he should not do. That is how powerful Māyā is. We should know that we are actually in danger in this material world because Māyā can catch us at any time if we are a little inattentive. As Prabhupāda says in his commentary, if we are thinking that now we have performed our duty, it does not mean that we can rest. Māyā is so powerful that we must always be alert. She does not rest; she is always very nicely engaged in her service. If we are a little inattentive, she will catch us, because she is much more powerful than we are and she is never inattentive. The devotee has to understand this position of danger in the material world—the danger of the illusory energy of the Lord and its great power.

To be able to overcome lust is not simply based upon the strength of our own intelligence. We may think we can discriminate and identify what lust is, but we need strength to carry through with not engaging in those activities. We cannot do that on our own strength. A devotee must always feel himself dependent on Kṛṣṇa. That is the safest position for a devotee. As soon as he thinks, “I can overcome this by my own strength,” he will be defeated by māyā. Our strength in comparison to the strength of the illusory energy is very insignificant.

Prabhupāda gives the example in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam of how material desires are like the waves of a river. One may enter into the river and try to stop the movement of the waves by his own strength. He may flap his arms to push back the waves, but he will have very little effect upon the influence of those waves. However, when the waves of the river enter into the ocean, then because the ocean is more powerful than the river, the ocean will push back the influence of the river’s waves. Because the ocean is more powerful than the waves of the river, one should take shelter in the ocean of devotional service. By the power of devotional service, we can be protected from the waves of material desires. One who takes shelter of devotional service is protected by Kṛṣṇa, and by the power of Kṛṣṇa, the waves of material desires can be pushed back.

Our business is to be fully dependent on Kṛṣṇa and to take His shelter. Therefore we must be able to discriminate between what is favorable and unfavorable for devotional service. To be able to discriminate means we should also have the strength to carry it out. That strength comes from Lord Balarāma, the source of all spiritual strength, who gives devotees strength to overcome the obstacles of conditional life. Without spiritual strength, it is impossible to achieve the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.

Prabhupāda quotes a verse from Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad in Kṛṣṇa book: nāyam ātmā bala-hīnena labhyaḥ—one cannot attain the supreme platform of self-realization without being sufficiently favored by Balarāma.

Bala means spiritual strength; not physical or material strength. No one can attain spiritual perfection by physical strength.

It is said in Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (3.2.4): The Supreme Personality of Godhead never reveals Himself to those who have no spiritual strength, who are wild and careless and whose austerities are inappropriate. The Supreme Lord reveals Himself to those who are always endeavoring to achieve Him by the right means. Only such persons enter into the spiritual world.

Therefore, we must make the endeavor, and by so doing, we will also be bestowed with the strength to overcome difficulties.

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura gives a very interesting analysis in his Caitanya-śikṣāmṛta. He describes how the different demons in Vṛndāvana are compared to the various obstacles of devotional service. Kṛṣṇa killed demons in Vṛndāvana, such as Pūtanā Witch, and Balarāma also killed demons, one of which was Dhenukāsura. Dhenukāsura was the ass-demon. He symbolizes ignorance. Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says that Dhenukāsura stimulates the ignorance about one’s spiritual identity. It makes one forget that he is a servant of Kṛṣṇa. Also due to the influence of Dhenukāsura, one gets misconceptions about the eternal nature of the holy name of the Lord. By the influence of the ass-demon Dhenukāsura, ignorance is created, binding the living entity. However, Lord Balarāma killed that Dhenukāsura demon.

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says that before one chants the holy name of the Lord by his own endeavors, he must pray to the Lord to overcome these different obstacles in chanting His holy name. First these demons have to be fought by our own endeavors and then Lord Balarāma comes and gives us strength and helps us to overcome them. Thus we must endeavor.

The Supreme Lord reveals Himself to those who always strive to achieve Him by the right means. We have to have the power to discriminate and know where to focus our endeavors. We should not be like the foolish asses that are full of ignorance and have no power of discrimination. The ass carries a big, heavy burden on its back. Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains that the Dhenukāsura demon also carries the heavy burden of ignorance about our spiritual identity and misconceptions about the holy name of the Lord and about that which is worshipable and that which is not worshipable. These misconceptions have to be destroyed by the power of Lord Balarāma, which will come to us when we try to overcome the obstacles in chanting the holy name of the Lord. We may know what is right and what is wrong. However, if we do not try to overcome these obstacles, we will not have the spiritual strength to carry it through, to know how to execute it, to know how to stay away from those things that are destroying our spiritual life, and how to have the power to say “no” to such things. This requires strength.

We should compare lust to our own will power and examine how many times we fall victim to our lust and lose. We need some strength to overcome the power of that lust. We have to make the endeavor, while being dependent upon the Lord. We see this in the example of the Pāṇḍavas who were very powerful and worked very hard with courage. Yet they were always dependent on the good will of the Lord who always helped them. Although the Pāṇḍavas were very powerful warriors and had great strength, they were always conscious of Kṛṣṇa’s protection in everything they did. Having firm faith that Kṛṣṇa will always protect us is one of the six divisions of surrender.

A nondevotee, by dint of his ignorance, thinks himself to be the doer of activities:

*prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni*  
*guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ*  
*ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā*  
*kartāham iti manyate*

**The spirit soul bewildered by the influence of false ego thinks himself the doer of activities that are in actuality carried out by the three modes of material nature. (Bg. 3.27)**

That is the nondevotee’s ignorance or misconception. Another example about the ass is used in this context. During India’s summer season, all the grass dries up. The ass is eating and eating, but in reality it is not eating anything, because there is no grass to eat. Although he is not eating anything, he thinks, “I’ve eaten everything!” Therefore he gets fat. In the winter season, there is so much grass everywhere and the ass is eating. Everywhere he looks, he sees that there is still so much grass. Even though he is eating so much grass, he is thinking, “I haven’t eaten anything!” Therefore, he gets skinny, thinking he is not eating so much grass. The abundance or absence of grass during winter and summer seasons occurs independently from the ass. Yet the ass is thinking, “I’m not eating anything” or “I’m eating so much,” based upon his own mentality. This is the ass! Prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ—everything is happening by material nature, but he is personally thinking, “No, I am doing it! I must be eating so much grass because there is nothing around!” Such is the mentality of the ass. That is mūḍha, a foolish person.

Similarly, a devotee can also sometimes have that same kind of ass-like mentality: “Look what I am doing! I am doing so many things. I am distributing so many books, opening so many temples, doing so much service. I am doing everything!” Yet if he sits down and chants Hare Kṛṣṇa and tries to absorb his mind in the holy names of the Lord, remember the pastimes of the Lord, and absorb himself in hearing the Lord’s pastimes, then he thinks, “What have I done today? I have not done anything! I have to do something.” Thus he has an ass-like mentality, thinking that doing something means doing it externally. Actually, really doing something means doing it internally.

We should not be like the ass, simply thinking that our achievements are always external achievements. There are also internal achievements that need to be accomplished. Therefore we have a responsibility to increase our Kṛṣṇa consciousness by hearing and chanting every day.

We find so many ways to absorb our consciousness because we do not want to make the endeavor to remember Kṛṣṇa. By not making the endeavor, we will not get the strength, we will not get Lord Balarāma’s mercy, and we will not get the mercy of the spiritual master who represents Lord Balarāma and gives us instructions on how to discriminate between what is right and what is wrong.

Therefore, Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains that killing this ass-demon first requires our own endeavors. When we make the endeavors ourselves, Lord Balarāma gives us the extra strength to carry it through.

We have to be able to discriminate between what we need and what we want. To have this power or strength, there must be sādhana. Every day a devotee must execute sādhana: hearing and chanting the holy name of the Lord. Before he begins his chanting, he should pray to Lord Balarāma, “I am in ignorance. I cannot get rid of this big heavy load that I am carrying by my own strength. I am completely dependent upon You to dispel my ignorance. Please give me the strength! I don’t have it on my own. Please, give me the strength to chant my rounds attentively. Give me the strength to overcome these anarthas.” That is sādhana. If we do that every day, we will feel that we get some strength.

We want to get spiritual strength from Lord Balarāma because He is the source of it all. If we want this strength of Lord Balarāma, then we should dedicate this day to making the endeavor to get it. We should pray for His mercy. We should pray for His strength to discriminate between what is right and what is wrong. We should pray for the strength to overcome the power of illusory energy and pray for the strength to defeat lust. Lord Balarāma will be very merciful to us. He is so kind that He will bestow upon us the strength that we need to overcome these obstacles. Just as He killed the demon Dhenukāsura, He will kill these heavy burdens of ignorance that we are carrying in our consciousness.

Lord Balarāma first appeared in the womb of Devakī and then He was transferred to the womb of Rohiṇī. After Lord Balarāma appeared, then Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared. Therefore, first we get the spiritual strength from Lord Balarāma, and then we get Kṛṣṇa’s mercy. Kṛṣṇa will appear in our minds and hearts, and will engage us in His loving devotional service.

Everything we do must be in connection with Kṛṣṇa. If we do something without seeing its connection to Kṛṣṇa, then we get lost in the labyrinth of duality. This labyrinth of duality is very difficult to get out of, because we always try to counteract a bad situation by a good situation, and in the attempt, we continue creating bad situations.

*mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya*  
*śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ*  
*āgamāpāyino ’nityās*  
*tāṁs titikṣasva bhārata*

**“The nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.” (Bg. 2.14)**

The only way we can tolerate these dualities of this material world is by remembering Kṛṣṇa. Any other shelter is an illusion. It appears to be shelter like a mirage in a desert. However the shelter that one gets from Kṛṣṇa consciousness is lasting shelter. Unless we endeavor to remember Kṛṣṇa, we will never transcend the duality of the material world. Kṛṣṇa says, “In all endeavors, depend on Me and work under My protection.” If we don’t make the endeavor, then Kṛṣṇa will not manifest in our minds.

*nāyam ātmā bala-hīnena labhyo*  
*na ca pramādāt tapaso vāpy aliṅgāt*  
*etair upāyair yatate yas tu vidvāṁs*  
*tasyaiṣa ātmā viśate brahma-dhāma*

**“A person devoid of strength in devotional service cannot achieve the Supreme Soul, the Lord. Only one who is eager to practice devotional service through the process of chanting His holy names can enter the supreme abode of the Lord.” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3)**

Without spiritual strength, the Lord will not manifest to a person—neither before him, nor in his mind, nor in his heart. Lord Balarāma infuses one with spiritual strength to overcome the obstacles of material life. He gives that strength to those who always strive to achieve Him by the right means. He does not give strength to those whose austerities are inappropriate and to those who are wild and careless.

We see many people willing to undergo so many personal inconveniences for fruitive (material) gain. These are inappropriate austerities. Those who are wild and careless are those who perform these austerities and do not make any effort to remember the Lord. They are careless in the application of their austerities, and they are not fixed in the goal. The result is that such persons will never enter the spiritual world and will never perceive the Lord. Therefore, one has to have spiritual strength, which comes from the Supreme Lord Balarāma. It is described in Caitanya-bhāgavata that Nityānanda Balarāma is the same as Ananta Śeṣa who is holding unlimited universes upon His hoods, yet not resting on anything.

One has to associate with those who have strength and get strength by remembering their instructions. There is no other way to tolerate the austerities of material life unless one has faith in the goal of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Such faith is the only requirement for pure devotional service and for obtaining real fruit. Whereas the false fruit of the material world is some temporary achievement, the real fruit of one’s spiritual endeavors and the real criterion for success is to achieve love for Kṛṣṇa. The topmost fruit is the pure holy name dancing on one’s tongue and causing his senses to become inert, which brings great joy within the courtyard of the heart. If we do not aspire for this fruit, and we have no faith in achieving it as the final goal, it is very difficult to make progress. Spiritual strength is thus required. We should therefore pray to keep ourselves in the association of persons who give us that strength.

That spiritual strength comes by the association of devotees whose instructions infuse us with faith in the goal. Even if such association is not available by physical proximity, we should keep their instructions within our heart. Similarly, if somebody gives you something very valuable and it means a lot to you, you will put it in a prominent place in your residence so that you can see it regularly or use it regularly. You will not put it in the closet. Thus if Vaiṣṇavas give something natural in the form of instructions, if it is valuable, we should put it in a prominent place. The most prominent place to put it is within the core of our heart. Those instructions will help us to remain steady on the path of devotion and prevent us from slipping again and again. Even though we are blind, we will still be able to make progress towards the goal because those instructions within the heart will lead us. However, if there is no faith, the heart will be empty and we will not be able to make progress and overcome the obstacles.

We should make our efforts towards achieving the right goal and depend on Kṛṣṇa. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura describes that even if we have so many foodstuffs that are meant for the Lord’s pleasure, if the Lord does not accept them, nobody will receive the remnants. Similarly, if we are not favored by the Lord, then even though we may have unlimited endeavors, we will never be successful. A devotee must always be dependent upon the mercy of the Lord.

**Question: By making some vratas or vows, does that give us spiritual strength?**

Kṛṣṇa says (Bg. 9.27), “Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, and whatever austerities you perform—do that, O son of Kuntī, as an offering to Me.”

Similarly, Prahlāda Mahārāja says to his classmates (Bhāg. 7.7.51-52):

“My dear friends, O sons of the demons, you cannot please the Supreme Personality of Godhead by becoming perfect brāhmaṇas, demigods or great saints or by becoming perfectly good in etiquette or vast learning. None of these qualifications can awaken the pleasure of the Lord. Nor by charity, austerity, sacrifice, cleanliness or vows can one satisfy the Lord. The Lord is pleased only if one has unflinching, unalloyed devotion to Him. Without sincere devotional service, everything is simply a show.”

Prahlāda Mahārāja explains that the secret ingredient is the austerities that are performed for Kṛṣṇa. Those will bear fruit if we remember the goal of our austerities. However, if we simply perform austerities for the sake of performing austerities, and if we are not careful, then the performance of austerities can also bring about recognition, and there will be no fruit.

This was shown in the pastime of the brahmacārī who tried to enter into the kīrtana of Caitanya Mahāprabhu. He begged Śrīvasa Paṇḍita, “Let me in! I perform austerities. I eat very little—just a little milk and fruit.” Śrīvasa invited him in and told him to hide so that he can see Caitanya Mahāprabhu’s kīrtana. However, Lord Caitanya was not satisfied by his austerities.

While the Lord was engaged in kīrtana, He said, “I am not experiencing the same ecstasy and devotion as usual. Something is present here that is disturbing My ecstasies. Who is in this house who is not a devotee?”

Śrīvasa could not hold it in, because he was responsible for having invited him in, and thus said, “Oh there is someone here, but he is a brahmacārī. He eats only fruits and drinks milk.”

Lord Caitanya responded, “What!? You think that simply by drinking milk you have the qualification to see My kīrtanas? No milk drinker can see My kīrtana!” He chastised him and told him to get out.

However, within his heart, the brahmacārī accepted the chastisement as mercy, and felt so fortunate to be a recipient of Mahāprabhu’s mercy. Thus as he was leaving the house by the order of Caitanya Mahāprabhu, the Lord understanding that his heart had changed and that he had accepted His mercy, called him back. Lord Caitanya then placed His lotus feet on his head and said, “Do not ever think again that simply by performing austerities you can achieve the right to attain My kīrtana.” Following that, the Lord said, “Let the kīrtana begin!”

Therefore, we cannot forget the goal of our austerities. Sometimes we may perform austerities for the sake of performing them, but we should always remember that the goal of our austerities is the satisfaction of the Lord. By so doing, we will be able to remember the Lord, and the Lord will help us to follow the austerities. When He helps us to remember Him, then such types of austerities are good.

## Transcending the Dualities of the Material World

*yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehas*  
*tat tat prāpya śubhāśubham*  
*nābhinandati na dveṣṭi*  
*tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā*

**In the material world, one who is unaffected by whatever good or evil he may obtain, neither praising it nor despising it, is firmly fixed in perfect knowledge. (Bg. 2.57)**

PURPORT

There is always some upheaval in the material world which may be good or evil. One who is not agitated by such material upheavals, who is unaffected by good and evil, is to be understood to be fixed in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. As long as one is in the material world there is always the possibility of good and evil because this world is full of duality. But one who is fixed in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is not affected by good and evil, because he is simply concerned with Kṛṣṇa, who is all-good absolute. Such consciousness in Kṛṣṇa situates one in a perfect transcendental position called, technically, samādhi.

In this verse, Kṛṣṇa is speaking about a person whom He also described in the previous verse as sthita-dhīr munir—a sage of steady mind, or one who is unaffected by upheavals of this world. Prabhupāda speaks about the nature of the material world in his purport, saying that there is always some duality in this world, and therefore there is always the possibility of good or evil, happiness or distress, or honor or dishonor.

The following verse from the prayers of Citraketu Mahārāja in the Sixth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam talks about how Kṛṣṇa creates these dualities in the material world for the living entities according to their desires.

*na tasya kaścid dayitaḥ pratīpo*  
*na jñāti-bandhur na paro na ca svaḥ*  
*samasya sarvatra nirañjanasya*  
*sukhe na rāgaḥ kuta eva roṣaḥ*

**The Supreme Personality of Godhead is equally disposed toward all living entities. Therefore no one is very dear to Him, and no one is a great enemy for Him; no one is His friend, and no one is His relative. Being unattached to the material world, He has no affection for so-called happiness or hatred for so-called distress. The two terms happiness and distress are relative. Since the Lord is always happy, for Him there is no question of distress. (Bhāg. 6.17.22)**

*tathāpi tac-chakti-visarga eṣāṁ*  
*sukhāya duḥkhāya hitāhitāya*  
*bandhāya mokṣāya ca mṛtyu-janmanoḥ*  
*śarīriṇāṁ saṁsṛtaye ’vakalpate*

**Although the Supreme Lord is unattached to our happiness and distress according to karma, and although no one is His enemy or favorite, He creates pious and impious activities through the agency of His material potency. Thus for the continuation of the materialistic way of life He creates happiness and distress, good fortune and bad, bondage and liberation, birth and death. (Bhāg. 6.17.23)**

PURPORT

Although the Supreme Personality of Godhead is the ultimate doer of everything, in His original transcendental existence He is not responsible for the happiness and distress, or bondage and liberation, of the conditioned souls. These are due to the results of the fruitive activities of the living entities within this material world. By the order of a judge, one person is released from jail, and another is imprisoned, but the judge is not responsible, for the distress and happiness of these different people is due to their own activities. Although the government is ultimately the supreme authority, the justice is administered by the departments of the government, and the government is not responsible for the individual judgments. Therefore the government is equal to all the citizens. Similarly, the Supreme Lord is neutral to everyone, but for the maintenance of law and order His supreme government has various departments, which control the activities of the living entities. Another example given in this regard is that lilies open or close because of the sunshine, and thus the bumblebees enjoy or suffer, but the sunshine and the sun globe are not responsible for the happiness and distress of the bumblebees.

These verses explain how Kṛṣṇa creates pious and impious activities through the agency of His material potency. For the continuation of those who are interested in the materialistic way of life, He creates happiness and distress, good fortune and bad, bondage and liberation, and birth and death. Prabhupāda gives the example that the sunshine causes the lilies to open and close, and the bumblebees suffer when the lilies are closed, but it cannot be said that sunshine is directly responsible for the suffering of the bumblebees.

*kṛṣṇa—sūrya-sama; māyā haya andhakāra*  
*yāhāṅ kṛṣṇa, tāhāṅ nāhi māyāra adhikāra*

**Kṛṣṇa is compared to sunshine and māyā is compared to darkness. Wherever there is sunshine, there cannot be darkness. As soon as one takes to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, the darkness of illusion (the influence of the external energy) will immediately vanish. (Cc. Madhya 22.31)**

Thus when we turn away from Kṛṣṇa, then we are under the separate material energy, which appears to act independent from the Lord. Kṛṣṇa says that the material nature works according to His direction, but for the living entity that turns away from Him, it appears to act independent from the Him. Thus the living entity, by turning away from Him, sees the dualities of this material world.

**“In this material world, every materialist desires to achieve happiness and diminish his distress, and therefore he acts accordingly. Actually, however, one is happy as long as one does not endeavor for happiness; as soon as one begins his activities for happiness, his conditions of distress begin.” (Bhāg. 7.7.42)**

Prahlāda Mahārāja very clearly explains that in the material world everyone is endeavoring for happiness and trying to mitigate his distress.

*bālasya neha śaraṇaṁ pitarau nṛsiṁha*  
*nārtasya cāgadam udanvati majjato nauḥ*  
*taptasya tat-pratividhir ya ihāñjaseṣṭas*  
*tāvad vibho tanu-bhṛtāṁ tvad-upekṣitānām*

**“My Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva, O Supreme, because of a bodily conception of life, embodied souls neglected and not cared for by You cannot do anything for their betterment. Whatever remedies they accept, although perhaps temporarily beneficial, are certainly impermanent. For example, a father and mother cannot protect their child, a physician and medicine cannot relieve a suffering patient, and a boat on the ocean cannot protect a drowning man.” (Bhāg. 7.9.19)**

Prahlāda Mahārāja gives this example that just like a physician and medicine cannot relieve a suffering patient, similarly the embodied souls, who due to the conditioned mentality are neglected by the Lord, cannot do anything for their betterment. They may become only temporarily relieved or temporarily happy. He gives the example that a person suffering from a terrible disease may all of a sudden look for the best doctor. The best doctor comes and says, “Yes, there is some medicine. I will administer it to you. Certainly we should see some signs of success.” However, there is no guarantee that it will actually be successful.

When I was with my dear godbrother Śrīdhara Mahārāja in Māyāpura before his departure, I could see that he was not deluded by this. One of our godbrothers named Tridandi from Italy said, “There is a doctor in South India. I know he can cure you.”

In his usual way, Mahārāja reacted to this by saying, “Oh alright, let him try.”

Tridandi went all the way to South India to find this doctor and brought him back.

The doctor said, “If you take my medicine, you will immediately see some dramatic change in just three weeks.” Śrīdhara Mahārāja willingly accepted, but you could see that he was really not convinced, and did not place much faith in it.

I left Māyāpura a week before Śrīdhara Mahārāja’s departure from this world. In fact, a lot of our godbrothers had left a week early. Śrīdhara Mahārāja had this way of diminishing the importance of his departure. Earlier, I had walked into his room, and Mahārāja said to me, “What are you doing here? Get out of here. Go to Moscow. Don’t you know I am going to be cured? I’ll see you in Moscow.” He kicked me out. “Why is everybody staying here? Go on, do your service. You should be preaching, not giving me so much attention.”

I therefore left, but I called him from Kiev on what turned out to be the night before he departed. Mahārāja said to me, “Mahārāja, you are going to have to preach to me to convince me that it’s worth staying here in this material world. You know, all these remedies are not doing anything. I think Kṛṣṇa knows. I think Kṛṣṇa has set the time for me to go. If everyone wants me to stay, then you all are going to have to preach to me and convince me that I should go on endeavoring to stay in this material world because I don’t see any reason for doing that.” He was speaking very openly and honestly with me.

Similarly, Prahlāda Mahārāja says that even if you have an expert physician and the best medicine, you may experience temporary happiness. However, it does not mean you are not going to die.

I brought up the example of Śrīdhara Mahārāja, because he seemed somewhat convinced that all of this was just another attempt to keep his body going. He was willing to do it because the devotees really wanted him to, but he was detached. I was with Mahārāja every night, going to his room and having kīrtanas. He was begging me to please come and chant for him.

There is one other thing he did that really amazed me. Mahārāja was bedridden at that time. One night I could not go to chant in his room, as I had a terrible headache after the GBC meeting. I used to go to his room just shortly after the meetings, but that day, I wrote a note and sent it to Mahārāja’s room, “Mahārāja, please forgive me but I am not going to be able to make it for the kīrtana.” I explained that I had a really bad headache and I promised I would be there the following night. However, when I was walking back to my room, I was thinking, “I have a headache, but look at what Śrīdhara Mahārāja is going through!” I felt really bad!

I decided to turn around, go back to Mahārāja’s room and have kīrtana. There were many devotees there. It is not like the kīrtana would not go on without me. However, I had a strong feeling that I should go because when Mahārāja first arrived in Māyāpura, I saw him and he embraced me, and asked me if I would come and chant with him every night. I therefore kept that fixed in my mind. I had already sent a message, but I thought, “I am going to go back and at least chant with the rest of the devotees.”

When I opened up the door of the room, Śrīdhara Mahārāja looked up at me, and then called out for me to come to him. He told me to sit on the bed next to him. Then he sat up and asked a devotee named Māyāpura to get some tiger balm. He started massaging my head for about 30 minutes like he was a completely healthy man. I was thinking, “Here is a devotee who is in so much pain, lying here bedridden, and he is thinking about my headache!” He just kept on massaging my head. He would not let me go. He was such an amazing personality, and such a valuable jewel we had in our midst. There is no wonder why we were all willing to try for him to stay longer in this world.

I remember another night when we had kīrtana. Mahārāja was lying down with so much poison and toxins in his body. He was really sick. His body was feverish. We thought he was going to leave that night. The doctor came and was supposed to get fluids drained from his abdomen. Mahārāja’s abdomen would get very bloated. His younger brother was crying at the sight of him.

The doctor came over and started to feel the fluids in his abdomen. Śrīdhara Mahārāja then turned to his brother and said, “It’s a boy!” His brother switched from tears to laughter. Śrīdhara Mahārāja was artfully dealing with everybody’s emotions. He was always trying to take away any emotion that would cause crying.

Somehow word got out to all the devotees that we were having kīrtana, and he got through that night. His fever subsided. The next night, when we had kīrtana, Mahārāja sat up after the kīrtana and gave a lecture to all devotees in his room about how we are not these bodies. That was one of the most profound lectures I have ever heard about how we are not these bodies. Although we hear those words all the time, when it came from the mouth of Śrīdhara Mahārāja that night, it was transcendental. You could see that he was not bewildered by what he was confronting—dhīras tatra na muhyati (Bg. 2.13). At the same time, Mahārāja would always deny his Kṛṣṇa consciousness and say, “I am not Kṛṣṇa conscious. I need all of you to help me be Kṛṣṇa conscious.” Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the only way to transcend the dualities of this world of birth and death. He very successfully transcended it in his detachment from all that was going on.

To transcend the dualities of the material world, the living entity has to control the mind, restricting it from the tendency to see things as separate from Kṛṣṇa. When the mind is thus controlled, one experiences fearlessness. If there is no Kṛṣṇa consciousness, then we are going to be faced with the dualities of the material world, which Kṛṣṇa has created for the living entities that turn away from Him. And just as we experience happiness and distress in relationship to the dream, which has no reality beyond our own imagination, we also experience happiness and distress in relationship to the daydream.

I remember that in the ‘70s, there was a time when lots of devotees were getting married, thinking that marriage was the solution. However, many unexpected distresses started to come to them. They were thinking everything would be like the nice daydream they were having. Our mind gets filled with the anticipation of happiness and the plans to avoid suffering.

*tasyaiva hetoḥ prayateta kovido*  
*na labhyate yad bhramatām upary adhaḥ*  
*tal labhyate duḥkhavad anyataḥ sukhaṁ*  
*kālena sarvatra gabhīra-raṁhasā*

**Persons who are actually intelligent and philosophically inclined should endeavor only for that purposeful end which is not obtainable even by wandering from the topmost planet \[Brahmaloka\] down to the lowest planet \[Pātāla\]. As far as happiness derived from sense enjoyment is concerned, it can be obtained automatically in course of time, just as in course of time we obtain miseries even though we do not desire them. (Bhāg. 1.5.18)**

Thus happiness and distress come in due course of time. We do not need to endeavor for it.

Prabhupāda tells the story of a sage who gives different kinds of blessings to different types of persons. To a prince, the sage says, “Better you live forever, because after your death, you do not know what is going to happen to you. You are going to get a hellish life. Better you live for some time. Go on with enjoying all your previous pious activities.”

To a brahmacārī who is working under the strict disciplinary guidance of a spiritual master, the sage says, “It is better that you die. Because you are so trained to enter into the kingdom of God, why should you take so much trouble in remaining here? It is better that you die and go straight back to Godhead.

To a saintly person the sage says, “May you live or die. It does not make any difference.”

To a butcher he says, “Don’t live and don’t die. Don’t live because by your living you are causing so much suffering. Don’t die either, because when you die there will be so much suffering for you.” He will be in a hellish condition that nobody can describe.

We may try to become happy by not suffering, but it is an illusion, because suffering will come by its own accord. Therefore, an intelligent person endeavors for neither. He knows that by endeavoring to please Kṛṣṇa and by remembering Kṛṣṇa, he can transcend happiness and distress, honor and dishonor.

In Bhagavad-gītā Kṛṣṇa says (6.6-7): “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his mind will remain the greatest enemy. For one who has conquered the mind, the Supersoul is already reached, for he has attained tranquility. To such a man happiness and distress, heat and cold, honor and dishonor are all the same.”

There is a verse from the Bhāgavatam (11.28.4), which Prabhupāda quotes in Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 4.175) in the story of Sanatāna Gosvāmī: “Anything not conceived in relationship to Kṛṣṇa should be understood to be illusion (māyā). None of the illusions uttered by words or conceived in the mind are factual. Because illusion is not factual, there is no distinction between what we think is good and what we think is bad. When we speak of the Absolute Truth, such speculations do not apply.”

For the Supreme Personality of Godhead, such speculations do not exist. Kṛṣṇa is transcendental to these things.

‘dvaite’ bhadrābhadra-jñāna, saba—‘manodharma’

‘ei bhāla, ei manda’,—ei saba ‘bhrama’

**“In the material world, conceptions of good and bad are all mental speculations. Therefore, saying ‘This is good’ and ‘This is bad’ is all a mistake.” (Cc. Antya 4.176)**

The word he used is manodharma, the religion of the mind. We are thinking in terms of mind’s projections. However, Kṛṣṇa clearly states (Bg. 2.57): “In the material world, one who is unaffected by whatever good or evil he may obtain, neither praising it nor despising it, is firmly fixed in perfect knowledge.”

There is always some upheaval in the material world, which may be good or evil. The dualities do exist. The conditioned soul’s experiences are real due to his conditioned intelligence, which is seeing things separate from Kṛṣṇa. “But one who is fixed in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is not affected by good and evil, because he is simply concerned with Kṛṣṇa, who is all-good absolute.” (Purport to Bg. 2.57)

**Question: Why did Kṛṣṇa create suffering for the living entities?**

**Although the Supreme Lord is unattached to our happiness and distress according to karma, and although no one is His enemy or favorite, He creates pious and impious activities through the agency of His material potency. Thus for the continuation of the materialistic way of life He creates happiness and distress, good fortune and bad, bondage and liberation, birth and death. (Bhāg. 6.17.23)**

The Lord is not directly responsible for the suffering of the living entities; just as the sun is not directly responsible for the sufferings of the bees when the lilies open and close. Prabhupāda also gives the example of the government:

(…) the government is not responsible for the individual judgments. Therefore the government is equal to all the citizens. Similarly, the Supreme Lord is neutral to everyone, but for the maintenance of law and order His supreme government has various departments, which control the activities of the living entities. (Purport to Bhāg. 6.17.23)

The Lord is seen as all-neutral in the same way as the judge who makes his decision according to the behavior of the defendant in court. Thus the Supreme Lord is also neutral, seated as the Supersoul within the heart to witness and give sanction. The living entity has his desires for independence, and therefore the Lord witnesses and gives sanction.

As previously explained, if a living entity is persistent in his desires and wants to enjoy, then although the Supersoul does not want him to do it, He witnesses and gives sanction to our desires. Not a blade of grass can move without the will of the Lord. He gives sanction, but it is by our misuse of our independence and by our choice that we create a situation that leads to suffering.

Prabhupāda explains that suffering in the material world, good fortune and bad fortune, bondage and liberation, and birth and death are all created by the Lord. Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the only way to transcend the dualities of the material world and to transcend the upheavals which, as Prabhupāda explains, will come automatically in the course of events in this material world. Kṛṣṇa—sūrya-sama, māyā haya andhakāra—we should endeavor every day to somehow remember Kṛṣṇa, speak about Kṛṣṇa and to try our best to overcome the dualities of materialistic life, which will ultimately only be a source of suffering. Even though we may temporarily experience some happiness, happiness is only a foundation for future distress. An intelligent person should understand this.

*nūnaṁ pramattaḥ kurute vikarma*  
*yad indriya-prītaya āpṛṇoti*  
*na sādhu manye yata ātmano ’yam*  
*asann api kleśada āsa dehaḥ*

**When a person considers sense gratification the aim of life, he certainly becomes mad after materialistic living and engages in all kinds of sinful activity. He does not know that due to his past misdeeds he has already received a body which, although temporary, is the cause of his misery. Actually the living entity should not have taken on a material body, but he has been awarded the material body for sense gratification. Therefore I think it not befitting an intelligent man to involve himself again in the activities of sense gratification by which he perpetually gets material bodies one after another. (Bhāg. 5.5.4)**

Persons who are pramattaḥ, mad after sense enjoyment, do not understand that all the suffering that they are experiencing in this life is simply due to all their attempts for happiness in their previous lives. Yet they are still addicted to all kinds of sinful activities. They are mad after sense gratification, thinking that it will relieve their suffering in this life. However, they do not see that their attempts to counteract these effects will lead to another set of effects that will create more suffering. As stated in the verse from the Fourth Canto of the Bhāgavatam, where Nārada Muni speaks to King Prācīnabarhi (Bhāg. 4.29.34):

“No one can counteract the effects of fruitive activity simply by manufacturing a different activity devoid of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. All such activity is due to our ignorance. When we have a troublesome dream, we cannot relieve it with a troublesome hallucination. One can counteract a dream only by awaking. Similarly, our material existence is due to our ignorance and illusion. Unless we awaken to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, we cannot be relieved of such dreams. For the ultimate solution to all problems, we must awaken to Kṛṣṇa consciousness.”

Similarly, a person may think he can counteract the effects of fruitive activities by manufacturing another activity that is devoid of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, but that is not possible. We are not counteracting the effects of fruitive activities; we are simply creating more suffering. It is like shifting a burden of weight from one shoulder to the other. We are still carrying the burden. In the same way, we are still carrying the burden of our reactions, aprārabdha-karma. In due course of time, it will bear fruit. We therefore try to counteract it by another fruitive activity, which results in more aprārabdha-karma. Therefore, as Nārada Muni says, the only way to counteract the effects of fruitive activities is to wake up from our dreams to Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

**Question: Due to the conditioned mentality, the living entity in the material world sees dualities. However, in the spiritual world there are no dualities; everybody is Kṛṣṇa conscious. Therefore, where does that desire to enjoy devoid of Kṛṣṇa come from?**

*jīvera ‘svarūpa’ haya—kṛṣṇera ‘nitya-dāsa’*  
*kṛṣṇera ‘taṭasthā-śakti’ ‘bhedābheda-prakāśa’*

(Cc. Madhya 20.108)

The living entity is taṭasthā, which means to be on the border. Thus the jiva, living entity, who is coming from a Mahā-Viṣṇu, is on the border. They are given a choice. As we know, love has to be of a voluntary spirit. Just as Kṛṣṇa is completely independent, the living entities must also have independence. The difference is that Kṛṣṇa is completely independent, and we have tiny independence. That tiny independence allows us to either choose Kṛṣṇa or the illusory energy.

From the platform of taṭasthā-śakti, that choice is there. Since time immemorial, there is beginningless karma, as Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura describes in Jaiva-dharma. It is very difficult to conceive or to understand by our tiny minds.

**Question: Kṛṣṇa is all-good, and thus everything that comes from Him is all-good. Is it a correct understanding that evil or bad things are created by the human minds because of the freedom of choice that has been given to us, and directly created by Kṛṣṇa?**

Kṛṣṇa says to Lord Brahmā in one of the four nutshell verses of the Bhāgavatam:

**“O Brahmā, whatever appears to be of any value, if it is without relation to Me, has no reality. Know it as My illusory energy, that reflection which appears to be in darkness.” (Bhāg. 2.9.34)**

The ability to see separate from Kṛṣṇa has also come from Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa says, “That is My separated material energy. If you see something of value, but you cannot see how it is connected to Me, then why is it valuable?” Something is valuable only when it is connected to the Lord; that is what gives its real value! However, if we think something is valuable, but we do not see it in connection to Kṛṣṇa, it is due to our perverted or distorted perception of the value of that particular object. We think, “I will derive happiness from this object and therefore it is valuable.” If we do not see its connection to Kṛṣṇa, then it is His illusory energy. Kṛṣṇa creates the illusory energy and the ability to see separate from Him. We always have the freedom to choose. At some point in time immemorial, we made a wrong choice!

**Question: Should we consider the illusory energy of Kṛṣṇa as evil or good?**

In one sense it is good. Just like the example that if you put the hand in the fire, the fire burns, which is good, because it causes you to take your hand out of the fire. Similarly, there is so much suffering in this material world which burns us, but can also helps us turn to Kṛṣṇa. Unfortunately, for most conditioned souls, suffering in the material world is something they do not want. They think, “It’s not my nature to suffer. Therefore, let me enjoy separate from Kṛṣṇa.” Such is the mentality of materialistic persons. They endeavor for happiness separate from Kṛṣṇa, and they try to counteract the distress, and therefore they act accordingly. As a result, they become caught up and entangled in the network of reactions, birth after birth after birth.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura describes in the Bhakti-tattva-viveka that the living entity’s sukṛtī, or qualification for beginning devotional service, is the result of some sukṛtī attained in the past. It begins due to living entities’ unfulfilled desires over a prolonged time or prolonged suffering over a prolonged time, in spite of their prolonged endeavors to enjoy. Then that spirit of detachment is awakened within one’s heart. However, being detached is not sufficient.

*ye ’nye ’ravindākṣa vimukta-māninas*  
*tvayy asta-bhāvād aviśuddha-buddhayaḥ*

**“O lotus-eyed Lord, although nondevotees who accept severe austerities and penances to achieve the highest position may think themselves liberated, their intelligence is impure. They fall down from their position of imagined superiority because they have no regard for Your lotus feet.” (Bhāg. 10.2.32)**

Real shelter is taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa. A person’s sukṛti is derived as a result of prolonged suffering or prolonged unfulfilled desires. When he achieves that spirit of detachment, and if by good fortune he comes into the association of devotees, this is called bhaktyā-mukhi-sukṛti. By his good fortune, he associates with the devotees and his faith that his ultimate goal of life is devotional service to Kṛṣṇa is awakened. Śraddhā then takes birth in his heart. Just as a mother protects the child from dangerous elements, in the same way, a devotee or a person who comes in contact with devotional service protects their śraddhā from karma and jñāna.

Hṛdayānanda Mahārāja gives the example in the Eleventh Canto of the Bhāgavatam that if you get on a plane from New York to Los Angeles, whether you sit in the front or back of the plane, you are still going to Los Angeles. Thus the living entity that is not surrendered to Kṛṣṇa still has some choice, but he has to accept the results of that karma.

**Question: When we see things such as flowers and peacocks, are these material or spiritual?**

Everything in this world is real, but temporary. It is real because it is Kṛṣṇa’s energy.

*etad-yonīni bhūtāni*  
*sarvāṇīty upadhāraya*  
*ahaṁ kṛtsnasya jagataḥ*  
*prabhavaḥ pralayas tathā*

**“All created beings have their source in these two natures. Of all that is material and all that is spiritual in this world, know for certain that I am both the origin and the dissolution.” (Bg. 7.6)**

In the material world, everything is temporary, whereas the spiritual world is transcendental, which means there is no temporary nature.

There is a verse that says that one who is unaffected by whatever good or evil he may obtain, neither praising it nor despising it, is firmly fixed in perfect knowledge. This verse is speaking about the person who does not praise anything for its material value. A person might say that the iPhone is not created by Steven Jobs, but by Kṛṣṇa, who gave this man the intelligence to create it. Thus, such things are not praised for their material value. Ultimately everything is coming from Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, a devotee praises these things only in terms of their connection with the Lord.

**Question: Kṛṣṇa is equal to the sufferings and enjoyments of the living entities, but sometimes people who are suffering approach Kṛṣṇa with their prayers. Does Kṛṣṇa remain indifferent or does He answer their prayers?**

Kṛṣṇa is neutral towards those who are suffering according to karma. However, for anyone who once approaches Him in devotion, Kṛṣṇa can never be indifferent. In devotion means that we have to approach Him through His devotees, because they are never indifferent towards the sufferings of the living beings. When a devotee feels suffering because of others’ suffering, then you get Kṛṣṇa’s attention. Kṛṣṇa cannot tolerate the sufferings of His devotees. However, if we try to get Kṛṣṇa’s attention ourselves, Kṛṣṇa remains neutral.

This is shown through the example of Advaita Ācārya who called the Lord to descend because he saw the condition of the living entities at that particular time. He saw how people were engaged in fruitive activities, and how they were destined to suffer so much. Feeling pain and compassion in His heart, He began calling upon the Lord: “Only You can deliver these people.” Because of the call of Advaita Ācārya, the Lord could not remain indifferent. He therefore descended as Lord Caitanya to relieve the sufferings of the people in Kali-Yuga. Thus the Lord will never be indifferent to the sufferings of those who are servants of His devotees.

**Question: Is it better for a devotee to direct his prayer for relief from material suffering through the devotee, rather than directly to Kṛṣṇa?**

Devotees should pray to the Lord for devotional service, because it is devotional service that relieves one from suffering, as well as from the root or seed of sufferings. The devotees are not interested in simply getting some temporary relief. We have to remove the seed of all suffering.

*kecit kevalayā bhaktyā*  
*vāsudeva-parāyaṇāḥ*  
*aghaṁ dhunvanti kārtsnyena*  
*nīhāram iva bhāskaraḥ*

**Only a rare person who has adopted complete, unalloyed devotional service to Kṛṣṇa can uproot the weeds of sinful actions with no possibility that they will revive. He can do this simply by discharging devotional service, just as the sun can immediately dissipate fog by its rays. (Bhāg. 6.1.15)**

Therefore, why should we pray to become relieved from suffering? If the cause of that suffering is still there in the heart, then it will only come back again. An intelligent person will pray for devotional service because that will uproot the weeds of all sinful actions without any possibility of reviving them.

The example is given that when you turn over the soil, it appears that nothing grows. However, everything is still underneath the soil. In due course of time, the weeds will grow up again. We may clear away our immediate suffering, but we have just turned everything underneath the soil. They will grow up again. However, Prabhupāda says that the fried seed cannot fructify. Therefore we have to burn the seed so it will never fructify. Devotional service does that. Devotional service can relieve both immediate reactions and all future reactions. It is therefore more intelligent to pray for devotional service than for freedom from sufferings.

## Returning to the Spiritual World

A devotee needs an opportunity to serve Kṛṣṇa. If he has that opportunity to serve, he is so satisfied by that service that he can be satisfied in any condition of life. That is the difference between a devotee and a nondevotee. A devotee is one who is satisfied with whatever the Lord provides for him. We see this in the example of Śuklāmbhara. He did not know the meaning of the word poverty, even though all he ate every day was a few grains of broken rice. Śuklāmbhara never felt impoverished; he was satisfied because the Lord was reciprocating within his heart.

The Lord is very much inclined to reciprocate with those devotees who fully depend upon Him. In this way, the devotee is satisfied, peaceful and happy. He is even happy to face death, which is the most difficult test to face.

We have to be dependent upon the mercy of the Lord. Such was the characteristic of the Pāṇḍavas, and therefore whatever situation they were put in, they accepted it as the arrangement of the Lord. That is a devotee: one who always wants to see the Lord in everything. If the Lord does it, then how can we ever reject it? Therefore the devotee prays, “I am happy with whatever You do! I do not want to be dependent upon anyone else! I am only dependent on You! Deal with me as You like.”

This is also shown through the example of Śrīla Bhakti Tīrtha Mahārāja, whose association we have lost. There was a very, very wonderful example that he showed just before his departure, which illustrates the point that I am making.

Bhakti Tīrtha Mahārāja prayed to Kṛṣṇa, “Please make me Your instrument. Do with me whatever You see fit and use me as You wish so that I may be an example to help other devotees become surrendered unto You.”

He was a bit surprised when he found out that he had cancer. He tried to understand, “Why has Kṛṣṇa put me in this situation? I prayed to the Lord to use me as He saw fit to teach other devotees.” After some continued contemplation, he began to realize that Kṛṣṇa wanted him to teach the devotees how to give up one’s body, and how to face death in a fearless way. In his heart, he was trying to fully accept the suffering that Kṛṣṇa put him in as a test for himself, and as an example for others to see how to overcome difficulties—especially at the time of death.

Towards his final days, he told me that his realization was that as long as he is still in the material world, it means Prabhupāda wants to use him in some way. He therefore wanted to use whatever breaths he had left in his life for serving Śrīla Prabhupāda’s mission. He was very inspired and he inspired so many other devotees. Many devotees would go to see him, and he would sit and preach, despite his condition. He would change their hearts. Many of the devotees who came to see him were devotees who had been alienated from the movement. Some of them had been gurukula children who had been abused in the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, but everyone who came to see him left crying—their hearts completely changed by having come in contact with him and having felt his compassion. He was feeling physical pain, but he accepted it and tried to overcome it in the ways that Lord Kapiladeva describes in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

*mad-āśrayāḥ kathā mṛṣṭāḥ*  
*śṛṇvanti kathayanti ca*  
*tapanti vividhās tāpā*  
*naitān mad-gata-cetasaḥ*

**“Engaged constantly in chanting and hearing about Me, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the sādhus do not suffer from material miseries because they are always filled with thoughts of My pastimes and activities.” (Bhāg. 3.25.23)**

Thus Bhakti Tīrtha Swami was trying to use his last days to preach as much as he possibly could to help others become more Kṛṣṇa conscious. His condition worsened to the point where he could no longer lecture or meet with devotees. He was preparing to give up his body. A few days before his departure, Bhakti Tīrtha Swami was experiencing a tremendous pain. The doctors were giving him measured doses of pain medication, because he wanted to keep his consciousness clear and he did not want his consciousness dulled by pain medication.

Just a few days before he departed, Śrīla Rādhānatha Mahārāja was alone with him in the room. Śrīla Bhakti Tīrtha Mahārāja was obviously in great pain, and Rādhānatha Mahārāja could see that. He took Rādhānatha Mahārāja’s hand. Understanding that Bhakti Tīrtha Mahārāja was in lot of pain, Rādhānatha Mahārāja began speaking about Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana, the cowherd boys and the gopīs, and describing Vṛndāvana in a very beautiful way. Rādhānatha Mahārāja then began chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. Bhakti Tīrtha Mahārāja did not have the strength to chant along with him very much, but he looked right into Rādhānatha Mahārāja’s eyes, and tears began flowing. He took Rādhānatha Mahārāja’s hand and kissed the back of it. Then he said to Rādhānatha Mahārāja, “Mahārāja, it just couldn’t get any better than this. And it is getting better every day.”

He was showing that in the face of suffering, adversity and pain, the safest thing is to somehow fix our consciousness on Kṛṣṇa and prepare for giving up this material body. Kṛṣṇa helps the devotee who always depends on Him. He helps the devotee who does not look for material formulas to mitigate his suffering, but looks to Kṛṣṇa only and says, “Kṛṣṇa, if You want to put me in a suffering condition, then let me suffer. However You deal with me—whether You put me in distress or in happiness—is my source of happiness as long as it is You, Kṛṣṇa, who is dealing with me. Please don’t let me become Māyā’s subordinate!”

Imagine how somebody could say something like that! Usually a person who is in a very difficult situation like that would say, “It just couldn’t get any worse than this. And it is getting worse every day!” But he was saying the opposite. It completely contradicts all material laws and all material conceptions. How can somebody lying in that physical state describe it as the best he has ever experienced and appreciate how it is getting better? It can only be there when there is some reciprocation taking place.

**Question: If we are ever able to go back to Kṛṣṇa’s abode, Vṛndāvana, what is the chance that we may mess up again and come back? Will we retain a little memory that this is a place to which we do not want to return?**

Prabhupāda gave the example that when a child puts his hand on the burner of the stove, he will not do it again. He will remember. Free will is still there, but he will not misuse it.

The potential is always there because we always have independence. However, Kṛṣṇa also says:

*janma karma ca me divyam*  
*evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ*  
*tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma*  
*naiti mām eti so ’rjuna*

**“One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.”**

**(Bg. 4.9)**

*avyakto ’kṣara ity uktas*  
*tam āhuḥ paramāṁ gatim*  
*yaṁ prāpya na nivartante*  
*tad dhāma paramaṁ mama*

**“That which the Vedāntists describe as unmanifest and infallible, that which is known as the supreme destination, that place from which, having attained it, one never returns—that is My supreme abode.” (Bg. 8.21)**

## Chapter 5 – Devotional Service

## The Nature of Devotional Service

Prabhupāda very nicely describes in his purport to Sāvaraṇa-śrī-gaura-mahimā, the nature of devotional service:

This is a song by Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura in praise of the glories of Lord Caitanya. Gaurāṅga refers to Lord Caitanya, who has a fair complexion. One who has a fair complexion is called gaura, and since Lord Caitanya was very fair, just like molten gold, He was also named Gaurasundara. Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura says, gaurāṅgera duṭi pada, jār dhana-sampada, se jāne bhakati-rasa-sār. Anyone who has accepted the two lotus feet of Lord Caitanya can understand the true essence of devotional service. Devotional service is very difficult. It cannot be understood by any ordinary man. As it is stated in the Bhagavad-gītā, out of many thousands of persons who are trying to achieve the perfection of human life, only some actually become perfect and realize the self. And out of many thousands of such self-realized persons, only one can understand Kṛṣṇa. Without understanding Kṛṣṇa, how can one engage himself in the service of Kṛṣṇa? Therefore, the devotional service of Kṛṣṇa is not an ordinary thing. But fortunately, if one follows in the footsteps of Lord Caitanya (gaurāṅgera duṭi pada) by following the path shown by Lord Caitanya—the process of simply chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa—he can very easily understand what devotional service is. Therefore, Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura prays that one take shelter of Lord Caitanya and follow in His footsteps, for then one can understand the essence of devotional service. (…)

Sāvaraṇa-śrī-gaura-mahimā means the glories of Śrī Gaurāṅga. It is a song by Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura, in which he emphasizes that we can understand devotional service if we accept the shelter of the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya. Otherwise, as Śrīla Prabhupāda explains in his commentary, devotional service is not such an easy thing to understand. Bhakti is eternal and has nothing to do with the affairs of this material world. Just as Kṛṣṇa is eternal, devotional service to Kṛṣṇa is also eternal. It has no beginning and no end. For an ordinary, materialistic person who is conditioned by the modes of the material nature, it is very difficult for him to understand what devotion is.

Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja Gosvāmī explains in Caitanya-caritāmṛta that Lord Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu is an ocean of transcendental mercy. Although the subject matter of bhakti is very difficult to understand, Lord Caitanya has made this understanding very easily accessible for the fallen souls in this Age of Kali.

When devotees go out to distribute Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books, people often ask the question, “Why are you doing this? Are you getting paid for this?” When told that we are not paid, they ask, “Then why are you standing here all day doing this?” They especially ask this when they see us standing in the freezing cold or in the pouring rain. It is expected that if somebody is making such a sacrifice, there must be some fruit. Thus, the first thing they ask is how much we are getting paid. Ordinary, materialistic people can never understand that we are doing this without getting paid.

Similarly, a person cannot taste honey by licking the exterior surface of the bottle. To understand the sweet taste of the honey, one has to open the bottle and taste its contents.

Thus if one wants to understand the nature of devotional service, he has to come in contact with the devotee of the Lord. We are most fortunate, because Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu appears in this Age of Kali as the hidden avatāra in the form of a devotee of the Lord to teach devotional service by practicing it Himself.

Previously when Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared, He instructed that we must surrender unto Him. Sarva-dharmān parityajya, mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ—“Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me.” (Bg. 18.66) He also instructed: man-manā bhava mad-bhakto, mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru—“Always think of Me, become My devotee, worship Me and offer your homage unto Me.” (Bg. 18.65) However, when Lord Kṛṣṇa gave these instructions, He only taught it in a theoretical way, and therefore had to appear once again as Caitanya Mahāprabhu—the topmost devotee of the Lord who is always absorbed in thoughts of Kṛṣṇa—to teach it by His own example. He even removed the aforementioned condition, requesting only that we simply take what He is offering.

## Eligibility for Devotional Service

Śrīla Prabhupāda came to spread the saṅkīrtana mission of Lord Caitanya. Saṅkīrtana is a collective effort. Thus Śrīla Prabhupāda created a society where the devotees work together. Within his books, he gives many very clear instructions about the necessity of working in cooperation within society. Prabhupāda’s formula for cooperation is the highest principle that he wanted us to work towards in spreading the saṅkīrtana mission.

There are many examples where Prabhupāda saw a devotee thinking that his service was above everyone else’s, and he would smash such a mentality. Although it appeared that everything was flourishing for that devotee, Prabhupāda would pull him out of that service. Prabhupāda was teaching that no one should think that his service is more important than anybody else’s; otherwise he becomes useless. Prabhupāda has established the formula for how to work in a cooperative way for expanding the message of Caitanya Mahāprabhu. His genius is beyond comparison, as his formula for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness in Kali-yuga has not been matched. He is the yuga-ācārya, he established our ISKCON society, and he wanted the devotees to cooperate within the society. To become free from pride will allow us to be useful in this society, and in the mission of the spiritual master.

Every fiber of Lord Nityānanda’s existence was in deep absorption of being a servant of Lord Caitanya. In fact, every member of Pañca-tattva had this mentality. Although we cannot imitate, we should learn to be so surrendered in a cooperative spirit for Śrīla Prabhupāda’s mission.

Lord Nityānanda explained to Jīva Gosvāmī that if one gets the mercy of a servant of Lord Caitanya, he can be accepted and become free from pride. Unless one becomes free from pride, he can never be a servant. Lord Caitanya says:

*tṛṇād api sunīcena*  
*taror api sahiṣṇunā*  
*amāninā mānadena*  
*kīrtanīyaḥ sadā hariḥ*

**“One can chant the holy name of the Lord in a humble state of mind, thinking himself lower than the straw in the street. One should be more tolerant than the tree, devoid of all sense of false prestige and ready to offer all respects to others. In such a state of mind one can chant the holy name of the Lord constantly.” (Śrī Śikṣāṣṭaka, Verse 3)**

This is the platform on which one has to come to be a servant of Lord Caitanya. Proud persons will not be accepted by Lord Caitanya as He cannot tolerate pride. Lord Nityānanda therefore prepares the devotee and makes him qualified to serve Lord Caitanya. Lord Nityānanda’s mercy is so expansive. Prabhupāda said, “Lord Caitanya went to the classes (high class people) and Lord Nityānanda went to the masses.”

Lord Caitanya, Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmīs, and Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya all went to the high class people, while Lord Nityānanda went and delivered everyone all over Bengal—even the most degraded offenders, preparing them to get Lord Caitanya’s mercy. This is what He did with Jagāi and Mādhāi. They were proud drunkards and womanizers. There was no sinful activity they had not committed. Lord Caitanya was going to kill them when they injured Lord Nityānanda. However, Lord Nityānanda said, “Please don’t kill them! Please deliver them. You are patita-pāvana! Certainly if You deliver these two, Your glories will expand throughout the entire creation for being the uplifter of the most fallen.” Lord Nityānanda thus took away the pride of Jagāi and Mādhāi and prepared them to get Lord Caitanya’s mercy.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says, “(ese) bṛndābane rādhā-śyāmer pa’be daraśan—if one wants to get the beautiful darśana of Rādhā-Śyāma in Vṛndāvana, first he has to get the mercy of Lord Caitanya—otherwise he can never enter.” To get the mercy of Lord Caitanya, we must get the mercy of Lord Nityānanda. Of course, when we speak about Lord Nityānanda, we are also speaking about Him as the original spiritual master. Therefore, we have to accept the representative of the original spiritual master who is supposed to help us to become free from our pride by helping with the cleaning work.

By the mercy of the servant of Lord Caitanya, one can become qualified to be a servant of Lord Caitanya, helping the living entity to become free from pride. After Lord Nityānanda explained this to Jīva Gosvāmī and gave him His mercy, He told him, “Lord Caitanya is now giving you the right to enter into Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma.” Lord Nityānanda then placed His lotus feet upon Jīva Gosvāmī’s head and infused him with spiritual strength. Jīva Gosvāmī became overwhelmed with ecstasy.

When all the Vaiṣṇavas heard that Jīva Gosvāmī was leaving Navadvīpa to go to Vṛndāvana, they all assembled, and Jīva Gosvāmī went to the lotus feet of each and every Vaiṣṇava and said, “You are my gurus! You are servants of Lord Caitanya! Please give me the dust from your lotus feet! Make me qualified to enter into Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma.”

Before leaving for Vṛndāvana, Jīva Gosvāmī wanted to go to the home of Śacīmātā to see her and get her blessings. Śacīmātā gave him the dust of her lotus feet and said, “Now go to Vṛndāvana and fulfill the order.” Jīva Gosvāmī left Navadvīpa and as he came to its outskirts, within his heart Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma manifested. He saw the Yamunā River, Giri Govardhana, and his uncles, Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmīs, who were there writing transcendental literature. Jīva Gosvāmī continued on his journey.

One night when Jīva Gosvāmī was resting, Lord Caitanya appeared to him in his dream and said, “You should worship Me in My form as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana. Always meditate on this form and serve this form of Mine very intimately. You and your uncles should write transcendental literatures.” Everything became revealed in Jīva Gosvāmī’s heart.

If we want to become qualified to become real servants, we should recognize that Lord Caitanya came to distribute the highest service.

*yuga-dharma pravartāimu nāma-saṅkīrtana*  
*cāri bhāva-bhakti diyā nācāmu bhuvana*

**\[Lord Caitanya says\]: “I shall personally inaugurate the religion of the age—nāma-saṅkīrtana, the congregational chanting of the holy name. I shall make the world dance in ecstasy, realizing the four mellows of loving devotional service.” (Cc. Ādi, 3.19)**

We cannot go anywhere if we do not become free from pride. That is the best way to become an instrument in the saṅkīrtana mission. Take the holy name of the Lord and pray very intently. The holy name is the cleansing agent. Thus, first we should become very serious about chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa and cooperate with the devotees, thinking ourself an insignificant servant. The most important service is to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa. For this particular service of chanting, we are allowed to think, “This is my service.” If anybody tries to get in the way of our service of chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, we can say, “No, I have to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa.” Everybody cooperates on that principle, as we all have to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa. This can be accepted as most important. For everything else, we must simply cooperate. If we go on chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa with deep faith, we will become very useful to Lord Caitanya’s and Śrīla Prabhupāda’s mission. Everything will be revealed in our heart, even without asking for it.

**Question: How do we overcome obstacles to facilitate cooperation?**

We have to watch our pride. In a purport in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Śrīla Prabhupāda states:

Everyone should be friendly for the service of the Lord. Everyone should praise another’s service to the Lord and not be proud of his own service. This is the way of Vaiṣṇava thinking, Vaikuṇṭha thinking. There may be rivalries and apparent competition between servants in performing service, but in the Vaikuṇṭha planets the service of another servant is appreciated, not condemned. This is Vaikuṇṭha competition. There is no question of enmity between servants. Everyone should be allowed to render service to the Lord to the best of his ability, and everyone should appreciate the service of others. Such are the activities of Vaikuṇṭha. Since everyone is a servant, everyone is on the same platform and is allowed to serve the Lord according to his ability. (Purport to Bhāg. 7.5.12)

**Question: How can we learn that we are not the possessor of the fruits of our activities?**

By offering them. Lust, anger, greed, illusion, and madness (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, and mada), as described by Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura, can be dovetailed for the service of the Lord. He says, “I will engage lust by offering the fruits of my activities for the pleasure of the Lord. I work hard for the fruits and I want to see the results, but when I get the result, I offer it to Kṛṣṇa. I will direct anger towards those who are envious of the Lord and His devotees. I will engage greed by becoming greedy to hear the topics of Kṛṣṇa consciousness in the association of devotees. I will feel illusioned or bewildered without achieving my worshipable Lord. I will be maddened while singing the glories of Kṛṣṇa.” Mātsarya (envy) however cannot be engaged in the service of the Lord. You just have to give it up.

## Cultivating Kṛṣṇa Consciousness

Śrīla Prabhupāda gave an arrival address in 1969 in London, where there were many reporters present asking questions. One reporter asked Śrīla Prabhupāda, “What have you come here to teach?”

Prabhupāda said, “I’ve come here to teach you what you have forgotten.”

The reporter said, “What is that?”

Prabhupāda responded, “Many people think that there is no God, God is dead, or God is impersonal. There are many different false conceptions about who is the Supreme Lord. However, I have come here to teach you what you have forgotten—that the Supreme Lord is a person, and one can see that person face-to-face in this life.”

Prabhupāda was very direct in his presentation of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Many of us, who experienced Śrīla Prabhupāda’s strong preaching in the early days of the movement, experienced that Prabhupāda gave a lot of his energy in removing our faith from the material world and simultaneously giving us faith in Kṛṣṇa. Such is the duty of the spiritual master—to introduce the highest goal of life, which is pure love of God, to his dependents.

When Prabhupāda came to the West, he could see that many people still had faith in materialistic science, materialistic medicines and materialistic teachings. He therefore invested a lot of energy in cutting away our faith in the material world. That cutting process can sometimes be painful, having placed so much of our faith in material arrangements, such as in accumulation of wealth, thinking that it can protect us; or in protection of family members, society and friends. We therefore make it difficult for ourselves to immediately accept the conclusive statement of Kṛṣṇa in the Bhagavad-gītā: “Abandon your faith in all the other processes of religion and all other methods of taking artificial shelter, and just surrender unto Me.” To be able to immediately make that step of full surrender is not easy. It is an ongoing process.

Sometimes we may artificially surrender everything and realize later that we really have not fully surrendered. Or sometimes one may have surrendered with a very sincere desire to give everything to the Supreme Lord, but may later realize that the surrendering process is not as easy as he thought it was when he first surrendered.

It is a very liberating feeling to give up material things and take shelter in the holy name, Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and devotional service. It brings about a certain sense of relief from distress. However, after time passes, one may begin to perceive that there are still so many things that he has not yet given up. Certain attachments begin to surface in the heart and thoughts, and one may even think that this process is not working. This is because they lose their faith, and they give up their practice in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. However, it is stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

“One who has forsaken his material occupations to engage in the devotional service of the Lord may sometimes fall down while in an immature stage, yet there is no danger of his being unsuccessful.
