**“Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from doubt and delusion, forgiveness, truthfulness, control of the senses, control of the mind, happiness and distress, birth, death, fear, fearlessness, nonviolence, equanimity, satisfaction, austerity, charity, fame and infamy—all these various qualities of living beings are created by Me alone.” (Bg. 10.4-5)**

PURPORT

The different qualities of living entities, be they good or bad, are all created by Kṛṣṇa, and they are described here.

Intelligence refers to the power to analyze things in their proper perspective, and knowledge refers to understanding what is spirit and what is matter. Ordinary knowledge obtained by a university education pertains only to matter, and it is not accepted here as knowledge. Knowledge means knowing the distinction between spirit and matter. In modern education there is no knowledge about spirit; they are simply taking care of the material elements and bodily needs. Therefore academic knowledge is not complete.

Asammoha, freedom from doubt and delusion, can be achieved when one is not hesitant and when he understands the transcendental philosophy. Slowly but surely he becomes free from bewilderment. Nothing should be accepted blindly; everything should be accepted with care and with caution. Kṣamā, tolerance and forgiveness, should be practiced; one should be tolerant and excuse the minor offenses of others. Satyam, truthfulness, means that facts should be presented as they are, for the benefit of others. Facts should not be misrepresented. According to social conventions, it is said that one can speak the truth only when it is palatable to others. But that is not truthfulness. The truth should be spoken in a straightforward way, so that others will understand actually what the facts are. If a man is a thief and if people are warned that he is a thief, that is truth. Although sometimes the truth is unpalatable, one should not refrain from speaking it. Truthfulness demands that the facts be presented as they are for the benefit of others. That is the definition of truth.

This chapter of the Bhagavad-gītā is called The Opulence of the Absolute. In this verse, Kṛṣṇa is describing some of the qualities of the living entities that He has created. Prabhupāda explains in the first sentence of the commentary that the different qualities of living entities—be they good or bad—are all created by Kṛṣṇa, although we know that Kṛṣṇa is all-good. Just as when one is facing the sunshine, everything is bright, but when he turns his back to the sun, he sees darkness, as he sees his shadow. The shadow does not exist between us and the sun. The shadow is only behind us. Thus to see darkness, we have to turn away from the sun. Similarly, Kṛṣṇa is all-good, but when we turn our face away from Him, we see darkness and the dualities of the material world. Therefore, dualities such as good and bad, heat and cold, and happiness and distress were created by Kṛṣṇa. Even illusion is created by Kṛṣṇa.

Kṛṣṇa explains to Lord Brahmā in the Second Canto of the Bhāgavatam that whatever we see of any value, if it has no connection to Him, we should know it to be His illusory energy or that reflection which appears in the darkness. If we see something very valuable, but cannot see its connection to Kṛṣṇa, then it is illusion, albeit created by Him.

*daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī*  
*mama māyā duratyayā*  
*mām eva ye prapadyante*  
*māyām etāṁ taranti te*

**“This divine energy of Mine, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is very difficult to overcome. But those who have surrendered unto Me can easily cross beyond it.” (Bg. 7.14)**

Kṛṣṇa says in many places in Bhagavad-gītā that for all that is material and all that is spiritual, He is both its origin and its dissolution. Both the material and spiritual energies are coming from the Lord. The material energy is simply a transformation of Kṛṣṇa’s spiritual energy. He can transform spiritual energy into material energy, and He can transform material energy back into spiritual energy.

Kṛṣṇa is inconceivable and it is very difficult to understand Him with the blunt material senses. Ataḥ śrī-kṛṣṇa-nāmādi, na bhaved grāhyam indriyaiḥ (Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu 1.2.234)—Kṛṣṇa cannot be understood by blunt material senses. He can only be understood with spiritual senses, which are being engaged in devotional service to Kṛṣṇa.

Eka-deśa-sthitasyāgner, jyotsnā vistāriṇī yathā (Viṣṇu-Purāṇa)—Kṛṣṇa is situated in the spiritual world and He spreads His energies throughout the entire creation, just as the sun distributes its rays throughout the entire universe. Kṛṣṇa is transcendental—beyond the perception of these blunt material senses. Kṛṣṇa therefore says, “It is very difficult for people to know Me and see Me, because they are covered by My illusory creative potency, yoga-māyā.”

Kṛṣṇa created this cosmic manifestation because there are living entities who want to forget Him. He gives the living entity that minute independence to choose, and He makes every effort to try to get the living entity to turn his attention towards Him. Therefore, as the Supersoul, He travels with us throughout our entire sojourn in the material universe from one body to the next. The Supersoul performs the function of being the witness and giving sanction to the living entity. Just as a person can understand the aroma of the flower by being close to it, the Supreme Lord understands the desires of the living entities by being right next to them in the heart, and He allows the living entity to do what he is persistent in wanting to do.

When Prabhupāda was a householder, he had a son who used to have an impulse to put his finger in the fan. Prabhupāda said, “No! Don’t do that!” But still the son was very persistent, and he would again put his finger very close to the fan and look at Prabhupāda.

A neighbor who was visiting Prabhupāda in the house was watching this little affair between Prabhupāda and his son. The neighbor asked, “Why don’t you just turn off the fan and let him put his finger in it when it slows down?”

Prabhupāda therefore unplugged the fan. The child walked up to the fan while it was unplugged and the blades were slowing down, and Prabhupāda said, “Go on.” His son put his finger in the fan, fell back, and never put his finger in the fan again.

In narrating this story, Prabhupāda said that this is just like the living entity in the material world. We are very persistent, but we cannot do anything without Kṛṣṇa’s sanction. Therefore Kṛṣṇa is sitting within the heart as Supersoul and is giving sanction to all our desires. When He sees that we keep going to the fan, trying to put our finger in it, finally Kṛṣṇa says, “Alright, go ahead and put your finger in it.” We do it, and then we cry, asking ourselves why we did it, as it has led to so much suffering.

Kṛṣṇa explains that when His devotee is engaged in His devotional service and at the same time wants the opulence of material enjoyment, he is like a fool who willingly gives up ambrosia to drink poison. He says, “Why should I give this fool material prosperity? Instead I shall induce him to take shelter of My lotus feet and make him forget.” When a devotee tries to satisfy his desires separate from the Lord, the Lord will fulfill his desires in such way that the devotee will not come back and ask for it again. That is the mercy of the Lord for His devotee.

Nārada Muni explains in the First Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam that one who gives up his material occupation to engage in the devotional service of the Lord may fall down in an immature stage, but there is no danger of his being unsuccessful. On the other hand, a non-devotee, even though perfectly engaged in his occupational activity, does not gain anything.

**“My dear Vyāsa, even though a devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa sometimes falls down somehow or other, he certainly does not undergo material existence like others \[fruitive workers, etc.\] because a person who has once relished the taste of the lotus feet of the Lord can do nothing but remember that ecstasy again and again.”(SB 1.5.19)**

This is Kṛṣṇa’s kindness. He never forgets any service rendered by His devotee.

*nehābhikrama-nāśo ’sti*  
*pratyavāyo na vidyate*  
*sv-alpam apy asya dharmasya*  
*trāyate mahato bhayāt*

**“In this endeavor there is no loss or diminution, and a little advancement on this path can protect one from the most dangerous type of fear.” (Bg. 2.40)**

The devotee’s future is always bright, even if he falls down and temporarily forgets the Lord. However, the non-devotee does not have such a bright future. His destiny is only to have to suffer repeated births and deaths in the material world.

The principle of this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is to give everyone the opportunity to get this little taste, because there is never any loss in obtaining it. Lord Caitanya is so kind that He has even taken away the conditions for getting that taste. He is so merciful that He is distributing freely ecstatic love of Godhead. Yet we see the living entities so foolish that they do not want to take it.

The spiritual master is just like a raincloud that pours its rain everywhere for the benefit of everyone. Still, the stones cannot take advantage of it, while the grass can. Or just as the sun spreads its rays everywhere, a blind man cannot take advantage of these rays of the sun in the same way as a man who can see. Thus the Lord is freely giving His mercy, making it accessible to everyone.

Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja Gosvāmī says, “I offer my respectful obeisances to Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, who is an ocean of transcendental mercy. Although the subject matter of bhakti is very confidential and very difficult to understand, He has nonetheless made it easily accessible in Kali-yuga.” Ordinarily, bhakti-yoga is extremely difficult to understand, but Lord Caitanya is so kind that He has made it so easily accessible.

Once I was invited to the yoga āśrama of yogī Amrit Desai, but we were told by the yogī, “No lecture. You can only have kīrtana.” He actually had a very favorable attitude toward Prabhupāda. There were about eight devotees that went, and the yogī had about three hundred followers in his āśrama. The devotees were so enthusiastic in their kīrtana that all the followers of Amrit Desai were spinning around, dancing and chanting very ecstatically. Amrit Desai then came in and sat down on his āsana and tried to look very aloof. He did not want to give the wrong impression to his followers. He wanted to make sure that they still saw him in the light as their guru. One of the devotees went over to Amrit Desai, grabbed his hand and pulled him into the kīrtana. The kīrtana continued for about a half an hour and Amrit Desai was waving his hands, chanting and dancing. After the kīrtana, his mood having changed, he said to me, “Okay, go ahead and speak.”

Prabhupāda once had a conversation with Amrit Desai, and one of the arguments that Amrit Desai presented to Prabhupāda was, “How are you going to make these people take up these principles?” Amrit Desai also knew about these principles of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, but he could not get his followers to follow them, and thus he was very skeptical of how it was possible for us westerners to follow these principles. Prabhupāda explained to him the potency of Lord Caitanya and how He is so merciful and kind that He has come to freely give that taste even without us having any qualification to obtain it.

Prabhupāda often quoted the verse from Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī: yena tena prakāreṇa manaḥ kṛṣṇe niveśayet—it is the duty of the spiritual master to get a disciple to somehow or other remember the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. All the rules and regulations will come later. This is the same principle that Lord Caitanya applied in His coming to this material world. He is so merciful and kind that He is giving that taste even though we did nothing in the past to qualify for it. Even one moment of that taste can never be forgotten.

Furthermore, a moment’s association with a devotee of the Lord cannot be compared to anything else, such as liberation from matter or worldly prosperity. Śukadeva Gosvāmī describes in the Second Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, “What is the value of prolonged life, which is wasted, inexperienced by many years in this world? Better one moment of full consciousness, because in that one moment one will continue to search after his ultimate interest.”

Trees live hundreds of years. However, a long life is not valuable if it is wasted. Much more valuable is one moment in full consciousness of Kṛṣṇa, as he will always continue to search after that ultimate interest, even if he forgets temporarily.

This is exemplified in the story of Priyavrata Mahārāja in the Fifth Canto of the Bhāgavatam. Priyavrata Mahārāja did not want to become a householder, but he was instructed by Lord Brahmā to become a king. However, he wanted renunciation, and did not want to become a king and get entangled in all these affairs. Lord Brahmā said, “It is required for universal affairs. You must take up this responsibility.”

Priyavrata Mahārāja did take up this responsibility, but then he began to enjoy his position. However, later in his life he remembered the instructions he had heard from Nārada Muni. He could not forget them, because they had entered into the core of his heart, and thus he again renounced everything just like a person gives up stool.

There is also the example of the sons of Dakṣa—the Savalāśvas and Haryaśvas. Prajāpati Dakṣa wanted his sons to become very good householders and sent them to perform austerities to prepare themselves for householder life. Nārada Muni saw them performing austerities and said, “Look at these ripe candidates for devotional service! Why should they get entangled?” Thus by the association of Nārada Muni and his preaching to them, they all took to the path of nivṛtti-mārga and did not become entangled in household life.

Such is the value of a moment’s association with a devotee. Such is the value of just even a slight taste of the holy name of the Lord. A slight taste is called ābhāsa-rūpā—a momentary glimpse of what the holy name of the Lord is like.

Once I was out on a Prabhupāda book distribution marathon, and it was very difficult. The weather was very bad and we had a car accident where our vehicle spun off the road and we were hanging over a cliff. The devotee behind me did not know what to hold on to, so he held on to my head and put his hands over my eyes while I was driving. He was chanting, “Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!”

I said, “What are you doing? I can’t see anything!” We were towing another vehicle which was already broken down and now our vehicle had spun off the road and we were hanging over the cliff. We all had to jump into the front seat of the car so the vehicle wouldn’t go over the cliff, and then wait for somebody to come and find us. There was one problem after the next, yet we remained very determined to distribute Prabhupāda’s books. It ended up being the biggest marathon we had ever had.

After returning to the temple for the first time and seeing the deities again, and after chanting and dancing before them, we had so much taste. I understood that Prabhupāda must have been so pleased by the austerities we had undergone. These tastes are not ordinary tastes.

Bhajanīya-parama-puruṣa-sukha-mātra-sva-sukhatvam—the living entity experiences his pleasure to the degree that Kṛṣṇa experiences pleasure in the activities of the living entity.

*bhaktiḥ pareśānubhavo viraktir*  
*anyatra caiṣa trika eka-kālaḥ*  
*prapadyamānasya yathāśnataḥ syus*  
*tuṣṭiḥ puṣṭiḥ kṣud-apāyo ’nu-ghāsam*

**Devotion, direct experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment from other things—these three occur simultaneously for one who has taken shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in the same way that pleasure, nourishment and relief from hunger come simultaneously and increasingly, with each bite, for a person engaged in eating. (Bhāg. 11.2.42)**

If you feel devotion, you know you are engaged in devotional service. If you feel your devotion is increasing, you know you are engaged in devotional service. If you are experiencing Kṛṣṇa’s presence in your life, you know you are engaged in devotional service. If you see you are losing your attraction for material things, you know you are engaged in devotional service. These three things come simultaneously. Just as a person who is eating experiences pleasure, nourishment and relief from hunger, we should live for this taste of devotional service, always being greedy for it. Pure devotional service can only be had by the intense greed to obtain it. Wherever one sees it, he must immediately purchase it without delay. However, Lord Caitanya is so kind that He gives us the taste first, even if we do not have any qualification for it. At that point, devotional service begins. That taste comes either by chanting, by associating with a devotee, or by honoring kṛṣṇa-prasādam. Once one has that taste, he wants more.

One has to be very careful, because if he commits offenses, he may lose his taste and may think that the taste for something else is more immediate and practical. However, Lord Caitanya says that is like a fool who gives up ambrosia to drink poison. The Lord thus induces us to take shelter of His lotus feet and makes us forget about the other things for which we have developed a taste. That is the unlimited mercy of devotional service and Gaura-Nitāi. We must simply be willing to accept that mercy, even though we may feel ourselves very unqualified to obtain it.

## Uprooting Sinful Activities

*idaṁ tu te guhyatamaṁ*  
*pravakṣyāmy anasūyave*  
*jñānaṁ vijñāna-sahitaṁ*  
*yaj jñātvā mokṣyase ’śubhāt*

**The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: “My dear Arjuna, because you are never envious of Me, I shall impart to you this most confidential knowledge and realization, knowing which you shall be relieved of the miseries of material existence.” (Bg. 9.1)**

*rāja-vidyā rāja-guhyaṁ*  
*pavitram idam uttamam*  
*pratyakṣāvagamaṁ dharmyaṁ*  
*su-sukhaṁ kartum avyayam*

**“This knowledge is the king of education, the most secret of all secrets. It is the purest knowledge, and because it gives direct perception of the self by realization, it is the perfection of religion. It is everlasting, and it is joyfully performed.” (Bg. 9.2)**

PURPORT

This chapter of Bhagavad-gītā is called the king of education because it is the essence of all doctrines and philosophies explained before. Among the principal philosophers in India are Gautama, Kaṇāda, Kapila, Yājñavalkya, Śāṇḍilya and Vaiśvānara. And finally there is Vyāsadeva, the author of the Vedānta-sūtra. So there is no dearth of knowledge in the field of philosophy or transcendental knowledge. Now the Lord says that this Ninth Chapter is the king of all such knowledge, the essence of all knowledge that can be derived from the study of the Vedas and different kinds of philosophy. It is the most confidential because confidential or transcendental knowledge involves understanding the difference between the soul and the body. And the king of all confidential knowledge culminates in devotional service. Generally, people are not educated in this confidential knowledge; they are educated in external knowledge. As far as ordinary education is concerned, people are involved with so many departments: politics, sociology, physics, chemistry, mathematics, astronomy, engineering, etc. There are so many departments of knowledge all over the world and many huge universities, but there is, unfortunately, no university or educational institution where the science of the spirit soul is instructed. Yet the soul is the most important part of the body; without the presence of the soul, the body has no value. Still people are placing great stress on the bodily necessities of life, not caring for the vital soul. (…)

Kṛṣṇa describes this knowledge as guhyatamaṁ, the most confidential knowledge. He further describes it as the king of education, the most secret of all secrets and the purest knowledge. Prabhupāda explains in his commentary that the type of knowledge that Kṛṣṇa is speaking about in the Bhagavad-gītā is not mere academic knowledge. He gives the example that there are many departments of knowledge in the universities all over the world, and these universities are teaching politics, sociology, physics, chemistry, mathematics, etc. However, there is unfortunately no university or educational institution where the science of the spirit soul is instructed.

One time when Prabhupāda was in Boston, he was giving a lecture at MIT, and he asked the assembled professors and students who were gathered for his lecture, “Can you please tell me, where in this university are they teaching the difference between the dead man and the living man?” Nobody could give an answer. He went on to explain that real knowledge means to know what matter is, what spirit is and who the controller of both is. To simply study mathematics, science, engineering and science of matter is incomplete knowledge; it is knowledge of the temporary nature of this material world.

Prabhupāda further explained that the science of the soul cannot be studied academically in a university. When one is studying science and wants to get a particular result, which can be obtained only by performing a scientific experiment, then he has to go to the laboratory and perform that experiment. Similarly to obtain the result of spiritual knowledge, which is vijñāna (realized knowledge), one has to perform certain activities which are conducive for understanding the existence of the soul, otherwise it is just theoretical knowledge.

To realize or understand the self as distinct from the temporary physical body, or to realize the most confidential knowledge of the Bhagavad-gītā, one must perform certain activities that are conducive for understanding the existence of the soul. Life does not come from a combination of chemicals, but rather the origin of life is life itself, and the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the original living being.

*nityo nityānāṁ cetanaś cetanānām*  
*eko bahūnāṁ yo vidadhāti kāmān*

(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.13)

Kṛṣṇa is the original living being and He is maintaining and supporting all other living beings.

*viṣṇu-śaktiḥ parā proktā*  
*kṣetra-jñākhyā tathā parā*  
*avidyā-karma-saṁjñānyā*  
*tṛtīyā śaktir iṣyate*

**The internal potency of the Supreme Lord, Viṣṇu, is spiritual, as verified by the śāstras. There is another spiritual potency, known as kṣetra-jña, or the living entity. The third potency, which is known as nescience, makes the living entity godless and fills him with fruitive activity. (Cc. Madhya 6.154, as quoted from Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.61)**

*na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin*  
*nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ*  
*ajo nityaḥ śāśvato ’yaṁ purāṇo*  
*na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre*

**For the soul there is neither birth nor death at any time. He has not come into being, does not come into being, and will not come into being. He is unborn, eternal, ever-existing and primeval. He is not slain when the body is slain. (Bg. 2.20)**

Kṛṣṇa begins his instruction to Arjuna in the Bhagavad-gītā by telling him that he is mourning for that which is not worthy of grief. He says that those who are wise lament neither for the living nor for the dead. Prabhupāda discusses that in this commentary (Bg. 9.2, Purport):

The Bhagavad-gītā, especially from the Second Chapter on, stresses the importance of the soul. In the very beginning, the Lord says that this body is perishable and that the soul is not perishable (antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ). That is a confidential part of knowledge: simply knowing that the spirit soul is different from this body and that its nature is immutable, indestructible and eternal. But that gives no positive information about the soul. Sometimes people are under the impression that the soul is different from the body and that when the body is finished, or one is liberated from the body, the soul remains in a void and becomes impersonal.

Prabhupāda goes on to explain the identity of the soul. We understand that the soul is not this body. It is eternal, whereas the body is temporary. Kṛṣṇa explains that just as a person puts on new garments, giving up the old and useless ones, similarly the living entity accepts a new body, giving up the old and useless bodies. When the living entity’s body grows old, becomes diseased and can no longer provide a suitable residence for the eternal soul, the living entity departs from that body. According to the activities performed in that life, the living entity in the human body has to accept another body according to the mentality that he has at the time of giving up his body.

Kṛṣṇa also explains (Bg. 15.8): “The living entity in the material world carries his different conceptions of life from one body to another as the air carries aromas. Thus he takes one kind of body and again quits it to take another.” Whatever desires one cultivates in the human form of life, then that desire will carry him (the soul) along with the assistance of the Supersoul. The soul exists within the body and is the knower of the field of activities of that body. There is the Super-knower (Supersoul), who is the Supreme Lord and is manifested in the heart of every living being, and He is the knower of all fields.

A person may have a plot of land and is quite aware of everything that goes on there (e.g. the gardens that he grows, the house that he builds, and so forth). He is thus the knower of his own field of activities. The king in the kingdom, however, is aware of what is going on in all the different plots of lands, and therefore he has various ministers and persons who go from one plot to the next, exacting taxes upon the citizens and explaining to the king what is existing on each of the plots of land.

Similarly, the living entity is the knower of his own field of activities (kṣetra-jña), but the Lord is the Supersoul, the Super-knower. The Lord knows what is going on in all the different bodies because He is present in the heart of every living being.

Just as the sun is situated in one place in the sky, it may be reflected in so many pots of water on the land, and thus you will see the reflection of the sun in each pot. In the same way, though the Supreme Lord is situated in the spiritual world, He is all-pervasive:

*ekadeśa-sthitasyāgner jyotsnā vistāriṇī yathā*  
*parasya brahmaṇaḥ śaktis tathedam akhilaṁ jagat*

(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.22.53)

Just as the illumination of a fire, which is situated in one place, is spread all over, the energies of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Parabrahman, are spread all over this universe.

He also explains in the Bhagavad-gītā:

*mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ*  
*jagad avyakta-mūrtinā*  
*mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni*  
*na cāhaṁ teṣv avasthitaḥ*

**“By Me, in My unmanifested form, this entire universe is pervaded. All beings are in Me, but I am not in them.” (Bg. 9.4)**

*vadanti tat tattva-vidas*  
*tattvaṁ yaj jñānam advayam*  
*brahmeti paramātmeti*  
*bhagavān iti śabdyate*

**Learned transcendentalists who know the Absolute Truth call this nondual substance Brahman, Paramātmā or Bhagavān. (Bhāg. 1.2.11)**

The Lord pervades this entire creation in His impersonal aspect by His diverse energies. He also pervades this cosmic manifestation as the Paramātma (Supersoul) manifestation. The third and topmost realization of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is His aspect of Bhagavān—the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śyāmasundara, who is manifested eternally in His three-fold bending form as Kṛṣṇa. He plays a flute, enjoys in the eternal realm of Goloka Vṛndāvana as an eternally fresh youth cowherd boy, and enjoys with His eternal associates—His parents, friends and lovers—in His transcendental realm of Goloka Vṛndāvana.

Depending upon the method of worship by the worshiper, he achieves a particular destination. For those who worship the all-pervading impersonal Absolute, they achieve entrance into the Brahman effulgence at the time of giving up this body. Those who worship the Supreme Lord as the Supersoul can achieve the same destination, although they may enter into the transcendental realm of Vaikuṇṭha, the spiritual world. But those who worship Kṛṣṇa in His personal form as Bhagavān and Śyāmasundara enter into the transcendental realm of Goloka Vṛndāvana.

Kṛṣṇa states in the Bhagavad-gītā:

*ye yathā māṁ prapadyante*  
*tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham*  
*mama vartmānuvartante*  
*manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ*

**“As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly. Everyone follows My path in all respects, O son of Pṛthā.” (Bg. 4.11)**

Kṛṣṇa is explaining the destination of those souls who worship Him in the three aspects of Brahman, Paramātma and Bhagavān. But the outcome for those souls who do not worship the Supreme Lord is explained very elaborately by Śrīla Prabhupāda in this commentary:

“This knowledge is the purest form of all activities, as explained in Vedic literature. In the Padma Purāṇa, man’s sinful activities have been analyzed and are shown to be the results of sin after sin. Those who are engaged in fruitive activities are entangled in different stages and forms of sinful reactions. For instance, when the seed of a particular tree is sown, the tree does not appear immediately to grow; it takes some time. It is first a small, sprouting plant, then it assumes the form of a tree, then it flowers and bears fruit, and, when it is complete, the flowers and fruits are enjoyed by persons who have sown the seed of the tree. Similarly, a man performs a sinful act, and like a seed it takes time to fructify. There are different stages. The sinful action may have already stopped within the individual, but the results or the fruit of that sinful action are still to be enjoyed. There are sins which are still in the form of a seed, and there are others which are already fructified and are giving us fruit, which we are enjoying as distress and pain.”(Bg. 9.2, purport)

It is also explained in the Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu and in the Padma Purāṇa that suffering or distress has three different causes: pāpaṁ (sinful activities), bījam (the sinful desire within the heart), and avidyā (ignorance). The root cause of all suffering is ignorance. Due to ignorance, one tries to enjoy separate from understanding his eternal relationship with the Lord. Not understanding his eternal identity, and thinking himself to be the temporary physical body, he tries to enjoy by engaging in some form of sinful activity, pāpaṁ.

Pāpam has two results: prārabdha and aprārabdha. Prārabdha-karma are results that have already fructified. As Prabhupāda explains in the Nectar of Devotion, if a person is suffering (for example, he may have a diseased body; he may be experiencing some legal implication; he may have taken a very low birth; or he may be born in a very suffering condition), this falls under prārabdha-karma. These are the results of some sinful activities performed in a previous life which are prārabdha—already manifest.

Aprārabdha-karma is described by Śrīla Prabhupāda in his commentary. He gives the example that just like a seed is sown in the ground, at first there is a small plant, then it assumes the form of a tree, it flowers and bears fruit, and when it is complete, the flowers and fruits are enjoyed by the persons who had sown the seed of that tree. Thus aprārabdha-karma means those sinful reactions which are still lying dormant, waiting to fructify; they have not yet manifested, but they will.

*kecit kevalayā bhaktyā*  
*vāsudeva-parāyaṇāḥ*  
*aghaṁ dhunvanti kārtsnyena*  
*nīhāram iva bhāskaraḥ*

**Only a rare person who has adopted complete, unalloyed devotional service to Kṛṣṇa can uproot the weeds of sinful actions with no possibility that they will revive. He can do this simply by discharging devotional service, just as the sun can immediately dissipate fog by its rays. (Bhāg. 6.1.15)**

The Bhāgavatam gives the example that when the sun rises in the morning, fog may still be manifest for some time. But as the sun rises in the sky, it gradually burns up the fog and it is dissipated. Similarly, for a person who engages in devotional service to the Lord, he can uproot the weeds of sinful desires just as the sun dissipates the fog by its rays.

The source of our suffering is sinful activities, and the source of those sinful activities is bījam—the seed of sinful desires within the heart. The sinful desires manifest in the heart, as they are one form of aprārabdha-karma.

When one engages in some kind of sinful activity, then in his next life he has a proclivity to do the same sinful activity. An example is given that just like a person engages in some sinful activity in this life, in his next life he has a natural proclivity to engage in thievery. In this example, that inclination towards stealing is kūṭaṁ (proclivity). Bījam is the seed of the desire to commit the theft. First there is a proclivity for thievery and then the desire is there to commit some thefts. When a desire is there, then one commits the theft, and as a consequence, the apprehension or punishment is there. Next, there is suffering.

There are two forms of suffering: One is when some implication comes in the form of suffering, and the other is when the desire to commit the sinful activity manifests again. It is a vicious circle—one commits a sinful activity and creates a sinful desire within the heart to commit the sin again. Therefore it is described in the Sixth Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam that real atonement does not mean to simply neutralize the effects of sinful reactions. One may try to neutralize the effects of the sinful reactions by engaging in some form of pious activity, such as performing austerities, giving charity or accepting vows. However, although the performance of pious activities neutralizes the reaction, these activities will not uproot the desires from within the heart to perform sinful activities again.

The example is given of an elephant that may enter into the water of the river to take its bath. However, when it comes out of the river, it again rolls in the mud. What is the value of such bathing? In the same way, what is the value of such atonement when one tries to neutralize the reactions so that he does not suffer the results of the sinful activities, but the desire to perform the sinful activity is still there within the heart?

An example is given in the Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu: A person may suffer due to unrestricted sex life by getting some venereal diseases from engaging in sexual activity. He then has to undergo some atonement or suffering to become relieved from his disease. However, if the desire to engage in unrestricted sex is still within the heart, then what is the value of such atonement? He will commit the activity again and will have to suffer again.

Therefore, the Bhāgavatam states that real freedom from reactions of sinful activities means to uproot the weeds of sinful desires within the heart—kecit kevalayā bhaktyā. Just as the fog is gradually burned by the rays of the sun, in the same way, unalloyed devotional service to Kṛṣṇa can uproot the weeds of sinful actions.

When weeding a garden, by turning over the soil to cover the weeds, the soil may look very clear or free from weeds for some time. You may think that you have gotten rid of all the weeds, but in due course of time, those seeds that are under the soil will gradually grow again. However, a fried or burned seed cannot fructify. Thus, the seeds of sinful desires within the heart can be burned up in the fire of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. A person who has adopted unalloyed devotional service to Kṛṣṇa can uproot the weeds of sinful actions with no possibility that they will revive. Thus this is possible by engaging in devotional service because of the nature of devotional service. Devotional service is very pleasing and satisfying to the Lord.

*viṣayā vinivartante*  
*nirāhārasya dehinaḥ*  
*rasa-varjaṁ raso ’py asya*  
*paraṁ dṛṣṭvā nivartate*

**“The embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, though the taste for sense objects remains. But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.” (Bg. 2.59)**

Kṛṣṇa says that a person may restrict himself from sense enjoyment or from the propensity of engaging in sinful activities, but until that seed of sinful desire has been burned up within the heart, the propensity or the tendency to commit the sin again and again remains within the heart. Devotional service eradicates the propensity or inclination to commit sinful activity by giving the living entity a superior form of pleasure.

Prabhupāda gave the example that a young child may be very attracted to play with knives, although it is a very dangerous affair. If the child wants to play with the knife and the parent tries to take it away from the child, the child will grab the knife in an attempt to keep it, and it becomes even more dangerous. Therefore, if the parent offers the child a nice, colorful toy, then the child will become attracted to the toy and will drop the knife. Similarly, for a person who has the bījam—the inclination to engage in sinful activity—when he experiences a higher pleasure in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, he will give up his inclination to engage in those sinful activities, which are a cause for his suffering.

We may not be fully conversant in the science of sinful activities. However, in Caitanya-śikṣāmṛta, Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura gives a very elaborate description of sinful activities to help us understand the causes of suffering. However, simply trying to restrain from sinful activities is not sufficient in itself, as the proclivity or inclination towards engaging in the sinful activity still remains within the heart, which is the cause of suffering.

We may know what the sinful activities are, however, as Kṛṣṇa explains in the Bhagavad-gītā:

**“While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises. From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.” (Bg. 2.62-63)**

Thus, one falls in the material whirlpool and engages in sinful activities. It begins with contemplating the objects of the senses, which causes one to develop lust and to want to satisfy himself. However, when his lust is not fulfilled, he becomes angry because his lustful propensities are somehow thwarted or obstructed, either by somebody else’s desire to thwart our attempt to satisfy ourselves, or by material nature, or by karma or any other thing. This kind of anger is known as virodha-yukta-krodha—anger which arises from attachment. Anger then causes bewilderment.

Sometimes when we become very angry at somebody, we may say something that we later regret. The anger consumes our mind and senses, and we lose control and become bewildered. Later we regret it, questioning how we lost control. This is another form of sin. To understand sinful activities helps us to understand the power of devotional service, and if we can understand the power of devotional service, we can appreciate the necessity to engage in devotional service.

*tais tāny aghāni pūyante*  
*tapo-dāna-vratādibhiḥ*  
*nādharmajaṁ tad-dhṛdayaṁ*  
*tad apīśāṅghri-sevayā*

**Although one may neutralize the reactions of sinful life through austerity, charity, vows and other such methods, these pious activities cannot uproot the material desires in one’s heart. However, if one serves the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead, he is immediately freed from all such contaminations. (Bhāg. 6.2.17)**

This verse is mentioned in the story of Ajāmila in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. Ajāmila had taken his birth in a brāhmaṇa family and was engaged in many brahminical activities. One day, while walking along the path, Ajāmila saw a śūdra and śūdrāṇī embracing one another and engaging in a relationship. Simply by seeing this, Ajāmila’s mind became overwhelmed by lustful desires, and later he came back, searched out this prostitute and married her.

After marriage, Ajāmila begot in the womb of the prostitute ten sons. It is described that he fathered children until the age of eighty-eight. To support his family, including himself, his wife and his ten children, he engaged in all kinds of sinful activities like thievery, gambling, taking intoxications, plundering and murder.

It just so happened that Ajāmila named his youngest son Nārāyaṇa. Finally, it was time for Ajāmila to give up his body, and he saw four fearful Yamadūtas coming with their ropes to snatch him out of his body, and to give him punishment for his life of sinful activities. At this time, he was thinking of his son, Nārāyaṇa, and he called out his name. By simply calling out the name of Nārāyaṇa—the Supreme Personality of Godhead—in this helpless state of mind, Ajāmila counteracted the reactions of his sinful life, although these Yamadūtas had come to arrest him with the ropes of Yamarāja to take him to the hellish planets for punishment.

Śukadeva Gosvāmī describes this story just after the Fifth Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam where there is a description of the hellish planets. That section describes all the different destinations that the living entities have to go to, and the torments and punishments they have to experience for all various types of sinful activities. When Parīkṣit Mahārāja heard these descriptions, he became overwhelmed and was thinking, “How can living entities avoid having to be punished and suffer this way?” His spiritual master, Śukadeva Gosvāmī, thus described this story of Ajāmila.

At the time when Ajāmila was destined to give up his body, the Yamadūtas had come to arrest him and to pull him out of his body to take him to the hellish planets for punishment. However, the Viṣṇudūtas, who are the representatives of the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, also appeared and said, “Stop! This person has counteracted his sinful activities by calling out the name of Nārāyaṇa at the time of giving up his body.”

A conversation between the Yamadūtas and the Viṣṇudūtas then ensued. The whole time, Ajāmila was lying there, hearing this discussion. The Viṣṇudūtas were describing the principles of religion and the power of the holy name of the Lord. The Viṣṇudūtas thus released Ajāmila from the ropes of the Yamadūtas and left for their own abode, and allowed Ajāmila to stay in his body. Thus he neutralized the reactions of his previous sinful activities by chanting out the name Nārāyaṇa. Although that was the name of his son, he remembered the real Nārāyaṇa. By hearing the Viṣṇudūtas defeat the Yamadūtas, Ajāmila’s heart became completely purified from all the residual attachments and lust. Not only did he become purified from the sinful reactions, but he immediately went to one sacred place by the name of Hardwar, and engaged in devotional service until the end of his life.

Later, when it was the destined time for him to give up his body again, the Viṣṇudūtas appeared in a flower airplane. Ajāmila remembered them, having seen them once before, and therefore at this time of death, it was just like lightning and illumination taking place simultaneously. There was no cause for fear whatsoever.

Similarly, when Dhruva Mahārāja gave up his body and death personified appeared before him, it was also said to be just like lightning and illumination simultaneously taking place. Instead of having to meet death personified, Dhruva Mahārāja simply stepped on the head of death personified, using it as a step to enter into the flower airplane and went back to Vaikuṇṭha—the spiritual world and the transcendental realm.

In the same way, Ajāmila went back to the spiritual world, being free from all contamination by having engaged in devotional service to the Lord. Thus we see that when one engages in devotional service to the Supreme Lord, one can not only neutralize the reactions of his previous sinful activities, but he is also immediately freed from all such contamination. Such is the power of devotional service. Therefore, becoming aware of these sinful activities helps us to at least understand what they are, but it should also create within us a desire to not only neutralize them, but to uproot the seed of sinful desires from within the heart.

When we see somebody else suffering, we immediately think that we do not want to suffer in the same way. However, a person conversant with the science of the soul knows that the soul is eternal and understands the cause of suffering. He knows that the results of one’s activities performed in a previous life are manifested in this life as prārabdha-karma, and it is lying in the form of a seed as aprārabdha-karma, waiting to fructify again in the next life. The intelligent person will think of how to avoid suffering in the future even though he may not be suffering right now.

However, sometimes we think that happiness means to not be suffering. However, that is not real happiness as defined in the Bhāgavatam. Real happiness is called brahma-sukham, which is transcendental to material happiness and continues forever. The soul, by nature, is meant to experience a superior happiness, which is spiritual happiness. This brahma-sukham is happiness derived from engaging in devotional service. Happiness derived from devotional service is eternal, satisfies the self, and gives one the impetus to eradicate not only the reactions of sinful life, but also to be constantly engaged in the service of the Lord.

Kṛṣṇa therefore describes the king of all knowledge as the purest knowledge, giving direct perception of the self by realization, everlasting, and joyfully performed. Devotional service is not simply some dry renunciation and austerities, but rather a joyful process—kevala-ānanda-kāṇḍa, as Locana Dāsa Ṭhākura describes in his song:

*parama koruṇa, pahū dui jana*  
*nitāi gauracandra*  
*saba avatāra-sāra śiromaṇi*  
*kevala ānanda-kanda*

**The two Lords, Nitāi-Gauracandra, are very merciful. They are the essence of all incarnations. The specific significance of these incarnations is that They introduced a process of chanting and dancing that is simply joyful. (Dhāmāli)**

He worships the two Lords, Lord Caitanya and Lord Nityānanda, who have given us a very joyful process which is not simply some dry form of renunciation, or some restraint from sense gratification that simply creates frustration. Rather, it is a process that is very satisfying to the self, and is therefore the perfection of religion. It is everlasting and joyfully performed. It gives one a superior form of pleasure. These are the glories of devotional service to the Lord as described in this verse (9.2) of Bhagavad-gītā, within the chapter entitled The Most Confidential Knowledge.

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura describes in the Caitanya-śikṣāmṛta that there are eleven principal sins: violence, cruelty, anger, wandering mind, lying, disobedience to a superior, lust, selfishness, impurity, rude conduct and destructiveness. He gives a very elaborate description of each of these things. It is very dangerous to have an uncontrolled mind and to have aprārabdha-karma—the results of our previous sinful activities still lying as a seed, waiting to fructify in due course of time. The danger of having bījam, sinful desires, within the heart, is that they will fructify in the form of sinful activities and will produce more prārabdha and aprārabdha-karma.

Padaṁ padaṁ yad vipadāṁ na teṣām (Bhāg. 10.14.58)—In this material world, there is danger at every step.

Once when Rādhānatha Mahārāja and I were in Kiev, Ukraine, there were some devotees who were being recommended for initiation to make their vows to receive Vaiṣṇava initiation before their spiritual master and to receive the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra. Rādhānatha Mahārāja happened to be very sick on the day of initiation and could not initiate them.

Just as Rādhānatha Mahārāja was getting ready to leave for the airport, the regional secretary asked him, “Mahārāja, these thirteen devotees are waiting to be initiated. What do you think should be done?”

Mahārāja said, “Well, let them go to the temple room and I will initiate them right now and they can sit before the fire sacrifice a little bit later.” He therefore went to the temple room, and these thirteen devotees received their spiritual names and their beads.

Mahārāja then had to rush because it was unexpected that he was going to give the initiation, and he needed to be at the airport. Five of these devotees jumped into the car to try to get to the airport before him, and there was a terrible car accident on the way. Mahārāja saw the car accident, but he had no idea that it was the devotees that were in the car. One of the devotees, who had just been initiated one hour before, left her body instantly. The other four girls who were in the car were all hospitalized with severe injuries. Padaṁ padaṁ yad vipadāṁ na teṣām—there is danger at every step and nobody can anticipate when something is going to happen. Of course, for these particular devotees, it was an auspicious day, as they had received initiation on that day and were accepted as disciples of Rādhānatha Mahārāja. However, some residual reaction was there and they had to also suffer in the way that they did.

We hear examples like this and we know that that is the nature of the material world—at every step there is potential danger. We don’t know what is lying ahead. Śrīla Prabhupāda says in his commentary in the Bhagavad-gītā that fear comes from the uncertainty of the future.

*bhajahū re mana śrī-nanda-nandana*  
*abhaya-caraṇāravinda re*

**“O mind, just worship the lotus feet of the son of Nanda, which make one fearless. Having obtained this rare human birth, cross over this ocean of wordly existence through the association of saintly persons.”**

The nine processes of devotional service, as given by Prahlāda Mahārāja in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, are:

*śravaṇaṁ kīrtanaṁ viṣṇoḥ*  
*smaraṇaṁ pāda-sevanam*  
*arcanaṁ vandanaṁ dāsyaṁ*  
*sakhyam ātma-nivedanam*  
*iti puṁsārpitā viṣṇau*  
*bhaktiś cen nava-lakṣaṇā*  
*kriyeta bhagavaty addhā*  
*tan manye ’dhītam uttamam*

**Hearing and chanting about the transcendental holy name, form, qualities, paraphernalia and pastimes of Lord Viṣṇu; remembering them; serving the lotus feet of the; offering the Lord respectful worship; offering prayers to the Lord, becoming His servant; considering the Lord one’s best friend; and surrendering everything unto Him (in other words, serving Him with the body, mind and words)—these nine processes are accepted as pure devotional service. One who has dedicated his life to the service of Kṛṣṇa through these nine methods should be understood to be the most learned person, for he has acquired complete knowledge. (Bhāg. 7.5.23-24)**

These are all very powerful processes, which can uproot and eradicate all the reactions of past sinful life and can situate one on the platform of devotional service, whereby one, at the end of this life, can remember the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa and go back home back to Godhead.

This is the nature of devotional service and that is described as pavitram-uttamam, the purest of all knowledge. In the Sixth Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, in the story of Ajāmila there is the following verse:

*etāvān eva loke ’smin*  
*puṁsāṁ dharmaḥ paraḥ smṛtaḥ*  
*bhakti-yogo bhagavati*  
*tan-nāma-grahaṇādibhiḥ*

(Bhāg. 6.3.22)

**Devotional service, beginning with the chanting of the holy name of the Lord, is the ultimate religious principle for the living entity in human society.**

This verse describes devotional service, beginning with the chanting of the holy names of the Lord, which is the most powerful method, as described in the Śikṣāṣṭaka prayers:

*ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanaṁ bhava-mahā-dāvāgni-nirvāpaṇaṁ*  
*śreyaḥ-kairava-candrikā-vitaraṇaṁ vidyā-vadhū-jīvanam*  
*ānandāmbudhi-vardhanaṁ prati-padaṁ pūrṇāmṛtāsvādanaṁ*  
*sarvātma-snapanaṁ paraṁ vijayate śrī-kṛṣṇa-saṇkīrtanam*

**Glory to the śrī-kṛṣṇa-saṅkīrtana, which cleanses the heart of all the dust accumulated for years and extinguishes the fire of conditional life, of repeated birth and death. This saṅkīrtana movement is the prime benediction for humanity at large because it spreads the rays of the benediction moon. It is the life of all transcendental knowledge. It increases the ocean of transcendental bliss, and it enables us to fully taste the nectar for which we are always anxious. (Śrī Śrī Śikṣāṣṭaka, Verse 1)**

**Question: How do we know what sin is? What is the authority that says that lying, cheating, lust, etc. are sins?**

We accept the authority of the Vedic literatures such as the Bhagavad-gītā and the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. They have been described in the Eleventh Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, and also summarized by one Vaiṣṇava-ācārya (or spiritual master). He summarized the content that is given in the Bhāgavatam and gave the essence in the form of the list that has been mentioned herein.

## Importance of Hearing

In the early days when Śrīla Prabhupāda established the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, he was very much focused on introducing everyone to the concept of accepting the Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, he presented Kṛṣṇa consciousness in a way that was very easily accessible to everybody, because the innate propensity to love God and to serve God is situated within the heart of every living being.

*nitya-siddha kṛṣṇa-prema ‘sādhya’ kabhu naya*  
*śravaṇādi-śuddha-citte karaye udaya*

**Pure love for Kṛṣṇa is eternally established in the hearts of the living entities. It is not something to be gained from another source. When the heart is purified by hearing and chanting, this love naturally awakens. (Cc. Madhya 22.107)**

Śrīla Prabhupāda had firm conviction, confidence and faith that everyone has the potential to become a devotee of the Lord, because it is not something that is artificial. It is a natural desire that is innate within everyone’s heart—to want to love and serve somebody. Thus Śrīla Prabhupāda, understanding that everybody had the potential to serve and love Kṛṣṇa, made Kṛṣṇa consciousness so accessible to everyone throughout the world. Although he started with a very simple and humble beginning to spread the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement in the west, things expanded beyond his expectation.

I am someone who personally witnessed how Kṛṣṇa consciousness expanded on the strength of Śrīla Prabhupāda’s personality, his preaching, and his firm conviction and faith. He always spoke with intense conviction about Kṛṣṇa being the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Because he had that firm conviction, he also understood how Kṛṣṇa is situated within the heart of every living being.

I had attended the Ratha-yātrā festival in 1975, in Philadelphia, America. I remember that when Śrīla Prabhupāda arrived at the Ratha-yātrā festival, there were thousands of people present. Śrīla Prabhupāda arrived a little bit late and the procession had already started going down the street. Lord Jagannātha and many devotees were on the big cart. When Śrīla Prabhupāda arrived, the cart stopped. He came up to the cart, and, in the middle of the road, he got down and offered his full obeisances to the Lord. Everybody was seeing how amazing Prabhupāda was! He was in the middle of the dirty street, but still he did not hesitate to offer his obeisances to the Lord. He was then assisted onto the cart. He sat down and was looking at the thousands of people who were there.

Devotees would often say that when Śrīla Prabhupāda casts his glance past you, immediately it penetrates into your heart. On this particular occasion, it was the second time I had seen Śrīla Prabhupāda. His glance swept across and he looked at everybody, and I could see that he looked at me. I then started dancing like a madman.

I had the same experience the following day when Śrīla Prabhupāda was giving the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam class in Philadelphia. Many devotees had come from all over the eastern United States to attend the festival. They were trying to find different places where devotees could stay all over the city. As it turned out, the place that we were staying was some place on the other side of the river, very far away from the temple. Therefore, we were completely dependent on getting a ride to the temple to attend Śrīla Prabhupāda’s Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam class.

Unfortunately we got a ride a little bit later than we had hoped. When our group arrived at the temple, the temple room was completely full, and nobody else could fit into the temple room. We were standing in the hallway and the devotee who was standing by the door decided that he would close the door so that nobody else would come in. Standing out there, our hearts fell into our stomach. Śrīla Prabhupāda got very disturbed. He said, “Why did you close the door? Open the door! Let them come in!” Śrīla Prabhupāda therefore gave the green light even though the room was completely full. I therefore immediately walked in and sat very close to the vyasasana. I felt completely confident that Śrīla Prabhupāda gave me permission to do this. Normally I would not have been so aggressive, but in those days, sometimes you had to be.

Upon finding a spot and sitting down, Śrīla Prabhupāda just looked at me. It was a really penetrating look. When Śrīla Prabhupāda looks at you, it just goes right through the eyes, into the heart, then into the soul, and immediately you feel completely exposed. Certainly I wanted to use every possible moment for looking at Śrīla Prabhupāda, but at that particular moment, all I could do was look down at the floor. That was the kind of penetrating glance that Śrīla Prabhupāda had when he would look at you. He did not see the body, but the soul. In his presence, we felt very low and fallen, but it inspired within the heart the desire to want to serve and please Śrīla Prabhupāda.

It is stated that simply by seeing such an elevated devotee of the Lord, one awakens the desire to engage in devotional service to the Lord. Simply by his glance, one gets his blessings. He seems to be calling out, “What are you doing here in the material world? Don’t you know that you have an eternal relationship with Kṛṣṇa? Why are you wasting your time here?” That is what Śrīla Prabhupāda’s glance would do to the heart, because he had the capacity to see Kṛṣṇa in everything and in everyone. Therefore, by the force of his preaching, he would attract so many people to come and take part in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. He established the Sunday Feast programs so that anybody who came in contact with books or devotees could come to hear and learn more about Kṛṣṇa.

Anyone who comes in contact with Kṛṣṇa, even for a moment, will derive eternal benefit. The nature of devotional service is such that once having come in contact with it, the desire for it is awakened within the heart, and one wants more. We obtain more by hearing more about Kṛṣṇa. Hearing is one of the methods of engaging in devotional service, and it is the most important. Simply by giving one’s ears in submissive aural reception, one is actually engaging in devotional service to the Lord.

*satāṁ prasaṅgān mama vīrya-saṁvido*  
*bhavanti hṛt-karṇa-rasāyanāḥ kathāḥ*  
*taj-joṣaṇād āśv apavarga-vartmani*  
*śraddhā ratir bhaktir anukramiṣyati*

**In the association of pure devotees, discussion of the pastimes and activities of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is very pleasing and satisfying to the ear and the heart. By cultivating such knowledge one gradually becomes advanced on the path of liberation, and thereafter he is freed, and his attraction becomes fixed. Then real devotion and devotional service begin. (Bhāg. 3.25.25)**

In the association of devotees, one gets the opportunity to hear about Kṛṣṇa. The more one hears about Kṛṣṇa, the more the desire within the heart is awakened to render service to Him.

There is a lecture in which Śrīla Prabhupāda speaks about the nine processes of devotional service. He was speaking to a young group of guests in 1969 in Columbus, Ohio. He was speaking about himself, and how his spiritual master recognized him because he had a desire to hear.

He explained how Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta was on parikramā, and many of the senior devotees were sitting and listening to his lecture. Śrīla Prabhupāda had a strong desire to go and hear from him. Some of the devotees went on parikramā to the Śeṣaśāyī temple while Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta was speaking. However, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta took note of the desire that Śrīla Prabhupāda had to hear. Śrīla Prabhupāda was not interested in going anywhere else.

Therefore, the process of devotional service begins simply by hearing. If one hears nicely, then next there will be kīrtanam. For one who hears nicely, he can go out and become a preacher and give Kṛṣṇa consciousness to others.

Taj-joṣaṇād āśv apavarga-vartmani śraddhā ratir bhaktir anukramiṣyati—as one gradually advances along the path of devotional service, then gradually he loses his attraction to material things, and his attachment to Kṛṣṇa will become fixed. Then real devotional service will begin.

The temple Sunday program was established so that people could come back to hear more, to honor Kṛṣṇa prasādam and to take part in chanting the holy names of the Lord. Śrīla Prabhupāda always emphasized that our Kṛṣṇa consciousness philosophy is very simple—chanting, dancing, and taking Kṛṣṇa-prasādam. This is what Lord Caitanya’s pastimes entailed. When the devotees would come from Navadvīpa to Jagannātha Purī to see Lord Caitanya and to take part in the Ratha-yātrā festival, there was chanting, dancing, and so many arrangements for the devotees to get nice prasādam that had been offered to Lord Jagannātha. Such activities are very purifying to the heart.

For even the most stone-hearted person who comes in contact with such a sublime way of living, his heart can change. Of course, as one advances in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, it is understood that he should awaken an attraction for these simple activities. The goal is to always be hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa. The devotees and the associates of Lord Caitanya always took complete shelter in that process.

Maintaining this human body through engaging in devotional service of the Lord is the best use of this human form of life. If one hears nicely, then he will chant Kṛṣṇa’s names and he will tell others about Kṛṣṇa. Then smaraṇam will come automatically—one’s mind and thoughts will become absorbed in thoughts of Kṛṣṇa.

Once I was sitting in Śrīla Prabhupāda’s lecture in 1976 in Māyāpura, and He was giving a lecture about austerities. He was saying that austerity does not mean that we have to sit in a circle of fire in the middle of the summer. Austerity does not mean that we have to sit in the freezing cold river in the middle of the winter. Our austerity is that we strictly follow the instructions of the spiritual master. Then all other austerities will be there. This is the process for self-realization. We should be very careful to not make a mistake and think that this human body is meant for our enjoyment.

Śrīla Prabhupāda therefore presented this message in this way that would appeal to everyone. Anyone who would come in contact with Śrīla Prabhupāda would feel the urgency behind his message: “Please take up this process of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Do not waste your human form of life.” If he would see somebody turn away from Kṛṣṇa then Śrīla Prabhupāda would feel so much compassion that he would cry. If we take full advantage of his message and all the gifts that he has given us for advancing in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, then our perfection in life is assured.

## Developing Loving Devotional Service

*teṣāṁ durāpaṁ kiṁ tv anyan*  
*martyānāṁ bhagavat-padam*  
*bhuvi lolāyuṣo ye vai*  
*naiṣkarmyaṁ sādhayanty uta*

**In this material world, every human being has a short span of life, but those who are engaged in devotional service go back home, back to Godhead, for they are actually on the path of liberation. For such persons, there is nothing which is not available. (Bhāg. 4.23.27)**

PURPORT:

In Bhagavad-gītā (9.33) Lord Kṛṣṇa says: anityam asukhaṁ lokam imaṁ prāpya bhajasva mām. The Lord here declares that this material world is full of miseries (asukham) and at the same time is very flickering (anityam). Therefore one’s only duty is to engage himself in devotional service. This is the best end to which human life can be put. Those devotees who are constantly engaged in the service of the lotus feet of the Lord achieve not only all material benefits but also all spiritual benefits, for at the end of life they go back home, back to Godhead. Their destination is described in this verse as bhagavat-padam. The word padam means “abode,” and bhagavat means “the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” Thus the destination of the devotees is the abode of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

In this verse the word naiṣkarmyam, which means “transcendental knowledge,” is also significant. Unless one comes to the platform of transcendental knowledge and offers devotional service to the Lord, one is not perfect. Generally the processes of jñāna, yoga and karma are executed life after life before one gets a chance to render pure devotional service to the Lord. This chance is given by the grace of a pure devotee, and it is in this way only that one can actually attain liberation. In the context of this narration, the wives of the demigods repented because although they had the opportunity of a birth in a higher planetary system, a lifetime spanning millions of years and all material comforts, they were not as fortunate as Pṛthu Mahārāja and his wife, who were actually surpassing them. In other words, Pṛthu Mahārāja and his wife scorned promotion to the higher planetary systems and even to Brahmaloka because the position which they were attaining was incomparable. In Bhagavad-gītā (8.16) the Lord affirms, ābrahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar āvartino ’rjuna: “From the highest planet in the material world to the lowest, all are places of misery wherein repeated birth and death take place.” In other words, even if one goes to the highest planet, Brahmaloka, he has to return to the miseries of birth and death. In the Ninth Chapter of Bhagavad-gītā (9.21), Lord Kṛṣṇa also asserts:

*te taṁ bhuktvā svarga-lokaṁ viśālaṁ*  
*kṣīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśanti*

“When they have thus enjoyed heavenly sense pleasure, they return to this mortal planet again.” Thus after exhausting the results of pious activities, one has to come again to the lower planetary systems and begin a new chapter of pious activities. It is therefore said in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.5.12), naiṣkarmyam apy acyuta-bhāva-varjitam: “The path of liberation is not at all secure unless one attains the devotional service of the Lord.” Even if one is promoted to the impersonal brahmajyoti, he runs every chance of falling down into this material world. If it is possible to fall down from the brahmajyoti, which is beyond the higher planetary systems in this material world, then what can be said of the ordinary yogīs and karmīs who can only be elevated to the higher material planets? Thus the wives of the denizens of the higher planetary systems did not very much appreciate the results of karma, jñāna and yoga.

This verse is being spoken by the wives of the demigods. They are observing the progress and destination of Pṛthu Mahārāja and his wife Arci, as it appears that they have surpassed them and have gone to higher regions beyond them. They have surpassed the residence of the demigods by having engaged themselves in resolute devotional service to the Supreme Lord. Prabhupāda therefore explains that Pṛthu Mahārāja and his wife scorned promotion to the higher planetary systems, even to Brahmaloka, because the position that they were attaining was incomparable.

This verse is emphasizing the superiority of devotional service above activities performed in karma-kāṇḍa and jñāna-kāṇḍa. Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura says in his Prema-bhakti-candrikā: karma-kāṇḍa, jñāna-kāṇḍa, kevala viṣera bhāṇḍa—both fruitive activities and mental speculation about the Supreme Lord are compared to be like pots of poison. Anyone who drinks this thinking it to be nectar will have to struggle in this material world life after life after life. Thus a devotee understands that devotional service is superior, because by it, one can attain the results of all these things automatically.

*vedeṣu yajñeṣu tapaḥsu caiva*  
*dāneṣu yat puṇya-phalaṁ pradiṣṭam*  
*atyeti tat sarvam idaṁ viditvā*  
*yogī paraṁ sthānam upaiti cādyam*

**A person who accepts the path of devotional service is not bereft of the results derived from studying the Vedas, performing austere sacrifices, giving charity or pursuing philosophical and fruitive activities. Simply by performing devotional service, he attains all these, and at the end he reaches the supreme eternal abode. (Bg. 8.28)**

Sometimes people will perform great sacrifices to achieve a higher destination; undergo great austerities in order to get some material benediction; or may give some charity so that they get some pious results or some benefits in the future. However, Kṛṣṇa explains in this verse that anyone who is engaged in devotional service gets the results of all of this.

*bhaktis tvayi sthiratarā bhagavan yadi syād*  
*daivena naḥ phalati divya-kiśora-mūrtiḥ*  
*muktiḥ svayaṁ mukulitāñjali sevate ‘smān*  
*dharmārtha-kāma-gatayaḥ samaya-pratīkṣāḥ*

**“If I am engaged in devotional service unto You, my dear Lord, then very easily can I perceive Your presence everywhere. And as far as liberation is concerned, I think that liberation stands at my doorstep with folded hands, waiting to serve me—and all material conveniences of dharma \[religiosity\], artha \[economic development\] and kāma \[sense gratification\] stand with her.” (Kṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta 107)**

This is Bilvamaṅgala Ṭhākura’s prayer. Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī describes:

*īhā yasya harer dāsye karmaṇā manasā girā*  
*nikhilāsv apy avasthāsu jīvan-muktaḥ sa ucyate*

(Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu, 1.2.187)

**One who engages in the transcendental service of the Lord in body, mind and words is to be considered liberated in all conditions of material existence.**

As Prabhupāda explains, one may try to perform many other activities to achieve spiritual perfection, but he is compared to be like the silver smith using a little hammer in the shop, hitting away at his work and doing a little at a time with his little hammer. Whereas the blacksmith takes a big hammer and with one blow finishes the work. Thus the blacksmith is like devotional service—with one blow you take care of everything; you do not have to make so many separate endeavors to achieve the happiness derived from sense gratification. Persons who are intelligent and are philosophically inclined do not endeavor for that sense gratification that is available from the highest planet, Brahmaloka, down to the lowest planet, Pātālaloka. He knows that as far as happiness derived from sense gratification is concerned, it can be automatically derived in due course of time just as in due course of time one can obtain miseries without asking for them.

Persons who are intelligent and philosophically inclined do not endeavor for sense gratification or miseries, because they know that they will come automatically. Those who are philosophically inclined simply endeavor to engage in rendering service to the Lord, because they know that service itself is superior and it will provide all the benefits automatically that can be obtained by these other methods.

Prabhupāda often quoted the following verse from Śrīla Prabhodānanda Sarasvatī:

*kaivalyaṁ narakāyate tri-daśa-pūr ākāśa-puṣpāyate*  
*durdāntendriya-kāla-sarpa-paṭalī protkhāta-daṁṣṭrāyate*  
*viśvaṁ pūrṇa-sukhāyate vidhi-mahendrādiś ca kīṭāyate*  
*yat kāruṇya-kaṭākṣa-vaibhavavatāṁ taṁ gauram eva stumaḥ*

**For those who have attained the merciful sidelong glance of Lord Caitanya, impersonal liberation becomes as palatable as going to hell, the heavenly cities of the demigods become as enticing as flowers imagined to be floating in the sky, the poisonous fangs of the untameable black snakes of the senses are broken, the whole world becomes full of joy, and Brahma, Indra, and all the other great demigods become as insignificant as tiny insects. Let us glorify that golden-complexioned Lord Caitanya. (Caitanya-candrāmṛta 5)**

The pleasure that one achieves from merging into the impersonal oneness of the Supreme Lord is like hell for one who has achieved the pleasure of devotional service. For them the heavenly kingdoms are like phantasmagoria, and the venomous serpents of the senses become like serpents with broken fangs—they no longer have any poisonous effects. It is most important for the devotee to understand that the senses are like venomous serpents, always looking for some object to strike. However, for anyone who receives the merciful glance of Lord Caitanya, these venomous serpents become like serpents with broken fangs; there is no longer any poisonous effect. Similarly, when the senses strike their sense objects, they become poisoned.

By contemplating the objects of the senses, attachment arises, from such attachment lust develops, from lust, anger arises, and then comes delusion, bewilderment, and finally intelligence is lost and one falls down again into the material pool. This is something that any sādhaka will learn, because he understands the nature of contemplation on objects of the senses. For one who is engaged in devotional service, the serpent’s fangs are broken, and there is no longer any poisonous effect. Thus devotional service is superior.

It requires great faith and determination to fully realize this. However, due to weakness of heart, we still commit sinful activities, although we know that they will lead to suffering.

In the Eleventh Canto of Bhāgavatam, Kṛṣṇa explains to Uddhava:

**“Having awakened faith in the narrations of My glories, being disgusted with all material activities, knowing that all sense gratification leads to misery, but still being unable to renounce all sense enjoyment, My devotee should remain happy and worship Me with great faith and conviction. Even though he is sometimes engaged in sense enjoyment, My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents for such activities.” (Bhāg. 11.20.27-28)**

Kṛṣṇa is describing the superiority of devotional service, which has its foundation in having faith in hearing the narrations of Kṛṣṇa’s glories, which includes hearing the glories of devotional service. It is described that hearing the superiority of devotional service is above and beyond anything else. It is like the prayer of Mādhavendra Purī:

**“The expert moralists may say that I am deluded, the Vedic religionists may insist that I am misled, and my associates may condemn me as uncultured. My own brothers may disrespect me and call me an idiot, the wealthy may say I am mad, and the sharp-witted philosophers may severely criticize me as being a great egotist. Nevertheless, my heart cannot budge in the slightest degree from its aspiration to serve the lotus feet of Śrī Govinda.” (Śrī Bhakta-vacanamṛtam, 7.18)**

Here we have an example of one of our great ācāryas who is also speaking the glories of the superiority of devotional service. So many verses substantiate this point in the Bhāgavatam, and by hearing the glories of devotional service, it will awaken faith and determination within our heart to continue to serve the Lord. Any pleasure that we get from anything else is so insignificant in comparison to this. Not only is it insignificant, but even if we get the result of sense gratification, of performing austerities, of karma-kāṇḍa and giving charity, the mind will not find any shelter in the results of these activities. It will always be looking for the need for a superior goal. Prabhupāda explains in the Bhagavad-gītā that due to a lack of attaining a higher goal, one will never feel sheltered in the fulfillment of any of these things. Therefore a person’s mind will never be peaceful, and thus he will never be happy.

*kṛṣṇa-bhakta—niṣkāma, ataeva ‘śānta’*  
*bhukti-mukti-siddhi-kāmī—sakali ‘aśānta’*

**“Because a devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa is desireless, he is peaceful. Fruitive workers desire material enjoyment, jñānīs desire liberation, and yogīs desire material opulence; therefore they are all lusty and cannot be peaceful.” (Cc. Madhya, 19. 149)**

We may ask ourselves why we are not experiencing bliss—ānandāmbudhi-vardhanaṁ. As long as there is any desire for sense enjoyment in our heart, or the desire for liberation, we will not be able to taste transcendental bliss. This is the unfortunate result of pursuing other activities independent from devotional service—the mind will never be peaceful.

In Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the wives of the demigods say: “Pṛthu Mahārāja and his wife Arci are going past us. We are stuck in the heavenly planets with a very long duration of life, experiencing so many different types of heavenly pleasures. Not only that, but we are stuck here for thousands of years, and after we finish our thousands of years of enjoyment, we will fall back down into lower planets. And after we exhaust the results of all of our pious activities, what is our next destination?” It is like a person who has accumulated so much money in his bank account, but if he keeps withdrawing funds and never makes any deposits, then at some point the account will be empty. The wives of the demigods are thus saying: “We are going to exhaust the results of our pious activities and live thousands of years of enjoyment, but then what will our destination be?”

However, Pṛthu Mahārāja had fully absorbed his mind and senses in devotional service to the Lord, and gave up his body in full Kṛṣṇa consciousness. His wife entered into the sacrificial fire, and both of them together went directly past the heavenly planets. The demigods were able to observe this and the higher destination achieved by Pṛthu Mahārāja. Thus the wives of the demigods understood that devotional service is superior to being stuck on the heavenly planets.

For persons who are engaged in devotional service, they get the benefits of everything, because they get happiness that is otherwise only partially obtained by anything else. Because such happiness is only partially obtained, it will be exhausted in due course of time. Therefore the devotee continues to worship the Lord with firm faith that complete happiness will be granted by the mercy of the Lord. Kṛṣṇa can fulfill the desires of His devotees even better than the devotees themselves can fulfill their desires. Kṛṣṇa will fulfill the desires of His devotees in such a way that they won’t come and ask for it again. Anyone who is engaged in devotional service will get such results.

Kṛṣṇa says that at the end, His devotee attains His eternal abode. The karmīs, jñānīs, siddhis and yogīs may get the results of their sacrifices performed, but they will not achieve the eternal abode of the Lord. Thus the wives of the demigods say that there is nothing that is not available to the devotees.

## Accepting a Higher Authority

*maitreya uvāca*  
*bhṛgv-ādayas te munayo*  
*lokānāṁ kṣema-darśinaḥ*  
*goptary asati vai nṝṇāṁ*  
*paśyantaḥ paśu-sāmyatām*
