**The great sage Maitreya continued: “O great hero Vidura, the great sages, headed by Bhṛgu, were always thinking of the welfare of the people in general. When they saw that in the absence of King Aṅga there was no one to protect the interests of the people, they understood that without a ruler the people would become independent and nonregulated.” (Bhāg. 4.14.1)**

PURPORT

In this verse the significant word is kṣema-darśinaḥ, which refers to those who are always looking after the welfare of the people in general. All the great sages headed by Bhṛgu were always thinking of how to elevate all the people of the universe to the spiritual platform. Indeed, they advised the kings of every planet to rule the people with that ultimate goal of life in mind. The great sages used to advise the head of the state, or the king, and he used to rule the populace in accordance with their instruction. After the disappearance of King Aṅga, there was no one to follow the instructions of the great sages. Consequently all the citizens became unruly, so much so that they could be compared to animals. As described in Bhagavad-gītā (4.13), human society must be divided into four orders according to quality and work. In every society there must be an intelligent class, administrative class, productive class and worker class. In modern democracy these scientific divisions are turned topsy-turvy, and by vote śūdras, or workers, are chosen for administrative posts. Having no knowledge of the ultimate goal of life, such persons whimsically enact laws without knowledge of life’s purpose. The result is that no one is happy.

In this verse, Maitreya Muni is describing that Bhṛgu Muni, seeing the state of the government, became very concerned that they do not have a proper ruler to protect the people. King Aṅga had left to go to the forest and had not left anyone behind to rule the kingdom. As a result of there being no one to protect the interests of the people, the citizens became independent and non-regulated.

Śrīla Prabhupāda takes the opportunity to explain how modern society is topsy-turvy, because they do not establish the ultimate goal of life for the interest of the citizens. The leaders of society are simply put in their positions by votes.

It is explained in the Bhāgavatam that men who are like hogs, dogs, camels and asses, glorify those men who have no attraction for hearing the pastimes of the Supreme Lord. Similarly, men who are hogs, dogs, camels and asses, simply glorify persons who are better hogs, dogs, camels and asses than themselves. They have no idea of the ultimate goal of life, and therefore they are put in positions where people will provide them the means to live like animals. There is a tendency that people do not want to be ruled at all. This is one of the symptoms of Kali-yuga.

It is described in the Sixth Canto of the Bhāgavatam, when Yamarāja was speaking to the Yamadūtas, that a driver of the bullock cart controls the bull by tying ropes to its nostrils and pulling him. The bull is resistant, but due to the pain, he has to move when somebody is pulling on the ropes. Similarly, the Supreme Personality of Godhead binds all men through the ropes of His words that are given in the Vedas, which set forth the names and the activities of different sections of human society.

In fear, men worship the Supreme Lord and offer Him the fruits of their respective activities. One must first become obedient to the laws of God. Most living entities in human society are still conditioned by the laws of material nature. They are not liberated souls and therefore are still bound by the laws of the Supreme Lord. Although liberated souls worship the Supreme Lord from a higher platform than fear, those who are still influenced by the modes of material nature have to follow the rules and regulations that are set forth by the Supreme Lord as given in the scriptures. Yamarāja therefore gives the example that men perform their respective duties out of fear.

The representative of the Supreme Lord is the king, and he is supposed to act in accordance with the direction and guidance coming from the great sages. The king’s responsibility is to see that everyone is performing their duties. If the king is not fulfilling his duties, seeing that everyone else is performing their duties, then society turns into chaos. Therefore, the king is supposed to be very powerful; he is supposed to wield a sword. However, in modern society, there are no qualified kings. Just as in Kali-yuga, kalau śūdra-sambhava—there are no qualified brāhmaṇas. Because human society does not have these four orders in place, everything is topsy-turvy.

In one of the Following Śrīla Prabhupāda videos that Yadubara Prabhu put out, there was some footage of Śrīla Prabhupāda being received in a very palatial building in Paris. It was a huge mansion, and the mayor of Paris and many other dignitaries were there to receive him. Prabhupāda took advantage of this reception to speak to all the assembled dignitaries. The devotee who was narrating this particular līlā explained that Prabhupāda was sitting on a chair, and when the mayor comes in the room, it is the responsibility of everyone who is sitting to stand up to receive him. Thus everyone stood up, except for Prabhupāda. Yogeśvara Prabhu whispered into Prabhupāda’s ear, “Prabhupāda, there was never a time when anybody sat down when the mayor has entered the room. Everybody stands. It’s the tradition.”

Prabhupāda turned to Yogeśvara and he said, “Stand up for whom?” Prabhupāda made it clear that he was not going to get up for anybody. The mayor became very flustered. He had to speak to give a reception, welcoming Śrīla Prabhupāda. However, he had never experienced someone refusing to rise when he entered the room.

Prabhupāda remained sitting, listening to the mayor receive him, and he was tapping his foot. (Sometimes when Prabhupāda was getting ready to lunge on an attack, he would tap his foot, like he did with Cardinal Danielou.) When the mayor finished, Prabhupāda stood up and lunged right for the jugular vein, so to speak. He immediately started preaching about how it is the duty of the leaders of society to see that everybody is advancing in spiritual life. If they do not perform such activities, their leadership is no better than animal life. A leader who does not understand the goal of life is not a leader at all and therefore should not be followed. Human society is meant to be led by spiritual principles. This talk was never recorded, but we have the remembrance of Jyotirmayī, who translated for Prabhupāda during his talk with the mayor.

Prabhupāda would often say that the laws of God cannot be manufactured in the fertile minds of men. Dharmaṁ tu sākṣād bhagavat-praṇītam (Bhāg. 6.3.19)—the principles of religion are coming directly from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and the laws of God are coming directly from God Himself. Therefore, just as people cannot sit in their home and say to someone, “Let’s create a law today,” the leaders of society cannot create laws that have no connection whatsoever to the laws of God. If they create such laws, it is only to protect their own economic interest and live like animals, and not in the interest of protecting the citizens.

Elsewhere Prabhupāda says, “Real protection of citizens of societies is to lead them in such a way that this is their last birth in this world.” For this to be our last birth in this world is the real goal of human society. Man-made laws meant to protect the economic interests of the citizens are not protective at all. They are simply preparing human society to become animals in their next life.

Thus, Prabhupāda explains that when there is no strong king who maintains the goals of human society based upon spiritual principles, then there is no purpose of life. Therefore, the kings or the leaders of society should be conversant with the laws of God.

*nārāyaṇa-parā vedā*  
*devā nārāyaṇāṅgajāḥ*  
*nārāyaṇa-parā lokā*  
*nārāyaṇa-parā makhāḥ*  
*nārāyaṇa-paro yogo*  
*nārāyaṇa-paraṁ tapaḥ*  
*nārāyaṇa-paraṁ jñānaṁ*  
*nārāyaṇa-parā gatiḥ*

(Bhāg. 2.5.15-16)

The Vedas are coming from the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇa is the goal of all the Vedas. Nārāyaṇa-parā lokā—all the planets are meant to be subservient to the will of the Supreme Lord. All the demigods are meant to perform sacrifices for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa. Nārāyaṇa-parā makhāḥ—all sacrifices are meant for His pleasure. Nārāyaṇa-paro yogo—all mystic yoga activities are ultimately meant to achieve the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa. Nārāyaṇa- paraṁ tapaḥ—all austerities are meant to satisfy the Supreme Lord. Nārāyaṇa-paraṁ jñānaṁ—all knowledge is meant for understanding who is the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa. Nārāyaṇa-parā gatiḥ—the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate destination of life.

This is what should be understood by the leaders of society, and they should lead the citizens properly according to the direction given in the scriptures and by the sages who are the real spiritual leaders of society.

Śrīla Prabhupāda gives the example in the Bhāgavatam that during the autumn season, due to the presence of the clouds, all the luminaries in the sky are covered and cannot be seen. One looks up and sees the glowworms in the trees and thinks that they are the luminaries in the sky. Similarly, these clouds are like the clouds of Kali-yuga. In the Age of Kali, people mistake the glowworms in the trees to be the real luminaries in the sky. We therefore see how men who are like dogs, hogs, camels and asses glorify those who are never interested in discussing the activities of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. However, the real luminaries are those who are conversant with the laws of God (those who study the Vedic scriptures). Human society does not glorify them or even recognize them. Instead, they have all their other luminaries that they glorify.

Human society does not even know what to look for in real leadership. They do not want someone who is going to rule them; they only want somebody who will facilitate their sense gratification. However, human society is meant to voluntarily be ruled by a higher authority. We are supposed to be ruled by śāstra and by those who are learned in the śāstra. We voluntarily submit ourselves to the ruler—to the authority of those who are conversant with the knowledge of revealed scriptures. In this way, we should allow ourselves to become bound by the words of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, which are given in the Vedic literatures.

Just as the bull is bound to the nostrils by a rope and is controlled, we should allow ourselves to become controlled by the statements of the Supreme Lord given in the revealed scriptures. It is voluntary submission. Unless we voluntarily accept this type of submission, it is very difficult to progress in human life.

Lord Ṛṣabhadeva instructed his sons to accept voluntarily austerities and penances (Bhāg. 5.5.1):

tapo divyaṁ putrakā yena sattvaṁ

śuddhyed yasmād brahma-saukhyaṁ tv anantam

One should accept divine austerities and penances to achieve the divine position of devotional service. By such activities, one’s heart is purified. One comes to that platform of transcendental happiness, which is superior to material happiness, and this continues forever.

Thus if one voluntarily accepts austerities and penances to achieve the divine position of devotional service, he will achieve real happiness.

## Proper Attitude

We should always take advantage of every facility for coming together for hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa. Prabhupāda wanted temples to be established, and he would try to establish the stability of the temples around the worship of the Deity. He emphasized that both the bhagavat-kathā and the paths of bhagavat-marga and pāñcarātrika-marga must go on simultaneously. In other words, the worship of the Deity must be there, but also the glorification of the Deity must be there by spreading the glories of the pastimes and the qualities of the holy name of the Supreme Lord. Kṛṣṇa consciousness will remain strong as long as both things go on in parallel. However, Śrīla Prabhupāda always emphasized that bhagavat-marga, the path of glorification of the Lord, is more important.

I remember that in 1975, Prabhupāda wrote a letter saying that all the devotees should go out and preach and leave one devotee back in the temple to worship the deities. We saw this by Prabhupāda’s own example. He came to the West to establish Kṛṣṇa consciousness and there were no deities. Preaching was Prabhupāda’s deity. By preaching Kṛṣṇa consciousness and giving Kṛṣṇa to others, he was awakening an attraction for Kṛṣṇa within the hearts of others. By awakening that attraction within the heart, the desire to render some service will automatically follow. Without the awakening of that desire and without inspiration, it is very difficult to establish temples. Temples will simply be buildings and we will simply become absorbed in maintaining the buildings if we do not know what lies in the heart of the temple: Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

Prabhupāda used to say that our temples are like embassies to the spiritual world. When you go to an embassy, you are going to that place where you get your qualification to go to your ultimate destination. However, simply by going to the embassy does not mean you have gone to the country it represents. Similarly, simply by going into our temples does not necessarily mean we are going to become Kṛṣṇa conscious. Even though a person is in the temple, he can still be very un-Kṛṣṇa conscious.

Sometimes we see devotees living in the temple, but they are simply meditating on what is outside. Thus, it is not the temple that makes us Kṛṣṇa conscious, rather it is what goes on inside the temple that does. There has to be bhagavat-kathā. Prabhupāda explained that he established these temples for people to come and hear about Kṛṣṇa, because when one hears about Kṛṣṇa, it awakens within the heart the desire to serve the Lord. When that desire is awakened, then it is natural inspiration. Devotional service has to be rendered in a voluntary spirit. That voluntary spirit or desire to do something to please the Lord has to be awakened from within the heart. That is the perfection of our service.

Prabhupāda said in a lecture in 1966 that it is not enough to only believe in God, but we actually have to desire to have an intimate relationship with Him. To believe in God is pious and good, but it is not everything. Generally people come to God and ask, “Please give us this day our daily bread,” or, “O God, please free me from distress.” Prabhupāda said that generally people think that God is the order supplier, but actually He is not our order supplier. We must become the order supplier for God. That is devotional service—when God becomes dependent upon us and wants something from us, and we fulfill His requests.

In Vṛndāvana, Mother Yaśodā is providing all of Kṛṣṇa’s necessities. He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead and the master of all universes, yet He is dependent upon His mother for all of His necessities. Her full absorption is in providing everything that Kṛṣṇa needs.

Similarly, we see this in the pastimes of Nimāi and His mother, Śacīmātā. Once, young Nimāi became very angry because Śacīmātā asked Him to wait a moment for her to bring the garlands for Him to worship the Ganges. He began throwing a temper tantrum, saying, “What do you mean you will bring?!’’ He was so angry that He started smashing everything in the house. He began smashing all the pots of ghee, rice, milk and yogurt. He broke them open and they started to form rivers in the house. He pulled down, one by one, all the items hanging from the rafters, and threw them on the floor. He started to destroy the house, beating the doors and windows. Then He went outside and started beating the ground. After finishing His devastation, He lay down on the ground and went into yoga-nidrā (sleep).

Śacīmātā was watching all of this from a distance. This was shortly after the departure of Jagannātha Miśra, and Śacīmātā was a widow. Externally it appeared that they were living in poverty. They did not have many things within the house, yet her son was destroying everything.

After Nimāi fell asleep, Śacīmātā got a garland and the oil that was required for the worship He wanted to do. Then she went back and wiped all the dust off the body of her son. She woke Him up and said, “Nimāi! Nimāi! Here is the garland. Now You can go and perform Your worship to the Gaṅgā.”

Nimāi awoke and took everything from His mother’s hands and went down to the Gaṅgā. Śacīmātā began cleaning everything. When Nimāi returned she was trying to understand, “Nimāi! Everything here belongs to You! However, You have destroyed everything that I have for serving You! What will I do? I have nothing now.”

Nimāi said, “Don’t worry, mother. Kṛṣṇa will provide.”

Thus our devotional service should be rendered in this spirit of being the order supplier for God. Everything that we have should be given to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Not only that, but we should come to the platform of rendering devotional service in a very intimate relationship with God. This type of devotional service is ultimately required by all of us for the satisfaction of the Lord. Many people worship God as the all-pervading Supreme Personality of Godhead, Bhagavān, the possessor of all six opulences—wealth, beauty, strength, knowledge, renunciation and fame—in full. However, if our goal is to satisfy the Lord, it means we should render that service that is most pleasing to Him, and the Lord is most pleased when a devotee renders spontaneous ecstatic loving devotional service to Him.

*gopy ādade tvayi kṛtāgasi dāma tāvad*  
*yā te daśāśru-kalilāñjana-sambhramākṣam*  
*vaktraṁ ninīya bhaya-bhāvanayā sthitasya*  
*sā māṁ vimohayati bhīr api yad bibheti*

**“My dear Kṛṣṇa, Yaśodā took up a rope to bind You when You committed an offense, and Your perturbed eyes overflooded with tears, which washed the mascara from Your eyes. And You were afraid, though fear personified is afraid of You. This sight is bewildering to me.” (Bhāg. 1.8.31)**

PURPORT

Here is another example of the bewilderment created by the pastimes of the Supreme Lord. The Supreme Lord is the Supreme in all circumstances, as already explained. Here is a specific example of the Lord’s being the Supreme and at the same time a plaything in the presence of His pure devotee. The Lord’s pure devotee renders service unto the Lord out of unalloyed love only, and while discharging such devotional service the pure devotee forgets the position of the Supreme Lord. The Supreme Lord also accepts the loving service of His devotees more relishably when the service is rendered spontaneously out of pure affection, without anything of reverential admiration. Generally the Lord is worshiped by the devotees in a reverential attitude, but the Lord is meticulously pleased when the devotee, out of pure affection and love, considers the Lord to be less important than himself. The Lord’s pastimes in the original abode of Goloka Vṛndāvana are exchanged in that spirit. The friends of Kṛṣṇa consider Him one of them. They do not consider Him to be of reverential importance. The parents of the Lord (who are all pure devotees) consider Him a child only. The Lord accepts the chastisements of the parents more cheerfully than the prayers of the Vedic hymns. Similarly, He accepts the reproaches of His fiancees more palatably than the Vedic hymns. When Lord Kṛṣṇa was present in this material world to manifest His eternal pastimes of the transcendental realm of Goloka Vṛndāvana as an attraction for the people in general, He displayed a unique picture of subordination before His foster mother, Yaśodā. (…)

Prahlāda Mahārāja describes that the Lord is pleased when one has unflinching unalloyed devotion to Him and He is not so pleased even if one becomes a brāhmaṇa, performs sacrifices, austerities, accepts vows, or is chaste. The Lord is pleased when one has unflinching unalloyed devotion to Him. Prabhupāda describes that even more relishable for the Lord is when out of pure affection and love the devotee considers the Lord to be less important (subordinate) than himself, just as is the mood of Mother Yaśodā. This is called anugraha, which means to look upon the Lord with mercy and compassion. Mother Yaśodā was thinking, “I have to be compassionate upon my son! I have to take care of Him! If I don’t take care of Him, then something terrible could happen!”

Mother Yaśodā thus regularly offers prayers to Lord Viṣṇu for the protection of her son, Kṛṣṇa. When the dangerous event happened with Pūtanā the witch, Mother Yaśodā told one friend that the reason why Kṛṣṇa was saved was because she and Nanda Mahārāja were regularly offering prayers to Viṣṇu for Kṛṣṇa’s protection. She never thought that Kṛṣṇa actually killed Pūtanā, or that He pulled down the yamala-arjuna trees with a grinding mortar. Mother Yaśodā’s conclusion about the trees was that it was because of strong winds that they fell down.

Kṛṣṇa is gopikā-suta, which means He is the son of Yaśodā. However, He is not understood as the son of Yaśodā by mental speculators, to those striving for self-realization by severe austerities and penances, or to those who consider the body the same as the self. He can only be understood by spontaneous loving devotional service to Him. This spontaneous loving devotional service is required.

We cannot artificially come to that platform. We may try to be spontaneous, but if there is no devotion, that will not fulfill the requirement. Kṛṣṇa explains in Bhagavad-gītā the consequences of such spontaneous activity:

*yaḥ śāstra-vidhim utsṛjya*  
*vartate kāma-kārataḥ*  
*na sa siddhim avāpnoti*  
*na sukhaṁ na parāṁ gatim*

**He who discards scriptural injunctions and acts according to his own whims attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme destination. (Bg. 16.23)**

Whimsical activity is not the criteria for satisfying the Lord. One has to awaken spontaneous love within the heart first by regulated devotional service. This regulated devotional service begins by regularly hearing about the activities of Mother Yaśodā, Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd boys and all the residents of Vṛndāvana.

Kṛṣṇa says:

*atha cittaṁ samādhātuṁ*  
*na śaknoṣi mayi sthiram*  
*abhyāsa-yogena tato*  
*mām icchāptuṁ dhanañjaya*

**“My dear Arjuna, O winner of wealth, if you cannot fix your mind upon Me without deviation, then follow the regulative principles of bhakti-yoga. In this develop a desire to attain Me.” (Bg. 12.9)**

Devotional service has to be rendered in this spirit. Prabhupāda explains in the Upadeśāmṛta that cultivation refers to that of our natural desire to serve and to please the Lord. However, before one can love Kṛṣṇa, first there must be obedience. When one becomes obedient to the Lord and to the devotees of the Lord, then he can cultivate by regularly hearing and rendering devotional service in a submissive spirit. This is the proper formula for success. There is no other way to awaken love within the heart.

*nitya-siddha kṛṣṇa-prema ‘sādhya’ kabhu naya*  
*śravaṇādi-śuddha-citte karaye udaya*

**Pure love for Kṛṣṇa is eternally established in the hearts of the living entities. It is not something to be gained from another source. When the heart is purified by hearing and chanting, this love naturally awakens. (Cc. Madhya, 22.107)**

By hearing about Kṛṣṇa, that pure love will naturally awaken within the heart. Therefore we can understand that our regulated devotional service includes hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa. This is why Śrīla Prabhupāda established temples—so that everyone can come together and regularly hear and chant about Kṛṣṇa. When devotees are hearing and chanting about the pastimes of the Supreme Lord, then it awakens within the heart the voluntary spirit of service. This is lying dormant in the heart of every living entity, but it needs to be awakened by the proper association.

*ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ*  
*mad-bhakteṣv abhidhāsyati*  
*bhaktiṁ mayi parāṁ kṛtvā*  
*mām evaiṣyaty asaṁśayaḥ*  
*na ca tasmān manuṣyeṣu*  
*kaścin me priya-kṛttamaḥ*  
*bhavitā na ca me tasmād*  
*anyaḥ priyataro bhuvi*

**“For one who explains this supreme secret to the devotees, pure devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me. There is no servant in this world more dear to Me than he, nor will there ever be one more dear.” (Bg. 18.68-69)**

Prabhupāda, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta, Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura, Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura, Jīva Gosvāmī, Rūpa Gosvāmī, Sanātana Gosvāmī and Lord Caitanya have all given guarantees that if you fix your mind upon the Supreme Lord, then certainly you will go to Him. We have to cultivate the desire to always remember Kṛṣṇa and never forget Him. We should be in anxiety if we are not thinking of Kṛṣṇa. It is very dangerous to forget Kṛṣṇa even for a moment.

Nārada Muni said to King Prācīnabarhiṣat, “O you who are free from sinful activity, one who tries to counteract the effects of fruitive activity by manufacturing another activity, which is devoid of Kṛṣṇa consciousness is just like a person who tries to counteract the effects of a bad dream with a bad hallucination.” Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the real wakeful state of the living entity. When Kṛṣṇa consciousness is there, then everything is revealed and all fear goes away.

To cultivate our devotional service, we should always be anxious to always remember the Lord. The goal of everything that we do—cooking, worshipping the Deity, distributing books, working, taking care of our children, taking care of our husband, etc.—is to somehow or other be able to remember Kṛṣṇa. Cultivation of Kṛṣṇa consciousness must be a daily practice of hearing and chanting in the association of devotees. Unless that is done first, we cannot talk about spontaneous devotional service.

**Question: Sometimes when we are given a particular service, it is taken away from us. How should we handle this and not feel discouraged in our devotional service?**

In rendering devotional service, nothing is ever taken away from the devotee’s Kṛṣṇa consciousness and advancement that he has made. Kṛṣṇa says:

*nehābhikrama-nāśo ’sti*  
*pratyavāyo na vidyate*  
*sv-alpam apy asya dharmasya*  
*trāyate mahato bhayāt*

**“In this endeavour there is no loss or diminution, and a little advancement on this path can protect one from the most dangerous type of fear.” (Bg. 2.40)**

It is natural that if we are given a particular project to work on, we will want to do our best, but we should be careful to understand that doing our best also includes the consciousness that we do it in.

In the Third Canto of the Bhāgavatam, there is a verse where Brahma was praying to the Lord for the potency to create the universe. Prabhupāda explains in the commentary that fortunate is that person who has been entrusted with responsible work, and if he is always conscious that he is subordinate to the will of the Lord, then whatever the result, it will be done nicely. If, however, he is not in that consciousness, even if the result may externally look very nice, the work was still not done properly. Thus, if we are given a particular work, and we put our heart into it, it means that we are always subordinate to Kṛṣṇa and His representatives. Even though our service may change, the heart should not. The project, whatever it may be, is valueless if we have not put our heart into it. Sometimes Kṛṣṇa reminds us and puts us into a situation where we have to remember how to keep putting our heart into what He wants us to do.

## Being Successful in our Endeavors

Certainly it is encouraging when we experience Kṛṣṇa’s direct presence in our lives. This will happen when we are always thinking about what is best to do for Kṛṣṇa’s service. If somehow we throw in other motivations in our decisions then we will not be able to perceive Kṛṣṇa’s direct presence in what we do, being unable to depend on Him. Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (18.57-58): “In all activities just depend upon Me and work always under My protection. In such devotional service, be fully conscious of Me. If you become conscious of Me, you will pass over all the obstacles of conditioned life by My grace. If, however, you do not work in such consciousness but act through false ego, not hearing Me, you will be lost.”

We can only depend on Kṛṣṇa when we see His instructions and desires in the execution of our duties. If Kṛṣṇa’s desires are not there, then why should we be interested in doing such duties? If Kṛṣṇa’s desires are not there and there is a little obstacle in what we are doing, we will say, “I can adjust according to my own desires,” thinking that the result is for ourselves. We immediately forget Kṛṣṇa. We cannot depend on Kṛṣṇa if we think that the result is for ourselves. However, if there is an obstacle and we know that Kṛṣṇa wants the result, then we can depend on Him. We therefore have to know His instructions and His desires. Kṛṣṇa says that in all activities we should depend upon Him. If we are rising in the morning, cleaning our bodies, accepting prasādam, going to work, going to distribute books, worshipping the deities, etc., we have to depend on Krishna. This is the science that we must practice internally. We will otherwise see devotional service as something external.

If one is not favored by Kṛṣṇa, even though he may make so many endeavors, he will never be successful. One must always be dependent upon the mercy of the Lord for his success. Mundane endeavors will always be unsuccessful.

This is exemplified in the story in Caitanya-bhāgavata of the brāhmaṇa who offered rice to his Deity, Gopāla. He was accustomed to simply wandering about, eating the fruits and roots in the forest. He had no fixed residence; his residence was wherever the Lord brought him. He was always fully dependent upon Śrī Gopāla, and always had the Deity of Gopāla around his neck wherever he would go. He had two deities: Gopāla and a śālagrāma-śilā. Wherever he would wander about, his deities were with him constantly. He would not eat anything except that which was offered to his Deity. He was accustomed to offering only fruits and roots from the forest wherever he would go, and when the Lord would accept his offering, that would be his only food for consumption.

Once, as he was wandering about, he appeared at the home of Jagannātha Miśra. Jagannātha Miśra could immediately recognize that he was a very elevated Vaiṣṇava. He invited the brāhmaṇa into his home, welcomed him, and asked him where he was from. The brāhmaṇa told him, “I have no fixed residence.”

Jagannātha Miśra requested, “Please use my home and prepare some food for your deities. In our home we will provide you the kitchen and all the ingredients.

The brāhmaṇa said, “No, I am accustomed to eating fruits and roots in the forest.”

Jagannātha Miśra insisted, “It is our duty to serve Vaiṣṇavas like you. Please let us provide you all the ingredients you need to prepare very nice food for Gopāla.” The brāhmaṇa agreed, and immediately Jagannātha Miśra prepared his kitchen. Everyone in the house gathered various ingredients for the brāhmaṇa to cook for his Deity.

The brāhmaṇa then prepared very nice, hot rice to offer to his Gopāla. As previously mentioned, he would never eat anything without first offering it to Gopāla. However, when he placed the offering before his Deity and began offering prayers, young Nimāi, the resident of the house of Jagannātha Miśra, came into the room. He took some rice and began eating it. When the brāhmaṇa saw this, he immediately called out, “Alas! Now the offering has been contaminated! I can no longer offer this rice to Gopāla.” Of course, we know that Nimāi did not contaminate the rice. However, at that particular time, the Lord had not revealed His divinity to anyone, and therefore this brāhmaṇa was simply thinking that this was some ordinary, young, mischievous boy who could not distinguish between right and wrong. He accepted it as the arrangement of providence, thinking, “I knew I wasn’t supposed to cook rice today for my Deity.” He accepted it as the Lord’s will and said, “I will offer some fruits and roots from the forest as I normally do.”

However, Jagannātha Miśra was very disturbed when he saw the mischievous behavior of his son and wanted to chastise Him. He ran towards Nimāi with a stick to beat Him, but the brāhmaṇa grabbed his hand and said, “No. Please, do not punish him. A young child cannot know what is right and what is wrong. How can you punish a young, innocent boy like this? It is Gopāla’s will. He wants fruits and roots from the forest as He normally takes. Please do not punish your son.”

Jagannātha Miśra felt so terrible and said, “I am simply a householder. It is my duty to serve great Vaiṣṇavas like you! I want to serve you, but you will not accept anything that is not offered to Gopāla! Please therefore let me serve you by providing the ingredients again. It makes no difference what endeavor is there for me! I am prepared for that endeavor. Please do not deprive me of the opportunity to render service unto you. Let me clean the kitchen again and get all the necessary ingredients once again. Please cook one more time for your Deity.”

The brāhmaṇa agreed, and immediately Jagannātha Miśra became very ecstatic from the opportunity to serve this Vaiṣṇava. Although his son was the Supreme Personality of Godhead, we can see how much pleasure he derived from serving Vaiṣṇavas. Jagannātha Miśra gathered all the ingredients, cleaned the kitchen, and then the brāhmaṇa went to cook once again, preparing a nice offering of the cooked foods.

When time came for making the offering, he decided to make sure that Nimāi was not in the house. They therefore arranged for Nimāi to be taken to the neighbors. While He was being taken out of the house, everybody was teasing Nimāi, saying, “Nimāi, you are eating from the brāhmaṇa! But You don’t even know where he is from and what family he is from!”

Nimāi replied, “I am a cowherd boy, a vaiśya. I always accept food from the hands of brāhmaṇas. How will I ever become degraded if I eat food from the hands of brāhmaṇas? Certainly I will benefit by eating food cooked by brāhmaṇas.” Everyone was laughing at Nimāi’s statements. They could not understand the deep meaning of His words and that he was actually describing His divine position as a cowherd boy. They thought He was just speaking out of innocence.

When Nimāi was brought next door, all the neighbors began to entertain Him so that He would be busy and would not disturb the brāhmaṇa during his next offering. However, when the brāhmaṇa brought the rice before his Deity, Gopāla, and began to offer it, in an unseen way, by the arrangement of yoga-māyā, Nimāi left the house of the neighbors. He immediately came to that place where the brāhmaṇa was making his offering to the Deity, Gopāla. While he was chanting his mantras to offer the rice, young Nimāi took another handful of rice and ate it. The brāhmaṇa again called out, “Alas! Alas! The offering has been contaminated again! What can I do? Certainly now we can see it is Gopāla’s desire for fruits and roots from the forest.”

When Jagannātha Miśra saw this, he became furious. This time he was not going to be stopped. He began running after Nimāi with a stick and was going to beat Him. All the family members and neighbors saw Jagannātha Miśra doing this, and they stopped him: “Please, Miśra, you can’t do this to your son!”

Jagannātha Miśra said, “No! He will not escape my beating today!”

When the brāhmaṇa saw Jagannātha Miśra in great anger, he pacified him with sweet words. The brāhmaṇa was so tolerant. In his mind, he was fixed on Lord Gopāla, and was not so disturbed by what happened. He begged Jagannātha Miśra, “Please, do not punish your son!”

After two attempts to make some offering, the brāhmaṇa was convinced that the next offering will be some fruits and wild roots from the forest. He said to Jagannātha Miśra, “What can be done?” Even if one may have unlimited varieties of food, but the Lord does not sanction, how can one eat the remnants?” Thus, only if the Lord accepts one’s offering, can he get the remnants from the Lord.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta explains that in a similar way, unless one is favored by the Supreme Lord, even though he may make so many endeavors, he can never be successful. Therefore, for success, one always has to be dependent upon the mercy of the Lord. Mundane endeavors will always end in an unsuccessful result.

For a devotee, the criterion of success is the pleasure of the Lord. As explained in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

*ataḥ pumbhir dvija-śreṣṭhā*  
*varṇāśrama-vibhāgaśaḥ*  
*svanuṣṭhitasya dharmasya*  
*saṁsiddhir hari-toṣaṇam*

**“O best among the twice-born, it is therefore concluded that the highest perfection one can achieve by discharging the duties prescribed for one’s own occupation according to caste divisions and orders of life is to please the Personality of Godhead.” (Bhāg. 1.2.13)**

If the Lord is not satisfied, then even though the result may look very nice, it only appears that way, because we are looking at it from an external point of view, seeing things in duality. One who is in external consciousness will always see duality. However, one who is in internal consciousness will always see Kṛṣṇa’s hand, and if Kṛṣṇa’s hand is there, then success must be there, even if it brings grief. Whatever Kṛṣṇa does—either giving punishments or benedictions—since His hand is personally in it, it is always for the benefit of the recipient. There is no value in being punished by the material nature unless we can see that Kṛṣṇa is behind it. If we do not see Kṛṣṇa behind it, we will simply get punished again and again by the material nature, and we will never make progress and will never be successful. The material nature will always punish the conditioned soul who forgets Kṛṣṇa. After all, that is her service. Kṛṣṇa says:

*daivī hy eṣā guṇa-mayī*  
*mama māyā duratyayā*  
*mām eva ye prapadyante*  
*māyām etāṁ taranti te*

**“This divine energy of Mine, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is difficult to overcome. But those who have surrendered unto Me can easily cross beyond it.” (Bg. 7.14)**

Material nature will reward us and punish us according to our past activities. However, whatever rewards we get are temporary, and we will have to end in distress. Such is the nature of the material life in forgetfulness of Kṛṣṇa. We must therefore always remember Krishna.

*nehābhikrama-nāśo ’sti*  
*pratyavāyo na vidyate*  
*sv-alpam apy asya dharmasya*  
*trāyate mahato bhayāt*

**In this endeavor there is no loss or diminution, and a little advancement on this path can protect one from the most dangerous type of fear. (Bg. 2.40)**

A devotee may experience some temporary setback, but he will be successful if he remembers the Lord. In whatever we are doing, we have to see Kṛṣṇa’s connection. If we cannot see Kṛṣṇa’s connection, then why are we doing it?

## Chapter 6 – Holy Name

## Potency of the Holy Name

Mantra meditation is a very ancient tradition, practiced by members of many different groups. A mantra is essentially meant to deliver the mind, and is a means for performing meditation or fixing the mind upon a sound vibration, which is invested with potency. The potency that is invested in the mantra will vary according to the type of mantra. The Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra is known as the mahā-mantra (the greatest mantra). The mahā-mantra is invested with the potency coming directly from the Supreme Lord Himself. He has invested Himself or all of His potencies in this mantra. The process of chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa is meant to control the mind.

In the Bhagavad-gītā, Lord Kṛṣṇa describes that for one who has controlled his mind, it is his best friend, and for one who fails to control it, it is his worst enemy. The mind is filled with many thoughts. Some of those thoughts can never be fulfilled. However, even when they are fulfilled, they may not sufficiently satisfy the self.

The mind is described to be like the reservoir of all ideas for enjoyment. There are different types of enjoyment. There is enjoyment that one experiences when the senses come in contact with the sense objects. However, that enjoyment is temporary and is insufficient for satisfying the self. The nature of the soul within the body is ānanda-mayo ’bhyāsāt—eternal and pleasure seeking.

There are different kinds of pleasure. By nature, the soul is meant to experience ānanda—spiritual pleasure. As opposed to temporary pleasure, which simply satisfies the senses and the mind, this spiritual pleasure has no beginning or end, and it satisfies the self. To experience this spiritual pleasure, one has to come to the platform of realizing the difference between the body and the self. The chanting of Hare Kṛṣṇa is the means for purifying our identification with this temporary body so that we can experience the real pleasure that we are all looking for, which is derived from coming in contact with the internal potency or the pleasure potency of the Supreme Lord.

There is also pleasure that is derived from contact with the sense objects, and pleasure that is derived from liberation, which is the pleasure that one experiences when there is the cessation of all material activities and of identification with the temporary physical body.

Many people look for liberation. Even from a material perspective, we see that there are many cultures, societies and individuals in the world who have been oppressed by some power greater than themselves, and they want to try to become liberated from that oppression and establish their own individuality and freedom. It is the natural characteristic of the eternal soul to be liberated from physical, social and mental oppression. However, that type of liberation or pleasure is described as the second type of pleasure. The third type of pleasure, ānanda, is that which one experiences through realization. Through realization, one not only negates his identity with the physical, but also identifies himself with his eternal identity in relationship with the Supreme Lord, which is beyond the platform of liberation.

Jīvera ‘svarūpa’ haya-kṛṣṇera ‘nitya-dāsa’ (Cc. Madhya 20.108)—the constitutional position of the living being is that he is an eternal servant of Kṛṣṇa. Our conditional nature is that we are servants of illusory masters. Thus, if we are not serving the Supreme, then we become subservient to other objects for service, which is service to the demands of the body, friends, families, society and nation. Everyone is rendering service in some way. That is our constitutional nature, but we are looking for that object of service that can really fully satisfy the self.

Thus, when one chants Hare Kṛṣṇa or performs this mantra meditation, what he is actually doing is coming in contact with the eternal potency of the Lord, which has the power to remove all the coverings that are temporarily obstructing our natural vision, which is to see everything connected to the Supreme. This is the natural constitutional vision of every living being.

In the Bhagavad-gītā, Kṛṣṇa says, “For one who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me, I am never lost to him nor is he ever lost to Me.” This is spiritual vision—seeing everything connected to the Supreme Lord—whereas material vision is seeing everything connected to oneself.

Lord Kṛṣṇa explains:

*ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavo*  
*mattaḥ sarvaṁ pravartate*  
*iti matvā bhajante māṁ*  
*budhā bhāva-samanvitāḥ*

**“I am the source of all spiritual and material worlds. Everything emanates from Me. The wise who perfectly know this engage in My devotional service and worship Me with all their hearts.” (Bg. 10.8)**

For one who sees everything connected to the Supreme Lord, he is not in duality. Examples of dualities of this world are pleasure and pain, happiness and distress, heat and cold, and honor and dishonor. These dualities are a constant source of anxiety. Usually we are calculating whether an action will produce the kind of result that will make us happy. Sometimes we think we have found the formula to achieve happiness, but it does not always work. Sometimes we may get what we want—a certain type of pleasure from coming in contact with the fulfillment of that desire—but it does not last. That happiness is described as capala-sukha—it has a beginning and an end.

Thus, chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa is a meditation, which enables us to experience our natural spiritual nature. Spiritual means that it is eternal, just as we are eternal. In Bhagavad-gītā (2.20) it is stated: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin—for the soul there is never birth nor death. Having once been does he never cease to be. He is unborn, undying, ever-existing and eternal. He is not slain when the body is slain.

Chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa is done either individually or, as is recommended in this age, congregationally. Because Kṛṣṇa has invested His potencies in His name, by chanting that name we begin to experience our spiritual nature.

Śrīla Prabhupāda gives the example that if you put an iron rod in fire and keep it in contact with the fire, it becomes red-hot. Although it is rod iron, because of being in contact with the fire, it burns just like fire, having taken on the same quality as fire. Similarly, Kṛṣṇa is pavitraṁ—completely pure. Because of our present condition, we need to cleanse these identifications, called upādhis, with this temporary world, and begin to understand our eternal relationship with the Supreme. The means to do this is by coming in contact with Kṛṣṇa’s name.

*sarvopādhi-vinirmuktaṁ*  
*tat-paratvena nirmalam*  
*hṛṣīkeṇa hṛṣīkeśa-*  
*sevanaṁ bhaktir ucyate*

**Bhakti, or devotional service, means engaging all our senses in the service of the Lord, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the master of all the senses. When the spirit soul renders service unto the Supreme, there are two side effects. One is freed from all material designations, and one’s senses are purified simply by being employed in the service of the Lord. (Nārada-pañcarātra, as quoted in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu (1.1.12))**

Kali-kāle nāma-rūpe kṛṣṇa-avatāra (Cc. Ādi, 17.22)—in the Age of Kali, the Lord has descended in the form of His name. For anyone who associates with Him in the form of His name, it is as good as associating with Him directly, and certainly he becomes delivered.

Normally, persons engage in meditation for many thousands of years to understand their spiritual nature. Sometimes people look for God and sometimes they look for many other processes through mystic yoga, āsanas, or meditation. There are many ways by which persons will try to search after the ultimate source. However, in this Age of Kali—the age of quarrel, where men are short-lived, quarrelsome, misguided, unlucky and disturbed—the Lord has made Himself so easily accessible by chanting. Chanting is ever-fresh because it develops more and more meaning for our lives. There is an internal experience that is manifest in one’s heart, which is indisputable, but it has to be experienced by trying it oneself.

Śrīla Prabhupāda gives the example that if someone gives you some very nice, sweet honey, you will not know how sweet it is simply by looking at it or hearing about how sweet it is. You must actually taste it. Similarly, because Kṛṣṇa is sweet, His name is also sweet. We may not experience the full sweetness when we begin chanting, but because it is also the means for experiencing that sweetness, when we chant Hare Kṛṣṇa, we get a little taste. From that little taste, our mind becomes controlled, our anxieties begin to diminish, and we derive a little pleasure. However, there is more. One begins to realize that there is so much more that is available in Kṛṣṇa’s name. One then becomes very eager to go on chanting more and more, because the experience becomes ever fresh. Because Kṛṣṇa is unlimited, He will give pleasure to our senses.

In Bhagavad-gītā (2.59), Kṛṣṇa says:

*viṣayā vinivartante*  
*nirāhārasya dehinaḥ*  
*rasa-varjaṁ raso ’py asya*  
*paraṁ dṛṣṭvā nivartate*

**The embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, though the taste for sense objects remains. But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.**

When we experience something higher, it is very easy to give up that which is low. Thus, we want to experience the pleasure of chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, which will make everything else look much less significant.

Hare is a word that is addressing the energy of the Lord. The Lord has energies, and is also the energetic source. We address the energies of the Lord, because it is through them that we can come in contact with Kṛṣṇa. The name Kṛṣṇa means all attractive. Rāma means the reservoir of pleasure. Thus, the chanting of Hare Kṛṣṇa is a prayer: “Please let me engage in Your service, Kṛṣṇa.” Sometimes we may pray for good health, long life, or welfare of a friend or family member. However the mahā-mantra is an exceptional prayer, requesting that we may realize ourselves in relationship to the Lord as His servant by being permitted to render some service.

Our nature is to serve, therefore, why not serve the highest? The Lord is always satisfied with any little service rendered to Him. The pleasure we derive from that service is far superior to any other service we may perform in this world, and it gives us the impetus to serve more.

**Question: Is there any significance attributed to chanting out loud versus within one’s mind?**

There is benefit from both. However, chanting out loud has twice the benefit—not only do you benefit, but others who hear can also benefit.

## The Greatest Gift

If one experiences something of great value at any moment in his life, then all the troubles, difficulties and problems that he has to undergo become much less significant.

It is described in the Bhāgavatam that when one attains shelter at Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, it is just like a person who has a long journey and finally comes home—a place of comfort. In the same way, when one experiences some value in relationship to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, all the other problems and difficulties become much less significant.

The Bhāgavatam (2.1.12) states: “What is the value of a prolonged life which is wasted, inexperienced by years in this world? Better a moment of full consciousness, because that gives one a start in searching after his supreme interest.” That moment of full consciousness is so valuable that everything else becomes pale in its presence. Even if one has a very long life and accumulates so many different experiences, what is the value of all of those experiences in relationship to Kṛṣṇa consciousness? They are not so valuable. Our journey here in the material world is filled with an accumulation of so many different types of experiences. However, the experiences of greatest value are the ones that enhance our Kṛṣṇa consciousness. If we get some experience that allows us to realize the greatness and value of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, then all the other problems and difficulties that we have to undergo are immediately forgotten.

Devotees once asked Śrīla Prabhupāda: “When we go back to Godhead, will we remember our journey in the material world?”

Prabhupāda replied, “We will remember just enough to know not to go back.” What is the value remembering all the different species of life and all the different substances eaten? When one goes back home, back to Godhead, the journey in the material world is not so valuable to remember because Kṛṣṇa consciousness is so valuable, and because Kṛṣṇa consciousness is ever fresh.

Those who are experiencing Kṛṣṇa consciousness do not think about māyā because the ever increasing pleasure in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is so powerful and absorbing that those devotees in full Kṛṣṇa consciousness are always remembering Kṛṣṇa. They do not know about māyā. They do not have to remember all the experiences of the material world, because Kṛṣṇa consciousness is such an overwhelming experience that it can attract every living entity completely. Even liberated souls are attracted to serving Kṛṣṇa because it is so valuable and wonderful. That is the whole meaning of the ātmārāma verse in the Bhāgavatam—that those who are on the path of self-realization—even those who are completely freed from all material bondage—are always eager to render devotional service to Kṛṣṇa. This means that Kṛṣṇa possesses transcendental qualities that can attract everyone—even the liberated souls. Such is the meaning of all-attractive. Everyone can be fully attracted. Any experience that gives us a little taste or glimpse of Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the most valuable experience we take with us. If we actually get that experience, then any other problems undergone in order to obtain it are very insignificant. The only problem is that if we do not get this experience, then there are so many problems and anxieties.

Rāmānanda Rāya told Lord Caitanya that the greatest cause of pain and suffering is to be bereft of the association of devotees.

*satāṁ prasaṅgān mama vīrya-saṁvido*  
*bhavanti hṛt-karṇa-rasāyanāḥ kathāḥ*

**In the association of pure devotees, discussion of the pastimes and activities of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is very pleasing and satisfying to the ear and the heart. (Bhāg. 3.25.25)**

The most valuable gift to give in the association of devotees is the holy name.

The following is the translation of Śrī Nāma-kīrtana, Song 4 (Bolo Hari Bolo), by Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura:

1\) Chant the name of Hari! O brothers, with blissful minds chant the name of Hari! Chant the name of Hari! Birth after birth in happiness, chant the name of Hari!

2\) Chant the name of Hari! O brothers, you have obtained a human birth, now chant the name of Hari! Chant the name of Hari! Whether you are in happiness or distress, chant the name of Hari!

3\) Chant the name of Hari! O brothers, whether in prosperity or misfortune, chant the name of Hari! Chant the name of Hari! Whether you live at home or in the forest, chant the name of Hari! Remaining in this material world for Kṛṣṇa’s purposes, chant the name of Hari!

4\) Chant the name of Hari! O brothers, give up the association of non-devotees and chant the name of Hari! Chant the name of Hari! Falling at the feet of the Vaiṣṇavas, chant the name of Hari!

5\) Chant the name of Hari! Chant the names of Gaura and Nityānanda! Chant the names of Gaura and Gadādhara! Chant the names of Gaura and Advaita!

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura very nicely describes how the holy name should be chanted under any condition in which one may find himself. He also describes the various conditions in which one should chant the holy name of the Lord.

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura also explains in his Navadvīpa-dhāma-māhātmya how to obtain sambandha (relationship with Lord Caitanya). If one wants to become a servant of Lord Caitanya, then it can only happen when he is chanting in a humble state of mind, thinking himself to be lower than the straw in the street, devoid of all sense of false prestige and ready to offer all respects to others. In that state of mind, he can chant the name of the Lord constantly.

A proud person who has no humility can never have a relationship with Lord Caitanya. The only hope for a proud person is to get the mercy of Lord Nityānanda or to get the mercy of a Vaiṣṇava—a devotee of the Lord who is a servant of Lord Caitanya.

Without service to Lord Caitanya, there is no way one can enter into Vṛndāvana. (Ese) bṛndābane rādhā-śyāmer pa’be daraśan, (gaura-kṛpā ha’le he)—one can get the beautiful darśana of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana only first if he has received Lord Caitanya’s mercy. Otherwise there is no darśana. One may get the darśana of Rādhā-Śyāmasundara in the form of arcā-vigraha. However, if one actually wants to see Rādhā-Śyāmasundara, to enter into Their līlās, and to enter into the dancing party of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, first he must catch hold of the lotus feet of Lord Nityānanda. By the mercy of Lord Nityānanda, one can become freed from material desires. By the mercy of the servant of the Lord, one can become freed from these anarthas that are within the heart. Therefore Lord Nityānanda is very merciful in the distribution of the holy name, because it is the holy name of the Lord that is our means for achieving our relationship with Kṛṣṇa.

Kṛṣṇa-mantra haite habe saṁsāra-mocana, kṛṣṇa-nāma haite pābe kṛṣṇera caraṇa. (Cc. Ādi, 7.73) Lord Caitanya has instructed that the holy name of Lord Kṛṣṇa is actually what will bring us to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. Out of all the ways of executing devotional service, the nine processes of bhakti are the most powerful because they contain the potency to deliver Kṛṣṇa and ecstatic love for Him. Of the nine processes of bhakti, the most important is the chanting of the holy name of the Lord. One who chants the holy name of the Lord without offense can very easily attain ecstatic love for Kṛṣṇa. Thus it is the holy name of the Lord that gives us the means for achieving the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa and becoming qualified to enter into the transcendental realm of Goloka Vṛndāvana, the place where nobody knows about māyā. All they know is Kṛṣṇa.

Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (9.13): “mahātmānas tu māṁ pārtha, daivīṁ prakṛtim āśritāḥ.” These mahātmās are always under the protection of the Lord’s divine nature. All they know and all they can speak and hear about is Kṛṣṇa. All they want to see is Kṛṣṇa’s face. He is always there, reciprocating with devotees. It is the holy name that brings us to that place, and it is the means by which the Lord has descended in this Age of Kali, and how He has made Himself so easily accessible to us.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains that only two realities exist in the material world: the living entity and the holy name. Everything else is simply a product of the illusory energy. However, contact with the holy name of Kṛṣṇa, is our first contact with Him. That is our contact with reality and our means for cleaning the heart and getting out of this material world.

Lord Caitanya says: ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanaṁ bhava-mahā-dāvāgni-nirvāpaṇaṁ. Ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanaṁ means cleaning the mirror of the heart. It is the only means by which we can clean our heart so that we can become qualified to go back home, back to Godhead.

In his bhajana, Bolo Hari Bolo, Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura gives so many nice instructions. He tells everybody, “Chant the names of Hari in whatever condition, whether in happiness or distress.” If one does not realize the necessity of chanting the holy name of the Lord under any circumstances, how can he ever realize the great gift that is present within the holy name? There is only one place for persons who forget about chanting the holy name of the Lord. It is the material world, which is filled with so many dualities and anxieties. It is described that if one does not dedicate himself to the service to Lord Caitanya, then he has to be filled with abominable anxiety-filled service of the material world. There are only two fruits that can be obtained in the world of duality: material happiness and material distress. Neither of them is of any value.

*‘dvaite’ bhadrābhadra-jñāna, saba—‘manodharma’*  
*‘ei bhāla, ei manda’,—ei saba ‘bhrama’*

(Cc. Antya 4.176)

When we think in terms of good and bad, it is simply mental speculation or manodharma (the religion of the mind). There is the religion of the soul and the religion of the mind. The religion of the mind is to see good and bad in the material world. The mind is very dedicated to perceiving things in relationship to good and bad. Anything not conceived in relationship to Kṛṣṇa is understood to be illusion. None of the illusions uttered by words or conceived in the mind are factual. Since this illusion is not factual, there is no difference whether we say that something is good or something is bad. In actuality, it is all bad because it is an illusion.

Under illusion, we think that we are happy. However, this is bad, because the only fruit of that happiness is suffering. In reality, there is only one fruit for the world of duality: Duḥkhālayam aśāśvatam—a condition that is temporary and full of suffering. Even material happiness leads to suffering, because as Prahlāda Mahārāja explains, it is creating all conditions for our future distress. In the material world, every materialist endeavors for happiness and tries to mitigate his distress, and therefore acts accordingly. However, one cannot be happy as long as he endeavors for happiness. As soon he begins his endeavors for happiness, immediately his conditions for distress will begin. Such is the fruit of duality.

If we do not have Kṛṣṇa consciousness, then all we have is duality, resulting from our anxiety-filled service to the illusory energy dictated by the mind and by the influence of Māyā. Māyā is very successful in her influence in the material world. In the spiritual world we say she has no influence, but the material world is her domain, where everybody gets jabbed by her trident of the three-fold miseries.

Prahlāda Mahārāja says that the perfect condition for chanting the holy name is to realize that one is living in the world of duality. First we have to have a fear of māyā. If we have no taste, at least we should be afraid of māyā. Prabhupāda said, “That is the difference between you and me. I will never fall down, because I am afraid of māyā.”

*enechi auṣadhi māyā nāśibāra lāgi’*  
*harināma-mahāmantra lao tumi māgi’*

(Aruṇodaya-kīrtana, Text 4)

“I brought you the medicine. Take your medicine; chant this holy name of the Lord. This is the best medicine to take to become freed from this world of birth and death.”

Lord Caitanya calls, “Wake up! How long will you sleep on the lap of the witch called māyā?” She is just lulling you to sleep, but Lord Caitanya is calling.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura is also saying that since you have attained the human birth, chant the name of Hari. Whether you are in happiness or distress, chant the name of Hari. Whether you are in prosperity or in misfortune, chant the name of Hari. Whether you are wealthy or completely poor, it does not make any difference. A person who lives in opulence and does not chant the holy name of Hari is living in hell, whereas a person who lives in poverty and chants the holy name of the Lord is in the spiritual world. Don’t waste your life simply so that you can live in opulence and forget to chant the holy name! In such a state, you have lost everything. Under illusion you think you have gained, but actually you have lost everything.

*kāmasya nendriya-prītir*  
*lābho jīveta yāvatā*  
*jīvasya tattva-jijñāsā*  
*nārtho yaś ceha karmabhiḥ*

**Life’s desires should never be directed toward sense gratification. One should desire only a healthy life, or self-preservation, since a human being is meant for inquiry about the Absolute Truth. Nothing else should be the goal of one’s works. (Bhāg. 1.2.10)**

Our whole purpose for maintaining our body in this world is so that we can chant the holy name of Hari. Otherwise, the body has no value.

Just as the holy name is valuable, so is the dust of the feet of the Vaiṣṇavas, which also include their instructions and blessings. We should fall at their feet and beg them, “Please help me to remember Kṛṣṇa. Help me to remember to always chant the holy name of the Lord. Help me to understand the importance of always chanting the holy name of the Lord so that I can go on cleaning my heart and get rid of these anarthas (obstacles) on the path of devotional service, so that one day I can become a servant of Lord Caitanya.” This should be our hope. The holy name of the Lord is the means for achieving that great hope. Please take this valuable gift, appreciate its importance, take these instructions with you and make your life successful.

## Faith in the Holy Name

*nāma cintāmaṇiḥ kṛṣṇaś*  
*caitanya-rasa-vigrahaḥ*  
*pūrṇaḥ śuddho nitya-mukto*  
*’bhinnatvān nāma-nāminoḥ*

**The holy name of Kṛṣṇa is transcendentally blissful. It bestows all spiritual benedictions, for it is Kṛṣṇa Himself, the reservoir of all pleasure. Kṛṣṇa’s name is complete, and it is the form of all transcendental mellows. It is not a material name under any condition, and it is no less powerful than Kṛṣṇa Himself. Since Kṛṣṇa’s name is not contaminated by the material qualities, there is no question of its being involved with māyā. Kṛṣṇa’s name is always liberated and spiritual; it is never conditioned by the laws of material nature. This is because the name of Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇa Himself are identical. (Cc. Madhya 17.133)**

Prabhupāda often said that the means and the end are the same in Kṛṣṇa consciousness—we are chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa. We ultimately want to chant the pure holy name. When one chants the holy name of the Lord and tears come to the eyes, his bodily hair stands up, and when he experiences different symptoms of ecstatic love, then he knows that he has come to the platform of pure chanting. Until such a time, he is a struggling sādhaka. Trying to purify himself, he goes through the different stages of chanting the holy name of the Lord. The first stage is called nāma-aparādha, chanting on the platform of committing some offenses to the holy name. Next is the clearing stage, nāmābhāsa. Finally, there is chanting of śuddha-nāma, which gives rise to kṛṣṇa-prema, or pure ecstatic love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

To approach the pure holy name, one needs to come to the platform of the clearing stage, where he is not committing any offenses and is endeavoring to overcome all of the anarthas within his heart, which are obstacles for chanting the pure name of the Lord.

The example given is that although the sun is always in a fixed position in the sky, always effulgent, and always giving off an endless light, our experience of the sun is affected by the presence of clouds and fog in the sky. Similarly, the holy name of the Lord is ever blissful, full of unlimited ecstasies, and is Kṛṣṇa Himself. However, if we are not experiencing Kṛṣṇa’s presence in His name, it is due to the presence of the clouds of anarthas and the fog of ignorance, which are obstructing our experience of the pure holy name.

We will discuss the subject of clearing the clouds of anarthas and destroying the fog of ignorance so that we can gradually chant at least on the platform of nāmābhāsa. Although nāmābhāsa can bestow many great benedictions, it does not give the pure holy name of the Lord, śuddha-nāma. However, nāmābhāsa, the clearing stage, dissipates the darkness of ignorance and eradicates the reactions of sinful life. This is in itself a very extensive topic. We will speak about chanting from that platform, more than falsely trying to present that everyone will suddenly be chanting śuddha-nāma; will be seeing Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa dancing before them; Kṛṣṇa playing His all attractive flute, which is attracting all the residents of Vṛndāvana; and Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī and all the cowherd girls entering into the forest at the sound of Kṛṣṇa’s flute; and that we will be able to enter into that call also, and experience the beautiful cowherd boy standing in the groves of Vṛndāvana, by chanting His name, seeing Him and experiencing Him with all of our senses. We can hanker for that, and certainly, we should aspire for it, as we should know that that is the goal of our chanting. There should be no doubt, and one should have faith in this goal. However, we will discuss herein chanting on the platform of nāmābhāsa.

Although we may be struggling sādhakas, we should still have faith that by chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa we can achieve all perfection.

*ajñaś cāśraddadhānaś ca*  
*saṁśayātmā vinaśyati*  
*nāyaṁ loko ’sti na paro*  
*na sukhaṁ saṁśayātmanaḥ*

**“But ignorant and faithless persons who doubt the revealed scriptures do not attain God consciousness; they fall down. For the doubting soul there is happiness neither in this world nor in the next.” (Bg. 4.40)**

Kṛṣṇa is speaking about three types of persons: ajñaḥ (the ignorant person), aśraddadhānaḥ (the faithless person) and saṁśaya ātmā (the person who is a doubter). There is distinction between each one. Kṛṣṇa says that ajñaḥ, which is compared to a fully ignorant person, is just like a foolish animal, which cannot achieve the pure state of God consciousness due to having insufficient brain substance. For the aśraddadhānaḥ, those who are faithless, they have some knowledge of the scriptures, but when they see some contradictions or hear contradictory statements spoken by different representatives of the scripture, they cannot have any faith in it. The doubter has some faith, but when he reads the scripture, he thinks, “This is nice, but I don’t know if it’s going to be effective in my case.” Thus, although he has faith, he always doubts and cannot apply himself with conviction, optimism and hope. Kṛṣṇa therefore says that even an ignorant person can experience some flickering happiness and sense enjoyment in this world, but the doubting soul can neither experience happiness in this world nor on the spiritual platform.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura has composed the following bhajana, entitled Dalalera-gītā—The Song of the Broker:

1\) I am singing news of the greatest happiness! At the place known as Surabhi Kuñja in Śrī Navadvīpa, the marketplace of the holy name has now been opened—and Lord Nityānanda Himself is the proprietor.

2\) Such wonderful things are going on in that blissful marketplace! Śrī Nityānanda Prabhu is selling the pure holy name wholesale, merely for the price of one’s faith.

3\) Seeing the assembly of devotees eagerly waiting to purchase the name, Lord Nityānanda first examines each of them to test their qualification; then He sells them the name by bargaining for His price accordingly.

4\) O my dear friends! If you really want to buy this pure holy name, then just come along with me, for I am now going to meet with this Nityānanda Mahājana.

5\) Thus, you will finally be able to acquire the pure holy name. I will also take my due commission, and in this way all three of us will fulfill our desires.

6\) Śrī Nityānanda Prabhu is so extraordinarily merciful— accepting only one’s faith in the holy name, He bestows the topmost divine bliss.

7\) When Nitāi sees a tear welling in someone’s eye upon chanting the name of Gaura! He instantly gives His support to that person; indeed, He bestows all divine opulences.

8\) He gives that person genuine realization of the pure teachings of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as found in the Bhagavad-gītā and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. While displaying all this inconceivable mercy, He pays no attention to one’s caste, material wealth, mundane knowledge, or physical ability.

9\) Now, dear friends, please reject all of māyā’s entangling snares. If you are a householder, then just remain at your home; if you are renounced, then just live in the forest. Either way, nothing more will trouble you.

10\) We no longer need to fear the terrible Age of Quarrel, for the most merciful Lord Nityānanda gives the holy name to anyone and everyone—even to the lowest among men.

11\) Bhaktivinoda loudly calls out and proclaims to all, “Other than then lotus feet of Lord Nityānanda, there is no shelter!”

This is Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura’s description of the marketplace of the holy name and how Lord Nityānanda distributes the holy name for the price of one’s faith. Faith is the most important commodity and asset that one can possibly obtain. If one has faith that by chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa he can become a lover of God, then he can go on struggling. Being a struggling sādhaka is not in itself considered to be something that is negative. It does not mean that one is fallen, incompetent or incapable. The fact that one is struggling is auspicious. Prabhupāda often said that when we are struggling, at least we are endeavoring to overcome obstacles. However, when we give up struggling, then Māyā, who is more powerful than us, will easily capture us, take us over and we can easily fall victim to the objects of sense enjoyment.

Kṛṣṇa says:

*teṣāṁ satata-yuktānāṁ*  
*bhajatāṁ prīti-pūrvakam*  
*dadāmi buddhi-yogaṁ taṁ*  
*yena mām upayānti te*

**“To those who are constantly devoted to serving Me with love, I give the understanding by which they can come to Me.” (Bg. 10.10)**

Thus, to be struggling is not a sign of a weakness, but rather of strength. However, when one stops struggling, then he becomes very weak. Faith is therefore required to go on chanting.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura speaks about patience in Śrī Bhaktyāloka and explains that everyone—the jñānīs, karmīs and bhaktas—is endeavoring for some result. The karmīs want some fruitive result for their sacrifice; the jñānīs want to achieve liberation as a result of their austerities; and the bhaktas want Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure. Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains that sometimes when bhaktas do not achieve their result, they give up their practices in sādhana due to weakness. Patience is therefore required. A devotee should be patient and should be convinced that he will get Kṛṣṇa’s mercy—either now, one year from now, ten years from now, a hundred years from now, or many lifetimes from now. This type of patience is required to achieve success in devotional service. Convinced of this, the devotee will go on chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa and endeavoring to please Kṛṣṇa.

To become convinced, we have to associate with those who have very strong faith. To determine if we are actually making progress, we should be looking to see if our faith in the process of pure devotional service, in the process of chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, and in the process of association with Vaiṣṇavas is becoming stronger.

For a devotee who is preaching to others, he is always very eager to see a result. Some may say that we are not supposed to look for results. However, a devotee is not looking for a result for himself. He simply wants to see others’ faith grow in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Prabhupāda explains that a person may take to a religious path simply to achieve some prestige, position, respect, or profit. However, when a person is preaching Kṛṣṇa consciousness, he is looking for faith, as it is the most valuable currency in the marketplace of the holy name of the Lord. Likewise, for one who is coming to associate with other devotees, he should be looking for someone who has strong faith, which will enable his currency to also grow.

We see that in the business world, people who want to increase their wealth tend to associate with somebody who can teach them how to make good investments. I remember hearing that there was some kind of seminar with Donald Trump and George Foreman. People were paying good money to get their association, as they are people who have demonstrated that they have success in the business world, and that they know how to make good investments and get good returns. Thus, the attendees were hoping that by investing some money in the seminar, they would learn how to take whatever money they have in their storehouse and make investments so that they can get good returns. This is the marketplace of the material world, where everybody is looking to increase their wealth, and thereby presumably increase their enjoyment. However, in the marketplace of the holy name of the Lord, the only currency that is accepted and which has value is faith. Thus, one who has a little faith thinks about how they can invest their faith and get a good return, which would be increased faith.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says:

4\) O my dear friends! If you really want to buy this pure holy name, then just come along with me, for I am now going to meet with this Nityānanda Mahājana.

5\) You will be able to acquire the holy name. I will take my commission, and in this way all three of us will fulfill our desires.” (Dalalera-gītā)

Sometimes a salesman will go and purchase the commodity, and then will go and sell all that he has purchased. Having obtained all his money back, he will purchase some more of the commodity. A broker (dālāl), however, will bring the purchaser directly to the wholesaler to obtain the pure holy name of the Lord, and he will just take a commission. The distributor simply wants to see everyone’s faith increasing.

Faith, being the only currency in the marketplace of the holy name, has the greatest value. However, even if we have no faith, Lord Nityānanda can distribute the holy name in such a way as to create that faith.

*śuśrūṣoḥ śraddadhānasya*  
*vāsudeva-kathā-ruciḥ*  
*syān mahat-sevayā viprāḥ*  
*puṇya-tīrtha-niṣevaṇāt*

**“O twice-born sages, by serving those devotees who are completely freed from all vice, great service is done. By such service, one gains affinity for hearing the messages of Vāsudeva.” (Bhāg. 1.2.16)**

In one lecture, Śrīla Prabhupāda had said to his disciples, “I have given you your faith.” Prabhupāda, the merciful representative of Lord Nityānanda, came selflessly, not wanting anything, living so austerely with persons who had no understanding whatsoever of Vedic culture, tradition, and etiquette, and yet extended himself to the most fallen. His method of distribution was so powerful that it created faith: “If Swamījī chants Hare Kṛṣṇa, then I’ll chant Hare Kṛṣṇa. If it’s good enough for the Swamījī, it’s good enough for me!” As Prabhupāda said, example is sometimes even more important than the precept.

*mahāprabhoḥ kīrtana-nṛtya-gīta-*  
*vāditra-mādyan-manaso rasena*

**Chanting the holy name, dancing in ecstasy, singing, and playing musical instruments, the spiritual master is always gladdened by the saṅkīrtana movement of Lord Caitanya Mahāprabhu. (Śrī Śrī Gurv-aṣṭaka, Verse 2)**

Similarly, when Lord Nityānanda would distribute the holy name of the Lord with tears in His eyes, He would go from door to door, begging, “Please, take up the chanting. Please chant Kṛṣṇa’s names. Worship Kṛṣṇa. Make Kṛṣṇa your life.” He would do it in such a selfless way that He would awaken faith.

The ācāryas give the example that when a person wants to sell a product, sometimes he will send out people into the street to give out a small free sample of the product. If somebody just uses that small sample and sees its benefits, he will go back and purchase a big bottle.

Lord Nityānanda and Śrīla Prabhupāda distributed the holy name in the same way. Seeing Śrīla Prabhupāda chanting, awakened faith in us to chant. By beginning with that little faith in someone who has deep faith, and by continuing to invest our faith in that person, the result is that we get a good return from our investment.

Thus the evolution of chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa is from chanting on the platform of faith. As an attempt to chant from the platform of faith, we try to increase our faith. Ultimately, we want to come to the topmost platform of devotional service where we have firm faith, never sway from the truth, and are personally experiencing Kṛṣṇa manifesting and dancing on our tongue.

*‘śraddhā’-śabde—viśvāsa kahe sudṛḍha niścaya*  
*kṛṣṇe bhakti kaile sarva-karma kṛta haya*

**raddhā is confident, firm faith that by rendering transcendental loving service to Kṛṣṇa one automatically performs all subsidiary activities. Such faith is favorable to the discharge of devotional service. (Cc. Madhya 22.62)**

Sometimes it is hard to maintain that conviction in the face of many other obligations that one has to confront when living outside the temple, working, maintaining family and maintaining one’s own body.
