When the heart becomes clean, then gradually we will begin to realize how we are simply the eternal servants of Kṛṣṇa and our eternal residence is there with Him in Goloka Vṛndāvana, serving the eternal associates of the Lord in His presence.

Prabhupāda came to this world from the spiritual world in the same mood as Lord Caitanya to give us the greatest and most valuable gift—the congregational chanting of the holy names of the Lord. Lord Caitanya stated:

*yuga-dharma pravartāimu nāma-saṅkīrtana*  
*cāri bhāva-bhakti diyā nācāmu bhuvana*

**“I shall personally inaugurate the religion of the age—nāma-saṅkīrtana, the congregational chanting of the holy name. I shall make the world dance in ecstasy, realizing the four mellows of loving devotional service. (Cc. Ādi 3.19)**

Śrīla Prabhupāda has appeared to fulfill that mission. Simply by chanting the holy names of the Lord in cāri bhāva-bhakti diyā, one will be able to realize these four ecstatic mellows of loving devotional service (dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya and mādhurya). Prabhupāda makes the point in Caitanya-caritāmṛta that the fifth bhāva (śānta) is not mentioned, because generally śānta-rasa is not present in Goloka Vṛndāvana.

Our goal should be to please Śrīla Prabhupāda, to please our spiritual master, make sacrifices, cultivate this Vṛndāvana mood of selfless service, and prepare ourselves for going back home, back to Godhead. That was Prabhupāda’s blessing upon all of us when he appeared in 1965 on the Jaladuta at Boston Commonwealth Pier and wrote Mārkine Bhāgavata-dharma. It is one of the most wonderful prayers to Kṛṣṇa, in which he says, “I wish that You may deliver them all.” We are the object of that wish. When the pure devotee makes such a wish to Kṛṣṇa, then Kṛṣṇa will always fulfill his desire. We all have the great fortune of receiving that blessing. Be assured that if we simply stay in the association of these Vaiṣṇavas, that blessing will be realized in the hearts of each and every one of us.

## Pleasing Prabhupāda

In the series called Following Śrīla Prabhupāda, Yadubara Prabhu has compiled all the footage that was ever taken of Śrīla Prabhupāda and put it together on DVDs. He has interviewed many of the devotees who were present during each of the līlās shown on the DVD. While you are watching Śrīla Prabhupāda, you are hearing all the devotees in the background who were present in that particular place, at that particular time, telling all their remembrances and experiences they had with Śrīla Prabhupāda. It actually makes you feel that you are right there, experiencing it.

There is one story of when Prabhupāda was in California. I was not there at that time, but the devotees were telling different stories of Prabhupāda’s visit to Los Angeles. One devotee was telling the story of when Prabhupāda decided to print seventeen volumes of Caitanya-caritāmṛta in two months. Hearing the complete narration of how the events unfolded was very moving and inspiring.

Many of the devotees from the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust (BBT) were on a morning walk with Śrīla Prabhupāda on Venice Beach in Los Angeles, and they were discussing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s translation work with him. Prabhupāda was inquiring why they were so far behind. He said that he was working so much on the books, but it was taking so long to publish them. Prabhupāda then turned to the devotee who was in charge of the BBT at that time and told him that he wanted the books to be published faster. He told the BBT devotees to go discuss among themselves to see how long it would take for them to publish the books.

The devotees could understand that Śrīla Prabhupāda really felt a sense of urgency to print these books quickly. They therefore stood aside, leaving Śrīla Prabhupāda and the other devotees to continue on the walk. They had a long discussion on how they could increase the pace of publishing his books. They came up with what they thought was a really good plan, and they wanted to bring it back to Śrīla Prabhupāda, expecting that he would be very pleased by their proposal.

They met up with Śrīla Prabhupāda and said, “Śrīla Prabhupāda, we have been talking among ourselves while you were walking, and we decided that we will be able to change the speed by which we can publish your books now.”

Śrīla Prabhupāda said, “Oh? Tell me how long will it take?”

They said, “By making all these different changes and arrangements, we concluded that we will be able to produce one book every two months.”

Prabhupāda responded, “What? Two months for one book? No, I want all books published in two months!” That meant seventeen books in two months! The devotees stood in shock. Their mouths dropped. One devotee explained on the DVD how his mind was completely suspended in time and space. His head and mind were reeling. When the spiritual master gives an instruction like that, especially in those days, you did not think to do otherwise. Therefore, when Prabhupāda said, “This is the way it has to be done,” then that is just the way it had to be done.

However, still this devotee said, “Śrīla Prabhupāda, I think it will be impossible to produce seventeen volumes in two months.” Prabhupāda took his cane, dug it into the sand, and looked very seriously into the devotee’s eyes and said, “Impossible is a word that is only in a fool’s dictionary. Two months!” Therefore, the devotees had to go back again and discuss how they were going to accomplish Prabhupāda’s order.

I specifically remember this time. Although I was not there at the time when this discussion took place, it was the topic in every temple. In those days, whatever Prabhupāda said, whatever Prabhupāda did, and as soon as he made some particular outstanding statement in a lecture, everybody was on the phone, calling devotees all over the world. There was no internet, so you couldn’t post the information on a blog. Therefore, everybody was on the phone, informing the other devotees, “Prabhupāda said this, and Prabhupāda said that.”

Once Prabhupāda told the temple president in Chicago during the marathon, “One devotee should stay back to worship the deities and everybody else should go out on saṅkīrtana.” Immediately after he said that, the devotees were on the phone, calling the other temples, saying, “Prabhupāda said that he wants one devotee back at the temple and everybody else out distributing books.”

Not only did the one devotee who stayed back have to prepare breakfast and lunch, but since most temples in the West at that time all had Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa deities, they had to prepare more than 6 offerings for the deities. Therefore, the devotee would have to cook all those offerings, transfer on the plates, wash the pots, etc. However, Prabhupāda would say it, and as soon as he would, the message would spread everywhere.

In another instance, I was the traveling saṅkīrtana-leader in 1975, and I was traveling in a van, distributing books. Prabhupāda was in Atlanta, speaking to many devotees from the Rādhā-Dāmodara traveling party. Prabhupāda said to the devotees, “Devotees who travel in vans and distribute my books get my extra special mercy!” That quote then immediately went out everywhere.

At that particular time, I was distributing books for probably ten to twelve hours a day, seven days a week. On Sunday, we would stay back in the afternoon and have our feast of fruit salad. Otherwise, we would be out distributing books, usually from 9 o’clock in the morning until 9 o’clock at night. On Saturday nights, we used to stay out until 1 or 2 o’clock in the morning. Therefore, I remember that when I heard this quote from Prabhupāda—“When you travel in a van and distribute my books, you will get extra special mercy”—I was thinking, “I am already getting so much mercy, and now Prabhupāda is saying he is ready to give some extra special mercy! I don’t know what that extra special mercy could possibly be, but whatever it is, I want it!”

Therefore, I sat down with the devotees in my saṅkīrtana party and discussed how we could get this extra special mercy. We decided to increase our time on saṅkīrtana, because we all agreed that if Prabhupāda is ready to give extra special mercy, then we should not miss out on this rare opportunity.

Although Prabhupāda’s statements were immediately circulated throughout the whole movement, sometimes it did not work well, because sometimes Prabhupāda would give a particular instruction that was specifically for one devotee, and not for everybody in general. If somebody would hear that Prabhupāda said it to that one devotee, then immediately they would get on the phone and say “Prabhupāda said…” when Prabhupāda did not mean it for everybody.

On one occasion, devotees were telling Śrīla Prabhupāda that they were distributing candy canes on saṅkīrtana. They were offering them to the deities and were distributing them as prasādam to everybody in a happy spirit while they were distributing books. Prabhupāda told the devotee, “Yes, for preaching, you can even offer these candy canes to the deities.” Within a few days, in all the temples, devotees offered candy canes to the deities on the altar. Everybody thought that Prabhupāda wanted the deities to have candy canes. This is just one of the many examples of how word would spread for anything Prabhupāda said.

Thus, in this way, I had also heard about the conversation that Prabhupāda had with the devotees about printing seventeen volumes of books in two months, as the word had spread very fast.

When Prabhupāda gave this order and said that impossible is a word in a fool’s dictionary, the devotees stepped back from the walk again. The first thing they had to do was accept what Prabhupāda wanted, and accept that they therefore had to do it. As soon as they accepted that collectively in their minds, they felt Kṛṣṇa’s reciprocation. Many ideas then started to come to their minds for things they could do. They decided that they would have to bring to Los Angeles all the New York devotees who were working on prepress (typing and transcribing), as well as all the artists. The devotees discussed, “We can get a whole backup team of devotees who can cook for these devotees and wash their clothes so that they can work all day long.” They went back to Śrīla Prabhupāda and told him their plan for finishing the books in two months. Prabhupāda said, “Do it!”

The devotees proceeded with this plan. The artists, transcribers, typists and everyone else would work until they dropped. When they dropped, a fresh person who had just gotten some rest would immediately be sent in to replace them and continue the work. They would alternate in this way, thus ensuring that the work was continuing 24 hours a day. As a result, many of the paintings in Caitanya-caritāmṛta were done by several artists. One artist would start, and when they could not keep their eyes open and would fall on the floor, they were pulled away, and another artist was sent in to continue. Many paintings had at least four or five artists working on them. Some of the paintings were completed so fast, and not very meticulously.

The devotees therefore came up with and executed this plan when Prabhupāda gave the order to publish the seventeen volumes in two months. Sometimes Prabhupāda had this capacity to really push very hard for a particular result, and the devotees would just have to surrender. At other times, however, he would be very soft and not push at all.

In 1975, Prabhupāda was really pushing book distribution. He was making so many statements that would drive the devotees mad to go out to distribute books, such as, “Ultimately, if you want to please me in the highest way, then you will preach and distribute my books.” 1975 was also the year that Prabhupāda was in Los Angeles and made the famous statement: “Just print as many books as possible in as many languages as possible and distribute them all over the world!” Many of the famous quotes that Prabhupāda made about book distribution that we have enshrined in our movement today were made in 1975. He was really pushing the devotees to go out and distribute his books.

As soon as the volumes of Caitanya-caritāmṛta started being published, Prabhupāda would immediately have them sent out to all the temples in America—each temple receiving their own quota. As soon as the books would arrive, we would unload them from the truck and go out and distribute them all. No one even thought about keeping some books in the temple. We did not think that Prabhupāda was also publishing these books for us. We were just so fixed that Prabhupāda wanted these books distributed. Finally, we realized that we did not have any books in the temple, as we had enthusiastically distributed all of them. We then had to make a special order to get more books so that we could make a library for the devotees to read the books at the temple.

We see in Govardhana-līlā how Kṛṣṇa established that He wants quantity. He wanted a large quantity of bhoga to be offered for Govardhana-pūjā. Even though all the residents of Vṛndāvana offered such large quantities of foodstuff for the pleasure of Girirāja, and Kṛṣṇa Himself even assumed the form of Girirāja to accept those offerings, still, after taking everything, Kṛṣṇa said “Aniyor! Aniyor! Give Me more! Give Me more!” They had already prepared mountains and mountains of different types of preparations. Yet Kṛṣṇa wanted the devotees to give Him more and more.

We also see this demonstrated by Lord Caitanya in the mahāprakāśa-līlā. During His ecstasy of 21 hours, He stood on the altar and revealed His divinity to His devotees. Before that, He would only from time to time reveal something special about Himself as being divine, and only very briefly, because He was in the mood of a devotee. However, in this particular pastime, for 21 hours He took the position of the Supreme Lord. He stood on the altar and told the devotees, “Now sing My abhiṣeka song!” The devotees then performed abhiṣeka.

The Lord started taking offerings from the hands of the devotees, and He would eat everything that they would bring to Him. When the devotees started to pick up on the Lord’s mood—that He wanted more and more—then they would go out to all the merchants and purchase everything from them and bring it back and give it to Lord Caitanya. Although Lord Caitanya would eat everything, the devotees could see that He still wanted more. Thus they would go to more places and bring back everything they possibly could, such as sandeśa, sweet rice, thousands of pots of Ganges water and fruits. As soon as they would offer it to Lord Caitanya, He would consume it immediately. The devotees could understand that the Lord simply wanted their offerings. This is therefore another example of how the Lord established quantity as a means for satisfying Him. Similarly, Prabhupāda also pushed for publishing seventeen books in two months.

Kṛṣṇa says in so many places that He is satisfied even with the smallest offering—even a leaf, fruit, flower, or a little water—if it is offered with love and devotion. There are so many examples in śāstra of how devotees did not have very much to offer the Lord, but the Lord would be so pleased by their offering that He would take it even before they would offer it. Thus quality is certainly an important factor in the attitude in which the devotee is making the offering for the pleasure of the Lord. Quality is when one makes their offering with love. The Lord is very eager to accept such offerings. Being very pleased, He will give us benedictions. Sometimes He will even take His devotee back home, back to Godhead, for such small services.

An example of this is given in Caitanya-caritāmṛta about the dog that was favored by Śivānanda Sena. Śivānanda Sena would make many arrangements for this dog to travel with them, and he would even pay the boatman for the dog’s passage.

One day, that dog could not be found, and Śivānanda Sena sent ten men out to look for it. Śivānanda Sena fasted, refusing to eat until the dog was found. The men could not find the dog. The next day, they arrived at Purī, and when they came to Lord Caitanya, they saw Him feeding coconut pulp to the dog. Śivānanda Sena immediately got down to offer his daṇḍavats to the dog, because he realized, “This is not an ordinary soul.” The next day the dog disappeared and went to Vaikuṇṭha, because he was the recipient of the favor of the Lord’s devotee.

There are many examples in śāstra, where the soul did not have to do very much to obtain the mercy of the Lord. There is a dichotomy here. Sometimes the Lord accepts just the quality and the essence of the offering, but sometimes the Lord wants a lot. Sometimes His devotee also wants a lot, just like Prabhupāda did, when he said, “Seventeen volumes in two months!” Therefore, we have to be prepared for whatever the Lord or His devotee wants.

We should not be satisfied with only offering a little. We should try our best to offer as much as we possibly can—especially if we consider that Kṛṣṇa wants everything we have. When a devotee offers everything to the Lord and accepts whatever is set aside as his quota, then that is prasāda.

There are many examples in the scriptures of how the Lord requests more and more from His devotees. If we have the fortune to be put in that situation, then we should accept it as an opportunity for increasing our service to the Lord.

There is the example of Sanātana Gosvāmī, who would go on a parikramā of Govardhana every day. When he did parikramā, he did not take the usual path, which is about 22 kilometers. Rather, he would take the road by Candra-sarovara and go all the way around, which is about 40 kilometers. He would do this parikramā every day. That was his worship of Girirāja. Even when he was getting so old that it was becoming very difficult for him to do this parikramā, he would do it anyway. He never thought about doing a shorter parikramā.

One day, a young boy came to Sanātana Gosvāmī and said, “You are getting old! Why are you walking such a long distance? It is certainly becoming very difficult for you to do this! Why do you need to undergo this austerity? You should walk much less now.”

Sanātana Gosvāmī said, “No, it is my vow to do this parikramā every day.”

The little boy went to Govardhana Hill and took a stone from there that had an imprint of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet on it. Girirāja would oftentimes go into ecstasy because Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma were walking on Him. When He would go into ecstasy, then all the stones on His body would melt under Kṛṣṇa’s feet. Thus Kṛṣṇa’s footprint would be left in many places all over Girirāja where He would walk. The boy took this stone with Kṛṣṇa’s footprint and gave it to Sanātana Gosvāmī and said, “From now on, you should just walk around this stone. That will be as good as walking around Govardhana Hill.”

Sanātana Gosvāmī took the stone, and when the boy left, he realized that that boy was actually Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa knew how much Sanātana Gosvāmī was committed to walking around Girirāja every day. He therefore personally appeared before him and said, “Now you walk around this stone, because you are getting old and it is becoming too difficult for you.” Thus Kṛṣṇa knows how much we can push ourselves.

The same thing happened with Mādhavendra Purī when he was carrying one maund (about 82 pounds) of sandalwood and camphor. The Lord appeared to Mādhavendra Purī in a dream and said, “Instead of carrying all this sandalwood back to Me, just put it on the body of Gopīnātha. It is as good as putting it on My body!”

Thus the Lord knows when we are giving everything that we have and doing everything that we possibly can for Him. He will make the arrangements so that we do not have to push ourselves beyond what we are physically capable of doing. However, sometimes He wants us to push ourselves, and if that is His will, we should be ready to do it for Him or for His devotee. By pleasing Prabhupāda, we will certainly please the Lord.

**Question: Why did Śrīla Prabhupāda push so hard for the publishing of his books?**

He knows that others in this world under the influence of Kṛṣṇa’s external energy are destined to suffer. Out of compassion, the devotee thinks of how he can induce them to do something for Kṛṣṇa. He feels that compassion burning in his heart.

That is how Śrīla Prabhupāda was thinking when he was present here on this planet. His heart was burning with compassion: “How can I get this message to as many people as possible?” The devotees who were present during Śrīla Prabhupāda’s manifest presence in this world felt Prabhupāda’s sense of urgency. His own spiritual master, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Gosvāmī Mahārāja, told Śrīla Prabhupāda, “This message is urgent. It cannot wait.”

Prabhupāda had that same sense of urgency. His heart was filled with compassion, and he wanted everybody to get the opportunity to get a little of that taste. Kṛṣṇa arranges it in such a way that you can get that taste by serving His pure devotee. By doing something that will please him, you can please Kṛṣṇa. You can please Prabhupāda and you can please Kṛṣṇa at the same time. Prabhupāda had that potency to express his desire, and he expressed it in such a way that the devotees became mad about fulfilling Prabhupāda’s desires. Prabhupāda just had to say what his desire was, and immediately the devotees were driven like mad, running after the opportunity. During Śrīla Prabhupāda’s manifest presence, what his followers had to do if they wanted to please him was crystal clear in their eyes.

## Taking Shelter of a Spiritual Master

**Question: Sometimes when we see one guru leading very nice kīrtanas, we become very much inspired by those kīrtanas. Then when we see another guru giving wonderful lectures, we become inspired by those lectures. Sometimes we become inspired by the personality of another guru based on his dealings with us. Additionally, there is a large number of spiritual masters in ISKCON. What is the basis of choosing a spiritual master when you feel inspired by different aspects of different spiritual masters?**

You should accept the spiritual master within whom you see Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇa’s will. A spiritual master is Kṛṣṇa’s representative. The whole process of devotional service is the development of faith. Someone may create or awaken faith within our hearts, but whose instructions are actually nurturing that faith, nourishing it, and causing that faith to establish that connection with Kṛṣṇa? Whose instructions do we fall back on when we are facing some difficult moments or tests? Whose instructions become the stick that we carry to help us to continue to walk on the path even though our feet may slip?

Thus, there has to be substance in a relationship. It cannot be based upon some fleeting, potentially sentimental notion about a relationship that we may wish to establish with someone because of their good kīrtana or because they happen to give a nice class. That is a very sentimental foundation for accepting a spiritual master. You have to go deeper than that.

If one really wants to accept a spiritual master, he has to be prepared to do the ground work. It is not such a cheap thing for Kṛṣṇa to manifest Himself before us as guru. The ground work is to be praying for it every day as part of our bhajana: “Kṛṣṇa, please reveal Yourself to me through the words of my spiritual master.” If we have that sincere desire and sincerely pray in that way, then we will get help.

Prabhupāda explains that by accepting the spiritual master, one gets help from the Lord within the heart. He then also gets help externally from the manifestation of guru who is the external manifestation of the Supersoul.

When that instruction is confirmed in our hearts by testing (not by blindly accepting) that faith by applying their instructions through vāṇī, then we will see that our faith will build around the instructions of a particular personality who may be our shelter. If we continue to pray daily, then Kṛṣṇa will direct us to accept Him through the words of a particular Vaiṣṇava. One will then receive initiation, which is the beginning.

Some people think that initiation is the end. However, Prabhupāda very clearly states that once you have taken shelter of the bona fide spiritual master and have taken initiation from him, then that is the beginning. We should not try to position ourselves in just the right way to get the recognition or recommendation that we want to get the personality we want. We cannot externally get the attention of the spiritual master and expect that to be our methodology for achieving Kṛṣṇa.

There was a maidservant of Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura whose name was Dukhī. Every day she would bring water for Lord Caitanya’s bath and would leave it in front of the door. The Lord would come and see the water there every day, but Dukhī was never standing there saying, “Look at me. I brought the water.” She was always some place far away. After seeing the water there every day, the Lord asked, “Who has brought this?”

“It was Dukhī.”

Lord Caitanya said, “Dukhī (sad)? No, within my heart she will always be Sukhī (happy).”

By serving in that way with faith, Kṛṣṇa will manifest before us through the words of the spiritual master.

Accepting a spiritual master is not based upon something external, but rather on something very internal—our faith and application of their instructions. Kṛṣṇa will then reveal Himself to us.

**Question: Although we hear lectures of various spiritual masters in ISKCON, it is often hard to get their personal time. Therefore, how can we determine who should be our spiritual master?**

It is not a cheap thing for Kṛṣṇa to manifest Himself in our heart and for us to get confirmation that the instructions of a particular spiritual master are the foundation for our faith in devotional service. Prabhupāda gave the analogy that you must first prepare the soil before the seed can be planted. Similarly, we have to do our work to prepare ourselves.

It is according to scriptural injunction that one has to test the spiritual master before accepting him, and the spiritual master has to test the disciple. There are various ways of associating with the spiritual master through his representatives, which enables us to test him. Prabhupāda said in a purport in Bhāgavatam that the disciples have to be representatives and have to be prepared to defeat others’ arguments on behalf of the spiritual master. They have to be able to defeat the arguments of the candidates for devotional service, and nourish their faith. Thus the spiritual master also has representatives. So if one may not have direct association with the spiritual master, then the spiritual master is thinking of how to give his association in other ways to make himself personally accessible.

If the spiritual master is somebody from whom we regularly hear, who awakens some faith in our hearts, then we should also seek out those who properly represent him, and see how they can help us overcome our doubts and nourish our strength in devotional service. We should see them as representing the spiritual master, which is as good as getting the association of the spiritual master. Once that faith is awakened, it has to be nourished. Without puṣṭiḥ, it is very difficult to advance in spiritual life. One has to become very eager to seek it out.

**Question: What kind of personal experience did you have with Śrīla Prabhupāda?**

I did not have much association with Śrīla Prabhupāda. I saw him several times. However, Prabhupāda knew better and always kept me at a distance.

I was with him in Māyāpura when he was giving lectures in 1976. I saw him in Ratha Yātrā in New York in 1976. I also saw him in New York in 1975. I cleaned his room for him in Vṛndāvana in 1976, but before Prabhupāda entered the room his servants said, “Everybody get out of here. Prabhupāda is coming!” Therefore, my observation was always from a distance. I never had personal association with Prabhupāda.

However, usually when anyone asks me when I first met Prabhupāda, I always tell them that it was in 1972. It was in the bookstore on Connecticut Avenue in Washington D.C. I went in, looking for a book on yoga, and I saw Bhagavad-gītā As It Is sitting on the bookshelf. I opened it up, and I landed on the page with the picture of the yogī sitting in meditation and his soul is going to the spiritual world. I said to myself, “This looks like a very good book on yoga. I am going to purchase it.” That was my first meeting with Śrīla Prabhupāda. I started to read the book every night after work. In fact, I found out many years later from a devotee that he had placed that Bhagavad-gītā in the bookstore; it was not part of the bookstore’s stock. The bookstore simply charged me the price that was indicated on the back of the book. That is how I met Prabhupāda for the first time.

## Serving the Mood and Instructions of the Spiritual Master

**Question: How can we develop our taste for serving the spiritual master?**

Sometimes devotees are very enthusiastic when they are in the physical presence of guru, but when he leaves, then somehow that enthusiasm and steadiness dissipates. Steadiness comes from the following: faith, chanting, hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā, devotion, inspiration, discipline, the desire to please the guru, and understanding and serving the internal mood of the spiritual master. It is very important to serve the mood and instructions of the spiritual master.

Spiritual life does not work without spiritual inspiration. Somebody may be inspired to work very hard, but if it is not spiritual inspiration, it is simply for the purpose of getting something material. However, work done from spiritual inspiration is not with the aim of getting anything material. In other words, they are not inspired to work very hard because they are getting a lot of money, a comfortable situation, prestige, or any position. If it is not spiritual inspiration, it will not last long; it may last for some time, but it will distract one from spiritual life. Then when one is exposed to some spiritual inspiration, it will be perceived as something material. He will then think, “Why should I do these things that are spiritually inspiring if I am getting so much inspiration from something else? I get more inspiration from being comfortable, having money, material security, etc. Why should I associate with people who have some attraction for spiritual life? There is no inspiration there.”

However, everybody needs spiritual inspiration. Without it, it is very difficult to be motivated to work hard and to do something without the aim of getting some material fruit from it. Inspiration comes from association with devotees. When we learn how to appreciate the association of devotees, then we can be very inspired to be in their association and to do the things that devotees should naturally be doing.

Someone may say that it is difficult to find inspirational devotees where they live. That may be the case, but the more one associates with devotees who really do inspire him, the more he will begin to appreciate the qualities even in the devotees who appear to not be inspirational.

To associate with devotees also means understanding the mood of the spiritual master. It is one thing to superficially take the instructions of the spiritual master, but it is another thing to understand the internal mood of the spiritual master. For example, if the spiritual master instructs us to associate with devotees, then understanding the internal mood of the spiritual master means developing the vision to see all the good qualities in the association of devotees. The spiritual master has his internal mood and vision. We must look at what it is that inspires him to preach. He never looks at everybody and says, “Everybody is not so advanced! They have so many bad qualities. Why should I want to associate with all these people? Maybe I should just sit in my room, read Prabhupāda’s books, chant Hare Kṛṣṇa, become a bābājī or go to Rādhā-kuṇḍa. Forget about all these people. There is nothing good in any of them. Nobody has real inspirational qualities!”

Therefore, why is the spiritual master inspired to preach? What is his internal mood that gives him that inspiration to give Kṛṣṇa consciousness to others? His internal mood is that he sees Kṛṣṇa in the hearts of others. He sees the potential for devotional service in their heart. He sees that everybody is a potential devotee of Kṛṣṇa. We simply have to inspire them to serve Kṛṣṇa by giving them an opportunity to come in contact with Kṛṣṇa. If they are not inspired to serve Kṛṣṇa, then we should be thinking, “I have not really given them an opportunity to come in contact with Kṛṣṇa.”

Thus the spiritual master preaches because he sees Kṛṣṇa in everyone’s heart and he sees the potential for devotional service in everyone’s heart. He therefore sees that everyone has these good qualities. They are coming for a reason! They are coming to hear because they want something. Therefore, there must be good qualities in them. Even if they want something material, there is a potential to serve Kṛṣṇa in their hearts.

Sometimes people come to the temples with motivations such as wanting to see a guru to obtain blessings to get a good job, a pretty wife, a wealthy husband, etc. Even though they may not have pure motives, the potential to serve Kṛṣṇa is in their hearts. Therefore, if such people are coming, we should be thinking, “If we can simply give them Kṛṣṇa in some way, we will not be giving them a good job, a wealthy husband or a beautiful wife, but we will give something much better. They are here for some reason. Kṛṣṇa has sent them! Let us therefore give them something of greater value. Let us give them the opportunity to hear about Kṛṣṇa and we will see if they come back for more. If they come back for more, they must be sincere. If someone continues coming back even though we are not giving them something material, there must be something sincere there.”

This is the internal preaching mood of the spiritual master. The spiritual master also has his bhajana (meditation)—the things that absorb him in understanding the association of devotees who may not be surrounding him immediately. He may also be aspiring to associate with other devotees. That kind of internal inspiration is also there in the spiritual master. There are other devotees besides those who are coming to hear from him. There may be devotees who are speaking to him. Or there may be devotees who are serving Kṛṣṇa so nicely that we aspire to associate with them so that we learn how to serve Kṛṣṇa as nicely as they do. However, it is very important to understand the preaching mood of the spiritual master. By understanding it, we will never be without the association of devotees. We will associate with our spiritual master through his instructions and we will associate with other devotees by seeing their potential for devotional service. We will thus come up to a higher platform in devotional service.

**Question: It is said that to get Kṛṣṇa’s mercy, one has to get Lord Caitanya’s mercy. To get Lord Caitanya’s mercy, one has to get Lord Nityānanda’s mercy. And to get Nityānanda’s mercy, we need to get the spiritual master’s mercy. What kind of service will satisfy you to get your mercy?**

I am most satisfied when the devotees are always endeavoring to remember Kṛṣṇa and to never forget Him. In other words, I put more emphasis on sādhana. I am a firm advocate that if devotees have good sādhana, then they will be able to do anything for Kṛṣṇa. If they do not have good sādhana, then whatever they do will not last very long, and then there will be disappointment that they were not able to follow the instructions of the spiritual master. It is better to avoid being put into that disappointing situation.

If you want to satisfy me, you will rise early every morning and chant your rounds attentively. You will listen to my lectures about chanting the holy name and understand my instructions on the proper method and consciousness that one should have in chanting. Every day you will read from Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books. You will associate with devotees for the purpose of hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa. I promise that if you do this, understanding it to be the most important service to me, everything else will follow.

**Question: You have instructed that one should attentively chant the mahā-mantra. I play a recording of you chanting the mahā-mantra, and I chant along with you. Does this disturb you?**

No. Whenever I am in the temple, I am always chanting with the devotees in the temple room. It is only in instances when I am staying very far from the temple that I do not chant with the devotees in the temple. Therefore, how would I be disturbed by hearing others chanting? I am generally doing it every day.

## Chapter 8 – Vaiṣṇava Relations

## Vaiṣṇava Etiquette

Śrīla Prabhupāda has given many instructions on Vaiṣṇava etiquette in his lectures and letters. Some excerpts on this topic can be found in Prabhupāda Śikṣāmṛta. Prabhupāda Śikṣāmṛta is based on many different topics, such as chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, business and money, book distribution, the Bhaktivedanta Institute, and devotional service. The section on Vaiṣṇava Etiquette is broken down in four subtopics: general Vaiṣṇava etiquette, dress, death, and the definition of a Vaiṣṇava.

It is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:

*smartavyaḥ satataṁ viṣṇur vismartavyo na jātucit*  
*sarve vidhi-niṣedhāḥ syur etayor eva kiṅkarāḥ*

**Kṛṣṇa is the origin of Lord Viṣṇu. He should always be remembered and never forgotten at any time. All the rules and prohibitions mentioned in the śāstras should be the servants of these two principles. (Padma Purāṇa, as quoted in Cc. Madhya 22.113)**

Etiquette consists of the rules and codes of behavior that are positive for the proper exchange not only between human beings, but all living beings. Etiquette also encompasses avoiding the niṣedhas, which are prohibited activities that one should avoid since the result could be the commission of an offense or aparādha. The etymological root of the word aparādha is rādhāt arthāt ārādhanat-apagataḥ, which means to be turned away from the service of Rādhārāṇī and Her maidservants.

We must be careful about Vaiṣṇava aparādhas, as it is dangerous for our advancement in devotional service. A Vaiṣṇava is one who is the worshiper of the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, and whose aspiration is to achieve pure devotional service to Kṛṣṇa. We must be careful of anything that obstructs advancement towards pure devotional service. There is proper etiquette that must be followed in dealing with Vaiṣṇavas who are more advanced; in dealing with those who are our peers; in dealing with those who are less advanced; and even in dealing with all human beings and other species of life. A Vaiṣṇava would never think of unnecessarily committing an act of violence or killing any living being. Unnecessarily causing harm to another living being or shortening its life span within that particular body will cause it to take another birth within that particular body. Therefore, the devotee does not want to untimely end a life.

According to the codes of conduct for a human being, it is described that there are pañca-mahā-yajña—the five types of sacrifices that are supposed to be performed by householders—because, as the householder engages in daily activities, whether it is cooking or cleaning, they are causing harm to other living entities. Therefore, according to the codes of conduct, one should perform certain sacrifices to alleviate himself from the reaction of causing harm to other living beings. Of course, a Vaiṣṇava automatically performs all these sacrifices by the performance of the saṅkīrtana-yajña, which is the supreme sacrifice. Nevertheless, the point remains that according to the codes of behavior, one has to be very careful to not commit any activity that would be an act of violence or cause unnecessary disturbance to others.

There are two kinds or standards of morality: ordinary morality according to religious codes of ethics, and Vaiṣṇava morality. There is a distinction between the two. The highest platform of Vaiṣṇava morality is that whatever is pleasing to the Supreme Lord has to be accepted, and anything that is not pleasing to the Lord has to be rejected. Therefore, even if something apparently causes harm or disturbance to others, but it is the desire of the Lord, then one has to accept it as favorable for pleasing the Lord. The Bhagavad-gītā is founded on that principle—Arjuna’s unwillingness to take part in what he perceives to be the battle, not wanting to have to kill the members in the opposing army. He was choosing to take the path of least resistance and becoming a pacifist. However, Kṛṣṇa did not want that. He had a higher purpose He wanted fulfilled, and He wanted Arjuna to take part. Therefore, for Arjuna, morality meant killing.

Prabhupāda, of course, makes the distinction that there is authorized killing and unauthorized killing. He gives an example of a person who was previously engaged in military service. That person may come back from fighting in the battlefield to his homeland. If he gets into a fight, kills somebody, and is then arrested, he may offer the argument: “Why are you arresting me? I killed only one man; however I have a Medal of Honor for killing hundreds of men in battle. How is it that you are arresting me now for having killed one man?” He is arrested because the killing of the one man is unauthorized killing, whereas the killing on the battlefield was authorized.

We must be careful about discussing such things, because in modern times, people have taken so called authorized killing to an extreme, which really has no place in Vaiṣṇava etiquette or Vaiṣṇava principles. The word that is used in relation to these individuals is extremists. They have misunderstood the religious principles.

According to Vedic standards, such acts of killing were only to take place between kṣatriyas—warriors who were equally matched in power, and who had agreed and understood military ethics. They accepted them and fought on those principles. For example, they did not fight at night; they only fought during the day, and only amongst warriors. The Mahābhārata outlines in great detail the ethics that they followed.

However, nowadays, justification for killing on religious principles has been taken to the extreme where innocent civilians, including women and children, are now targets for political ambitions. We must therefore be careful when speaking about authorized killing. Today there are not any kṣatriyas like those who took part on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra.

Such is one of the symptoms of Kali-yuga—the varṇāśrama institution cannot be applied, because everyone is lower than a śūdra. We do not even see the śūdras, what to speak of kṣatriyas, and even brāhmaṇas. Kalau śūdra-sambhava—in Kali-yuga everyone is lower than a śūdra because of improper training and performance of saṁskāras.

The basis of Arjuna’s argument for not taking part in the Battle of Kurukṣetra was that if he were to kill the opposing members on the battlefield, then there would be no one to protect the women. Furthermore, if the women were not protected, then there would be varṇa-saṅkara, unwanted progeny. When there is unwanted progeny without having performed proper saṁskāras, the result is that human society becomes increasingly degraded.

Arjuna’s argument had substantial moral value. However, Kṛṣṇa had an even higher principle, and He wanted Arjuna to take part in the Battle of Kurukṣetra to fulfill His purpose, which was as follows:

*paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ*  
*vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām*  
*dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya*  
*sambhavāmi yuge yuge*

**“To deliver the pious and to annihilate the miscreants, as well as to reestablish the principles of religion, I Myself appear, millennium after millennium.” (Bg. 4.8)**

To know all the different rules of Vaiṣṇava etiquette and to apply them perfectly is not an easy task. However, we should try to understand some of these principles to avoid committing offenses unto other living beings. A Vaiṣṇava is one who is aspiring for the service of Lord Viṣṇu. However, the result of an offense or aparādha is to be kicked away from devotional service. One should therefore know what these offenses are and try to apply the Vaiṣṇava principles in his life.

One of the offenses in chanting the holy name of the Lord is called kuṭi-nāṭi, or fault-finding. This is a prevalent symptom in the Age of Kali, or the age of quarrel. In this age, people’s minds are so disturbed that just by a little provocation, there is fighting between one human being and another, between communities, and between nations. This is due to there being so much tension in the atmosphere. People’s minds are also disturbed by envy.

The following is a letter written by Śrīla Prabhupāda, wherein he talks about the interactions between Vaiṣṇavas, finding faults, how to understand envy, and how to overcome it.

Please accept my blessings. I am in due receipt of your very nice letter of January 10, 1972, and I am very much pleased by the sentiments expressed therein. It is not so much that because there may be some faults in our godbrothers and godsisters, or because there may be some mismanagement or lack of cooperation, that this is due to being impersonalists, no. It is the nature of the living condition to always have some fault. Even in the Spiritual World there is some fault and envy—sometimes the Gopis will quarrel over Krishna’s favor, and once Krishna was so much attracted to Radharani that by mistake he tried to milk the bull instead of the cow, and sometimes when the Gopis used to put on their dress and make-up for seeing Krishna, they would be too much hasty and smear kumkum and mascara in the wrong places and their ornaments and dresses would appear as if small children had been trying to dress themselves and they were not very expert, like that. There are so many examples. But it is not the same as material fault or material envy, it is transcendental because it is all based on Krishna. Sometimes when one Gopi would serve Krishna very nicely, the others would say, Oh, she has done so nicely, now let me do better for pleasing Krishna. That is envy, but it is transcendental, without malice. So we shall not expect that anywhere there is any Utopia. Rather, that is impersonalism. People should not expect that even in the Krishna Consciousness Society there will be Utopia. Because devotees are persons, therefore there will always be some lacking—but the difference is that their lacking, because they have given up everything to serve Krishna—money, jobs, reputation, wealth, big educations, everything—their lackings have become transcendental because, despite everything they may do, their topmost intention is to serve Krishna. “One who is engaged in devotional service, despite the most abominable action, is to be considered saintly because he is rightly situated.’’ The devotees of Krishna are the most exalted persons on this planet, better than kings, all of them, so we should always remember that and, like the bumblebee, always look for the nectar or the best qualities of a person. Not like the utopians, who are like the flies who always go to the open sores or find the faults in a person, and because they cannot find any utopia, or because they cannot find anyone without faults, they want to become void, merge, nothing—they think that is utopia, to become void of personality. So if there is sometimes slight disagreements between devotees, it is not due to impersonalism, but it is because they are persons, and such disagreements should not be taken very seriously. The devotee is always pessimistic about the material world, but he is very optimistic about the spiritual life; so in this way, you should consider that anyone engaged in Krishna’s service is always the best person. (Letter to Ātreya Ṛṣi—Bombay, Februay 4, 1972)

Prabhupāda is explaining that whatever appears to be a mistake in the spiritual world is actually perfect. In whatever fault or envy there seems to be, there is never any malice towards another living being. In the material world, envy is when one wants to do better than the other person by making that person look bad. That is envy with malice. One will even step on another person’s head and push him down so that he can appear to be higher.

However, in the spiritual world, one is thinking that he wants to do better. His envy is always aimed towards increasing his own determination, enthusiasm and inspiration to do something that is pleasing to Kṛṣṇa, but never in any way does it obstruct the service of another. In fact, in the spiritual world, the appearance of envy only enhances Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure; it never diminishes the service to Him, as there is no malice.

In the spiritual world, there are different camps of devotees who are trying to please the Lord, and there is competition between these camps. This competition heightens Kṛṣṇa’s ecstasy and the love the devotees have for Him. For example, Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī is Kṛṣṇa’s topmost servant, and Candrāvalī is there to increase the ecstasy of having competition between the gopīs. It adds flavor to the relationship, and Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure increases as a result of that competition. Therefore, there is no malice, as Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure is increasing.

Prabhupāda makes the point that in the spiritual world, everything is meant for Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure and everyone’s actions are always meant to please Him. Even though externally there may appear to be some fault, it is not really a fault. A fault is something that obstructs Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure, and that does not exist in the spiritual world.

However, in the material world, there are so many faults. Although the utopians say that there should be no fault, Prabhupāda explains that we actually have to look at things properly. We have to look at the motive behind the action. If there is a commission of some fault between us and another person, we must not look at it externally and judge it based on the disturbance caused to us, rather than based on Vaiṣṇava standards. We are not the center of the universe, and we are not the sole criterion of what is right and what is wrong.

According to Vaiṣṇava etiquette, a Vaiṣṇava is one who always wants to please the Supreme Lord and never wants to obstruct anybody else’s efforts to please Him. Sometimes there may be some fault externally, but if we trust that another person’s is to genuinely do something to please the Lord, then there is no question of enmity. Prabhupāda also speaks about this point (Purport to Bhāg. 7.5.12):

Everyone should be friendly for the service of the Lord. Everyone should praise another’s service to the Lord and not be proud of his own service. This is the way of Vaiṣṇava thinking, Vaikuṇṭha thinking. There may be rivalries and apparent competition between servants in performing service, but in the Vaikuṇṭha planets the service of another servant is appreciated, not condemned. This is Vaikuṇṭha competition. There is no question of enmity between servants. Everyone should be allowed to render service to the Lord to the best of his ability, and everyone should appreciate the service of others. Such are the activities of Vaikuṇṭha. Since everyone is a servant, everyone is on the same platform and is allowed to serve the Lord according to his ability. As confirmed in Bhagavad-gītā (15.15), sarvasya cāhaṁ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca: the Lord is situated in everyone’s heart, giving dictation according to the attitude of the servant. However, the Lord gives different dictation to the nondevotees and devotees. The nondevotees challenge the authority of the Supreme Lord, and therefore the Lord dictates in such a way that the nondevotees forget the Lord’s service, life after life, and are punished by the laws of nature. But when a devotee very sincerely wants to render service to the Lord, the Lord dictates in a different way. As the Lord says in Bhagavad-gītā (10.10):

*teṣāṁ satata-yuktānāṁ*  
*bhajatāṁ prīti-pūrvakam*  
*dadāmi buddhi-yogaṁ taṁ*  
*yena mām upayānti te*

“To those who are constantly devoted and worship Me with love, I give the understanding by which they can come to Me.” Everyone is actually a servant, not an enemy or friend, and everyone is working under different directions from the Lord, who directs each living entity according to his mentality.

Prabhupāda is speaking from a very elevated perspective about the Vaikuṇṭha mentality. There are different categories of devotees. The mahābhāgavata is the topmost devotee that sees everyone serving Kṛṣṇa except himself. The madhyama-adhikārī, however, makes the discrimination between the Supreme Lord, devotees of the Lord, people who are innocent, and people who are atheistic. To be able to make those distinctions, one has to be qualified.

Prabhupāda explains that the spiritual master, or a person who is on a more advanced platform, has the ability to discriminate between what is right and what is wrong, and it is his responsibility to correct—whether the person is doing something wrong or if his motive is wrong. Following proper Vaiṣṇava etiquette also means knowing how to deal with different levels of Vaiṣṇavas.

*dadāti pratigṛhṇāti*  
*guhyam ākhyāti pṛcchati*  
*bhuṅkte bhojayate caiva*  
*ṣaḍ-vidhaṁ prīti-lakṣaṇam*

**Offering gifts in charity, accepting charitable gifts, revealing one’s mind in confidence, inquiring confidentially, accepting prasāda and offering prasāda are the six symptoms of love shared by one devotee and another. (NOI, Text 4)**

When dealing with more advanced devotees, we should inquire and learn from them about how to make progress on the path of devotional service. Sometimes the person who is on the advanced platform has to accept the position of being on the superior platform in order to serve other devotees, even though he does not think himself to be on the superior platform and thinks of himself to be the servant.

Prabhupāda gave a lecture in Uppsala University in Stockholm, Sweden in 1975 about the four classes in society. There was one envious man in the audience who was listening to Prabhupāda glorify the brāhmaṇas as being the topmost. The envious man was finding faults: “By glorifying the brāhmaṇas, you are simply glorifying yourself, because you are telling us that you are a brāhmaṇa. That is why you are sitting on that fancy seat with all those flowers there, and you have all these worshipers sitting at your feet.” He was criticizing Prabhupāda for presenting the position of the brāhmaṇa as the upper rank of society and projecting himself to be one.

However, Prabhupāda very humbly defused all the arguments. He said, “No, I never said that. I am not a first class man. I have to speak what Kṛṣṇa says about the four classes, but I am a fifth class man because I am the servant of all four classes.” He was not just saying it to defuse the arguments, but rather, it was said in a state of complete humility and innocence. To any sensitive heart that heard Prabhupāda speaking, it was obvious that Prabhupāda’s heart was filled with humility. Thus, sometimes it is the duty of a person, out of humility and service to others, to point out some faults and discrepancies, because Kṛṣṇa has given the standard. When one sees that there are some discrepancies or deviations, the best way that he can serve that person is by pointing out the fault. By doing so in the mood of service, it is a lot easier for somebody to accept it. However, if he points it out in the mood of malice or envy, then the statement may not have the same effect.

Execution of the principles of Vaiṣṇava etiquette is always done in the mood of service and promoting the service of the Lord. It is still proper etiquette to point out some fault in dealings between the more advanced and the less advanced Vaiṣṇava, but only if it is done in a proper attitude of service to the Supreme Lord and service to the other Vaiṣṇavas. It is not done in the right mood if one does it based on kuṭi-nāṭi (faultfinding), pratiṣṭhāśā (desiring name and fame and for high position), jīvahiṁsā (being envious of other living entities), and pūjā (hankering for popularity). These are all faults and are called anarthas. They are like particles of dust, or little weeds that are within the heart. We must carefully clean them out of the heart. The essence of association with devotees, chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa and hearing Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and Kṛṣṇa’s instructions in the Bhagavad-gītā is to cleanse the mirror of the heart from these anarthas, thus allowing us to gradually realize our true spiritual identity. Ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanaṁ bhava-mahā-dāvāgni-nirvāpaṇaṁ—“Let there be all victory for the chanting of the holy name of Lord Kṛṣṇa, which can cleanse the mirror of the heart and stop the miseries of the blazing fire of material existence.” (Śikṣāṣṭaka, 1)

There are many more subtle aspects of Vaiṣṇava etiquette. There is a compilation of a course on Vaiṣṇava etiquette that was given by His Holiness Bhakti Caru Swami, which has more details on Vaiṣṇava etiquette. There are different rules and prohibitions that we should follow if we want to get to our desired destination. If we strictly follow these prescribed activities and strictly avoid the prohibited activities, then advancement will be more rapid. Kṛṣṇa says in the Bhagavad-gītā (9.27): “All that you do, all that you eat, all that you offer and give away, as well as all the austerities that you may perform, should be done as an offering unto Me.” By accepting these vidhis and niṣedhas for the purpose of trying to please the Lord, advancement in devotional service will come.

*smartavyaḥ satataṁ viṣṇur vismartavyo na jātucit*  
*sarve vidhi-niṣedhāḥ syur etayor eva kiṅkarāḥ*

**Kṛṣṇa should always be remembered and never be forgotten at any time. All the rules and prohibitions mentioned in the śāstras should be the servants of these two principles. (Padma Purāṇa, as quoted in Cc. Madhya 22.113)**

**Question: If someone follows the instructions of their spiritual master, but they have some personal motive, are they making any spiritual advancement?**

Śrīla Prabhupāda nicely answers this question within one of his purports in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam.

**The Supreme Personality of Godhead then said: O Brahmā, O depth of Vedic wisdom, be neither depressed nor anxious about the execution of creation. What you are begging from Me has already been granted before. (Bhāg. 3.9.29)**

PURPORT

Any person authorized by either the Lord or by His bona fide representative is already blessed, as is the work entrusted to him. Of course, the person entrusted with such a responsibility should always be aware of his incapability and must always look for the mercy of the Lord for the successful execution of his duty. One should not be puffed up because he is entrusted with certain executive work. Fortunate is he who is so entrusted, and if he is always fixed in the sense of being subordinate to the will of the Supreme, he is sure to come out successful in the discharge of his work. Arjuna was entrusted with the work of fighting on the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra, and before he was so entrusted, the Lord had already arranged for his victory. But Arjuna was always conscious of his position as subordinate to the Lord, and thus he accepted Him as the supreme guide in his responsibility. Anyone who takes pride in doing responsible work but does not give credit to the Supreme Lord is certainly falsely proud and cannot execute anything nicely. Brahmā and persons in the line of his disciplic succession who follow in his footsteps are always successful in the discharge of loving transcendental service to the Supreme Lord.

In other words, even if something appears to be perfectly done externally, if one does not remember the Lord, is not conscious of being subordinate to the Lord, and is proud thinking himself to be the doer, then it is actually imperfect. Such a person cannot execute anything nicely. However, if the person is always conscious of his subordinate position to the Lord, his offering will be acceptable and pleasurable to the Lord, even it does not look perfect externally. The Lord looks at the motive in the heart, and not at the externalities.

Prabhupāda also gives a very good example of Rāmānujācārya to illustrate the point about the spiritual motive that a Vaiṣṇava may have behind his actions. Rāmānujācārya’s spiritual master told him that he would give him a mantra only if he would not give it to anybody else. He said that by chanting this mantra he will establish his eternal relationship with the Lord. Rāmānujācārya therefore agreed not to give it to anyone.

However, when he received the mantra, he started to think that his spiritual master was so merciful to have given him a mantra that can immediately deliver anyone who chants it. He therefore decided to stand on the roof of the building and call all the local townspeople—hundreds of whom gathered. He said, “Please come closer. I am going to give you a very special mantra. I want you to chant and repeat after me: Oṁ namaḥ nārāyaṇāya.”

Everyone became so ecstatic chanting this mantra, and when word got back to Rāmānujācārya’s spiritual master, he became so angry. He said, “What have you done?!”

Rāmānujācārya replied to his spiritual master, “I did this because I understand your purpose. I know that your desire is to deliver so many suffering living entities. Therefore, if that meant that I have to go to hell for disobeying your instruction, then I was prepared to go to hell so that everyone else could get this mantra and be delivered.”

His spiritual master then understood the heart and motive of Rāmānujācārya and began to cry. He fell at Rāmānujācārya’s feet, embraced them, and said, “You are my spiritual master.” He began glorifying Rāmānujācārya for the spirit of his service. Thus, for the service of his spiritual master, Rāmānujācārya was prepared to disobey his instructions and go to hell. However, the result was that his spiritual master became very pleased.

Śrīla Prabhupāda further explains:

The story of Ramanujacarya as stated by you is not disobedience. It was a great fervor for the disciple to advance the missionary cause of the Spiritual Master. Such rare instances are sometimes visible in many places. The story is like this: Caitanya Mahaprabhu after taking His lunch would rest for a while and Govinda was daily massaging His feet. So one day Caitanya Mahaprabhu fell asleep very soon and keeping His head on the threshold. So while He was sleeping, Govinda came crossing the body of Caitanya and massaged His Feet. But he was sitting there, so when Caitanya Mahaprabhu was awake He saw that Govinda was sitting there although it was too late. So He inquired, “Govinda, you have not taken your Prasadam, you are sitting here?’’ So he replied, “Yes, I shall go now to take Prasadam.’’ Caitanya Mahaprabhu inquired, “Why so late?’’ He replied, “I could not go on the other side because You were lying on the threshold.’’ Caitanya Mahaprabhu said, “How did you come in?’’ He flatly replied, “By crossing You.’’ Then He inquired, “Why did you not go out by crossing Me?’’ Govinda said, “That I cannot do. I came crossing You inside the room for Your service, but I cannot go out crossing You for taking my lunch. That would be for my sense gratification.’’ The idea is for service of the superior sometimes such violation appears to be in the scene. Ramanujacarya violated the order of the Spiritual Master to advance the cause of the Spiritual Master. The Spiritual Master’s mission was to deliver fallen souls, therefore Ramanujacarya considered that if the mantra was so powerful to deliver the persons, why not deliver it to everyone as soon as possible. That was a little tactic to advance the cause of the Spiritual Master. So everything has to be judged by the motive, and as the motive of such apparent violation was very good, Ramanuja’s Spiritual Master embraced him. This is not actually violating the order of the Spiritual Master. But such actions are very rarely to be done.” (Letter to Satsvarūpa Mahārāja, November 14, 1968)

## Real Loving Relationships

Our whole spiritual life is based upon association. We read so many examples of great Vaiṣṇava ācāryas who always aspire for the association of devotees. In the purport to Mānasa Deha Geha, Prabhupāda explains what Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura is saying in this song, which is essentially: “I am not so interested to take a birth as Lord Brahmā, because if I do, but don’t have association with devotees, then what is the value? Taking birth as an insect in the house of Your devotee would be far superior to taking birth as Brahmā, because by so doing, I will have an opportunity to hear about the glories of Kṛṣṇa, and by hearing the glories of Kṛṣṇa, my devotional life will be nourished. Thus, even birth as an insect in a house of a devotee would be far better than as Brahmā.”

There are many other examples of Vaiṣṇavas who pray to the Lord for benedictions to have the opportunity to come back again in the association of His devotees. Thus, if devotees are given an opportunity by the Lord to receive some benediction, and they ask for the association of devotees above anything else, they are showing us by their example the great value of association. This is most important for spiritual advancement.

We should know how to associate. Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura has given details about what is association and what is not association within an essay on saṅga-tyāga (giving up the association of nondevotees) in Śrī Bhaktyāloka. The essay is one of many of his commentaries on Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Śrī Upadeśāmṛta. In this particular essay, Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura writes about how householder devotees can live a life without being affected by being in the constant presence of nondevotees. Usually nondevotees associate with each other to fulfill similar ambitions—they share each other’s convictions, and they give support to each other.

There are many different types of association between nondevotees. For example, in the West, there is a group called Alcoholics Anonymous, where people come together and associate to help each other with their drinking problems. There are also associations for family members of alcoholics, where they come together, open their hearts, share their experiences and try to help each other overcome obstacles that result from living with a family member who is an alcoholic. Another example is that of book clubs, where people gather every week and talk about a common book they are reading. Thus, association is common to everyone. It is said, “No man is an island unto himself.” By nature, we are social beings, and we are very much affected by the association we keep.

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura describes how we can give up the association of nondevotees:

There are two types of saṅga—association and attachment. Association is of two types-with nondevotees and with women. Similarly, attachment is also of two types—attachment for prejudices and attachment for assets. Those mahatmas who wish to attain perfection in devotional service should carefully give up saṅga in the form of association and attachment. Otherwise this saṅga will gradually and surely ruin everything. As stated in the Bhagavad-gītā (2.62-63):

*dhyāyato viṣayān puṁsaḥ*  
*saṅgas teṣūpajāyate*  
*saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ*  
*kāmāt krodho 'bhijāyate*

*krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ*  
*sammohāt smṛti-vibhramaḥ*  
*smṛti-bhraṁśād buddhi-nāśo*  
*buddhi-nāśāt praṇaśyati*

“While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises. From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”

A practitioner should always remember this instruction of the Lord. If a practitioner engages in prohibited association, then gradually his attachment increases. The more this attachment increases, the more his firm faith in the supreme goal diminishes. (Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

This emphasizes the statement of the Bhagavad-gītā (2.62): “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.” The more that attachment increases for that which is material, the more that faith in the supreme goal diminishes.

Although we may feel that our faith is very strong, if we are not careful, and we begin to cultivate our attachments, it is possible to lose faith in very simple devotional activities, which are meant to increase our attachment to Kṛṣṇa. One of the offenses against the holy name is to maintain material attachments even after hearing so many instructions on the matter.

Sometimes Kṛṣṇa very mercifully arranges, either Himself or through the association with His devotees, for us to be forced to confront our attachments. Each time we are forced to do so, we may not deal with that confrontation in an appropriate way, especially if we start becoming offensive. Rather than looking at the attachment within our own heart as an obstacle, we begin to look for faults in others, or in the process itself. This is the result of harboring attachments without the desire to give them up. We become fearful of losing them, and thus we protect them.

If we want to purify our hearts from these attachments, we have to continue hearing and chanting about the Lord with firm faith, and serving devotees who are free from attachments, as that is the most powerful method of cleansing our heart from attachments.

*śuśrūṣoḥ śraddadhānasya*  
*vāsudeva-kathā-ruciḥ*  
*syān mahat-sevayā viprāḥ*  
*puṇya-tīrtha-niṣevaṇāt*

**“O twice-born sages, by serving those devotees who are completely freed from all vice, great service is done. By such service, one gains affinity for hearing the messages of Vāsudeva.” (Bhāg. 1.2.16)**

Those who are impatient after prolonged sādhana sometimes lose faith and give up their sādhana. Both Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura and Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura in the Mādhurya Kaḍambinī explain that if one loses the mercy of the holy name of the Lord, he can no longer chant or hear about the Lord. To the degree that we associate (engage in saṅga) with our attachments, to that degree our faith in the ultimate goal will decrease. Until one’s attachments have been spiritualized, he actually becomes attached to Kṛṣṇa and His devotees, and becomes attached to hearing and chanting about the Lord, he has to protect his devotional creeper. By the mercy of our guardians of devotional service, our devotional creepers are protected.

Particularly since Kali-yuga is a period that is filled with so much bad association, if one is aspiring to advance in spiritual life, then he has to know how to keep good association. Good association is the kind of association that helps us maintain our spiritual values and remain fixed upon the path of bhakti. We must understand that there is both good and bad in relationship to both material and spiritual things.

Rūpa Gosvāmī says: “ānukūlyasya saṅkalpaḥ prātikūlyasya varjanam—Of the six principles of surrender, one principle is to accept everything favorable for devotional service and the other is to reject everything unfavorable for devotional service.” (Hari-bhakti-vilāsa 11.676)

Similarly, there is good association and bad association. Lord Caitanya instructs us:

*asat-saṅga-tyāga ei vaiṣṇava-ācāra,*  
*strī-saṅgī eka asādhu kṛṣṇābhakta āra*

**A Vaiṣṇava should always avoid the association of ordinary people. Common people are very much materially attached, especially to women. Vaiṣṇavas should also avoid the company of those who are not devotees of Lord Kṛṣṇa. (Cc. Madhya 22.87)**

Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura quotes one verse from Mādhurya Kaḍambinī: How can one attain that which is in the East by going west? Prabhupāda would also use a simple analogy to make this point: How can one light fire by pouring water on it at the same time? In other words, if we want to advance in spiritual life, we have to restrict ourselves from certain tendencies. Therefore, we need to know what the dangerous creatures are on our path of devotional service. Without knowing this, devotees will have a tendency to flirt with māyā, thinking that it is alright to flirt just a little bit, yet remain protected. However, this is dangerous if one is not careful, as he will lose his power of discrimination.

Therefore, it is necessary to both restrict from bad association and to keep good association. To restrict from bad association, we have to know who is a non-devotee. Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains in his Śrī Bhaktyāloka:

First we will consider the association of nondevotees. Who is a nondevotee? Those who are not subordinate to the Lord are called nondevotees. The jñānīs are never subordinate to the Lord. They think that they can become one with the Lord on the strength of their knowledge. They think, “Jñāna is the topmost object; the Lord cannot keep one who attains jñāna under His control; the Lord became Supreme by the strength of this jñāna, and I too will become Supreme.” (Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

This is a little bit of an introduction into the mentality of a jñānī. He is somebody who thinks that his knowledge is attained by jñāna, and it is so powerful because it is non-different from the knowledge which even the Lord achieved by jñāna. They think that ultimately the Supreme is impersonal and, therefore, they think that by this method of jñāna they will achieve the same reality as the Supreme, becoming one with the Supreme.

Therefore all the endeavors of the jñānīs are to become independent of the Lord. The Lord’s power does not act on one who achieves liberation in the form of merging with the Lord, which is attained by jñāna. This is the attempt of the jñānīs! The jñānīs and mundane scholars do not depend on the mercy of the Lord. They try to achieve everything on the strength of their knowledge and reasoning, they do not care for the Lord’s mercy. (Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

They think that because of their own ability to achieve the Supreme, they neither need the Lord nor any mercy which is, of course, the exact antithesis of a devotee. They may be temporarily interested in Kṛṣṇa’s mercy, but only until they achieve their goal. This mentality of the impersonalists was described in a story of Prabhupāda in Māyāpura. When Prabhupāda was crossing over a ditch, one devotee took his hand to help him cross. Prabhupāda got to the other side and then pushed the devotee away. The devotee was shocked. How could Prabhupāda do that? Śrīla Prabhupāda said that this is what the impersonalists do. They take help from the guru, and then as soon as they achieve what they want, they push him aside. Therefore, they may temporarily try to get some mercy, but the mercy they are interested in is only to achieve their goal, which is to become one with the Supreme.

The impersonalists are one of the categories of materialistic or worldly people whose association should be avoided, which are described in Śrī Bhaktyāloka: (1) Māyāvādīs and atheists, (2) sense enjoyers, (3) those who are fond of the sense enjoyers, (4) women (which he clarifies later means illicit association with the opposite sex), (5) womanizers, (6) the hypocritically devout, dharma-dhvajī, and (7) the ill-behaved foolish outcastes, or persons who are just simply addicted to all kinds of sinful activities.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains that for men, women are māyā, and for women, men are māyā when the association is illicit (not within marriage). He also explains that association with the dharma-dhvajī who pretends to be very devotional is the worst kind. Such persons pretend to be very devoted and attract people by the external potential of devotion; however, internally they are simply calculating how to fulfill their material ambitions. The association of these seven types of categories of materialistic persons should be avoided.

However, it is stated in the Bhāgavatam:

*kirāta-hūṇāndhra-pulinda-pulkaśā*  
*ābhīra-śumbhā yavanāḥ khasādayaḥ*  
*ye ‘nye ca pāpā yad-apāśrayāśrayāḥ*  
*śudhyanti tasmai prabhaviṣṇave namaḥ*

**Kirāta, Hūṇa, Āndhra, Pulinda, Pulkaśa, Ābhīra, Śumbha, Yavana, members of the Khasa races and even others addicted to sinful acts can be purified by taking shelter of the devotees of the Lord, due to the Lord being the supreme power. (Bhāg. 2.4.18)**

Thus, even those who are addicted to the most sinful acts can become purified if given the right association. However, those who are householders and those who are not very advanced in spiritual life should be very careful about associating with the seven types of materialistic people, because by associating with them, they can develop their qualities. Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains in Bhaktyāloka, however, that a householder who has to be with them can survive and not develop these bad qualities.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura writes the following about giving up the association of nondevotees:

What is association and giving up association? Many people have doubts about this. Doubts may be there, because if just by coming close to a materialist of material object is considered associating with them, then there is no way to give up this association. As long as the material body is there, how can one give up the proximity of these things? How can a gṛhastha Vaiṣṇava give up his family members? One cannot give up the association of deceitful persons, even if they are renunciates.. One will have to come across materialists in one’s life, whether one is a gṛhastha or renounced. Therefore the limit for giving up the association of materialists is prescribed in Śrī Upadeśāmṛta as follows:

*dadāti pratigṛhṇāti*  
*guhyam ākhyāti pṛcchati*  
*bhuṅkte bhojayate caiva*  
*ṣaḍ-vidhaṁ prīti-lakṣaṇam*

Offering gifts in charity, accepting charitable gifts, revealing one’s mind in confidence, inquiring confidentially, accepting prasādam and offering prasādam are the six symptoms of love shared by one devotee and another.

(Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

These are the six types of exchanges of love. A devotee associates through these exchanges—by giving and accepting—as real love is a reciprocal relationship. You may give food to somebody, but if a Vaiṣṇava wants to reciprocate and give something back, then you must accept. That is love. If you do not accept, then there is no reciprocation, and therefore no love. Of course, when something is offered with love, it is done without any expectation of receiving anything in return. This is one criterion for love. Love is selfless. Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī explains in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu that real love means to be able to repose all of one’s affections on one object exclusively, forever. The impetus to go on loving that object comes from the exclusive desire to please the beloved, which means that the devotee is fully satisfied with one thing only—the opportunity to serve.

Loving exchanges can only be experienced between devotees. Devotees are pleased even by the smallest gift of anything that is connected to Kṛṣṇa. We can give something to the devotee that is connected with Kṛṣṇa with love, such as prasādam, a gift, or dust from Vṛndāvana.
