Even Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā that He will accept a fruit, leaf, flower or water if it is offered to Him with love. He sets the standard of loving exchanges, and He completes the exchange. The nature of loving exchanges is not only giving, but also accepting. When Kṛṣṇa accepts something, the devotee is ecstatic, and that is the perfection of his life.

Similarly, devotees have the same standard of loving exchanges. The nature of loving exchanges between the devotees is to give something with the desire to please them; not wanting to get something back from them. The greatest gift we can get back from them is when they accept our offering with gratitude. Gratitude is a natural form of reciprocation. Even Kṛṣṇa is always grateful for the love of His devotees, and is always eager to reciprocate that love. When He wants to give something back to His devotees, since the devotee only desires for Him to be his master and to be allowed to be His servant, Kṛṣṇa gives His heart. Such are the loving exchanges between the Lord and His devotee. When you get Kṛṣṇa’s heart, you get everything. Similarly, if you have the heart of the devotee, you get Kṛṣṇa. There is no greater gift, and naturally you will want to give something in return.

Prabhupāda says:

This Society was started single-handedly, but because people are coming forward and dealing with the give-and-take policy, the Society is now expanding all over the world. We are glad that people are donating very liberally to the development of the Society's activities, and people are also eagerly accepting whatever humble contribution we are giving them in the shape of books and magazines dealing strictly with the subject matter of Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

(…) In this way our Society is successfully spreading all over the world, and the intelligentsia of all countries is gradually appreciating our Kṛṣṇa conscious activities. The life of the Kṛṣṇa conscious society is nourished by these six types of loving exchange among the members; therefore people must be given the chance to associate with the devotees of ISKCON because simply by reciprocating in the six ways mentioned above an ordinary man can fully revive his dormant Kṛṣṇa consciousness. (Śrī Upadeśāmṛta, purport to Verse 4)

They associate with the devotees of ISKCON because they were experiencing loving exchanges with Prabhupāda. Prabhupāda gave the greatest gift. The only desire in his heart was to give Kṛṣṇa to others. He was not interested in anything else. He said that many times. That is the nature of a preacher, and of loving exchanges between devotees who know what is most valuable.

Whereas when there is love between devotees and where we can reveal our mind in confidence and inquire confidentially, Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura warns that we have to protect ourselves from engaging in exchanges with the materialist. How can you reveal your mind in confidence to a materialistic person and not become affected by it?

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains what association is:

Generally there is some love involved in confidential speaking, therefore it is association. While meeting a materialistic friend, one should speak only what is extremely necessary. At that time it is better not to exhibit heartfelt love. But if that friend is a proper Vaiṣṇava, then one should accept his association by speaking to him with love. This type of behavior with relatives and friends creates no hostility. There is no association in ordinary talk. One should behave with ordinary people as one externally behaves with a stranger while buying something in the market. The same dealings with a pure devotee of the Lord should be done out of love. If one is obliged to feed hungry people, needy people, and teachers, he should do so as a host dutifully cares for his guest, there is no need to exhibit love. Care for them, but not out of love. One should feed pure Vaiṣṇavas with love, and when required accept the remnants given by them with love. If one can behave in this way while giving in charity, accepting charity, speaking confidentially, hearing confidentially, feeding, and accepting food with one’s wife, children, servants, maidservants, strangers, and whoever else one meets, there will be no unholy association, only good association. (Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

In other words, when you actually have real association with devotees, it will be so relishable and attractive that even though you have to be in the physical proximity of so many materialistic people, you will not be affected. Loving exchanges is what Kṛṣṇa consciousness is all about, and it is also our method for preaching.

Lord Caitanya personally taught this by His own example. When He sat with Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya who spoke for seven continuous days, Lord Caitanya did not associate confidentially with him, as He did not listen to anything. Afterwards, He said, “I am listening to the Vedānta Sutra from you, but I am not listening to your interpretations, because you have clouded all Vedānta Sutra with your nonsense interpretations.” However, He then preached to Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya.

Lord Caitanya converted 60,000 Māyāvādī sannyāsīs. Of course, we should be very careful, as Prabhupāda warns us that we should not imitate the mahā-bhāgavatas. Lord Caitanya showed by His own example how to share this love with non-devotees. For one continuous year, He only associated with His intimate devotees. The non-devotees were not allowed into kīrtanas in Śrīvāsa Paṇḍita’s house. The devotees simply relished kīrtana with the Lord. However, following that, they went out and demonstrated these loving exchanges by beginning the saṅkīrtana movement.

This is how we distribute and introduce others to Kṛṣṇa’s love—by bringing them into the experience of these loving exchanges between devotees. In this way, Śrīla Prabhupāda spread the saṅkīrtana movement and taught us, by his own example, how to understand the meaning of the loving exchanges, as outlined in Śrī Upadeśāmṛta (Verse 4):

*dadāti pratigṛhṇāti*  
*guhyam ākhyāti pṛcchati*  
*bhuṅkte bhojayate caiva*  
*ṣaḍ-vidhaṁ prīti-lakṣaṇam*

Furthmore, in engaging in loving exchanges in devotional service, devotees never fear any condition of life, being only interested in serving the Lord:

*nārāyaṇa-parāḥ sarve*  
*na kutaścana bibhyati*  
*svargāpavarga-narakeṣv*  
*api tulyārtha-darśinaḥ*

**Devotees solely engaged in the devotional service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Nārāyaṇa, never fear any condition of life. For them the heavenly planets, liberation and the hellish planets are all the same, for such devotees are interested only in the service of the Lord. (Bhāg. 6.17.28)**

This is exemplified in the pastime of when Lord Caitanya took the pieces of broken rice from Śuklāmbhara Brahmacārī. Although Śuklāmbhara did not offer it, the Lord grabbed it because He wanted something from the hands of His pure devotee.

In Caitanya-bhāgavata, Vṛndāvana dāsa Ṭhākura explains that the materialistic millionaires cannot understand such pastimes between the Lord and His devotee—how the Lord is so inclined to reciprocate an insignificant offering from a devotee with love. Even though one may have so much wealth, he cannot get the Lord to accept anything from him simply by his wealth. The Lord is inclined to see the love.

It is explained in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

**“The Supreme Personality of Godhead becomes very dear to those devotees who have no material possessions but are fully happy in possessing the devotional service of the Lord. Indeed, the Lord relishes the devotional activities of such devotees. Those who are puffed up with material education, wealth, aristocracy and fruitive activity are very proud of possessing material things, and they often deride the devotees. Even if such people offer the Lord worship, the Lord never accepts them.” (Bhāg. 4.31.21)**

Although love is exclusively reposed upon Kṛṣṇa, there is also love between devotees. One gives to another without expecting in return, and therefore the other devotee also gives and does not expect anything in return.

There is a story in Caitanya-caritāmṛta of two brāhmaṇas who were going on parikramā (pilgrimage). The young brāhmaṇa was helping the older brāhmaṇa. The older brāhmaṇa was so grateful for the assistance of the younger brāhmaṇa, and wanted to give something in return. He therefore offered his daughter in marriage.

Younger brāhmaṇa: “I served you out of love because you are very dear to Kṛṣṇa. I do not want anything from you.”

Elder brāhmaṇa: “But I want to give something in return.”

Younger brāhmaṇa: “But you are from a very aristocratic family. I am a very poor brāhmaṇa. How can you offer your daughter to me? Certainly your family members will object. Please do not offer your daughter. I do not want your daughter in marriage. I just wanted to serve you.”

Older brāhmaṇa: “No, I must. I want to reciprocate! Please take my daughter in marriage.”

Younger brāhmaṇa: “All your family members will certainly object to this, and you will therefore not be able to keep your promise.”

The elder brāhmaṇa therefore brought him before the Gopāla Deity to make his promise: “Before You, I promise that I will give my daughter to this brāhmaṇa in marriage.”

Younger brāhmaṇa: “Yes, and if it is necessary in the future, we may have to call upon You as a witness.”

Such was their loving exchange.

The younger brāhmaṇa said to the elder brāhmaṇa, “If you make a promise before the Deity, then certainly your promise will have to be kept intact.”

When the two brāhmaṇas returned to Vidyānagara, the younger brāhmaṇa raised the question of this marriage, but the elderly brāhmaṇa, due to obligations to his friends and wife, answered that he could not remember his promise. Because of this, the younger brāhmaṇa returned to Vṛndāvana and narrated the whole story to Gopālajī. Thus Gopālajī, being obliged by the young man’s devotional service, accompanied him to southern India. Gopālajī followed the younger brāhmaṇa, who could hear the tinkling sound of Gopālajī’s ankle bells. When all the respectable gentlemen of Vidyānagara were assembled, Gopālajī testified to the promise of the elderly brāhmaṇa. Thus the marriage was performed. Later, the king of that country constructed a fine temple for Gopāla.

As Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī has explained, giving gifts, accepting gifts, giving prasādam, and accepting prasādam—when done with love—is association.

Of course, we must be careful with whom we associate. Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains:

One must accept proximity with both bad and good people as one passes his life. This equally applies to householders and renunciates. Proximity must be there, nevertheless one should not engage in bad association. Giving in charity, accepting charity, revealing one’s mind, hearing one’s mind, accepting foods and giving foods—if done with love, these are called saṅga, association. Giving some foodstuffs to a hungry person or accepting some charity from a pious man is done out of duty, not out of love. (Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

We know that reciprocal love is selfless, and if anything is offered with love, we should reciprocate with love. However, if there is no love, and if something is offered with some other motivation, then we should be very careful to not reciprocate such relationships in a loving way. We must therefore protect ourselves. We may accept other kinds of offerings as a matter of duty, but it is not out of love. Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura further explains:

Even if they are materialists, this type of engagement is not considered association. But if they are pure devotees, then such activities are performed out of love. When acts are performed out of love, then it is association. Therefore giving charity to pure Vaiṣṇavas and accepting items or wealth from them becomes sat-saṅga. Giving charity to a materialist or accepting charity from one, if done out of love, becomes asat-saṅga. When a materialist approaches you, whatever is required to be done should be done only out of duty.

One should not speak confidentially with a materialistic person. Generally there is some love involved in confidential speaking. Therefore this is association. While meeting a materialistic friend one should speak only what is extremely necessary. At that time it is better not to exhibit heart felt love. But if that friend is a proper Vaiṣṇava, then one should accept his association by speaking to him with love. This type of behavior with relatives and friends creates no hostility. There is no association in ordinary talk.

One should behave with ordinary people as one externally behaves with a stranger while buying something in the market. The same dealings with the pure devotee of the Lord should be done out of love. If one is obliged to feed hungry people, needy people and teachers, you should do so as the host dutifully cares for his guest. There is no need to exhibit love. Care for them, but not out of love. One should feed pure Vaiṣṇavas with love, and when required accept the remnants given by them with love.

If one can behave in this way while giving in charity, accepting charity, speaking confidentially, hearing confidentially, feeding and accepting food with one’s wife, children, servants, maidservants, strangers and whoever else one meets, there will be no unholy association, only good association. There is no hope of achieving devotion to Kṛṣṇa until one gives up unholy association in this way.

A gṛhastha Vaiṣṇava should accept prasāda-grains and drinks in the house of another gṛhastha who has pure character. One should always be cautious about taking prasāda in the house of a non-devotee and one with bad character. There is no need to speak further about this subject. Due to their pious activities those who have developed faith in devotional service have a little intelligence by the mercy of Kṛṣṇa. Due to that intelligence, they can easily understand the essence of the ācāryas instructions. Therefore only a few words are needed to instruct them. Those who have no pious credits have no faith. Even if they are given volumes of instructions, they will not understand anything. Therefore, Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī has given only a few words of instruction in Śrī Upadeśāmṛta. (Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Section 11: Saṅga-tyāga)

In this section of Śrī Bhaktyāloka, Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura instructs us how to associate. It is especially difficult if one comes under the association of materialistic people, because one can be very negatively influenced. However, Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura has written this article to explain how we can protect ourselves so that we can live and work with others. Wherever we go, there is always some exchange with others. However, if we are not careful and do not discriminate the type of exchanges we have, we can become influenced and forget about the real devotional values in life.

As previously explained, the criterion of a loving exchange is when something is offered without any expectation in return, and only with the desire to please the Lord by serving His devotee. To serve the Lord, we must serve the Lord’s devotees, which are those persons who are always giving to the Lord without any expectation of something in return. When we serve the devotees without any expectation of something in return, we get recognized by the Lord.

In the Ādi Purāṇa, Kṛṣṇa explained to Arjuna, “My dear Pārtha, one who claims to be My devotee is not so. Only a person who claims to be the devotee of My devotee is actually My devotee.” The Lord goes wherever His devotees go. By the dust of the lotus feet of His devotees, He desires to purify this entire material world, which is situated within Him. He says He will always follow in the footsteps of His devotees who are always chanting His glories, are equal to everyone, and who are never indifferent to others.

*nāhaṁ tiṣṭhāmi vaikuṇṭhe*  
*yogināṁ hṛdayeṣu vā*  
*tatra tiṣṭhāmi nārada*  
*yatra gāyanti mad-bhaktāḥ*

**“I am not in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of the yogīs. I remain where My devotees engage in glorifying My activities.” (Padma Purāṇa)**

If we serve such devotees, we can serve the Lord.

Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura explains that a devotee may give charity to a hungry person, as the host dutifully cares for his guest. However, since love is reciprocal, one should be careful about offering love, because what he gets back may not help him in his Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and he may end up taking asat-saṅga.

Lord Caitanya says:

*asat-saṅga-tyāga,—ei vaiṣṇava-ācāra*  
*‘strī-saṅgī’—eka asādhu, ‘kṛṣṇābhakta’ āra*

(Cc. Madhya 22.87)

**“A Vaiṣṇava should always avoid the association of ordinary people. Common people are very much materially attached, especially to women. Vaiṣṇavas should also avoid the company of those who are not devotees of Lord Kṛṣṇa.”**

Asat-saṅga has to be given up. A devotee can thus learn how to live in the world and not be influenced by it, which will help keep him in the association of pure devotees. The materialists will become attracted by seeing these loving exchanges, and it will awaken within their hearts a desire to love. Even the greatest materialists can become devotees simply by coming into the association of devotees. Association becomes real association when there is love.

**Question: Sometimes when associating with devotees, we may develop an inferiority complex, seeing that we do not have the same spiritual qualifications as them. This becomes a barrier in building relationships with them. How can we deal with this?**

We should always try to keep ourselves in the association of devotees who we can see as superior. We should not feel discouraged. It is due to our false ego that we may feel discouraged in the presence of someone who is superior, thinking ourselves a failure. However, that sense of being a failure should never be in the heart of a devotee. A devotee who thinks that way is lacking faith in the process of chanting the holy name and in the association of devotees. The real progress in life that we should be aspiring for is to increase that faith. We should therefore seek out the devotees who can give us more faith. Seeing others more successful than ourselves in Kṛṣṇa consciousness should actually give us faith that this process is possible for us.

When we read examples in the scriptures about associates of the Lord who achieved such perfection, we may think that it is because they are associates of the Lord, but that we are just an ordinary jīva. Again, we should not be discouraged. Those examples are actually meant to build our faith. Prabhupāda once said that we should not think that we cannot become like mother Yaśodā and serve Kṛṣṇa as she does. Everybody can have this opportunity.

When we see others who have strong faith, which is the real criterion of success, then we can have real association with them to build our own faith. In the marketplace of the holy name, the only currency that is used is faith. To increase our own faith, we look for somebody who has more faith and in whom we can invest our faith. By investing our faith, we get good returns. We should associate with the purpose of increasing our faith. Material qualification is irrelevant, unless it is dovetailed in devotional service.

Although people saw Śuklāmbhara Brahmacārī as a beggar, he never knew the meaning of the word poverty, because he was always satisfied in his heart. Although he externally appeared to not have anything, in actuality, he had the most valuable jewel—the gem of complete faith in the Lord. He was so pleasing to the Lord that the Lord wanted to take something from his hand even before he offered it.

Thus, if we see somebody has more faith, instead of feeling inferior, we should invest our faith and reveal our mind in confidence to him. We should feel fortunate to have the opportunity to associate with this devotee who has more faith in the Lord. It is possible for us to advance if we make the right investment. There is no failure in this type of endeavor in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Kṛṣṇa gives His assurance of this.

We should realize that we are the most unqualified. However, Lord Caitanya has come to deliver those who are the most unqualified. Our qualification for spiritual life is this genuine feeling of unqualification. Kṛṣṇa therefore gives us the association of those who can help us become more qualified in our spiritual life. If we always see things in that perspective, we cannot fail in Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

**Question: How can we develop open relationships with devotees?**

Having open relationships is not something that can be mechanically accomplished. There has to be trust for there to be an open relationship. However, the tendency is to mistrust the motives of others, because motives cannot always be easily ascertained, and we have been conditioned by so many past experiences, both in this life and in previous lives. Because we are carrying so much baggage with us into our relationships with devotees, in the beginning, we are skeptical about what we see. Therefore, we have to create faith, but not blind faith where we immediately start trusting everybody.

We can build faith by associating with someone with whom we have some trust. When we establish a relationship with a Vaiṣṇava with whom we have some trust, who understands the history of our condition from millions of births and is kindly intervening into our life for our benefit, then our heart opens and we can have open relationships. We see that such a Vaiṣṇava simply wants to serve Kṛṣṇa and has no other motive. He is transparent and gives us an opportunity to come in contact with Kṛṣṇa. Until we meet such a person who can open our heart, there will always be doubts. Therefore, the primary goal of our life is to come into contact with that person who can open our heart. Such a person not only shows us how to love Kṛṣṇa, but also how to love all of Kṛṣṇa’s parts and parcels.

Of course, when one comes to the madhyama platform, he has to make distinctions. He has love for the Lord, he makes friends with devotees of the Lord, he is merciful to those who are innocent, and he avoids those who are atheistic. Thus, we do not act blindly; we have to discriminate and associate with everyone according to their particular status. To come to the madhyama platform, we have to associate with devotees who are more advanced than ourselves. We have to be willing to open our hearts to try to test.

Prabhupāda explains in his introduction to the Bhagavad-gītā that even if you cannot accept Kṛṣṇa as God and that God was the speaker of the Bhagavad-gītā, at least theoretically accept that Kṛṣṇa is God. Prabhupāda had one hundred percent faith that Kṛṣṇa is present in Bhagavad-gītā, and that He spoke it. Because he was purely presenting Kṛṣṇa’s motive for presenting Bhagavad-gītā, he had complete faith that if somebody theoretically accepted that, and if they were sincere, then they would come to understand beyond the theoretical platform.

Prabhupāda used to say that because there are so many counterfeit coins, it means that in some place, there is something genuine. Thus we should have faith that there are genuine relationships, and we should trust that those genuine relationships can be built in the association of those who are devotees of Lord Kṛṣṇa. Keep on testing and have a little faith. By continuing to test, our trust and taste for devotee association will become stronger, and we will become more open. There are no material formulas for open relationships. They are built based on our faith in Kṛṣṇa and in the Vaiṣṇavas speaking on behalf of Kṛṣṇa.

**Question: Sometimes we see that there are loving relationships between devotees, but over a period of time, they become inimical to each other. Why does this happen?**

It happens because of impurities in the heart. We should look within our own heart to see if we are pure. We should become such an example that other devotees will be inspired.

## Spiritual Relationships versus Material Relationships

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta states in his Amṛta Vāṇī:

Of what should we be careful?

Everything in this world belongs to Kṛṣṇa. If one uses anything for his own enjoyment, he will have to face the consequences. Those who are averse to hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā will become materially attached and bound to this world. Therefore, pious persons who desire their eternal benefit should take utmost care to hear kṛṣṇa-kathā from real devotees. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Association, Part 22)

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta puts these three statements in quotes, as being sinful thoughts:

“I serve the Lord so much.” “I have already served the Lord,” or “I have become a Vaiṣṇava”—these are sinful thoughts. One must give up such madness and humbly beg to attain the Lord’s service.

To make a show of serving Kṛṣṇa without serving the spiritual master and the Vaiṣṇavas is like keeping water in a broken pot. Such pretense is simply pride. One must seek constant association with devotees. I am so weak that I am unable to survive without the association of devotees. If I do not associate with devotees constantly, I will certainly develop a strong desire to become the master, and various sinful thoughts will disturb me. Material existence is the gateway to hell. Even though it appears pleasing in the beginning, it will disappoint me in the end. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Association, Part 22)

Many of these points are very relevant to us. The first point that has been made is that everything belongs to Kṛṣṇa. The following quote supports this point.

How should we treat the material world?

We should see this material world and everything in it as full of ingredients for the Lord’s service. Everything in this world is meant for Kṛṣṇa’s service. The day when we can look at the world like this and become liberated from the material conception, we will be able to see the material world as the spiritual world, Goloka. We should treat all women as Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds. They are to be enjoyed by Him. Do not look at them with an enjoying spirit. They are meant to be enjoyed by Kṛṣṇa, never by the living entities. Treat your father and mother as Kṛṣṇa’s father and mother. Instead of considering your children your servants, treat them as friends of child Kṛṣṇa. Then you will not see the material world everywhere, but Goloka. (Amṛta Vāṇī, A Devotee’s Vision, Part 3)

We should try to cultivate this vision. It is takes training. When that vision is there, as Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta explains, then one will not see the material world, but will see Goloka Vṛndāvana. The mood of Goloka Vṛndāvana is that everything is for Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure.

This material world is simply a reflection of the spiritual world; it is not real. In the Bhāgavatam, Kṛṣṇa describes to Lord Brahmā how the material energy is actually His energy: “Anything that you see of value, but which has no connection to Me, you should know it to be My illusory energy.” He compares it to be like a projection of light into darkness. There is real light, which is the spiritual world where everything is self-illuminating. It is the actual substance, whereas the material world is simply a perverted reflection of the spiritual world. Our endeavor to experience happiness out of relationships in this world is like trying to enjoy a reflection.

Once I was in Kharkov. I was staying in someone’s home, and they had a very big guard dog. I was standing in the sunlight and the sun was hitting my watch and the reflection was projected onto the wall. The reflection on the wall was just moving, unknown to me, because of the movements of my arm. All of a sudden, I saw the dog lunge at the wall with its jaws to grab that reflection. It lunged several times, almost to the point where its mouth was cut, though not bleeding. It stood back, and when the reflection started to move again, the dog jumped against the wall. It wanted to catch that reflection, but there was no substance to catch. The same thing happens in the material world when we attempt to enjoy the relationships of this world. Yet, we are so foolish that we try to enjoy the reflection of this world. As a result, we suffer again, and again, and again, in the same way that the dog was lunging to try to get some substance from a reflection, though it was not there. There is no substance in this material world, unless everything is connected to the Lord and can be used in His service.

Prabhupāda explains in the Bhagavad-gītā that anything material that is engaged in the service of the Lord regains its spiritual qualities, because the material energy is also one of Kṛṣṇa’s energies. Kṛṣṇa says:

*etad-yonīni bhūtāni*  
*sarvāṇīty upadhāraya*  
*ahaṁ kṛtsnasya jagataḥ*  
*prabhavaḥ pralayas tathā*

**“All created beings have their source in these two natures. Of all that is material and all that is spiritual in this world, know for certain that I am both the origin and the dissolution.” (Bg. 7.6)**

Since Kṛṣṇa is the source of this material world, it is not false. It is connected to Kṛṣṇa, and it belongs to Him. However, it is temporary. That is the difference between matter and spirit. Therefore, the relationships of this world are all subject to destruction, whereas the relationships of the spiritual world are eternal. We see so many disastrous results in relationships that are based on sense gratification. We may not see them immediately. However, a devotee is one who knows the stringent laws of material nature, and who sees how those who are engaged in gross sense gratification are going to hell and will experience repeated birth, death and suffering.

In reference to the sons of Kuvera, Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva, Nārada Muni said (Bhāg. 10.10.8): “Among all the attractions of material enjoyment, the attraction of riches bewilders one’s intelligence more than having beautiful bodily features, taking birth in an aristocratic family, and being learned. When one is uneducated, but falsely puffed up by wealth, the result is that one engages his wealth in enjoying wine, women and gambling.”

Thus, those who try to accumulate and enjoy wealth in this world create so much distress for themselves in the future, because they simply use it to engage in sinful activities.

**Question: Should we renounce the association of those greedy for money?**

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta says:

Wealth is the source of all anarthas. It is best if wealth is used in Kṛṣṇa’s service. Otherwise, it will ruin our lives and bind us to material existence. Pious devotees should never be greedy for temporary wealth. We should hanker only after eternal wealth, spiritual life. May persons who desire auspiciousness be free of attachment to wealth, because as long as we are materially attached, we will not be able to develop attachment for spiritual life. Our lives will be useless. Please bless me that for the rest of my life, I will not have to see the faces of materialists, greedy for wealth. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Association, Part 5)

Śrīla Prabhupāda often quotes from the Bhāgavatam:

*kāmasya nendriya-prītir*  
*lābho jīveta yāvatā*  
*jīvasya tattva-jijñāsā*  
*nārtho yaś ceha karmabhiḥ*

**Life’s desires should never be directed toward sense gratification. One should desire only a healthy life, or self-preservation, since a human being is meant for inquiry about the Absolute Truth. Nothing else should be the goal of one’s works. (Bhāg. 1.2.10)**

Thus, because the body is an important vehicle for crossing over the material world, one therefore maintains it so that he can use it for self-realization and not waste it for sense gratification.

Lord Ṛṣabhadeva explains that of all living entities who have been awarded material bodies, one who has accepted the human form of life should not waste it in the pursuit of sense gratification like the hogs and dogs that eat stool. One should instead engage in divine austerities and penances to achieve the divine position of devotional service, because by such activities one’s heart is purified and one begins to experience real happiness, which is transcendental to material happiness and which continues forever. Those austerities are to engage in devotional service to the Lord and to use everything in the service of the Lord. If one uses anything for his own enjoyment, he will have to face the consequences.

Kṛṣṇa says to Uddhava:

**“Having awakened faith in the narrations of My glories, being disgusted with all material activities, knowing that all sense gratification leads to misery, but still being unable to renounce all sense enjoyment, My devotee should remain happy and worship Me with great faith and conviction. Even though he is sometimes engaged in sense enjoyment, My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents such activities.” (Bhāg. 11.20.27-28)**

That sincere repentance is also another form of suffering. However, it is purifying. For one who has to repeatedly suffer again and again for sense gratification, that suffering will not lead to advancement of spiritual life until he realizes that he is disgusted with it. Such a devotee has awakened faith in hearing the narrations of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, because he knows that it is the cure for his suffering.

Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura quotes the Lord:

*enechi auṣadhi māyā nāśibāro lāgi’*  
*hari-nāma mahā-mantra lao tumi māgi’*

**“O conditioned souls who are foolishly sleeping on the lap of the witch Māyā, I have brought an excellent medicine to cure the disease of your illusion. This medicine is called hari-nāma. It is My holy name, and by taking this medicine you will get all perfection in life. Therefore, I sincerely request you to please take this medicine that I have personally brought for you.”**

A devotee who is convinced of that will take the proper medicine. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura also explains, however, in his Mādhurya Kaḍambinī:

One may say that the offender against the holy name is condemned to develop aversion to God, making it impossible for him to remain firmly fixed in devotional service under the guidance of his guru. This is certainly true. It is also true that just as a very sick patient loses his appetite, a grievous offender to the holy name loses his attachment for hearing, chanting, and other devotional activities. However, just as the patient’s sickness abates after some time, his appetite gradually returning, so also, when the offender’s sensual cravings decrease after a long period of sense enjoyment, his interest in devotional service is rekindled.

The conclusion is that the offender again becomes eligible to render devotional service. To continue the analogy, a nourishing and healthy diet of milk cannot fully revitalize a seriously diseased man. It helps him slightly but does not kill the germs and bacteria. By proper medicines and diet, however, the patient is gradually able to regain good health. In this way, after again becoming eligible to perform devotional service, the devotee eventually manifests devotional symptoms such as sincere hearing, chanting, and serving.

*janmaiśvarya-śruta-śrībhir*  
*edhamāna-madah? pumān*  
*naivārhaty abhidhātum´ vai*  
*tvām akiṣcana-gocaram*

(Bhāg. 1.8.26)

Prabhupāda also explains in Teachings of Queen Kuntī that janma (high birth), aiśvarya (opulence), śruta (education), and śrībhiḥ (beauty) are all symptoms of the diseased condition of life. If one has a high fever and wants to become better, he has to bring the fever down by reducing his attachments to these things, as they cause bondage in this material world. However, that same attachment when applied to the self-realized devotees, mokṣa-dvāram apāvṛtam (Bhāg. 3.25.20) opens the door to liberation.

Lord Kapiladeva thus tells His mother, Devahūti,

*ta ete sādhavaḥ sādhvi*  
*sarva-saṅga-vivarjitāḥ*  
*saṅgas teṣv atha te prārthyaḥ*  
*saṅga-doṣa-harā hi te*

**“O My mother, O virtuous lady, these are the qualities of great devotees who are free from all attachment. You must seek attachment to such holy men, for this counteracts the pernicious effects of material attachment.” (Bhāg. 3.25.24)**

Associating with Vaiṣṇavas means hearing from their mouths. Lord Kapiladeva therefore qualifies this verse with the previous one:

*mad-āśrayāḥ kathā mṛṣṭāḥ*  
*śṛṇvanti kathayanti ca*  
*tapanti vividhās tāpā*  
*naitān mad-gata-cetasaḥ*

**“Engaged constantly in chanting and hearing about Me, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the sādhus do not suffer from material miseries because they are always filled with thoughts of My pastimes and activities.” (Bhāg. 3.25.23)**

Thus, to the degree that we see things in connection with Kṛṣṇa, remember Kṛṣṇa, speak about Kṛṣṇa, and hear about Kṛṣṇa in the association of Vaiṣṇavas, attachment and the fever of illusion will gradually decrease, and we will become healthy. We should learn to see things according to the vision of liberated souls.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta gives a perfect and profound quote: “We should treat all women as Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds. They are to be enjoyed by Him. Do not look at them with an enjoying spirit. They are meant to be enjoyed by Kṛṣṇa; never by the living entities.” We must develop this vision, and women must think of themselves as belonging to Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds cleanse and ornament their bodies, because they are always thinking about how to increase Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure. They are not interested in attracting anyone else; they want only to attract Kṛṣṇa because their hearts belong to Him. Therefore everything they do is meant to increase His pleasure.

We have to base our relationships on the spiritual platform and see things in proper spiritual perspective. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta further says, “Treat your father and mother as Kṛṣṇa’s father and mother.” We speak in great reverence about mother Yaśodā and Nanda Mahārāja who are always in anxiety about how to protect their son. Furthermore, instead of considering children as our servants, treat them as friends of child Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa has so many friends with whom He goes to the pasturing grounds and He plays with every day. They bring great pleasure to Kṛṣṇa, and are thus very valuable. If something has no connection to Kṛṣṇa, then it is māyā.

Prabhupāda said that the impersonalists always pride themselves on rejecting everything and having nothing to do with this material world. Prabhupāda, however, said, “I will take everything! I will use it for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness.” His vision was to utilize everything for spreading the glories of the Lord; but not for sense gratification. Sense gratification leads to suffering, but everything in this world becomes valuable when it is dovetailed for the service of the Lord.

We should always be looking at how to increase our service to the Lord. Becoming proud and thinking that we have served the Lord enough is sinful. As Bhaktisiddhānta says, we must give up such madness and humbly beg to attain the Lord’s service. In the service of the Lord, we can never do too much.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta goes on to explain:

To make a show of serving Kṛṣṇa without serving the Vaiṣṇavas is like keeping water in a broken pot. Such pretense is simply pride. A Vaiṣṇava’s duty is to make his companions and dependents fearless, free from anxiety, happy and to deliver all conditioned souls from Māyā’s hands. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Association, Part 22)

We should never think that we have direct service to Kṛṣṇa. We should serve and assist Vaiṣṇavas in their service to their spiritual master. If we do not seek constant association with devotees, being dependent upon them for survival, we will certainly develop a strong desire to become the controller of this world. However, this is not possible, as our position is as servants of Vaiṣṇavas.

A Vaiṣṇava wants to see others happy and free from anxiety. We should always try to faithfully serve Vaiṣṇavas by spreading the glories of Kṛṣṇa consciousness for the welfare of others. This was the mission of our previous ācāryas. Service to Vaiṣṇavas is real service to Kṛṣṇa. Vaiṣṇavas are para-dukha-dukhī—they see others’ anxieties as their own. Thus, to serve Vaiṣṇavas, we must think of how we can relieve their anxieties that they have taken on behalf of others who are suffering. We can see why Śrīla Prabhupāda always wanted us to strongly and vigorously preach Kṛṣṇa consciousness. By doing this, we will please Śrīla Prabhupāda, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta and our entire guru-paramparā. We will relieve the anxieties of others and we will see that our own anxieties will also go away.

Prabhupāda said that when you take care of others, Kṛṣṇa will take care of you. When you help others to become Kṛṣṇa conscious, you become Kṛṣṇa conscious yourself. Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the only solution, as recommended by our previous ācāryas.

## Vaiṣṇava Behavior

*dharma-sthāpana-hetu sādhura vyavahāra*  
*purī-gosāñira ye ācaraṇa, sei dharma sāra*

**“A devotee’s behavior establishes the true purpose of religious principles. The behavior of Mādhavendra Purī Gosvāmī is the essence of such religious principles.” (Cc. Madhya 17.185)**

This verse was spoken by Lord Caitanya to the Sanoḍiyā brāhmaṇa about the example of Mādhavendra Purī.

*tarko ’pratiṣṭhaḥ śrutayo vibhinnā*  
*nāsāv ṛṣir yasya mataṁ na bhinnam*  
*dharmasya tattvaṁ nihitaṁ guhāyāṁ*  
*mahājano yena gataḥ sa panthāḥ*

**“Dry arguments are inconclusive. A great personality whose opinion does not differ from others is not considered a great sage. Simply by studying the Vedas, which are variegated, one cannot come to the right path by which religious principles are understood. The solid truth of religious principles is hidden in the heart of an unadulterated, self-realized person. Consequently, as the śāstras confirm, one should accept whatever progressive path the mahājanas advocate.” (Cc. Madhya, 17.186)**

Lord Caitanya was citing these verses to give Mādhavendra Purī as an ideal example of religious principles, and how he set the standard of religious principles by his behavior. This happened at the time when Lord Caitanya was traveling to Vṛndāvana. He came to Viśrāma-ghāṭa, where He took His bath. Then when he entered Mathurā, anyone who would see Him would become filled with ecstasy and achieve ecstatic loving devotional service.

While walking into Mathurā, one brāhmaṇa came and fell at the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya and then touched them. Lord Caitanya picked him up in His embrace. As they were embracing each other, they were saying, “Chant the name of Hari! Chant the name of Hari!” with tears flowing from their eyes. They were manifesting such ecstatic symptoms.

Lord Caitanya then took this brāhmaṇa aside and said, “You appear to be a very sincere, learned and elderly brāhmaṇa. Can you tell Me from where have you gotten such ecstatic love for Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa? I think you must have had the association of Mādhavendra Purī. Otherwise how could such a display of ecstasy be manifest?”

The brāhmaṇa said, “Yes, Mādhavendra Purī was once traveling to Mathurā. He came to my home and accepted me as his disciple and initiated me into devotional service.” Although a Sanoḍiyā brāhmaṇa is not supposed to offer food to a sannyāsī, Mādhavendra Purī took food from the hands of this brāhmaṇa and became very ecstatic upon eating it.

Lord Caitanya immediately said to the brāhmaṇa:

*dharma-sthāpana-hetu sādhura vyavahāra*  
*purī-gosāñira ye ācaraṇa, sei dharma sāra*

**“A devotee’s behavior establishes the true purpose of religious principles. The behavior of Mādhavendra Purī Gosvāmī is the essence of such religious principles.” (Cc. Madhya 17.185)**

Thus even the Lord looks to the example of a devotee for His own behavior. Lord Caitanya quoted Bhagavad-gītā (3.21):

*yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas*  
*tat tad evetaro janaḥ*  
*sa yat pramāṇaṁ kurute*  
*lokas tad anuvartate*

**“Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”**

Lord Caitanya was telling many stories about Mādhavendra Purī to all the devotees who were traveling with Him, causing Him to become ecstatic. He explained how Mādhavendra Purī set so many examples of Vaiṣṇava behavior. Once, Mādhavendra Purī was at Govardhana, and he was absorbed in deep meditation upon the pastimes of the Lord. He did not even know whether it was day or night, or whether he was standing or lying down on the ground. One day while sitting beneath the tree near Govindakuṇḍa, the Lord, as a young cowherd boy, came to Mādhavendra Purī and offered him a clay pot of milk: “The women taking water from the well nearby saw that you are fasting. However, in this village, nobody fasts. I therefore want you to take this milk.” Mādhavendra Purī thus took the milk.

During the night, in his ecstasy, Mādhavendra Purī fell into a dream-like state. That same cowherd boy appeared to him in his dream and said that His name is Gopāla and that He had been hidden during the invasion of the Muslims in the dirt underneath the brush, and He had been sitting there for a long time, waiting for Mādhavendra Purī to come. He told Mādhavendra Purī exactly where He was and that He wanted to be pulled out from the ground to be served by Mādhavendra Purī. Mādhavendra Purī thus went and rescued the Gopāla Deity with many of the villagers, and established His worship.

Upon establishing Gopāla’s worship at Govardhana by performing an annakūṭa ceremony, all the neighboring villagers performed annakūṭa and worshiped Gopāla. The king who had seen such elaborate worship of Gopāla also came and decided to build a huge temple for Gopāla.

Gopāla then appeared to Mādhavendra Purī again in another dream and told him that He was still hot from being under the hot sun for so long, and He wanted Mādhavendra Purī to go to Purī, Orissa to get camphor and eighty-two pounds of sandalwood to cool His body.

Mādhavendra Purī had to undergo many austerities and difficulties to obtain this camphor and sandalwood, as it was not easy traveling at that time. There were many toll collectors, tax collectors, borders that needed to be crossed, rogues, thieves and dacoits. However, Mādhavendra Purī did not consider any personal inconvenience when he undertook the order of the Lord.

We understand by this example how the Lord takes notice when the devotee is willing to accept personal inconvenience and difficulties on His behalf. It is so inconvenient to travel such a distance with such a large quantity of sandalwood. When Mādhavendra Purī stopped at Remuṇā, the Lord appeared again for the third time in a dream and said, “Now take all the sandalwood that you have been carrying and grind it into a paste and put it on the body of Gopīnātha. Gopīnātha is nondifferent from Me. Therefore, when Gopīnātha feels the cooling effect of that sandalwood and camphor, it will be the same as cooling Myself.” The Lord appreciated Mādhavendra Purī so much that He wanted to make it easier for him by not having to carry the sandalwood and camphor all the way back to Govardhana. The Lord wanted to show by this example that He will help the devotee by making it easier for him to fulfill his desire to please the Lord.

Lord Caitanya gave another example of Mādhavendra Purī who composed one verse:

*ayi dīna-dayārdra nātha he*  
*mathurā-nātha kadāvalokyase*  
*hṛdayaṁ tvad-aloka-kātaraṁ*  
*dayita bhrāmyati kiṁ karomy aham*

**“O My Lord! O most merciful master! O master of Mathurā! When shall I see You again? Because of My not seeing You, My agitated heart has become unsteady. O most beloved one, what shall I do now?” (Cc. Madhya 4.197)**

Mādhavendra Purī recited this verse at the time of giving up his body. The only ones who knew and understood this verse were Lord Caitanya, Rādhārāṇī and Mādhavendra Purī.

Mādhavendra Purī is described as the root of feelings of ecstatic love of God in the mood of separation. From him came Īśvara Purī, and then Lord Caitanya became the trunk of that tree.

When Īśvara Purī was reciting verses that would help Mādhavendra Purī remember the Lord at the time of giving up his body, Rāmacandra Purī said to Mādhavendra Purī, “Why are you lamenting? Don’t you know that you should be fixed on Brahman and there will be no disturbances?”

Mādhavendra Purī said, “Get out of my sight! If I give up my body while seeing your wretched face, I will never achieve the Lord of my heart.” He condemned Rāmacandra Purī for committing such an offense. An offense committed to the devotee is considered to be the same as an offense committed to the Lord. Thus Rāmacandra Purī showed an example of wrong behavior.

Conversely, Īśvara Purī showed the example of good behavior. When Mādhavendra Purī was elderly and unable to take care of himself, Īśvara Purī would clean up his stool and urine with his own hands. Īśvara Purī would speak to Mādhavendra Purī in such a way that he would help him to remember the Lord in the mood that Mādhavendra Purī was in. Mādhavendra Purī thus recited the aforementioned verse prior to his giving up his body. This type of viraha (separation) is the same as the mood of the gopīs when Kṛṣṇa leaves Vṛndāvana and goes to a distant place and stays away for a long time. This type of separation is called sudūra-pravāsa.

There are four types of separation. The first is called pūrva-raga, which is a separation that one feels before seeing someone—either as a result of hearing about or seeing a picture of that person. Thus when all the gopīs were very young, they developed feelings of pūrva-raga, or attachment to Kṛṣṇa. Although they had not yet seen Him, they were very anxious to do so, as they were hearing from the nitya-siddha gopīs about Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, the gopīs continue to have this pūrva-raga even after seeing Kṛṣṇa, because each time they see Him, it is like seeing Him for the first time. For a sādhaka who is still aspiring for the association of the Lord, this is the only kind of separation that we can feel, since we have not yet seen Kṛṣṇa.

The second type of separation is called māna, which is separation due to anger. Sometimes when there is a display of anger between Rādhārāṇī and Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa feels separation from Rādhārāṇī, and Rādhārāṇī feels separation from Kṛṣṇa. While Rādhārāṇī is manifesting Her anger, Kṛṣṇa will try in different ways to get Rādhārāṇī’s mind back to allowing Him to associate. Sometimes He even takes His own flute and places it at Her feet, begging for forgiveness.

The third type of separation is called premā-vaicittya, which is feeling separation although the individuals are still in the association of each other. In this type of separation, one thinks that they could lose the association at any moment. This type of separation is also exemplified in the pastime where Kṛṣṇa and Rādhārāṇī were sitting next to each other, and Rādhārāṇī looked into Kṛṣṇa’s eyes, saw Her reflection, and thought that Kṛṣṇa was with another gopī. She fainted and fell on the ground, feeling separation from Kṛṣṇa.

On another occasion, Rādhārāṇī and Kṛṣṇa were sitting together and there was a bee buzzing around. Madhumaṅgala chased the bee out of the kuñja. When he came back, he said, “Madhu (the honeybee) is gone.”

Rādhārāṇī said, “Madhu is gone?!” Immediately She thought he was referring to Kṛṣṇa (Madhu). She thus fell on the ground in feelings of separation, even though Kṛṣṇa was just beside Her.

The fourth type of separation is pravāsa, which is the feeling that one has when Kṛṣṇa goes out for a short period of time. This is exhibited by mother Yaśodā when Kṛṣṇa goes to the pasturing grounds every day. Not wanting Kṛṣṇa to leave, Mother Yaśodā looks for various excuses for Him to remain at home. All the cowherd boys assemble in front of the house, and are calling for Kṛṣṇa to come with them to the pasturing grounds. However, mother Yaśodā comes out, looks at Kṛṣṇa, and then before He leaves, she gives Him something to eat. She then turns back around and says, “I should give Kṛṣṇa something to drink. He may be thirsty.” She then brings Him some fruits and juice.

As she is walking away, she stops, turns around, and comes back. She does not want Kṛṣṇa to leave, so she finds another excuse for Him to stay: “Kṛṣṇa’s clothes look disheveled. Maybe I should go and straighten up His clothes.” She thus begins to straighten His clothes and His turban to make sure that everything looks just right.

She walks back towards the house, stops, and again looks back at Kṛṣṇa. Staring at Him, tears come to her eyes. She thinks, “Maybe I should tell all His friends to protect Him, because Kṛṣṇa is always getting Himself into trouble when He goes out to the pasturing grounds.”

She says, “Balarāma, you stand in front. Śrīdāmā, you stand on the side, and you stand behind. You all protect Kṛṣṇa. Make sure nothing happens to Him. Sometimes when He comes back home, I see there are so many scratches on His body. He is going too deep into the brush, and He’s getting scratches from the thorns. You should protect Him.”

She turns around and walks back to the house, but then stops, turns around, and looks at Kṛṣṇa again.

Finally, Kṛṣṇa comes up to mother Yaśodā and grasps her lotus feet and says, “Mother, please, go home! Please let Me go. All My friends are waiting for Me. Please just go home. I will be back.”

Mother Yaśodā stands there and watches as Kṛṣṇa leaves with His friends. It is described that she looks just like a mother cow, displaying love for her calf, standing there just like a painted picture, not moving. She watches Kṛṣṇa go off with the dust of the calves’ hoof prints rising in the air. She feels separation, even though Kṛṣṇa will just be at a short distance.

There are also examples of feelings of separation experienced when Kṛṣṇa leaves the gopīs to go away at a long distance. They felt this separation when they saw Akrura coming and Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma were on the chariot. The only reason the gopīs do not give up their bodies is because they think that if they give up their bodies, Kṛṣṇa will not be able to live without them. Thus they do not give up their bodies, but they feel such torment of separation.

It is with this same feeling of separation that Mādhavendra Purī recited the verse just prior to giving up his body (Cc. Madhya 4.197): “O My Lord! O most merciful master! O master of Mathurā! When shall I see You again? Because of My not seeing You, My agitated heart has become unsteady. O most beloved one, what shall I do now?” However, a devotee tolerates all kinds of adverse conditions, continues to engage in Kṛṣṇa’s service, and continues to glorify Kṛṣṇa. A devotee lives by hearing and chanting the glories of Kṛṣṇa in the association of the devotees and by bringing Kṛṣṇa consciousness to others. A devotee also cares for the welfare of others. This not only captures the attention of those who are poor in spiritual understanding, but also that of the Supreme Lord. The Lord says: “By the dust of the lotus feet of My pure devotees I desire to purify the entire material world which is situated within Me. Thus I always follow in the footsteps of My devotees who are always equally disposed towards everyone and who are always fixed in chanting My glories.” Kṛṣṇa says: “I follow in their footsteps and I take their dust.” Kṛṣṇa’s attention is captured by the devotee, who is fixed in devotional service.

The devotee never wants any attention. In another instance, Gopīnātha stole a pot of sweet rice, and when the pūjārī went after it, Gopīnātha told him, “There is a sannyāsī whose name is Mādhavendra Purī. He is sitting nearby. You should bring the sweet rice to him.”

The pūjārī said, “Where is this sannyāsī named Mādhavendra Purī? Mādhavendra Purī, please, show yourself to me! Gopīnātha has stolen some sweet rice for you.”

When the pūjārī found Mādhavendra Purī, Mādhavendra Purī took that sweet rice and said, “The Lord has stolen sweet rice for me? When people will find out about this, surely I will be surrounded by so many people.” In the middle of the night he decided to leave so that he would not get any recognition or any reputation. However, it is described in Caitanya-caritāmṛta that reputation follows a devotee wherever he goes. Therefore, even though Mādhavendra Purī left that place, because of his ideal example, the Lord recognized him, and then so many others also recognized him.

When the nondevotees hear about the example of such devotees, they become purified and attracted to the lotus feet of a devotee and therefore also become attracted to the lotus feet of the Lord.

## Serving in Unity

*śrī-bhagavān uvāca*  
*varaṁ vṛṇīdhvaṁ bhadraṁ vo*  
*yūyaṁ me nṛpa-nandanāḥ*  
*sauhārdenāpṛthag-dharmās*  
*tuṣṭo ’haṁ sauhṛdena vaḥ*

**The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: My dear sons of the King, I am very much pleased by the friendly relationships among you. All of you are engaged in one occupation—devotional service. I am so pleased with your mutual friendship that I wish you all good fortune. Now you may ask a benediction of Me. (Bhāg. 4.30.8)**

PURPORT

Since the sons of King Prācīnabarhiṣat were all united in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, the Lord was very pleased with them. Each and every one of the sons of King Prācīnabarhiṣat was an individual soul, but they were united in offering transcendental service to the Lord. The unity of the individual souls attempting to satisfy the Supreme Lord or rendering service to the Lord is real unity. In the material world such unity is not possible. Even though people may officially unite, they all have different interests. In the United Nations, for instance, all the nations have their particular national ambitions, and consequently they cannot be united. Disunity between individual souls is so strong within this material world that even in a society of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, members sometimes appear disunited due to their having different opinions and leaning toward material things. Actually, in Kṛṣṇa consciousness there cannot be two opinions. There is only one goal: to serve Kṛṣṇa to one’s best ability. If there is some disagreement over service, such disagreement is to be taken as spiritual. Those who are actually engaged in the service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead cannot be disunited in any circumstance. This makes the Supreme Personality of Godhead very happy and willing to award all kinds of benediction to His devotees, as indicated in this verse. We can see that the Lord is immediately prepared to award all benedictions to the sons of King Prācīnabarhiṣat.

This verse very nicely describes the best means by which we can please others: to recognize the potential in every living being as a servant of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Every living entity has the potential or the desire to love, please, and serve somebody, but this desire cannot be fulfilled until there is a proper receptacle for that desire. If we try to satisfy the material desires of others, we will only become frustrated, because nobody can be satisfied by the fulfillment of their material desires. This is a source of great frustration in this world. Everybody is struggling to please others, but with some personal motive or personal ambition. This is described as the mercantile mentality.

Prahlāda Mahārāja said to Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva, “Please don’t tempt me by offering benedictions to me; I don’t want to be a merchant. I don’t want to serve You with the idea of getting some benediction back from You. If You have to give any benediction, then give me the benediction that You will always be my master and I will always be Your servant.”

The sincere devotee of the Lord is always praying for the opportunity to satisfy the Lord and to satisfy others by helping them to increase their attachment to the service of the Lord. There is no other way to satisfy anybody in this material world. They may get some flickering happiness because of some material achievement. However, in their heart there will always be something lacking. Everybody is feeling that intense lacking in this material world. It is rare for a person to understand the need to hanker for the service of the Supreme Lord; however that potential spark is within the heart of every living being. A devotee of the Lord sees that spark in everyone—that by nature, everyone has a desire to serve Kṛṣṇa. This is the real sense of unity that exists on the platform of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. This is the real sense of unity that Śrīla Prabhupāda is speaking about with reference to this verse in the Bhāgavatam.

Prabhupāda says:

There is only one goal: to serve Kṛṣṇa to one’s best ability. If there is some disagreement over service, such disagreement is to be taken as spiritual. Those who are actually engaged in the service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead cannot be disunited in any circumstance. (Purport to Bhāg. 4.30.8)

Thus to be in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the platform for unity. In the material world, the only thing lacking is Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Everything else is available if we want it. We should be aspiring to be Kṛṣṇa consciousness. To be on the platform of unity in service to the Lord is a state of consciousness. Sometimes we think unity is when we are doing everything together. This is beneficial when we are collectively endeavoring to engage in the saṅkīrtana movement—to distribute the glories of the Lord, to maintain Śrīla Prabhupāda’s temples, to worship the deities, etc. However, doing service together does not only mean being physically together; it also means sharing a common consciousness or goal in those endeavors. That common consciousness is the desire to please the Lord without anything in return for that service. Devotees who work together in Kṛṣṇa consciousness in this way will see that here is no disunity.

However, Prabhupāda says:

Disunity between individual souls is so strong within this material world that even in a society of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, members sometimes appear disunited due to their having different opinions and leaning toward material things. (Purport to Bhāg. 4.30.8)

Everybody in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is always transparent in their activities. They are not thinking that their way is the right way and that only they are serving the higher order. Trying to please superior Vaiṣṇavas is the means for satisfying the Supreme Lord.

We have to remove our ego and false identity of possessiveness, thinking that everything has to be done “my way.” That is the main obstacle in engaging in devotional service, and is the main source of conflict in the material world. It is described in the Second Canto of the Bhāgavatam that persons who are bewildered by the illusory energy of the Lord are always absorbed in the topic of “I” and “this is mine.” However, our true mood should be as a servant, simply representing the superior order. We should be looking to see that desire in others to please the Supreme Lord, the potential in everyone else, and try to encourage them in Kṛṣṇa consciousness and in serving the Supreme Lord.

It is said in the Bhāgavatam (7.5.12, Purport):

Everyone should be friendly for the service of the Lord. Everyone should praise another’s service to the Lord and not be proud of his own service. This is the way of Vaiṣṇava thinking, Vaikuṇṭha thinking. There may be rivalries and apparent competition between servants in performing service, but in the Vaikuṇṭha planets the service of another servant is appreciated, not condemned. This is Vaikuṇṭha competition. There is no question of enmity between servants. Everyone should be allowed to render service to the Lord to the best of his ability, and everyone should appreciate the service of others. Such are the activities of Vaikuṇṭha.

In the spiritual world, Vaikuṇṭha, this mentality is all-pervasive. Everyone appreciates the service that others render for the Supreme Lord’s pleasure, and the Lord is displeased if He sees any disunity or anyone obstructing the service of others. This is seen in the Bhāgavatam in the example of when Jaya and Vijaya obstructed the four Kumāras from trying to enter Vaikuṇṭha. Of course, this was a līlā, and it was the will of the Lord that it take place. However, it still gives a very graphic description of how displeased and concerned the Lord becomes when someone obstructs the service of another devotee.

The four Kumāras are practically the oldest beings in the universe, being the sons of Lord Brahmā. Although they have the appearance of five year old boys, they have a great depth of Vedic wisdom. They would wander about naked. They passed through six gates of Vaikuṇṭha, and when they approached the seventh gate, the two gatekeepers who were standing there, Jaya and Vijaya, stopped them and obstructed them from entering into the kingdom of Godhead. They had the external judgment that these were just four little boys, wandering around naked, and thus they refused to allow them entrance through the seventh gate.

Although a young child generally can go anywhere without any obstruction because they are innocent, when the four Kumāras tried to pass through that seventh gate, Jaya and Vijaya manifested a disposition that was quite unpalatable to the Lord. They blocked these four boys with their staffs. The four Kumāras became very angry, as they were very anxious to see the lotus feet and personal form of the Supreme Lord. Their anger, however, was not the anger of the material world. The four Kumāras are completely liberated souls. Their anger was due to their service to the Lord having been obstructed, and thus they wanted to curse Jaya and Vijaya.

\[The four Kumāras said\]: “Who are these two persons who have developed such a discordant mentality even though they are posted in the service of the Lord in the highest position and are expected to have developed the same qualities as the Lord? How are these two persons living in Vaikuṇṭha? Where is the possibility of an enemy’s coming into this kingdom of God? The Supreme Personality of Godhead has no enemy. Who could be envious of Him? Probably these two persons are imposters; therefore they suspect others to be like themselves. In the Vaikuṇṭha world there is complete harmony between the residents and the Supreme Personality of Godhead, just as there is complete harmony within space between the big and the small skies. Why then is there a seed of fear in this field of harmony? These two persons are dressed like inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, but wherefrom can their disharmony come into existence? Therefore let us consider how these two contaminated persons should be punished. The punishment should be apt, for thus benefit can eventually be bestowed upon them. Since they find duality in the existence of Vaikuṇṭha life, they are contaminated and should be removed from this place to the material world, where the living entities have three kinds of enemies.” (Bhāg. 3.15.32-34)

They thought that since they were not enemies, but were being treated as such, they should go to the material world where they have real enemies—the enemies of desire, lust and anger. In the material world, we have personal material desires, we have lust towards the objects of sense enjoyment and we become angry when those objects or desires are unfulfilled.

Kṛṣṇa describes in Bhagavad-gītā that there are three gates leading into hell: lust, anger and greed. There are no enemies in the Vaikuṇṭha mentality. Everyone is seen as a servant of the Supreme Lord and their service is recognized and appreciated. The best way to help them in their service is to remind them who they are serving so they can render service in the proper consciousness, and not to obstruct their service.

Everyone is hankering to have genuine reciprocal relationships on the spiritual platform. The natural desire in the heart of every living entity is to have a loving relationship with someone. If we cut ourselves off from having loving relationships, then we are left to deal with the enemies of the material world—lust, anger and greed. These enemies influence everything we do in this world, and impact our attempts to have personal relationships. When lust, greed or anger dominates, we cannot have a personal relationship with anybody. The best way to become free from lust, anger and greed is to have a loving relationship on a spiritual platform. It is the most powerful force that can undo these influences that are dragging us to hell.

The Vaikuṇṭha mentality means seeing everyone’s potential to love and serve Kṛṣṇa, and trying to help them remember Him, the object of their service—not by instructing them in their service and having them to do it “my way.” The Lord does not like this mentality. When the gatekeepers, Jaya and Vijaya, behaved in this way, the Lord was not pleased. In fact, when they were cursed by the four Kumāras, the Supreme Lord immediately came before them with the Goddess of Fortune. He prostrated on the ground and folded His hands before the four Kumāras and said, “I have to beg your forgiveness because these two people claim to be My servants. A wrong act committed by My servant leads the people in general to blame their master, just as a spot of white leprosy on any part of the body spoils all of the skin.”

The Lord said to the four Kumāras, “The punishment you have given them is appropriate. I will accept it, but please let them come back to Me afterwards. Anybody who bathes in the nectar of hearing My glories, pastimes and names is very dear to Me. I will even cut off my own arm if it is found hostile to you.” This is how displeased the Lord becomes when this mentality of enmity manifests in the Vaikuṇṭha atmosphere.

Thus the Lord is pleased to see how everyone is united in devotional service. Vaikuṇṭha consciousness is when no one obstructs the service of others who are endeavoring sincerely to please the Lord, but instead, encourages and reminds them of who is the object of their service. He does not feel threatened by the competition. If we start to become envious that someone else is getting more recognition for their service, then we should question whether what we are doing is pleasing to Kṛṣṇa. We cannot serve Kṛṣṇa if we are possessed with this mentality, and we may be committing an offense by having such a mentality. We should therefore be very careful. We should always recognize that we are subordinate to the Supreme Lord in everything that we do. We should not take credit for the service that we render, and we should consider it a privilege to have the opportunity to be given some service.

*śuśrūṣoḥ śraddadhānasya*  
*vāsudeva-kathā-ruciḥ*  
*syān mahat-sevayā viprāḥ*  
*puṇya-tīrtha-niṣevaṇāt*

**“By serving those devotees who are completely freed from all vice, great service is done. By such service, one gains affinity for hearing the messages of Vāsudeva.” (Bhāg. 1.2.16)**

To see if we are becoming free from envy, we can check to see how much our taste for hearing the glories of Kṛṣṇa is manifesting in our heart. Conversely, if we want to see how much it has not gone away, we will see it by how much the tendency to speak about ourselves and to speak about the topics of the material world is present. We can awaken our attraction for hearing and chanting by serving the devotees of the Lord. Seek out the association of these devotees, try to serve them selflessly, please them, and develop a personal relationship with them. Then you will be able to pour that personal loving relationship into all your other relationships in this world. However, if we hold back and serve our own selfish desires for pride, recognition, greed, and profit, then that will also spill out in all relationships with everyone in this world. Then we will become increasingly frustrated, filled with lust, anger, and greed, and we will not be able to appreciate the good qualities in anyone. This is a hellish state of consciousness. We should therefore try to develop the Vaikuṇṭha consciousness, let these loving relationships with Vaiṣṇavas spill into our relationships with everyone else in this world, and live with the genuine desire to seek our advancement in Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

**Question: If someone hurts us, how can we shield ourselves emotionally, yet not take any offense by their actions?**

Bhagavad-gītā (10.4-5) describes both the good and bad qualities that Kṛṣṇa has created. In his purport to these verses, Prabhupāda describes that tolerance means that one should be willing to overlook the minor offenses of others. We are still conditioned souls, and sometimes we may find ourselves in a situation where a devotee may say something out of frivolity, or a statement may slip out of his mouth that may affect us emotionally and hurt our false ego, and we will want to protect ourselves. Ultimately, however, it is due to false ego that we become affected. We cannot immediately give up false ego. As we progress in spiritual life, the false ego is the most difficult thing to give up, and it takes time to do so. We have these anarthas within our heart, because we still identify ourselves with this external body and our external qualities and characteristics.

We can protect ourselves by keeping good association with devotees who are always encouraging us, and, by willingly overlooking the minor offenses that are committed by others in the process of engaging in devotional service, we have to expect that these things will happen from time to time. If they cause us to become too withdrawn and fearful of putting ourselves in a situation where such feelings could arise, then it is a good impetus for us to pray very deeply to Kṛṣṇa to help us to overcome this shortcoming within ourselves. Praying like this is a very important part of our practice of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and it will give us strength.

We should pray in accordance with the prayers of the previous ācāryas. We should find a verse from Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura or from the Bhāgavatam which resonates with a particular shortcoming that we see within ourselves, and we should make that a daily prayer. We will then get strength. We must always be in the association of devotees. If we develop any tendency to withdraw from devotees, it can be very dangerous for our spiritual life. If we find ourselves in a situation like that, one way to get strength is by praying daily to overcome that obstacle in spiritual life and to overlook the minor offenses that are committed by others.

**Question: Sometimes in our attempts to do our service, we may be strict with others. How can we execute our service without ruining our relationships with the other devotees?**

When performing some duty that is coming from Kṛṣṇa, we should try to do it in a way that is satisfying. We should be nonenvious in our dealings with others. In other words, we are strict with ourselves, but we should be more liberal in our dealings with others. If our service requires that we have to be stricter with others, then we should first be strict with ourselves. By so doing, we can inspire others to become stricter by our good example. Devotees need to be inspired to serve. Sometimes it is not easy to force devotees to do something they do not want to do. Yet, there has to be certain standards maintained by devotees who live in the temple. If devotees are not cooperative and are not willing to make that commitment, then rather than forcing them, you should bring it to the attention of the higher authorities. Everybody living in the temple should be expected to follow the established standard, and that should be understood before they even move into the temple.

Prabhupāda said in the Fifth Canto of the Bhāgavatam that our temples are not hotels for lazy people. Thus we have to be strict with those who are not willing to do their service, and we should tell the higher authorities. If we cannot get others to do what they are asked, then we can just be strict with ourselves. Kṛṣṇa knows the heart.

**Question: In Bhagavad-gītā Kṛṣṇa says that for one who is on this path, even a small endeavor will not be lost. He gives His assurance that He will preserve what a devotee has and give him what is lacking. If a devotee performs some severe kind of offense, such as Vaiṣṇava aparādha or nāma-aparādha, will Kṛṣṇa still preserve the assets that the devotee gained in the practice of devotional service?**

The result of his offenses is that he will lose his taste for devotional service. For example, there was a seed of fruitive desire within the heart of Rāmacandra Purī, and when he offended his spiritual master, Mādhavendra Purī, the seed fructified. Rāmacandra Purī then fell from his position. This is what happens to us when we offend an advanced Vaiṣṇava—the seed for fruitive desire will grow within our heart, and when it fructifies, we will lose our taste. When we lose our taste, we can no longer engage in devotional activities.

There is, however, a way to redeem everything that we had previously gained from our devotional service; it is not lost. We can be redeemed if we beg forgiveness from the Vaiṣṇava that we offended. If that Vaiṣṇava does not forgive us, then we can still take shelter of the holy name, feeling ourselves to be completely fallen and unworthy of its mercy, but worthy of punishment, for having offended a Vaiṣṇava. With the heart full of contrition, we can take shelter in the constant chanting of the holy name of the Lord. The holy name can bestow forgiveness upon us, and we can be reinstated. However, without forgiveness, we cannot be reinstated.

**Question: If we see a senior devotee not preaching in accordance to Śrīla Prabhupāda’s teachings, and we tell him about it—either directly or through another senior devotee, is it an aparādha on our part?**

It is not an aparādha if you present it to a senior devotee for them to determine whether or not it is a deviation. He will then take the appropriate action. Do not get directly involved.

## Receiving and Giving Shelter

Everyone is looking for shelter. However, shelter cannot be manufactured by artificial means. It can only be obtained by coming under the protection of the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord which is the only shelter for all living beings.

Śrīla Prabhupāda explained in a lecture:

*kṛṣṇa-bhakta—niṣkāma, ataeva ‘śānta’*  
*bhukti-mukti-siddhi-kāmī—sakali ‘aśānta’*

(Cc. Madhya 19.149)

Kṛṣṇa-bhakta, one who is fully Kṛṣṇa conscious, he is śānta. He is fully confident. Kṛṣṇa consciousness or God consciousness, he is fully confident that “Kṛṣṇa, I have surrendered to Kṛṣṇa. I have taken shelter of Kṛṣṇa, and He has promised, ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi \[Bg. 18.66\]. Then where is the cause of my anxiety?” Therefore he can become... He has understood Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality, almighty, all-powerful, full of all opulences. “So if he has taken my charge, then where is my anxiety?” That is śānti. That is śānti. And so long we are taking shelter of māyā, asat, which will not stay...

Suppose we are taking shelter, child is taking shelter of the father, mother, or the citizens is taking shelter of the state, of the government. So one has to to take shelter of something else for protection, for security. But they are not actually security. Therefore we are always full of anxiety. You may be a citizen of a great state like United States of America. But you are not without any anxiety because that shelter is not sufficient. That will not stay. Just like recently in America they had to dethrone Mr. Nixon because they were not free from anxiety. So you cannot become free from anxiety by taking shelter of anything material. That is not possible. Sadā samudvigna-dhiyām asad-grahāt \[Bhāg. 7.5.5\]. Asat and sat. Sat means eternal, and asat means temporary. So we are eternal. Na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre \[Bg. 2.20\].
