We are not annihilated after the annihilation or destruction of this body. Therefore we have to take shelter of the eternal. Then we’ll be happy. And so long we shall take shelter of the temporary thing, asat, this material world, material society, friendship, love, state, community, nation—anything you take, they are not permanent—so you cannot be happy. But if you take shelter for security at the lotus feet of the Supreme, then you are actually secure. (Śrīla Prabhupāda lecture—Bombay, January 18, 1975)

Because we are eternal, we have to take shelter of something eternal. We will never be free from anxiety as long as we are taking shelter of something material. We must therefore give up our materialistic conceptions about shelter.

Śrīla Prabhupāda explains in the Seventh Canto of the Bhāgavatam that one should not take shelter of a person who cannot control the senses. Such persons who are still bound by the ropes of fruitive labor, which are made of very strong cords, still have to undergo repeated birth and death in the material world. They are compared to be like the blind who lead the blind. How can somebody who is blind lead somebody else who is blind? One has to take shelter of somebody who has proper vision of how to take shelter of the Supreme Lord. Similarly, when one comes under the shade of a big tree, then automatically he feels sheltered from the heat.

Regarding material shelter, Prabhupāda quotes the verse spoken by Prahlāda Mahārāja to Hiraṇyakaśipu (Bhāg. 7.5.5): sadā samudvigna-dhiyām asad-grahāt. When Hiraṇyakaśipu asked Prahlāda Mahārāja to tell him something that he had learned, Prahlāda Mahārāja replied:

**“O best of the asuras, King of the demons, as far as I have learned from my spiritual master, any person who has accepted a temporary body and temporary household life is certainly embarrassed by anxiety because of having fallen in a dark well where there is no water but only suffering. One should give up this position and go to the forest \[vana\]. More clearly, one should go to Vṛndāvana, where only Kṛṣṇa consciousness is prevalent, and should thus take shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”**

Asad-grahāt means taking shelter of the material body or of temporary household life. However, there is no shelter; it is an illusion. Persons who seek this shelter will have to be embarrassed by so much anxiety.

Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura gives a very graphic analogy in connection to this verse, which helps us get a sense of what Prahlāda Mahārāja was telling his father. The example is of a king who went to the forest to hunt. A tiger began to chase him. He decided that he would temporarily take shelter in a well. He thought that if he could temporarily take shelter, the tiger would go away. When he jumped into the well, he grabbed onto two branches and lowered himself further into the well, which had no water. He waited for the tiger to go away.

Similarly, Prahlāda Mahārāja describes in this verse that one has entered the well where there is no water but only suffering. The king was at the bottom of the well, where many poisonous snakes were very eager for him to come down a little further. They were lurching up trying to capture him, but he had taken shelter of the two branches higher up. First he thought he was going to take shelter of the well, but there was no shelter in the well. Therefore, he then took shelter of the two branches. However, holding on, he looked up and saw that there were two rats that were chewing the branches. One was black, and the other was white.

Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura explains that the tiger represents death, the snakes at the bottom represent all the troubles that exist in household life, the two branches represent pious and impious activities, and the two rats that are chewing the branches represent day and night. Thus, day and night, or time, is passing, and one has taken shelter in this well. However, time is ultimately destroying everything, just as these two rats will ultimately be successful at severing the branches from the trunk. Furthermore, the tiger of death is not going away, and there are poisonous snakes below. This is a very fearful condition to be in.

Despite being in this condition, the king sees that there is a honeycomb in the branches. Because he is shaking in fear, the honey is gliding down the side of the branch, next to his mouth. He tastes the honey and thinks that it is very nice. Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura explains that this is the happiness that one obtains in the material condition of life. He is in such a precarious situation, yet he derives pleasure from the honey. Prabhupāda therefore says that one should not take shelter of that which is asat (temporary).

Prahlāda Mahārāja also says that one who has accepted temporary householder life is embarrassed by anxiety. However, for one who is taking shelter of householder life, he must also take shelter in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, as householder life is not full shelter.

There are many other examples of taking shelter of that which is temporary. Many people go to America thinking they will find shelter and will live in opulence. However, opulence is not real shelter. It is only material shelter, and is therefore an illusion. As long as we take shelter of something that is temporary, we will be in anxiety.

*ā-brahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ*  
*punar āvartino ‘rjuna*

**Kṛṣṇa says, “From the highest planet in the material world down to the lowest, all are places of misery wherein repeated birth and death take place.” (Bg. 8.16)**

It is our natural state of life to be sheltered. However, we have to take shelter in that which is sat—eternal. We must therefore take shelter of the association of devotees—those who help us to take shelter of the Supreme Lord. When devotees pray for benedictions, they pray to live in the association of devotees, as that is where there are always discussions about the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In this Age of Kali, the most powerful method to obtain shelter of the Lord is through the association of devotees.

Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī says in his Mādhava-mahotsava: “Though one usually ignores others in attaining one’s own goals, those aspiring for premā accept dependence on others with similar goals and tastes. Thus, cooperating with each other, they work together, keeping in mind the goal of premā.”

In Teachings of Queen Kuntī, Prabhupāda explains that in the material world, to be dependent on the mercy of someone else is the utmost sign of misfortune. But in the case of our transcendental relation with the Lord, it is the most fortunate case when we can live completely dependent on Him. To be dependent upon the Lord means to also be dependent upon the association of His devotees. It is only in the association of devotees that we can cooperate together and help each other in a common goal—the goal of being Kṛṣṇa conscious. We may engage in various projects together, which may create a sense of unity and harmony, but if Kṛṣṇa is not at the center, it will only produce more anxiety.

**Question: Can one give shelter if he himself is not sheltered?**

No. In order to give real shelter, one must be sheltered. Otherwise, it will only be artificial shelter.

*kṛṣṇa-bhakta—niṣkāma, ataeva ‘śānta’*  
*bhukti-mukti-siddhi-kāmī—sakali ‘aśānta’*

(Cc. Madhya, 19.149)

**Because a devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa is desireless, he is peaceful. Fruitive workers desire material enjoyment, jñānīs desire liberation, and yogīs desire material opulence; therefore they are all lusty and cannot be peaceful.**

Thus, one of the symptoms of one who has shelter is that he is peaceful; he is not agitated by external conditions.

Arjuna had asked Kṛṣṇa, “What is the symptom of a man who is situated in divine consciousness?” When a man gives up all desires for sense satisfaction which arise from mental concoction and he finds satisfaction in the self, he is in transcendental consciousness, and he is satisfied.

*nārāyaṇa-parāḥ sarve*  
*na kutaścana bibhyati*  
*svargāpavarga-narakeṣv*  
*api tulyārtha-darśinaḥ*

**Devotees solely engaged in the devotional service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Nārāyaṇa, never fear any condition of life. For them the heavenly planets, liberation and the hellish planets are all the same, for such devotees are interested only in the service of the Lord. (Bhāg. 6.17.28)**

The symptom of someone who is sheltered is that he is peaceful and satisfied in any condition. Because he is satisfied, he can give shelter. One who is not satisfied wants something for himself. He may want to increase his prestige by having many followers. He is therefore not sheltered and cannot give shelter.

Prabhupāda explains in Teachings of Queen Kuntī that Kṛṣṇa comes to this world for the sake of His devotees—either to protect them or to give them pleasure. He is not coming to get anything for Himself.

Similarly, for the devotee who is satisfied in his service to Kṛṣṇa, he gives Kṛṣṇa consciousness to others; not for anything for himself. His source of happiness is Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure.

Kṛṣṇa says that to the gopīs, “I am self-satisfied. I do not need anything. But by any service rendered, I am always grateful to you for that service.” The devotee who is taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa can give shelter to others, but if he is not taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa, he cannot be peaceful. If he is not peaceful, he cannot give real shelter to somebody else; it will only be temporary shelter, and will only result in anxiety. One must be sheltered to give shelter.

## Holding Festivals to Facilitate Association

Amṛta Vāṇī, or Nectar of Instructions for Immortality, is a book compiled of Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura’s teachings from various sources, such as his lectures and writings. The essence was put into a question and answer format. The contents are relevant to our society today. Reading this book increased my appreciation of Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura’s endeavors for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness on a very large scale. It further increased my appreciation of Śrīla Prabhupāda—seeing how much he was following in the footsteps of his spiritual master by establishing the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, and how he was always thinking of how to expand Kṛṣṇa consciousness on a very large scale.

To expand Kṛṣṇa consciousness is something that is not so easy to do in the Age of Kali, because there are many obstacles that need to be overcome for expanding pure devotional service. Some of those obstacles are discussed in the instructions of Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī. The obstacles begin with the potential impurities that are present within the heart, as they are the major obstacles on the path of devotional service. However, by expanding Kṛṣṇa consciousness, opening many temples and increasing the number of devotees, there are also many obstacles in the organization of the society. In organizing a society of Vaiṣṇavas, we have to be careful not to lose the essence.

There are dangers of considering form before substance, or of losing sight of what is the actual purpose behind the organization. In the Age of Kali, Kali will find a way to get in and disrupt the organization or expansion of a spiritual movement. Therefore, we have to be able to sit back and assess if we are moving in the right direction, which is pure devotion to the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. The organization is meant to facilitate advancement in pure devotional service.

As a part of our organization, our festivals are therefore also meant to facilitate our spiritual progress. Our festival in Ukraine has evolved over a few years into what it is today. Today it is a big organization. It takes a lot of work, effort, anxiety in a lot of people’s minds, and a lot of faith. It really takes faith that something like this can happen. Over the past few years, I tried to instill faith in the hearts of the devotees who are organizing this festival that if we depend on Kṛṣṇa and try to serve Him without any personal motive, He will facilitate our endeavors.

Several years ago, I remember going to maṅgala-ārati at the festival and seeing that many devotees were being refused entrance. One of my disciples from the West was attending the festival that year and she forgot to bring her pass, and she was told that she could not go in for maṅgala-ārati. She told me about it, and I began to think that there must be a better way to handle this. How is it possible that we were telling devotees not to go to maṅgala-ārati or to Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam class? I was bewildered. The whole purpose in organizing that festival was to create the facility for as many devotees as possible to come and hear hari-kathā. Should it be that if a person cannot afford to come and pay for all the expenses that they are banned? Or in other words, that the poor people cannot hear hari-kathā? I thought that there must be a better way of organizing the festival so that we do not have to refuse devotees from going to maṅgala-ārati and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam class.

I therefore suggested that we try to organize it on a voluntary basis. There was some resistance in the minds of some devotees, thinking that it would be too difficult, given that more and more devotees were coming.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura says the following in his Amṛta Vāṇī where he is explaining the importance of holding festivals:

Is it necessary to live with devotees to get their association?

Certainly association with devotees is essential. However, we attain association according to our own qualification. It is not a fact that simply by living together we can take advantage of good association. And it is true that we can associate with devotees even when we live at a distance from them. Association does not necessarily mean living in the same room. However living with devotees makes it easier to hear from them, whereas such hearing is more difficult over a distance.

We conduct festivals in the temple to give everyone the opportunity to associate with devotees, to destroy their attachment for material life, to display compassion for all living entities, to develop a taste for chanting the holy name, and to engage in the service of Hari, guru, and the Vaiṣṇavas. The Maṭha’s main purpose in holding festivals, reciting Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, and discussing hari-kathā is to awaken the soul’s constitutional propensity to serve Kṛṣṇa. If we hear hari-kathā in the association of devotees, we revive awareness of our constitutional position and attain the ultimate goal of life. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Association, Part 11)

Here, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta is giving the different purposes for conducting festivals. First he qualifies that they are meant to give everybody the opportunity to associate with devotees. However, he clarifies that associating with devotees does not mean simply living in the same room with them. Association means hearing from them. Therefore, if there is a facility to live closer to devotees, then it is beneficial, because one has a greater opportunity to hear from such Vaiṣṇavas.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta expresses that another purpose for organizing festivals is for hearing from Vaiṣṇavas, as it is supposed to eradicate obstacles on the path of devotional service or to help cleanse the heart from the unnecessary weeds of material desires.

Organizing festivals is also meant to display compassion for all living entities; not for some living entities. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta had a vision for everyone. He does say that we attain association according to our own qualification. Qualification also means one’s desire for association, which is an essential factor for attaining association. We want to associate with those who are going to help us make progress on the path of devotional service. To display compassion for all living entities means that we have to feel the sufferings of others and to think of a way to alleviate their sufferings. Everyone should be given the opportunity to associate. However, association has to be in the right mood.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta also says that if one gets genuine association, the result is that the heart changes. It becomes purified, and then one begins to develop a taste for chanting the holy name and engaging in the service of Hari, guru and Vaiṣṇavas, which is the next purpose stated by Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta for organizing festivals.

Therefore, regarding the Ukraine festival, I started to think that there must be a better way to organize a festival so that as many people as possible can get the association of advanced Vaiṣṇavas. I felt that the service that I could render to all Vaiṣṇavas was to facilitate to as many living beings as possible the opportunity to fulfill these objectives.

Of course, organization is not everything; substance also has to be there. As Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta explains, the Vaiṣṇava’s duty is to make his companions and dependents fearless, free from anxiety and happy, and to deliver all conditioned souls from Māyā’s hands. If a devotee actually has substance and has the desire to please Kṛṣṇa in the core of his heart, then he genuinely wants to see others spiritually happy; not materially happy or complacent and satisfied with material life.

In the Nectar of Devotion, Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī has divided happiness into three categories: (1) happiness derived from material enjoyment, (2) happiness derived by identifying oneself with the Supreme Brahman, and (3) happiness derived from Kṛṣṇa consciousness. The first kind of happiness is that which one derives from material enjoyment and is not real happiness. It has a beginning and an end, and it only leads to suffering.

Prahlāda Mahārāja states in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (7.7.42): “In this material world, every materialist desires to achieve happiness and diminish his distress, and therefore he acts accordingly. Actually, however, one is happy as long as one does not endeavor for happiness; as soon as one begins his activities for happiness, his conditions of distress begin.” Prahlāda Mahārāja is explaining the nature of material happiness—as soon as we begin our endeavors for material happiness, we are actually creating our future distress, due to karmic reactions. Such is the illusion of material happiness.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta prayed that he would never have to look into the face of a materialistic person who is simply interested in sense enjoyment. He first describes the danger of association of materialistic people and then he expresses his own intense fear of having to look into the face of a materialist. When a Vaiṣṇava wants to see others happy, he actually wants to see them getting some taste from spiritual life and getting spiritual happiness, which is superior to material happiness. It is such a superior happiness that makes us lose our attraction for the materialistic way of life. Association with Vaiṣṇavas is meant to produce that kind of result.

Thus, when we come to festivals and associate and get the opportunity to hear and chant; get an opportunity to live in the proximity of devotees for so many days; and get such an intense absorption in hari-kathā and chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, there should be some result of having gotten that opportunity to associate with devotees who have substance. The result is that there should be a decrease in our desires for material enjoyment and an increase in our desires for spiritual life.

Even though we may know that material desires are futile, and we cannot completely give them up, we should at least recognize them and know that we do not want them as they lead to suffering. We should cultivate the desire to give them up. The association of Vaiṣṇavas is the way to cultivate that desire. A Vaiṣṇava is somebody who wants to see others getting the third type of happiness, which is derived from Kṛṣṇa consciousness. This happiness is superior to both material happiness and that which is derived from liberation or from the relief of suffering.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura continues in his Amṛta Vāṇī:

A devotee is saintly. He is neither a material enjoyer nor a dry renunciant. By associating with saintly devotees, we can understand that just as material enjoyment is sinful, the path of dry renunciation is also sinful. Confused about what to do, the pseudo-renunciants adopt the path of renunciation. Being attached or simply detached from the material world are both signs of aversion to the Supreme Lord. Unless we give up these forms of aversion—material enjoyment and dry renunciation—we cannot attain complete shelter in devotional service. If we fail to understand the meaning of pure devotional service, we will end up either as material enjoyers or dry renunciants \[both of which are sinful\]. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Association, Part 11)

*kṛṣṇa-bhakta—niṣkāma, ataeva ‘śānta’*  
*bhukti-mukti-siddhi-kāmī—sakali ‘aśānta’*

**Because a devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa is desireless, he is peaceful. Fruitive workers desire material enjoyment, jñānīs desire liberation, and yogīs desire material opulence; therefore they are all lusty and cannot be peaceful. (Cc. Madhya 19.149)**

The dry renunciants described here are those who have no knowledge of devotion to the lotus feet of Lord Kṛṣṇa. They simply see that this world is a place of suffering, and therefore they try to renounce it. However, their renunciation is incomplete, because they fail to understand how everything is ultimately coming from Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, real renunciation is yukta-vairāgya.

Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī states:

*anāsaktasya viṣayān*  
*yathārham upayuñjataḥ*  
*nirbandhaḥ kṛṣṇa-sambandhe*  
*yuktaṁ vairāgyam ucyate*  
*prāpañcikatayā buddhyā*  
*hari-sambandhi-vastunaḥ*  
*mumukṣubhiḥ parityāgo*  
*vairāgyaṁ phalgu kathyat*

**When one is not attached to anything but at the same time accepts anything in relation to Kṛṣṇa, one is rightly situated above possessiveness. On the other hand, one who rejects everything without knowledge of its relationship to Kṛṣṇa is not as complete in his renunciation. (Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu 1.2.255-6)**

The devotees find the correct means by which everything can be utilized in the service of the Lord. (Commentary on Text 3, NOI)

Yukta-vairāgya means that one should use everything for the service of Kṛṣṇa. Unless you become a sannyāsī, you can never attain kṛṣṇa-premā. Of course, the real meaning of sannyāsa is when one does everything for Kṛṣṇa and nothing for himself. Therefore, there are householder-sannyāsīs. We saw how Śrīla Prabhupāda’s householder disciples even spread Kṛṣṇa consciousness far superior than some sannyāsīs who previously attempted before them.

Therefore, we should not be interested in dry renunciation of this world, as it is false renunciation, and cannot give real happiness. Rather, it leads to further suffering, because the lusty desires are still present in that false renunciation. As long as there are lusty desires for enjoyment, there will have to be suffering. Therefore only devotees of Kṛṣṇa can be peaceful. Kṛṣṇa-bhakta niṣkāma—devotees of the Lord have no material desires. Such is the happiness which is derived from devotional service.

A genuine Vaiṣṇava wants to see others developing the same kind of happiness. Thus many festivals are held, and many devotees who have substance are coming to give their association and to help make others happy; not just make others happy during the festival, but also to carry that happiness with them afterwards. They want to see others become free from anxiety, because anxiety is also a source of so much suffering.

Śrīla Prabhupāda says that this material world is called kuṇṭha, a place of anxiety. The spiritual world is vaikuṇṭha, where there is no anxiety. As long as one is in the material world, he must accept anxiety.

There are two types of anxiety: material and spiritual. Material anxiety is that which we get from the pursuit of sense gratification, which is the cause of bondage. Spiritual anxiety is liberating. We should become anxious for the service of the Lord. We can see if we are advancing in devotional service by the degree to which we are becoming anxious to do more to please Kṛṣṇa.

Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī describes in Bṛhad-Bhāgavatāmṛta that a devotee always feels a need for more mercy, and feels unqualified for the mercy that he has received. He never thinks that he has enough love for Kṛṣṇa and he never thinks that he has done enough for Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, spiritual anxiety means the awakening of these desires. This anxiety is purifying. When we associate with Vaiṣṇavas, we should feel that kind of push.

Therefore, festivals are established for that purpose. There are many devotees who are organizing the Ukraine festivals, and they have a lot of anxiety to organize it in such a way that it is accessible to all the devotees who wish to come. I felt that I had put them in this anxiety. I therefore preached to them: We have to depend on Kṛṣṇa! If we simply try to please these senior Vaiṣṇavas who are coming to relieve the material anxieties and awaken the spiritual anxiety of those attending this festival, and if we try to facilitate their devotional service by bringing as many living entities as possible into their association, then we should not be fearful, because it is a genuine spiritual service—to facilitate service to Hari, guru and Vaiṣṇavas. As explained by Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta, this is one of the purposes of organizing festivals—to develop a taste for chanting the holy names and to engage in the service of Hari, guru and the Vaiṣṇavas.

## Chapter 9 – Preaching

## Book Distribution

During his manifest presence in this world, Prabhupāda emphasized book distribution, and the importance of establishing this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement on the authority of his books. He also demonstrated this by his own example, as shown by the amount of time he dedicated every day for translating. Wherever Śrīla Prabhupāda would go, not only would he lecture, take care of managerial affairs, and take personal care of the devotees, but he was also translating Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and Caitanya-caritāmṛta.

Prabhupāda said:

Regarding printing our books and literatures, I may inform you in this connection that I saw one bulletin of ‘Indian Railways’ in which it was specifically advised that every railway servant should see to it that the wheels of the carriages or vehicles must be moving always, which means that the railway is going nicely. Similarly all of us should see that our literatures are profusely distributed. That means that our missionary work is going on nicely. Otherwise we are simply sleeping and eating. The literature we have already designated as brhad mrdanga. So distribution of literature means great sankirtana. (Letter to Karāndhara—Nairobi, October 9, 1971)

Śrīla Prabhupāda took great pain and spent so much energy translating books, and he wanted them to be the basis of this movement for many generations to come. In Śrīla Prabhupāda’s concluding words in Caitanya-caritāmṛta, he describes how he feels that his spiritual master inspired him within the heart to produce these books. He quotes the following verse:

*oṁ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*  
*janmādy asya yato ’nvayād itarataś cārtheṣv abhijñaḥ svarāṭ*  
*tene brahma hṛdā ya ādi-kavaye muhyanti yat sūrayaḥ*  
*tejo-vāri-mṛdāṁ yathā vinimayo yatra tri-sargo ’mṛṣā*  
*dhāmnā svena sadā nirasta-kuhakaṁ satyaṁ paraṁ dhīmahi*

**“O my Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, son of Vasudeva, O all-pervading Personality of Godhead, I offer my respectful obeisances unto You. I meditate upon Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa because He is the Absolute Truth and the primeval cause of all causes of the creation, sustenance and destruction of the manifested universes. He is directly and indirectly conscious of all manifestations, and He is independent because there is no other cause beyond Him. It is He only who first imparted the Vedic knowledge unto the heart of Brahmājī, the original living being. By Him even the great sages and demigods are placed into illusion, as one is bewildered by the illusory representations of water seen in fire, or land seen on water. Only because of Him do the material universes, temporarily manifested by the reactions of the three modes of nature, appear factual, although they are unreal. I therefore meditate upon Him, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is eternally existent in the transcendental abode, which is forever free from the illusory representations of the material world. I meditate upon Him, for He is the Absolute Truth.” (Bhāg. 1.1.1)**

Just as Lord Brahmā was inspired from within the heart by the Lord, Prabhupāda explained that he similarly felt that his spiritual master was always in his heart, guiding him in his translations, publication and distribution of books.

After quoting this verse from Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Prabhupāda thanked all of his followers for assisting him in fulfilling the desire of his spiritual master and Lord Caitanya. He concluded by saying that the publication and distribution of books such as Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and Śrī Caitanya-caritāmṛta should be the foundation of our Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement for future generations. Śrīla Prabhupāda thus emphasized the importance of his books for establishing the basis of this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement. It is certainly the mission of those who call themselves his followers to continue to distribute his books for many generations to come.

One of the most important reasons for distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books is to please our predecessor ācārya. Prabhupāda said repeatedly in his lectures, letters and books that this is what pleases him. Not only is he pleased, but other living entities who have forgotten their relationship with the Lord can ultimately become satisfied by making contact with Śrīla Prabhupāda in the form of his books.

Śrīla Prabhupāda also emphasized this as the method for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness throughout the whole world. It is meant for the ultimate enlightenment and welfare of the entire human society. Distributing Kṛṣṇa consciousness through the distribution of Kṛṣṇa’s holy name and transcendental literature is the method that Śrīla Prabhupāda gave us for our self-purification and advancement in spiritual life.

The demigods prayed to the Lord:

O Lord, who resembles the shining sun, You are always ready to fulfill the desire of Your devotee, and therefore You are known as a desire tree \[vāñchā-kalpataru\]. When ācāryas completely take shelter under Your lotus feet in order to cross the fierce ocean of nescience, they leave behind on earth the method by which they cross, and because You are very merciful to Your other devotees, You accept this method to help them. (Bhāg. 10.2.31)

When great ācāryas, such as Śrīla Prabhupāda, take full shelter under Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet and cross the ocean of material existence, the Lord is very much inclined to fulfill and satisfy their desires. He accepts the method by which they cross this ocean of material existence. He gives complete shelter to that devotee who goes beyond the material world and takes full shelter under Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet in the transcendental abode. He accepts the method that that devotee adopted for attaining that shelter. This is not only for the benefit of the ācārya, but also for the benefit of everyone else who is left to follow his example and instructions, so that those who are still on the other side of this material ocean can cross over it by this same method by which the previous ācāryas crossed. For our benefit, the Lord is so merciful that He accepts that method by which our previous ācāryas went to the spiritual world.

If we examine Śrīla Prabhupāda’s life and final pastimes in this world, we see that he was obviously very much absorbed in distributing Kṛṣṇa consciousness for the welfare of humanity. Just days before he departed, Śrīla Prabhupāda was lying in bed, and devotees were holding the microphone to his lips so that he could translate the Tenth Canto, Thirteenth Chapter of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. Prabhupāda’s absorption and method for crossing this material ocean is clear to anyone who sees that footage. He was always thinking of the welfare of human society, and he was always thinking of how to inculcate Kṛṣṇa consciousness within the hearts of his followers. Therefore, Śrīla Prabhupāda himself established the importance of the distribution of transcendental literature by his own example. Because the Lord accepted Prabhupāda’s method of worship, the Lord Himself also certified this process as a way for transcending the material world:

*ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ*  
*mad-bhakteṣv abhidhāsyati*  
*bhaktiṁ mayi parāṁ kṛtvā*  
*mām evaiṣyaty asaṁśayaḥ*

**“For one who explains this supreme secret to the devotees, pure devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me.” (Bg. 18.68)**

*na ca tasmān manuṣyeṣu*  
*kaścin me priya-kṛttamaḥ*  
*bhavitā na ca me tasmād*  
*anyaḥ priyataro bhuvi*

**“There is no servant in this world more dear to Me than he, nor will there ever be one more dear.” (Bg. 18.69)**

Kṛṣṇa has also certified that the publication and widespread distribution of transcendental literatures containing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s commentaries, in which this supreme secret is explained, is an important method of worship.

Distribution of Kṛṣṇa conscious literature is very important because it is pleasing to Prabhupāda and it is beneficial for human society. However, we should personally feel the importance for distributing Kṛṣṇa conscious literature, because by pleasing Śrīla Prabhupāda, by pleasing his followers, and by pleasing the predecessor ācāryas, we also have a method by which we can please the Lord, and thus we benefit. We must therefore take to this process.

By standing on the streets and trying to introduce Kṛṣṇa conscious literatures into the hands of the non-devotees, you develop a lot of important qualities. Certainly you learn the quality of tolerance, and although sometimes we may not feel compassionate for the conditioned souls, as we should, book distribution is one way to display that compassion. Sometimes it is difficult to feel compassion due to the way people treat us on the streets; however, I have learned that by serving somebody who is compassionate, we can develop this quality. We can see the difference between our own sense of compassion, and the compassion that was so perfectly manifested in Śrīla Prabhupāda. We can therefore take shelter in remembering that by serving somebody who is compassionate, some day we may be able to develop that quality.

When we develop tolerance and compassion, we can experience real satisfaction of the self by having pleased the devotee of the Lord. There is nothing more satisfying than when you feel the confirmation within your heart that by your activities, you are pleasing your spiritual master and Śrīla Prabhupāda. Despite so many external obstacles, anxieties and pressures that you may experience, even a moment of feeling satisfaction can immediately subdue all the other anxieties and distresses in the mind. There is a long list of qualities that one can develop by distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books.

*yasyāsti bhaktir bhagavaty akiñcanā*  
*sarvair guṇais tatra samāsate surāḥ*  
*harāv abhaktasya kuto mahad-guṇā*  
*mano-rathenāsati dhāvato bahiḥ*

**“One who has unflinching devotion for the Personality of Godhead has all the good qualities of the demigods. But one who is not a devotee of the Lord has only material qualifications that are of little value. This is because he is hovering on the mental plane and is certain to be attracted by the glaring material energy.” (Bhāg. 5.18.12)**

Thus the distribution of Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books is also very important for our own purification and progressive advancement in spiritual life, as it cleans the heart of unwanted desires. It benefits others, pleases Prabhupāda, and benefits ourselves.

I was present during Śrīla Prabhupāda’s manifest presence before he departed from this world in 1977. Because I had already been a member of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement for five years prior to his departure, I personally witnessed his very strong, compelling desire to see that his books were distributed throughout the world. I felt pushed by simply hearing that desire. Although I felt pushed during those years, I have no feelings of regret whatsoever. In fact, it has helped me to more fully understand the personality of His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Śrīla Prabhupāda, his motivations, his purpose, and his purity. It also enabled me to experience a very sweet taste that comes from making personal sacrifices for the pleasure of a pure devotee of the Lord. It is a taste that is incomparable to any other pleasure that one may aspire for or experience in this world.

It is, however, a mystery for those who do not understand the purpose of the teachings and instructions of a pure devotee of the Lord. From an external perspective, it looks like somebody is giving up their independence and making big sacrifices for no apparent remuneration. One who looks at it in this way will certainly not be able to understand the mystery of the teaching of the Lord’s pure devotees. However, it can be understood internally only by one who takes up a mood of service with a desire to please Kṛṣṇa’s pure devotee.

In the early 1970s, I was distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books on the streets, trying to introduce people to his teachings. They sometimes looked at me amazed and bewildered, wondering why I was undergoing such austerities for no apparent remuneration. Many times I was standing in sub-zero weather—sometimes even minus 20-30 degrees Fahrenheit, in the middle of the winter. I was questioned by the people I was trying to stop about how much I was getting paid. Naturally people may judge from an external perspective that what I was doing was crazy, unless I was getting a lot of money for it. I would tell them that I was not getting paid anything, and that it was strictly voluntary. They thought I must be crazy. People cannot understand the kind of pleasure that one experiences internally within the heart from voluntarily accepting some sacrifice or austerity to please the Lord or the Lord’s pure devotee. That is practically what all followers of Śrīla Prabhupāda experienced during his manifest līlā, especially in the 1970s.

It was 1972 when the first marathon for distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books began spontaneously. I was only visiting temples at that time; I was not living in the āśrama, although I did move in very shortly thereafter. In my first days of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, I was introduced to distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s literature. At that particular stage in my spiritual development, it was something I found to be very difficult, but at the same time, I found it to be very important, as I was introduced to the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement and to Śrīla Prabhupāda by having received a copy of Bhagavad-gītā As It Is.

When people ask me when I first met Śrīla Prabhupāda, I refer to this incident and answer that it was in the fall of 1972. Receiving that copy of Bhagavad-gītā As It Is was really my first meeting with Śrīla Prabhupāda. Physically, the first time I saw Śrīla Prabhupāda was in March, 1975. I was already his initiated disciple, having received both first and second initiation from him without seeing him physically.

When I first met Śrīla Prabhupāda through reading Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, I was living in Washington D.C. I was self-employed as a carpenter, and I used to remodel people’s homes. I was twenty years old and I was very interested in Eastern philosophy. I had read many books that, at that particular time (in the sixties and seventies), were very popular among the hippie generation. Two such books were Autobiography of a Yogī, by Paramahaṁsa Yogānanda, and Be Here Now, by Baba Rāma das. I had already been dabbling with Eastern philosophy in my teenage years, having read many books independently from my studies in school and university. Having been exposed to different types of Eastern philosophy, I was very much interested in finding a philosophy that I felt was consistent with my aspirations in life, although, honestly, at that time in my life, I did not know what they really were. All I knew was that I was looking for something that was consistent with what I thought would make me happy.

At that time, I was also a very impressionable youth, and whatever philosophical book I read became my philosophy at the time until I read a different philosophical book. As soon as I read one book, I would speak about that philosophy and about the book’s author, and I would try to embrace his teachings. Then, when I would read another book, I would embrace that philosopher, with his teachings. However, I gradually began experiencing some internal conflict when I saw that there were contradictions between these different philosophers and their conclusions. I was therefore about to be even more challenged by purchasing Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, because I was already a little skeptical about what new contradictions I might find.

I came to acquire Bhagavad-gītā As It Is when I was living in Washington D. C. and walked into a bookstore looking for a book on yoga. I immediately went to the Eastern Philosophy and Yoga section. I picked up different books, looked through them, and then saw Śrīla Prabhupāda’s Bhagavad-gītā As It Is. It was printed by the Macmillan Company in 1971. I immediately opened it to a picture of a yogī, sitting in meditation, and the soul was going through the body and finally exiting to an unknown place. I thought it looked like a very interesting book on yoga, and therefore I purchased it for the price listed on the back.

Many years later, I found out that that book was never part of the inventory of the book store. There was one devotee who put that book on that shelf in the bookstore. He explained to me that from time to time, he would go into different bookstores and just place Prabhupāda’s books on the bookshelves. I therefore happened to be the person who picked up that one copy that was in that bookstore. Although it was not part of their inventory, the bookstore was happy to charge me the price that was printed on the back of the book.

Prabhupāda once said that his books are like torpedoes, because you never know where they are going to land. This definitely applied in my particular case.

After coming home from work, every night I would read a few pages from Bhagavad-gītā As It Is until I finished the book. Upon finishing it, I thought that that book seemed a little different than the other philosophy books I had read. The arguments seemed to be very convincing and very practical. Yet I felt that they seemed to require a level of commitment that I was not yet ready for. Prabhupāda often commented that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Lord, and He wants absolute surrender unto Him. I found that to be a little bit too restrictive in comparison to the way I was living, which was an independent lifestyle. I therefore said to myself, “The philosophy in this book looks nice, but I think I will put it away on the bookshelf and get back to it some other time.”

However, subconsciously, my whole world view had been affected. Everywhere I looked, and in everything I did, these words that I had read in Bhagavad-gītā As It Is were resonating in my heart. I could no longer see things in the same way as I had previously seen them. At one point, I thought that I should completely forget everything that I read in that book. However, it would not let me go; it was a power beyond my control. Unknown to me at that time, it was Śrīla Prabhupāda calling me. I gradually began to realize that when one reads something, or hears something spoken from the lips of a pure devotee of the Lord, if one is genuinely searching for the truth, then he will also get confirmation from within the heart that the words he is hearing are true.

When one gets confirmation within the heart about something that is absolutely true, it is very difficult to give it up. Kṛṣṇa explains in the Bhagavad-gītā that He is situated within everyone’s heart. He is giving everyone remembrance, knowledge and forgetfulness, and out of compassion for all living beings, He, who is dwelling within everyone’s heart, destroys with the shining lamp of knowledge the darkness born of ignorance. Therefore, one of the manifestations of the Supreme Lord is the Supersoul, or witness who gives sanction for all of our desires and who is situated within the heart of every living being. Śrīla Prabhupāda titled his book Bhagavad-gītā As It Is because he always emphasized that his presentation of Bhagavad-gītā and his commentaries were to give Kṛṣṇa’s message of Bhagavad-gītā, the song of God, as it was intended by the speaker Himself, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Kṛṣṇa’s specific intention when He was speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra was to enlighten His devotee with transcendental knowledge and to help him realize his eternal position as that of an eternal servant of the Supreme Lord, whose constitutional position was simply to act according to the direction of the Supreme Lord. Kṛṣṇa was instructing Arjuna to give up his false sense of independence and proprietorship and to fully depend upon the Lord in all of his activities. There are so many verses in Bhagavad-gītā that emphasize Kṛṣṇa’s teachings to Arjuna. However, these words are sometimes interpreted by different commentators of the Bhagavad-gītā to mean something different than which Kṛṣṇa intended.

Śrīla Prabhupāda therefore spoke many times about the need for presenting a version of Lord Kṛṣṇa’s teachings as it was intended by the Lord Himself. Therefore, Śrīla Prabhupāda’s commentaries would always keep Kṛṣṇa’s purpose intact. He was fully surrendered to the same teachings that were spoken by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, and thus Prabhupāda’s words had potency. His words would therefore act in such a way as to enter into the ear and then go into the heart, where the Supreme Lord resides as the Supersoul and witness of all of our desires. For advancement in spiritual life, one requires assistance both from within and from without. Kṛṣṇa dictates from within the heart according to one’s surrender to Him.

Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna, “Ye yathā māṁ prapadyante, tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham, mama vartmānuvartante, manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ—As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly. Everyone follows My path in all respects, O son of Pṛthā.” When one hears the instructions of Kṛṣṇa’s devotee, he gets help externally from that devotee. That devotee is speaking the same message and has the same purpose as the Lord, who is dictating from within the heart.

Śrīla Prabhupāda never demanded that we surrender unto him. Rather, he would always say, “Surrender to Kṛṣṇa!” He emphasized that surrender is ultimately meant for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Because he was so transparent in his presentation of Kṛṣṇa consciousness—both within Bhagavad-gītā and in his lectures to his disciples—an evolution of surrender awakened within the heart of anyone who heard from him. They were convinced that following his words was as good as following Kṛṣṇa’s words, and that serving his desires was as good as serving Kṛṣṇa’s desires. Their words are nondifferent. This consciousness, however, requires faith.

When I was first exposed to the teachings of Bhagavad-gītā, I experienced a number of challenges. One of the questions I would always ask myself was, “How do I know if Prabhupāda is pulling the wool over my eyes?” I could never really answer that question myself. However, one thing I did know was that everything seemed logical and compelling. Everything seemed to be a better proposal than everything else that I was doing at that time. Thus it seemed that Prabhupāda was pulling me along by a string, and was always one step ahead of me. This gave me a sense of purpose and hope.

I did not have a lot of wealth, but I had everything that one from my generation could possibly want. I grew up in the sixties, and in the hippie culture in America. I even externally had the appearance of being somewhat of a hippie; I had very long hair down to my lower back. I was part of a countercultural revolution. I did not want to be a part of the system, but at the same time, I was trapped because I realized I needed to make money. However, if I was going to make money, I was going to do it my own way, and did not want to work for anybody. I was therefore self-employed, and I would get work by going to different people’s homes and asking if they needed any renovation work done.

I renovated one home in Washington D.C. It belonged to a couple who were professors at American University. They were wealthy people who had a beautiful home in downtown Washington. They gave me the keys to their car; asked me to take their children to school; gave me the keys to their house; and gave me access to anything I wanted in the whole house while they were away during the day. They completely accepted that I was an honest person. I would spend my days there fixing their house while both of them were at work. They were thrilled by the work that I did, and would call all their friends and refer me to do any repairs they needed. I never had any lack of work or income. I had everything I needed. I had a guitar, I had a dog, I had a girlfriend, and my own car. I had everything that somebody in those years would aspire for. However, I realized after reading Prabhupāda’s Bhagavad-gītā that I did not actually have everything. Although by external vision I had anything I could possibly want, I still did not have peace and satisfaction. Prabhupāda emphasized in Bhagavad-gītā the necessity of peace.

I especially remember reading the verse in the Second Chapter of the Bhagavad-gītā, where Kṛṣṇa says, “How can there be any happiness if there is no peace?” That verse, among many others and their commentaries, had a lot of influence on me.

Bhagavad-gītā meant a lot to me, because it was my first contact with Śrīla Prabhupāda. After I finished reading Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, I sent a request to the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust to purchase more books by the same author. At that time, the only books that were available were Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, Kṛṣṇa book, and the First Canto, First Volume of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. I therefore purchased Kṛṣṇa book and the First Volume of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. After I finished reading those books, I realized that I had to do something. I therefore decided to go and visit a Hare Kṛṣṇa temple.

I was living in Cape Cod, in the southern part of Massachusetts, in a house on the beach. I was still building houses and doing the same type of construction work. Then I decided to drive seventy miles and go visit the temple. I parked the car in front of the temple, and looked for a long time at the entrance of the temple. I saw the sign on the temple, which said, “International Society for Krishna Consciousness.” I sat there for about a half hour, thinking, “If I go in there, I may never come out.” Then I turned the engine on, and drove seventy miles back to Cape Cod.

A couple of weeks passed, and I decided that I really needed to go to the temple. I was still reading, and everything that I was doing was just a part of that search. Everybody who knew me was asking what had happened to me. I used to live with about 15-20 people. We were all hippies. We lived close together to keep our expenses down. I was popular among my friends. They could not understand why I was reading these books, and why my personality had changed. They thought I was undergoing an identity crisis.

All of the people I lived with were vegetarians, and I had become a vegetarian long before I read Prabhupāda’s books. From reading his books, however, I learned about offering food to Kṛṣṇa. I used to think that the kitchen should be clean, and that whatever I at least cooked for myself, I wanted to offer to Kṛṣṇa. However, nobody ever washed their own dishes, so every time I entered the kitchen, I would have to clean the entire room before I could cook anything for Kṛṣṇa. Sometimes I would become very resentful, wondering why I had to clean up after everybody, just to make a simple offering to Kṛṣṇa. I would not say anything, but internally, I was very frustrated.

After continuing to read Prabhupāda’s books, I felt very compelled to go back to the temple again, and worked up enough courage to actually enter the temple. I rang the bell, and a bright-faced devotee answered the door. He welcomed me in and asked what my name was. I told him my name and why I had come. He immediately brought me to one of the senior devotees to speak to me, because he could see that I was a person who obviously had some contact with Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books. We sat, spoke for some time, and I was very impressed by his knowledge of the philosophy.

He asked me if I was chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, and I told him that I was not chanting. He then introduced me to chanting and gave me my first set of japa beads. I gladly took the beads and began chanting on them according to the way he taught me. Then he asked me if I would like to do some devotional service. I was happy to do so. Another devotee came to me and asked me to come with him. He brought me into the back room, where there was a sink with a huge stack of pots, and asked, “Would you like to wash Kṛṣṇa’s pots?”

I was thinking, “Is this a joke?” Then I realized that this is actually service. I therefore agreed to do it. It was the biggest stack of pots I had ever seen before. It made the stack of pots back in our commune look insignificant. I started washing the pots, and then the same devotee came over to me, probably seeing that I was a little frustrated, looked at me with a big smile on his face and said, “When you clean Kṛṣṇa’s pots, you clean your heart.”

I just meditated on that. It was like a complete transformation of consciousness that immediately took place in my heart. It was such a simple statement, but my whole attitude changed 180 degrees. I became so blissful and joyful, washing the pots. That was my first exposure to devotional service after reading Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books.

I continued to visit the temple and became exposed to more service. I eventually decided that I wanted to move into the temple. At that time, however, the devotees were not just letting anybody move into the temple. They said that if I wanted to live in the temple, then first I should live downstairs in the basement on the concrete floor for a couple of weeks. They wanted to see if I was sincere.

I therefore did as they asked. Later I was begging them to allow me to shave my head. I wanted to dedicate myself completely to Prabhupāda’s teachings, and I felt that shaving my head was a real indication of surrender, especially for a long-haired hippie like me. They told me to wait until I was ready. I told them that I was ready. Finally, after a couple more weeks of persistent pleading with them, they agreed to shave my head. However, electric buzzers did not exist in those days. They therefore cut my hair with scissors and a razor blade. It took a long time. When they were done, it literally looked like I had been through a battlefield. My head was full of scars, and was still bleeding a little. They used a septic pencil to get the bleeding to stop. Then with my head looking like that, they told me to go out to distribute books.

Thus the very same day that my head was shaved, they gave me a bag filled with booklets called Reservoir of Pleasure and Back to Godhead magazine. Prabhupāda’s Bhagavad-gītā and Bhāgavatam were not available for mass distribution at that time. They brought me into the downtown streets and encouraged me to distribute books. That was my first exposure to distributing Śrīla Prabhupāda’s books, which meant a lot to me, as I was introduced to Kṛṣṇa consciousness through reading Prabhupāda’s books.

Prabhupāda said that as our movement expands, first people will ridicule us, then they will persecute us, and then they will accept us. In the seventies, a lot of ridiculing was taking place, but a lot of persecution had also started surfacing, as our movement had somewhat of an image in America of being a cult. Many of the accusations that were being made against our society were that people were brainwashing us to join the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement. They thought that only a brainwashed person would stand on the streets in minus 20-30 degree weather selling books and not getting paid for it. However, I always told people that no one brainwashed me, because I had never even met a devotee before becoming convinced. The only contact I had was from reading books. The first time I actually met and spoke with a devotee, I had already read Prabhupāda’s books, and I was already committed to the philosophy. It was therefore impossible for me to have been brainwashed.

Prabhupāda emphasized that our books are our evidence. When you go into a court room, the lawyer will always present evidence from the previous decisions of higher courts. Similarly, Prabhupāda explained that our books are our evidence that this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is not newly manufactured. It presents the conclusions of the higher courts from thousands of years ago. What we are presenting was spoken by the original person Himself. Thus Prabhupāda’s books are our evidence that we are not a cult. Prabhupāda emphasized the importance of his books for establishing a solid foundation for the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement.

In 1976, there was a lawsuit against ISKCON for brainwashing people. I knew the person whose parents were bringing the suit against the movement, as I had distributed books with him. The court case was in New York City, and it was becoming a very high profile case. Prabhupāda specifically instructed the devotee who was representing ISKCON in the court room to bring in all of our books and make the prosecutors read them. He said that the books are our evidence in court that we are not brainwashing anybody. The story is narrated in Śrīla Prabhupāda-līlāmṛta. Prabhupāda always spoke so much about the importance of his books and of publishing them.

In 1975, Prabhupāda said in Los Angeles, “My spiritual master has told me ‘Whenever you get money, you should print books.’ Therefore I am asking you, where is book? Where is book? Where is book? You should print as many books in as many languages that exist throughout the whole world and distribute them everywhere. Then this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement will spread automatically.” Prabhupāda made that statement when the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust was established, and around the time when he also requested his disciples to print seventeen volumes of Caitanya-caritāmṛta in two months.

Prabhupāda was not interested in becoming a famous author. He was not interested in becoming wealthy. He had no personal interest. Any money that came in from selling his books, he would immediately use for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness. He always proved that he would be self-satisfied in any condition of life—whether he was staying in some fancy place, or in a hut in the heat of the Māyāpura sun. He was not pushing to distribute his books for some personal gain. He was doing so because his spiritual master ordered him from the very first day that he met him to bring this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement to the West and to print books.

All of us who joined the movement in the early 1970s were nurtured with this purpose of pleasing Prabhupāda by publishing and distributing his books.

The Christmas marathon spontaneously manifested in December 1972. Prabhupāda was placing more and more emphasis on his books and on their distribution. Therefore, the devotees in Los Angeles, where the books were being published, spontaneously, without even talking to each other, decided to stay out late just to distribute Prabhupāda’s books. One particular devotee, who was managing the BBT, explained in the Śrīla Prabhupāda-līlāmṛta that he had stayed out one evening until eleven o’clock at night to distribute books. Nobody ever stayed out that late. They would usually finish by nine, after having been out for about twelve hours. However, since it was Christmas time, and all the stores were open late and all the shoppers were out very late, he thought it a good opportunity to stay out later and distribute books to them.

Although it had reached eleven o’clock, and he wanted to stay out even later, he figured that all the other devotees would be waiting for him back at the temple. It was the tradition to wait for all the devotees to come back, and then discuss amongst themselves how many books had been distributed that day. Not wanting to keep everybody waiting for him, he returned to the temple. When he walked into the room where all of the book distributors would meet, he saw that nobody was there. He thought that they must have gone to sleep. However, one devotee came into the room and told him that he was the first one back. On that particular night, everybody spontaneously decided to stay out late. The remaining devotees started coming back at around one-thirty in the morning.

For the next few days up until Christmas, the devotees all stayed out very late. They distributed approximately twenty-seven thousand books. They wrote a letter to Śrīla Prabhupāda and told him how many books they had distributed. Prabhupāda wrote back a letter saying that he was very pleased by disciples who worked so hard to distribute so many books, and who had personally undergone inconveniences for satisfying their spiritual master. He also said that the devotees who go out and distribute his books like this are guaranteed to go back to Godhead in this life. That quote circulated throughout the whole world.

The devotees then continued the Christmas Marathon in the following years, and it became the time when all the devotees would optimize their time as much as possible for distributing Prabhupāda’s books. We would sleep less and take care of our basic necessities in as little time as possible, so that we could engage as many people as possible to increase book distribution for Prabhupāda’s pleasure.

We would distribute books from nine in the morning until nine at night. On the weekends, we would usually stay out until two in the morning. The marathon would begin at the end of November, after Thanksgiving Day in America, until Christmas day. We would maximize our efforts and work together collectively to please Prabhupāda by increasing the distribution of his books.

In November 1977, Prabhupāda was in Vṛndāvana, and he was very ill. Devotees were coming from all over the world, because it appeared that Prabhupāda was going to leave this world. His body had become very emaciated because he had not eaten for months. He had given an indication that he was not going to stay much longer. For Kṛṣṇa’s pure devotee, to leave this world and to leave his body means he is going to join Kṛṣṇa in the spiritual world. There is no source of lamentation whatsoever for the devotee who departs and returns to Kṛṣṇa’s transcendental abode. However, certainly for those who are dependent upon the association of that devotee, it is a great cause for lamentation.

One day, Prabhupāda gave an indication that Kṛṣṇa had given him the choice to stay, or to go. Therefore, the devotees who had assembled in Vṛndāvana at that time decided that they would discuss this amongst themselves, because although Prabhupāda had indicated that he was inclined to go, he also indicated that Kṛṣṇa gave him the choice. The devotees were worried that asking Prabhupāda to stay would be selfish. They thought that they should let him do whatever he wished to do. They continued discussing for a long time whether or not they should ask Prabhupāda to stay or to let him go. Finally, they decided that since Śrīla Prabhupāda had not yet finished translating Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, they should ask him to stay to finish it, which was his life’s work.

They went into Śrīla Prabhupāda’s room, and pushed forward the devotee that was selected as the spokesperson. They all stood behind the spokesperson, patting him on the shoulder, rubbing his back, encouraging him to go ahead. He broke down crying, followed by all of the other devotees. He said, “Śrīla Prabhupāda, if Kṛṣṇa has given you the choice to stay, or to leave, then we are asking you, please, stay. We need you to finish the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. It is your life’s work. We need you to guide us. We are fully dependent upon you.

Prabhupāda responded, “Do you want me to stay?”

By that time, the devotees were so overwhelmed by their emotions and were crying. However, they felt that they all had to stay firm on their decision, and thus said, “Yes, Prabhupāda.”

Prabhupāda very casually said, “OK, I will stay.”

As soon as Prabhupāda said that, the devotees were phoning the other temples all over the world to inform them that Prabhupāda said he was going to stay. This encouraged devotees to go on with their service.

Shortly afterwards, I was driving with a number of devotees to another temple. I had to stop and call the temple president to tell him that we were all coming to Boston, but that we were going to be a little bit late for the program. As soon as I called, he told me, “Prabhupāda departed.” You can imagine the impact on the heart—the bewilderment, pain, separation—especially since we thought that he was going to stay. It was totally unexpected. I never cried like that in my life.

For whatever reason, Prabhupāda decided to leave. This was just two weeks before the month of December. All the devotees around the world knew that if we wanted Prabhupāda to be at the center of our movement again, there was only one way to bring him—through the distribution of his books. The 1977 marathon was therefore the biggest marathon in the history of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. We realized that although Prabhupāda left and we were like a ship without a rudder, Prabhupāda still made it very clear that if we wanted to please him, we should go on distributing his books. Therefore, everyone got the strength, courage and enthusiasm. It has thus become a tradition for everybody to work collectively to bring Prabhupāda’s desires back into focus, particularly during the Christmas marathon. That same focus that everybody had during Prabhupāda’s manifest presence is also created again and again, year after year, during the Christmas marathon. We felt a burning desire to fulfill Prabhupāda’s desire.

Thus, for anyone who has not experienced a taste of what it is like to push and push for Prabhupāda, book distribution opportunities are available for your benefit. Take advantage of them. Do not let this lifetime pass without at least once experiencing this taste of pushing for Prabhupāda. Prabhupāda is not a miserly person. That same taste that he gave to his direct followers is just as accessible for many generations to come. At the same time, it is also a mystery; it cannot be experienced unless that desire has been awakened within the heart to do something that really pleases Prabhupāda.

We may have our own particular services and means for pleasing Kṛṣṇa’s devotees and Prabhupāda. However, particularly during the Christmas marathon, there is an emphasis for everyone to get the opportunity to do a little bit more. It is available for anyone who wants to take part. Nobody is going to push anyone. However, all opportunities are there. If we actually feel the pushing from within, it is a great opportunity to become Prabhupāda conscious and to really meditate on what is so dear to his heart. It is a once in a lifetime opportunity that we should not miss out on. Do not let this lifetime pass without at least once experiencing what it is like to taste a marathon for Śrīla Prabhupāda’s pleasure. I say that from my heart and from my own direct realization and experience. I leave these words with you, and I invite you to please take advantage of Śrīla Prabhupāda’s mercy.

## Expansion of Kṛṣṇa Consciousness

We want to see the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement expanding. Expansion means increasing the family members. But what keeps the family together is when everybody has a common respect for the elders. We must expand our Kṛṣṇa consciousness in such a way that every devotee is increasing his Kṛṣṇa consciousness and giving and sharing that Kṛṣṇa consciousness with others. Expansion is something that is not always calculated by some external criteria. We have a tendency in the material world to see how things are expanding in terms of economic growth. However, accumulation of wealth is not simply the accumulation of material necessities. Real wealth means the development of our love for Kṛṣṇa. Expansion of Kṛṣṇa consciousness is something that is both individual and collective. It makes everybody feel some sense of responsibility for expanding Kṛṣṇa consciousness. If we are not careful, or if we are even a little inattentive, then we may lose our attraction and taste for Kṛṣṇa conscious activities.

However, Nārada Muni said to Vyāsadeva:

“One who has forsaken his material occupations to engage in the devotional service of the Lord may sometimes fall down while in an immature stage, yet there is no danger of his being unsuccessful. On the other hand, a nondevotee, though fully engaged in occupational duties, does not gain anything.” (Bhāg. 1.5.17)

“My dear Vyāsa, even though a devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa sometimes falls down somehow or other, he certainly does not undergo material existence like others \[fruitive workers, etc.\] because a person who has once relished the taste of the lotus feet of the Lord can do nothing but remember that ecstasy again and again.” (Bhāg. 1.5.19)

Even though one may be perfectly engaged in his occupational duties, there is no gain for him. The previous ācāryas, Vaiṣṇavas and speakers of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam use a different barometer for real success. They do not measure it in terms of economic growth. Rather, they measure it in terms of growth that takes place within the heart, and the growth that takes place in the relationships with Vaiṣṇavas. When affection begins to grow within the heart through the association of Vaiṣṇavas, then envy and the tendency to find faults in others begins to leave the heart. Śrīla Vṛndāvana dāsa Ṭhākura quotes Lord Caitanya:

“A person who never blasphemes any living entity, and who chants, ‘Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!’ easily conquers Lord Caitanya, who is never conquered by anyone. All the scriptures declare, ‘A person who blasphemes others will not attain the Lord.’” Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam teaches that one should respect everyone. (CB Madhya 10.313-314)

All the scriptures declare that the one should always offer respects to everyone, and one who blasphemes others will never find shelter at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. One of the offenses to the holy name is to blaspheme the devotees of the Lord. We are therefore often very careful to not blaspheme a pure devotee, but then we start judging who is not a devotee, and who we can get away with blaspheming and not have to suffer any consequences. However, Lord Caitanya originally recited this verse: “One who never blasphemes any living entity will achieve the shelter of My lotus feet.”

Raising His arms, fair Lord Caitanya declared to the entire world, “Renouncing criticism of others, everyone please chant Lord Kṛṣṇa’s name. I will personally deliver anyone who does not criticize others and who once chants ‘Kṛṣṇa!’ That is the truth. It is the truth.” (CB Madhya 20.213-214)

Expansion of Kṛṣṇa consciousness means a development of all of these devotional qualities within our hearts. Śrīla Prabhupāda often quoted the verse:

*yasyāsti bhaktir bhagavaty akiñcanā*  
*sarvair guṇais tatra samāsate surāḥ*  
*harāv abhaktasya kuto mahad-guṇā*  
*manorathenāsati dhāvato bahiḥ*

**All the demigods and their exalted qualities, such as religion, knowledge and renunciation, become manifest in the body of one who has developed unalloyed devotion for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vāsudeva. On the other hand, a person devoid of devotional service and engaged in material activities has no good qualities. Even if he is adept at the practice of mystic yoga or the honest endeavor of maintaining his family and relatives, he must be driven by his own mental speculations and must engage in the service of the Lord’s external energy. How can there be any good qualities in such a man? (Bhāg. 5.18.12)**

If you are engaged in devotional service, automatically you will attain all good qualities; the natural qualities of the soul will become manifest. In the meantime, however, we have to practice becoming nonenvious, avoid finding fault in others, and to see the good qualities in others. Vaiṣṇavas are actually adoṣa-darśī, which means they never see any bad quality. A natural Vaiṣṇava quality is to see the potential for devotional service in the heart of every living entity. One who always sees the bad qualities, but does not see the potential for devotional service, cannot effectively preach and make others Kṛṣṇa conscious. Jīva Gosvāmī has explained that if one cannot have respect towards other devotees, then he is practically useless for preaching.

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura says in his Amṛta Vāṇī:

Those who are proud cannot preach. Those who are proud only consider themselves great when they speak about Kṛṣṇa to others. The Absolute Truth does not reveal Himself to such persons. Thus it is impossible for them to preach and therefore to help others. Mahāprabhu instructed us to chant the holy name while remaining lower than the straw in the street and ready to offer all respect to others. (Amṛta Vāṇī, Section on Preaching, Part 9)

Similarly, Lord Caitanya instructs:

*tṛṇād api sunīcena*  
*taror api sahiṣṇunā*  
*amāninā mānadena*  
*kīrtanīyaḥ sadā hariḥ*

**“One should chant the holy name of the Lord in a humble state of mind, thinking oneself lower than the straw in the street; one should be more tolerant than a tree, devoid of all sense of false prestige, and should be ready to offer all respect to others. In such a state of mind one can chant the holy name of the Lord constantly.” (Śrī Śrī Śikṣāṣṭaka, Verse 3)**

Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta explained that this verse is the siddha-praṇālī for Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas. It is not by going to Rādhā-kuṇḍa or some other holy place that one can achieve their siddha-praṇālī—relationship with Kṛṣṇa by finding out their actual eternal identity in their service. If you want to achieve perfection, then meditate on this verse. Wear it like a garland around your neck.

Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja Gosvāmī also describes in Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 20.23): “When a tree is cut down, it does not protest, and even when drying up, it does not ask anyone for water.” Thus one should become more tolerant than a tree, thinking himself to be lower than a blade of grass. To think of oneself as very insignificant is so hard. It seems so theoretical. However, advancement in Kṛṣṇa consciousness means the development of faith.

*‘śraddhā’-śabde—viśvāsa kahe sudṛḍha niścaya*  
*kṛṣṇe bhakti kaile sarva-karma kṛta haya*

Śraddhā is confident, firm faith that by rendering transcendental loving service to Kṛṣṇa one automatically performs all subsidiary activities. Such faith is favorable to the discharge of devotional service. (Cc. Madhya, 22.62)

Conversely, even if we perfectly fulfill all our subsidiary duties, but do not have any faith in chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa, then it is of no gain.

**“The Supreme Personality of Godhead becomes very dear to those devotees who have no material possessions but are fully happy in possessing the devotional service of the Lord. Indeed, the Lord relishes the devotional activities of such devotees. Those who are puffed up with material education, wealth, aristocracy and fruitive activity are very proud of possessing material things, and they often deride the devotees. Even if such people offer the Lord worship, the Lord never accepts them.” (Bhāg. 4.31.21)**

Certainly one may have possessions, but they are not material possessions when his primary possession is to be engaged in devotional service to Kṛṣṇa. A devotee takes that as his real wealth. Prabhupāda explains that for those who are not engaged in devotional service, they may accumulate so many assets in this life, but at the time of death, nothing goes with them except their sinful reactions. Everything else is left behind. Prabhupāda has opened up our eyes to the reality of the material world. He spent gallons of blood in his preaching just to convince us how this material world is no place for a gentleman. He has given us everything—the means to achieve the perfectional state. However, there are still so many unwanted things and so many nondevotional tendencies—especially pride—in our heart. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī thus explains that those who are proud cannot preach.

A proud person thinks that he is a great devotee because he is speaking about Kṛṣṇa. However, a devotee is actually one who is not proud and always thinks that he is an instrument—always subordinate to the superior order. He sees the potency to execute that superior order is already impregnated in the words of that order, and if any good qualities manifest in him or any abilities to induce others to develop good qualities to become Kṛṣṇa conscious, it is only because he is following the Lord’s instructions.

For one who is proud, his whole psyche is completely forgetful of the fact that he is actually subordinate. However, the best person to give Kṛṣṇa consciousness to others is he who teaches by his own example how to be a servant. He is thus subservient to the superior order. That was the criterion for Prabhupāda’s success. Of course, Prabhupāda is nitya-siddha (eternally liberated); he came from the spiritual world just to give us Kṛṣṇa consciousness. However, he showed us the perfect example throughout his whole life by giving every fiber of his existence in serving the higher order given by his Guru Mahārāja. He never forgot that position in everything that he did. While crying, he said, “My Guru Mahārāja has sent all of you to me simply so that I can serve his order.” He always felt such overwhelming gratitude in his heart. This is humility.

Expansion of Kṛṣṇa consciousness does not mean increasing the collection of assets, bank accounts and positions. These are external things, at which Kṛṣṇa does not look. Kṛṣṇa decides who is attractive and who is not. He validates whether or not one is valuable. Of course, all the living entities are valuable, but for those devotees who think themselves to be very low, very humble, and to be always meditating on pleasing the Lord and satisfying the Lord, Kṛṣṇa considers them to be like valuable jewels.

Queen Kuntī prayed:

*janmaiśvarya-śruta-śrībhir*  
*edhamāna-madaḥ pumān*  
*naivārhaty abhidhātuṁ vai*  
*tvām akiñcana-gocaram*

**“My Lord, Your Lordship can easily be approached, but only by those who are materially exhausted. One who is on the path of \[material\] progress, trying to improve himself with respectable parentage, great opulence, high education and bodily beauty, cannot approach You with sincere feeling.” (Bhāg. 1.8.26)**

Prabhupāda explains that material prosperity (wealth, education, etc.), are external symptoms, just as a fever is the external symptom of an unhealthy body. If one has a fever, and if you want him to become healthy, then you must bring the symptoms of the fever down. Similarly, for these different symptoms of material prosperity to come down, Kṛṣṇa can take it all away, or we can use it in Kṛṣṇa’s service—yukta-vairāgya.
