*anāsaktasya viṣayān yathārham upayuñjataḥ*  
*nirbandhaḥ kṛṣṇa-sambandhe yuktaṁ vairāgyam*

**“When one is not attached to anything, but at the same time accepts everything in relation to Kṛṣṇa, one is rightly situated above possessiveness. On the other hand, one who rejects everything without knowledge of its relationship to Kṛṣṇa is not as complete in his renunciation.” (Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu 2.255–256)**

By using things for the service of the Lord, the fever will come down. In this way, we can try to become spiritually healthy, and that will be our process of expansion. We need more and more spiritually healthy devotees who can go out and preach and show by their example what it means to be Kṛṣṇa conscious. Kṛṣṇa consciousness will then expand unlimitedly. I ask you all to please help spread the mission of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Become fixed up devotees in Kṛṣṇa consciousness and go out and make others Kṛṣṇa conscious. Make your life successful, and at the same time make others’ lives successful. You will become happy, and they will become happy.

**Question: How do we preach to a person in a way to give him what he needs, rather than in a way that may be inspiring to us, but not necessarily to him?**

The whole process of Kṛṣṇa consciousness is centered on the development of faith—śraddhā ratir bhaktir anukramiṣyati. Thus, as preachers, for the development of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, we have to learn how to see what we can do to help another increase his or her faith. Sometimes we may have a tendency to think of what that person can do for our movement. While it is also beneficial for the person to be engaged in service, if we simply think about the person being engaged in service, but we do not think about their faith, that faith may become weakened. If one loses faith, it is very difficult to come back. Thus, for a devotee’s progressive advancement in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, we must see his potential for devotional service and his potential for faith in guru and Kṛṣṇa. If we have our own convictions in our own realizations, and if they are genuine and based on faith, then we are helping them even though our faith may be based upon a particular taste that they may not have. We are giving at least what we have realized and we are not trying to give something that we have not realized.

We should always try to speak from our own realizations. If we have a great conviction in what has nourished us in our Kṛṣṇa consciousness—even if it may not be a particular aspect of another person’s nourishment—that conviction will still be contagious and will help others to increase their faith in the process of devotional service. By giving in that way, Kṛṣṇa helps us within our heart to know the right way to preach to every individual. That comes from advancing in Kṛṣṇa consciousness and both from the help of the Lord within the heart and by a devotee’s sincere desire to give somebody Kṛṣṇa consciousness. The single motivation in our efforts to preach to somebody else should be to make them attached to guru and Kṛṣṇa and increase their faith in the process of devotional service. If we see our preaching in that way, then Kṛṣṇa will inspire us to speak in the way that they need to hear to advance in Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

**Question: Can we become successful in our Kṛṣṇa consciousness simply by the potency of a preacher, and by associating with him?**

The analogy is given that if the husband is potent and the wife is fertile, then impregnation takes place. In the same way, if a speaker is potent and the hearer is very eager to hear and to accept the instructions, then prolonged association may not be required. Similarly, a stone cannot derive benefit from the rain, whereas the grass can derive benefit from it. Likewise, a blind man cannot derive the benefit from the sun. Thus, success is dependent on the quality of the receptacle.

Pure love of Kṛṣṇa is situated in the heart of every living being; it does not come from any other source. When one hears about Kṛṣṇa, śravaṇādi-śuddha-citte, then pure love will naturally appear. However, hearing also depends on the quality of the receptacle, and how eager one is to hear the message that is delivered. One who is very eager will carefully listen, remember what has been said, and act on it.

Similarly, if you have a physical emergency and are bleeding profusely, when you go to the doctor, you will listen very attentively to his instructions on how to stop the bleeding. Due to the emergency, there is a quality of the receptacle, as you are very eager to hear how to deal with what is the most immediate problem.

Thus, in spiritual life, if you see what the immediate problem is, if you relate to that problem, and if you see how you can become part of that solution, then when you hear an instruction that is very relevant, then by association you can carry the instruction with you and execute it. If one does not realize the relevance of the instructions in dealing with the emergency, then he needs more association to develop this realization. Once he realizes the relevance, then he can take the instruction and act on it.

**Question: If a congregation member is visiting the temple, but is not yet asking questions for his advancement, should the preachers awaken in his heart such questions, or should they wait for these questions to be naturally generated by the congregation member?**

It is the responsibility of the preachers to awaken within the heart those questions which are relevant to spiritual life. That is what our whole movement is based upon. When you give to others something that is very relevant and valuable without any expectation of anything in return, then, not only the message, but also the method of giving, will act on the heart in such a way that one will begin to ask the questions. Therefore, it is the duty of the preachers to selflessly give themselves and give Kṛṣṇa to others in such a way that the hearts of others will be changed.

The secret in the distribution is the selflessness with which the preachers give themselves and Kṛṣṇa to others. That is how Lord Nityānanda and Haridāsa Ṭhākura were able to awaken Kṛṣṇa consciousness in the hearts of others when they went into the streets. Their method of distribution was so awesome that the hearts of anyone who would see them would change. That changing of the heart is what evokes questions about how to love Kṛṣṇa. To preach is to awaken the desire in others to serve Kṛṣṇa. To be an effective preacher, one has to be an example.

**Question: If mātājīs are not so active in preaching to the newcomers at the temple, what should be done so that either the brahmacārīs or unmarried senior devotees from the congregation are not left to preach to them?**

It is very important to establish a bona fide gṛhastha āśrama for the future of our movement. If devotees are properly situated in the gṛhastha āśrama, their example can serve the community of devotees in a very important way. Householder couples should preach together and show the proper example of how to live as householders and how to have proper relationships between men and women. We should strictly follow the principles of relationships between men and women.

Quite honestly, sometimes I am completely disgusted by the way men and women associate in our movement—particularly at festivals. It is a terrible example. I see brahmacārīs in saffron cloth sitting and speaking alone with women. It is frivolous behavior. I want to stop this disgusting behavior. Devotees must be shown how important it is for householders to preach and be examples for others. Without a section of our society of genuine householders who are preaching and taking care of others, we are going to lose other very important aspects of our preaching. In addition, if the brahmacārīs or the unmarried men continue preaching to women alone, then it is going to create such a bad example for our society, and it will gradually degrade to a complete apasampradāya.

Already, sometimes when people in India see the behavior of our devotees, they are shocked. In Māyāpura, the different Gauḍīya Maṭhas see the inappropriate way men and women mingle in our society; and in Vṛndāvana people would not accept our society because of seeing the way men and women mingle. No credibility is given.

The way the unmarried women behave in Vṛndāvana has become the worst. They do not have any protection. All women need to be protected. However, the proper protection for them is not from the unmarried men. That is ridiculous. If an unmarried man takes care of an unmarried woman, it is a terrible example. The only thing worse is if a sannyāsī does it. Therefore, we have to bring up the householders to be preachers and take care of the women properly. Husband and wife together should be taking care of women.

If the brahmacārīs start preaching to the women, then when the women start coming to the temple, they become attached to the brahmacārīs, or the brahmacārīs become attached to the women. Certainly brahmacārīs will preach to women on the streets and will encourage them to come to the temple. We are not fanatics. However, as soon as they come to the temple, there should always be another woman or a married couple to take care of them. However, even when it is a married couple, it is the wife who should take care of the women and the husband should simply support the wife. If a married man talks to another woman, he should talk via the wife or together with the wife. A man, even though married, should not speak alone with a woman. By so doing, the atmosphere of the temple remains very pure.

When people are coming to the temple with all kinds of mixed motives, looking to find an unmarried man or woman, this pollutes the atmosphere. People get disturbed by it, although they might not even be conscious of it. There should be a proper standard in preaching. If one is not properly situated in his āśrama, he cannot be an example, and thus should not preach. Otherwise, everybody will think that the bad example is the right example.

**Question: Is it possible for brahmacārīs to regularly take part in nāma-haṭṭa programs if mātājīs are present?**

There is certainly nothing wrong for a brahmacārī to give a lecture to a group of people that includes mātājīs. There is a difference between giving a general talk to a group of people with women present, and preaching alone to a woman. In fact, it is one of the duties of a brahmacārī, who is a preacher, to go out and preach to the community of devotees. If, however, he is too disturbed by women being present, then he should not preach.

## Organized versus Unorganized Preaching

There is a diversity of experiences throughout the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, and not every yatra is organized the same way. There are different methods for organization, and organization is essential if we really want to make a collective effort to do something positive in spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Although some organization is required in every yatra, there is a problem when religion becomes too organized, as the essence can be potentially lost. Many people are frustrated by seeing organization without substance.

Śrīla Prabhupāda’s mission, however, was to combine both. He wanted us to be organized. Prabhupāda said that his American and European disciples have come from wealthy backgrounds, and they should use their experience together with the wisdom of the East and spread Kṛṣṇa consciousness all over the world. We can see that Śrīla Prabhupāda had deep spiritual vision, as well as a very keen organizational vision.

Prabhupāda was the original organizer of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. First he inspired people to take up the practices of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and then when they came forward enthusiastically, he directed them on how to dovetail their abilities and their skills for spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness.

There are different ways to organize things throughout the movement. However, organization alone will not successfully spread Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Certainly we need organizers, but we also need spiritual vision.

Prabhupāda explained that if preaching is there, then management will follow like a shadow. In other words, if devotees are giving Kṛṣṇa consciousness to others, then inspiration will be there to be organized. Devotees will naturally want to do their service in best way that they can. Devotees will be inspired to put their energies, efforts, intelligence, wealth, and everything else that they have towards Kṛṣṇa’s service.

Organization should not be forced; otherwise it will only be temporary. Prabhupāda always said that this is a voluntary movement. In his letter to Karāndhara on December 22, 1972, he said that it is the duty of the leaders to bring up this voluntary spirit and to fan it so that Kṛṣṇa consciousness becomes an ever-fresh experience. In his letter, Prabhupāda was blasting certain devotees for their organizational scheme, because the leaders were creating a big organization, which was stifling the individuality of many of the other leaders in the movement and making them all financially dependent upon these few leaders. Prabhupāda chastised them, saying that it is the duty of the leaders to inspire the devotees and create ever-fresh opportunities for surrendering to Kṛṣṇa.

In explaining how we should take the organization of the West and combine it with the vision of the East, Prabhupāda gave the example of a blind man and a lame man. He said that India was lame and the West was blind. However, if a lame man would get up on the shoulders of a blind man, then together there could be progress in spiritual life. Thus, Prabhupāda wanted us to be organized, and he often spoke very encouragingly to the devotees in America, saying that his American and European disciples have come from wealthy backgrounds. They should use their experience together with the wisdom of the East, and spread Kṛṣṇa consciousness all over the world.

Prahlāda Mahārāja instructed his classmates (Bhāg. 7.7.53): “My dear friends, O sons of the demons, in the same favorable way that one sees himself and takes care of himself, take to devotional service to satisfy the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is present everywhere as the Supersoul of all living entities.” Thus, the same energy that everybody uses to take care of their own personal needs should be utilized in serving the Supreme Lord. Taking care of one’s personal needs is what one does in the material world. Being self-centered, everybody first thinks of themselves and then of others.

Prabhupāda even explains that philanthropists, who are apparently always thinking about others, are also thinking first of themselves, because they are thinking that they are part and parcel of the others. Thus, if they think of the welfare of others and take care of them, then they will ultimately also benefit. This means that they are still selfishly motivated.

To find selflessness in the material world is a very difficult search. Therefore, as Prahlāda Mahārāja instructed, just as we see and take care of ourselves, we should take that same energy and utilize it for the service of the Supreme Lord. By such focused devotional service, Kṛṣṇa will take better care of us than we can possibly take care of ourselves. Kṛṣṇa gives us everything that we need because He helps us to be satisfied in any condition of life. Without that, we can never be satisfied, even if we have everything we need.

We cannot create an organization for taking care of Kṛṣṇa’s devotees unless there is a feeling within the heart of devotees that they are being taken care of in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. This feeling cannot be evoked managerially. However, in the association of his peers, a devotee can get shelter. By feeling this shelter, one is enabled to give shelter to others. This is something that is very important. Sometimes a person thinks that inspiration or shelter can only come from one place. However, by such thinking, one is not on a very high level of devotional service.

If one is looking at Mount Everest from a distance, all he will see is a very high peak. As he comes closer, though, he will see that there are many subordinate peaks, hills and mountains that are surrounding Mount Everest. Similarly, when we see only one person who is the source of inspiration for us, that means that we are far away, because we cannot see that there are many other persons who are also assisting him and fulfilling a similar function of giving us inspiration, knowledge and care. We should try to get closer by seeing that through Kṛṣṇa’s arrangement, there are many others who can help us. We are meant to have relationships with them too. Shelter also comes from the association of our peers.

To effectively associate with others, we have to learn how to develop the ability to see the good qualities in others. To develop the ability to see the good qualities in others, we have to look within our own hearts to see the anarthas that are preventing us from seeing that. This is the success of the nāma-haṭṭa preaching of Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura. The following is the first verse recited in his Śrī Śrī Godruma Kalpatavi:

*nāma cintāmaṇiḥ kṛṣṇaś*  
*caitanya-rasa-vigrahaḥ*  
*pūrṇaḥ śuddho nitya-mukto*  
*‘bhinnatvān nāma-nāminoḥ*  
*(Padma Purāṇa)*

The marketplace of the holy name is the place where the pure holy name is distributed. This pure holy name cleanses the heart of all the anarthas. If a devotee wants to be successful in giving shelter to others, he has to be an ideal example in a way that he is visibly chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. Others should see how he is chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa; how he is chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa with others; and how chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa is the foundation of his spiritual life. When he is not chanting japa, he is chanting in kīrtana.

A leader can help others if he can always see the good in them. A preacher will think, “If somebody needs to develop good qualities, then as a preacher, I am partially responsible if that person does not have those qualities. The person will not improve unless he has the association of somebody who can help him and who cares about him.” Thus, devotees can help each other by seeing the good qualities in each other. By so doing, we can encourage them so that they will feel sheltered, and will then automatically want to come up to a higher standard. Such are Vaiṣṇava relationships.

## Counselor System

The counselor system referred to herein has been established in a number of areas, primarily in the former Soviet Union. In some places it is an effective system, while in other places it is not a very effective system. It is effective where there are devotees who actually understand their responsibilities as counselors. They are exemplary counselors who have already established genuine relationships with their counselees on the strength of their own example and preaching. For them to be counselors is very natural, because the relationship is already there. When it is forced, then it is not as effective. The primary purpose for the counselor system is so that devotees have trusting relationships with other devotees. The authority for one’s spiritual life cannot be established simply by designating somebody as an authority. Lord Caitanya’s movement is a voluntary movement, which means that we have to voluntarily give ourselves to an authority, on the basis of some substance of faith. When we voluntarily give ourselves to an authority, then we take greater responsibility for following their instructions, because we have faith that the instructions are beneficial for the objective we wish to achieve in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. To designate a counselor to a devotee is not effective unless the counselor is a person in whom the counselee has deep faith. Without faith in achieving a superior state of consciousness by the association of devotees, there is no spiritual life, and no advancement.

Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī has written in the Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu: sadho saṅgaḥ svato vare—a devotee should associate with devotees who are more advanced. The counselor system is meant to fulfill this principle. When you associate with somebody who is more advanced, then you can get the opportunity to exchange according to the teachings of Rūpa Gosvāmī—to reveal your mind in confidence and to inquire confidentially. If you do not have that kind of spiritual relationship in life, it is very difficult to make progress. Often that relationship does not exist because we are not willing to be humble. We are not willing to look for superior qualities that exist in others. We are not willing to accept that somebody may actually have something that they can offer us in our spiritual life. For a beginner in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, that is very dangerous, as it means that he is beginning spiritual life from a very dangerous platform. If pride exists within the heart, it is very difficult to advance spiritually. The Lord is very much attracted to humility in His devotees. Wherever there is humility, there are genuine exchanges between one devotee and another.

On the other hand, it is also the responsibility of the person who is supposed to be in the superior position to be an example, to be caring, to not be interested in respect, to not demand respect, and to not use his position for controlling others. Rather, he should have a relationship exclusively with that person for the purpose of helping him. The most important aspect is to help somebody without an expectation of getting something in return. If one cannot do that, then he is not qualified for taking care of others. One must be trustworthy, and the dependent should see that such a devotee has no other agenda in their relationship, other than wanting to help him in his spiritual life.

Therefore, the counselor system cannot be forced upon others. It has to be earned by those devotees who are actually serving in the capacity of counselors, coming up in their level of realizations, and becoming qualified both on the strength of their example, and on the strength of their preaching to help others. Sometimes devotees do not have faith in the authority structures of the temple. Thus, if the authority structure simply appoints somebody to be a counselor, then there will be no faith, and relationships will be very formal, with the counselee having an agenda of obtaining a recommendation. Such a relationship is practically useless. It is the responsibility of the neophyte newcomers to Kṛṣṇa consciousness to learn humility, and it is the responsibility of the counselors to not abuse the humility of others. When those two qualifications exist, we will have an effective counselor system. That should be the primary goal. Unless there are these kinds of relationships, we will be unable to create a very strong impression in the minds of the newcomers to Kṛṣṇa consciousness that there is such a thing as genuine Vaiṣṇava relationships. It starts in the temple, and then grows to the congregation who are connected to the temple. It should grow naturally, organically, and voluntarily, on the spiritual platform. It will not happen just because someone has been designated as an authority.

There are devotees who are actual authorities, and we should be humble enough to recognize those who have the qualities of an authority. In Vaiṣṇava relationships, the bond is based upon the genuine humility that is displayed between one Vaiṣṇava and another. A Vaiṣṇava sees others as his superior. He never thinks that he is superior to everyone else with whom he associates.

This is illustrated in the example of Duryodhana and Yudhiṣṭhira Mahārāja. Yudhiṣṭhira Mahārāja was told to go throughout the kingdom and to look for somebody who is more fallen than himself. Duryodhana was sent to look for somebody who was more advanced than himself. Thus, they both went out searching and came back to give their reports. Yudhiṣṭhira Mahārāja, who was the emperor, said, “I could not find anybody who was lower than myself.”

Duryodhana said, “I could not find anybody who is superior to me.” Duryodhana was thus labeled as offense-personified because he was so proud.

It is very important that the devotees understand that there is a very good reason for establishing the counselor system. It is a very good sign in a new devotee when he can find somebody who is better than himself.

**Question: Does a counselor have to be a preacher?**

To have an effective counselor system, the counselors have to be preachers. However, a counselee cannot relate with the counselor if they only see a counselor as a person who preaches to them. That would be a very formal and weak relationship—especially if the only time they see a counselor preaching is when they come into the room and a counselor starts telling them what they are doing wrong. To develop faith in the counselor, they have to see the counselor as a preacher who is taking care of others besides just themselves. That will build trust.

It is possible that there can be some relationships between the counselor and a counselee where the counselor is not a big preacher. However, it is a general principle that the counselors must also be preachers, and they must have a capacity to inspire others by their preaching and by their example. Devotees will then naturally come forward to take advice from them. The relationship between the counselor and counselee should be natural; not artificial.

Thus, the counselors should be preachers and should be satisfied in preaching. If they are not satisfied in preaching, and they do it because they are told to, they cannot really give shelter.

It is also very good for the counselors to be teaching subjects like Vaiṣṇava etiquette, guru and disciple relationships, association with Vaiṣṇavas, and even the holy name. The holy name is such an integral part of devotional service that devotees do not fully understand the inner relationship with it. They should discuss subjects that really refer to the Vaiṣṇava qualities.

Of course, the counselors also have to be good examples, otherwise they cannot be counselors. They have to be stable in their own situation. They should know how to associate with all levels of Vaiṣṇavas—those who are junior to them, those who are equal to them, and those who are superior to them. Teaching by example is very important for creating faith. The counselee should not only see how the counselor associates with him as an authority, but he should see how the counselors associate with his superiors and with his equals as well. The counselee will thus learn how to associate with his superiors and with his own equals. As a counselor, one is forced to be an example. Sometimes people try to create faith by an image they create. However, for there to be trust, they must also have substance; not just the image.

I am convinced that the counselor system has to create counselors who are not managers. It does not mean that they cannot manage, but they have to know how to manage in such a way that they do not abuse their managerial authority when counseling the devotees. Furthermore, the managers have to trust the counselors even though they are not managers. These kinds of harmonious relationships must exist.

Sometimes the managers try to designate counselors who will support the management. However, devotees who have some differences of opinion will not trust the counselors. It is therefore good to have counselors who are not part of that management system, who are independent thinkers, but strictly principled.

Trust has to be created so that the devotees will be less formal in their counselor relationships. Without trust, there is no meaning to the counselor system; it is simply a show.

**Question: It has been said that a devotee who is going to be a counselor should have good sādhana, should himself have shelter, and have social status and stability. If there are not many devotees who are qualified according to these criteria in the community, should we lower the standards for the short term, and then gradually raise them? Or should devotees just not be designated as counselors until they possess those qualities?**

The main objective is to find proper examples of devotees in their particular āśrama who can give attention to the counselees, properly train them and give them proper instructions. We must not stop everything that is going on. If we are not properly situated to take care of somebody, we have to find the right examples, establish them as the proper examples, and then point to them. Even though we may have been taking care of somebody, we have to bring them to the proper examples. If we are not the right example, we must admit that. However without the right example, everyone must not stop in their efforts. We have to get the right example and the right standard, and honestly recognize it. By encouraging devotees to rise to the standard, they will recognize where they are, and they will gradually work towards achieving that standard.

**Question: Should counselors be appointed to the counselee by the senior devotees in the yatra, or should the counselee choose a counselor amongst the appointed ones on their own?**

In some places I have asked the devotees to discuss amongst themselves and to present to me the potential candidates who could be accepted by everyone as good examples and thus as a counselor. I do not even want the local temple leaders to authorize them; I want to authorize them myself. I have tried to establish what the proper standard is, for the beginning at least, to act in a capacity as a counselor.

**Question: What should we do when devotees approach a counselor with the sole motivation of receiving initiation?**

There will always be people who are motivated in that way, but you can diminish it by proper training. However, I see mistakes taking place on both sides—there are those who are motivated only to get initiation, and there are leaders who are manipulating the devotees who are aspiring for initiation, trying to force them to be something that is against their nature just for some temporary time so that they can get a recommendation. This becomes a problematic situation because it creates a double standard. Devotees are told to be completely surrendered, but then the leaders are manipulating them to achieve the right standard.

In some cases, devotees are not very humble and are not qualified to be initiated. They do not like to be told that they are not qualified. Thus there are mistakes made on both sides. However, there is no excuse for the leaders. They should be careful to not manipulate devotees for initiation. Sometimes the leaders do not give their recommendation for initiation, but they will not tell the person why, and what they need to do to improve themselves.

To take care of someone does not mean just telling them that what they are doing is wrong. It means making the person feel cared for, and convincing them that you are actually thinking of them, so that they will want to try to improve.

If the devotee is sincerely endeavoring to try to improve, then it should be recognized and encouraged. Otherwise, they will think that the authority is just a person who is always pushing them down, while in actuality the authority should actually be a person who brings others up and inspires them.

**Question: In the counselor system, it is very important for a counselor to have shelter. What can be done so that he feels sheltered?**

There has to be proper Vaiṣṇava relationships with devotees who are exemplary. When you have shelter in the association of others, you can share it with everyone who is dependent upon you. There must be loving relationships with one another; not competition or envy. In addition, having shelter from a senior Vaiṣṇava can help us to be sheltered in relationships with others.

**Question: In addition to counseling other brahmacārīs, can a brahmacārī also counsel students, neophyte devotees and newcomers?**

It depends on his capacity. Certainly, if he has the capacity to counsel brahmacārīs and to preach to the new people, students, etc., then he should do it. However, still the separation of the sexes should be there. Mātājīs should be encouraged to preach to the women. Husband and wife should preach together. Unmarried women should have shelter. If women are going to preach, then they also need to be sheltered. However, they should get shelter from other women and married couples; not from the brahmacārīs.

Question: Should the proper standards be introduced immediately to the new people who come to our movement, or can it be done slowly?

There is a difference between counselor groups and nāma-haṭṭas. Certainly new people are not ready to immediately comply with strict standards and restrictions. By forcing it upon them, it might even turn them away. Therefore, there has to be something that is a little less rigid for the newcomers. However, when they start becoming more serious, they should know that there is something that is stricter that they should follow. They should be encouraged to move in that direction. It does not mean that we put all the devotees who are bad examples to preach to the new people. Those who preach to newcomers should be a good example, but they are less strict with them.

There is a verse in the Fifth Canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, in which Prahlāda Mahārāja prays for all the preachers to become nonenvious. Prabhupāda explains in the purport to that verse that a preacher should be very liberal in his social dealings towards others, but he is always strict with himself. Because he is very strict with himself, he does not push others down. Sometimes people are too strict with themselves, but when they are artificially strict, they are very dissatisfied. They become artificially strict because somebody else is forcing them to be strict. Because they are being forced, they then deal with everybody else in that manner. However, that is envy. A person should be free from envy. Thus he is happy by being strict with himself. His mind is peaceful. Therefore, he can be liberal with others and encourage them to come up. Śrīla Prabhupāda did the same with all the new devotees at the very beginning of the movement. Devotees are then attracted to become stricter, and to move into the programs that are more strictly defined. Thus, nāma-haṭṭa programs are meant for newer people, and there should be other programs where there are more senior devotees who are prepared to become stricter in their dealings with each other, especially between men and women. We should always avoid bad examples as preachers as much as possible.

**Question: It was said that householder devotees who counsel others should be financially stable and should not depend on money given by those whom they counsel. It is also said that in Vedic times, those devotees who were brahminical by nature were given charity. Is this to be applied today?**

A householder should have an honest means of livelihood, and their recreation should be preaching. Instead of spending one’s spare time on oneself, a devotee should use that time to try to do good for others. He will thus be much happier. Without obtaining some satisfaction from Kṛṣṇa consciousness, one will think that the only way to be satisfied is by increasing his wealth and material opulence.

**Question: What are some of the principles that should be followed by devotees that have the responsibility for taking care of others?**

Devotees must very closely associate with each other and take care of each other first and foremost. It is not that they are big leaders, or have a big group of people whom they are taking care of. For devotees who take care of other devotees, the most important relationships are the ones they have with each other. At Śrī Śrī Rādhā Gopīnātha Mandir, the devotees follow a particular formula for association: If they get up to twenty percent of association with their spiritual master, they are very happy; sixty percent of the association is with their peers; and twenty percent is with their counselees. When they come together regularly, they may discuss some management, but primarily they chant bhajanas and have classes together. They meet every week to do this. They help each other, and call each other on the phone if somebody has some difficulty.

Thus, shelter also comes with the association of one’s peers. To effectively associate with others, we have to learn how to develop the ability to see the good qualities in others. To develop the ability to see the good qualities in others, we have to look within our own hearts to see the anarthas that are obstructing us and preventing us from seeing.

The nāma-haṭṭa preaching as instructed by Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura is so effective. At the very center of nāma-haṭṭa preaching is nāma-cintāmaṇi-kṛṣṇaś caitanya-rasa-vigrahaḥ—the market place of the holy name is the place where the pure holy name is distributed, which cleanses the heart from all these anarthas.

If a devotee wants to be successful in giving shelter to others, he has to be an ideal example, visibly chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. Others should see how he is chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa with others, and how chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa is the foundation of his spiritual life. When he is not chanting japa, he is chanting in kīrtana. For devotees who come together to chant the pure holy name, it is the basis of their relationships, as they are cleaning their hearts and developing the ability to see the good qualities in each other and in their dependents. To have these nice loving relationships, one has to be able to appreciate the good qualities of others.

An important criterion of being a leader who can help others is to always see the good in others. If you cannot see the good in others, how can you help them? A preacher has to think that if somebody needs to develop good qualities, then as a preacher, he is partially responsible if that person does not have them. One will not improve unless he has the association of somebody who can help him and who cares about him. Thus, devotees help each other by seeing the good qualities in each other, and encouraging them so that they will feel sheltered. By feeling sheltered, they will automatically want to come up to a higher standard and improve. Such are Vaiṣṇava relationships.

If we always find ourselves surrounded by people whom we do not like and do not want to deal with, then we should be introspective and ask ourselves why this is the case. However, the external devotee will think that if they are always surrounded by people that they do not like, the solution is to avoid them all, and only associate and cooperate with people who like him.

Such a person, however, is not a preacher, and is not a madhyama. Rather, he is kaniṣṭha, as he does not know how to associate with his peers. A madhyama knows how to associate, because he knows how to appreciate the qualities of others.

The internal devotee will look within his heart; chant Hare Kṛṣṇa very attentively; and pray to Kṛṣṇa to help him to reveal and overcome the anarthas that obstruct him in his relationships with these devotees. He can see their good qualities and experience shelter and love. Devotees are not competitors; they love each other and are able to associate with each other by seeing their good qualities. To be successful in taking care of Kṛṣṇa’s devotees, follow this formula, and let all other managerial schemes go to the way side. Everything else will develop very naturally, because there will be some shelter to share. The ability to organize nāma-haṭṭas, bhakti-vṛkṣas, and other preaching activities will then manifest very naturally, as there will be some substance there. Prabhupāda says, “When preaching is there, then everything else will follow naturally.”

Preaching is not only in reference to the nondevotees. Kṛṣṇa says:

*ya idaṁ paramaṁ guhyaṁ*  
*mad-bhakteṣv abhidhāsyati*  
*bhaktiṁ mayi parāṁ kṛtvā*  
*mām evaiṣyaty asaṁśayaḥ*

**“For one who explains this supreme secret to the devotees, pure devotional service is guaranteed, and at the end he will come back to Me.” (Bg. 18.68)**

*na ca tasmān manuṣyeṣu*  
*kaścin me priya-kṛttamaḥ*  
*bhavitā na ca me tasmād*  
*anyaḥ priyataro bhuvi*

**“There is no servant in this world more dear to Me than he, nor will there ever be one more dear.” (Bg. 18.69)**

## Chapter 10 – Holy Dhāmas

## Eligibility to Enter the Holy Dhāmas

To become qualified to enter Vṛndāvana, one has to go through Lord Caitanya, and to get Lord Caitanya, one has to go through Lord Nityānanda. We accept the representative of Lord Nityānanda, a Vaiṣṇava, who helps us to clean the heart. This is so we can understand Lord Caitanya, understand real devotional service as taught by Lord Caitanya, and understand how to develop a relationship with Him.

*yuga-dharma pravartāimu nāma-saṅkīrtana*  
*cāri bhāva-bhakti diyā nācāmu bhuvana*

**\[Lord Caitanya said\]: “I shall personally inaugurate the religion of the age—nāma-saṅkīrtana, the congregational chanting of the holy name. I shall make the world dance in ecstasy, realizing the four mellows of loving devotional service.” (Cc. Ādi 3.19)**

Cāri bhāva-bhakti diyā—one can never understand these four ecstatic types of loving service to Lord Kṛṣṇa unless he becomes a servant of Lord Caitanya. When Lord Caitanya appeared, all of His associates appeared with Him in the mood of service to Him.

*pañca-tattva—eka-vastu, nāhi kichu bheda*  
*rasa āsvādite tabu vividha vibheda*

**Spiritually there are no differences between these five tattvas, for on the transcendental platform everything is absolute. Yet there are also varieties in the spiritual world, and in order to taste these spiritual varieties one should distinguish between them. (Cc. Ādi 7.5)**

The relationships that all of Lord Caitanya’s associates have with Him are in the mood of being His servant. Advaita Ācārya had become ecstatic when He finally achieved that most precious, valuable gift of becoming a servant of Lord Caitanya, when the Lord punished Him and beat Him. Advaita Ācārya said, “Now my life is finally fulfilled. He has accepted Me as His servant. Previously He was always giving Me respect as His master and superior.” Advaita Ācārya had even begun preaching Māyāvāda philosophy so that Lord Caitanya would come and beat Him. When Lord Caitanya heard this philosophy from Advaita Ācārya, the Lord came before Him, grabbed Him and pulled Him down.

Sītārāṇī, Advaita Ācārya’s wife, pleaded, “Stop! He is an old man. Please do not beat Him.”

However, while Lord Caitanya was pulling at Advaita Ācārya, Advaita Ācārya simply lay there in complete ecstasy, saying to Himself, “I am His servant! I am His servant! Why else would He treat Me this way, unless I am His servant?”

Similarly, every fiber and atom of Lord Nityānanda’s existence was in complete absorption in service to Lord Caitanya.

After Jīva Gosvāmī was infused with transcendental power by being touched by the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya, all the Vaiṣṇavas came and assembled at that place. Then one by one, Jīva Gosvāmī went to all superior Vaiṣṇavas and begged: “Please, give me your blessings so that I may become qualified to enter into Vṛndāvana. Only by getting the dust of the lotus feet of all of these wonderful associates of Lord Caitanya can I ever have hope to understand and enter into Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma.”

We should give all respect to Vaiṣṇavas, take the dust from their feet, and very fervently pray for this mercy so that we can get rid of this pride and the desire for respect and prestige. If we can develop some enthusiasm and taste to hear the pastimes of the Lord in the association of His devotees, then we can establish this sambandha (relationship) with Lord Caitanya, and the film which is covering Śrī Navadvīpa-dhāma can be removed so that we can actually enter into the dhāma and get the mercy of Lord Caitanya.

This thin film or covering of the dhāma is called prauḍhā-māyā. Even if somebody apparently seems to be in the dhāma and apparently calls Lord Caitanya’s name out of affection, he has no relationship with Lord Caitanya, as prauḍhā-māyā keeps him out. Lord Nityānanda tells Jīva Gosvāmī that there can be no material influence whatsoever in the dhāma, as it is a completely spiritual place.

Śrīla Prabhupāda explains that when one comes to Kṛṣṇa consciousness, Māyā will test him to see if he is coming to serve Kṛṣṇa or to disturb Kṛṣṇa. It is Māyā’s business to protect Kṛṣṇa from disturbances. Therefore, if we are coming to disturb Kṛṣṇa, Māyā will weed us out of her garden. The dhāma is always completely transcendental and is never influenced by any material qualities. It consists of the Lord’s sandhinī potency.

Lord Balarāma is in charge of the sandhinī potency, and is thus the predominating deity of sandhinī. This sandhinī potency of the Lord is that which creates transcendental form in the spiritual world. From Lord Balarāma comes the entire transcendental dhāma, which descends from the spiritual world into this material world. Prauḍhā-māyā protects the dhāma in this world from the materialistic.

This prauḍhā-māyā, which creates a thin covering or film over the dhāma to protect it, keeps all persons who are deceitful and full of pride from entering into the dhāma. A proud person—even though he has no real qualifications—thinks himself to be fully qualified, and he has no humility. However, Lord Nityānanda explains that such persons can never enter into the dhāma.

Jīva Gosvāmī once asked Lord Nityānanda, “How is it that somebody can live in the dhāma for such a long time and Kṛṣṇa bhakti will never manifest in his heart?”

Lord Nityānanda explained: “Dear Jīva, actually, they were never in the dhāma, because proud persons cannot reside in the dhāma, as prauḍhā-māyā is protecting it.” Therefore they are standing on what appears to them to be the dhāma, but the covering is protecting them from influencing it.

Sometimes we think that we want to enter the dhāma to see it. However, we must understand what it actually means to enter the dhāma. Lord Nityānanda explains that entering the dhāma means being recognized as a servant of Lord Caitanya. However, one can never have a relationship with Lord Caitanya as a servant if he is proud. A proud person is one who has no qualification but still thinks himself to be fully qualified and has no humility. Lord Nityānanda thus explains that they cannot enter, as Māyā will keep them out. However, by the mercy of Lord Nityānanda, even a proud person can enter the dhāma.

Lord Nityānanda gives hope that even a proud person can get in. However, he cannot get in with his pride. Rather, he must get the mercy of a servant of Lord Caitanya. If a servant of Lord Caitanya gives his mercy to a proud person, he will help this person to become free from his pride and will give him the spiritual strength to overcome his anarthas.

Lord Caitanya did not accept everybody. He was prepared to kill Jagāi and Mādhāi for the offense they committed to Lord Nityānanda. Yet it was Lord Nityānanda who begged Lord Caitanya to accept them. When a servant of Lord Caitanya begs Him to accept someone, then Lord Caitanya cannot refuse. Such is the power of a servant of Lord Caitanya. It is not a cheap thing.

Thus, by the mercy of a devotee of the Lord, even a proud person can become freed from his pride. Lord Nityānanda explains that to enter into the dhāma, one must have four qualifications: tṛṇād api sunīcena, taror api sahiṣṇunā, amāninā mānadena, kīrtanīyaḥ sadā hariḥ (Śikṣāṣṭaka 3)—one has to think himself to be lower than the straw in the street, devoid of all sense of false prestige, always ready to offer all respect to others and never want any respect for himself.

Furthermore, one of the characteristics of an advanced devotee is that he is attracted to always chanting the holy name of Lord Hari, and he is addicted to speaking about the qualities of the Supreme Lord. If a devotee has the aforementioned four qualities and is also always hearing and chanting about Kṛṣṇa, then he can enter into Navadvīpa-dhāma and have a relationship with Lord Caitanya.

Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī had entered into Navadvīpa-dhāma on parikramā with Lord Nityānanda. After they completed parikramā, Lord Nityānanda told Jīva Gosvāmī, “Now Lord Caitanya is giving you the right to enter into Vṛndāvana.” Although he had already entered Navadvīpa-dhāma, to enter into Vṛndāvana, Jīva Gosvāmī needed the mercy of Lord Caitanya.

As Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura says: bṛndābane rādhā-śyāmer pa’be daraśan, gaura-kṛpā ha’le he (Gītāvalī, Śrī Nāma-kīrtana, Song 2)—“One will be able to enter into Vṛndāvana and get the beautiful vision of Rādhe-Śyāma in Vṛndāvana, but first he has to get the mercy of Lord Caitanya.”

Just as one cannot get into Navadvīpa-dhāma unless he is freed from pride, one cannot enter Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma unless he gets the mercy of Lord Caitanya.

Upon telling Jīva Gosvāmī that Lord Caitanya had given him the right to enter into Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma, Lord Nityānanda placed His lotus feet upon the head of Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī. Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī then became infused with such transcendental ecstasy and great spiritual strength. He then fell on the ground at the feet of Lord Nityānanda, in great ecstasy, and tears were manifesting from his eyes. He was feeling himself to be so fortunate, having received the mercy of Lord Nityānanda. When devotees of Navadvīpa-dhāma heard that Jīva Gosvāmī was going to go to Vṛndāvana, many of them—servants of Lord Caitanya—assembled in that place, understanding the great fortune of Jīva Gosvāmī. Word spreads very fast when a devotee receives great fortune in the dhāma.

When all these Vaiṣṇavas assembled, Jīva Gosvāmī approached each and every one of them and said, “I accept all of you as my gurus because all of you are servants of the Lord. Please bless me. Give me the dust from your lotus feet, and give me your blessings so that I can traverse this journey to go to Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma.” Jīva Gosvāmī did this in complete humility. He is māna-śūnyatā—always feeling himself very humble even though he is very advanced.

*kṣāntir avyartha-kālatvaṁ*  
*viraktir māna-śūnyatā*  
*āśā-bandhaḥ samutkaṇṭhā*  
*nāma-gāne sadā ruciḥ*  
*āsaktis tad-guṇākhyāne*  
*prītis tad-vasati-sthale*  
*ity-ādayo ’nubhāvāḥ syur*  
*jāta-bhāvāṅkure jane*

**When the seed of ecstatic emotion for Kṛṣṇa fructifies, the following nine symptoms manifest in one’s behavior: forgiveness, concern that time should not be wasted, detachment, absence of false prestige, hope, eagerness, a taste for chanting the holy name of the Lord, attachment to descriptions of the transcendental qualities of the Lord, and affection for those places where the Lord resides—that is, a temple or a holy place like Vṛndāvana. These are all called anubhāva, subordinate signs of ecstatic emotion. They are visible in a person in whose heart the seed of love of God has begun to fructify. (Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu 1.3.25–26)**

These are the nine characteristics of an advanced devotee. Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī was manifesting all of these qualities. He felt himself to be totally unqualified, and therefore he approached each one of these associates of Lord Caitanya, begging for them to give him the dust of their lotus feet and their blessings so that he could make his journey to Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma.

When Jīva Gosvāmī completed his parikramā, he went to the home of Śacīmātā to get her blessings. She was very eager to see him. Jīva Gosvāmī fell at her feet and begged for her blessings to enter Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma. Śacīmātā took her lotus foot and placed it upon his head. Jīva Gosvāmī then proceeded to go to Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma, as he received both the right and the order to go.

Just as Jīva Gosvāmī was arriving at the outskirts of Navadvīpa-dhāma, Śrī Vṛndāvana-dhāma manifested within his heart, River Yamunā manifested within his heart, Govardhana manifested within his heart, and finally the associates of the Lord (Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmīs) manifested in his heart. He was totally absorbed in meditation upon Vṛndāvana.

One night on Jīva Gosvāmī’s journey, Lord Caitanya appeared to him in a dream. The Lord said to him, “Now you should go to Vṛndāvana, meditate upon My form of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, and serve that form there in Vṛndāvana. Also take up the service with your uncles of writing transcendental literature.”

Thus, we can enter into the dhāma by the mercy of a devotee who helps us to become free from pride. We can thus become qualified to enter Navadvīpa, and then when we get the blessings of Lord Caitanya, we can enter Vṛndāvana-dhāma. We can achieve the highest platform of ecstatic love of Kṛṣṇa by serving Lord Caitanya. By service to Lord Caitanya—by preaching the glories of the Lord and His holy names in this way—one actually becomes qualified to get Lord Caitanya’s mercy. Prabhodānanda Sarasvatī describes that to the degree that one renders service to Lord Caitanya, he becomes qualified to see Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes in Vṛndāvana. This is therefore our means for entering into the spiritual world.

However, if Lord Nityānanda sees that we are proud, He will help us by pointing out our anarthas. He chastises us and makes us qualified. A devotee will see the chastisement of the Lord as mercy.

There is a pastime of the brahmacārī who tried to enter into Lord Caitanya’s kīrtana by telling Śrīvāsa Paṇḍita that he only eats a few roots and berries from the forest and drinks a little milk, and is thus qualified to enter by his austerities. However, when Lord Caitanya became aware of his presence, He said to Śrīvāsa, “You think some milk-drinker can see My pastimes in your home? You think that is a qualification? That is not qualification!”

When the brahmacārī heard this, he felt that the Lord had bestowed so much mercy on him by having chastised him. In complete humility he walked to the door. The Lord being the all-pervasive Supersoul knew his heart and said, “Come here.” Lord Caitanya placed His lotus foot on his head and said, “Do not ever think again that you can become qualified to come into My kīrtana simply by drinking milk and performing your austerities. Austerities alone are not the qualification. One has to think himself to be very low and fallen. Then he gets mercy.”

Thus, being humble is our qualification for getting some taste of the holy name of the Lord—tṛṇād api sunīcena, taror api sahiṣṇunā—and then one can chant the holy name of the Lord constantly. Similarly, if we want to enter the holy dhāma, then we need to develop the qualification. We will be tested by māyā—to see if we are coming to serve Kṛṣṇa or disturb Kṛṣṇa. We should therefore express our intense desire to serve the Lord and to become qualified to become a resident of the dhāma.

## Learning Devotion from Girirāja

If we want to learn how to perform devotional service, then we must obtain the mercy of a devotee of the Lord. Otherwise, devotional service will always remain a great mystery. Even the gopīs, who are the greatest devotees of the Lord, think, “If we want to obtain the fulfillment of our desires, then we should worship a devotee.” The gopīs are the topmost devotees, yet they think in that way. They are the greatest receptacles of mercy from Lord Kṛṣṇa, yet they desire to serve a devotee of Kṛṣṇa so that they may be allowed to meet Kṛṣṇa. The gopīs proclaimed Girirāja as the best devotee. The following was spoken by the gopīs when Lord Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma entered the forest:

**“Of all the devotees, this Govardhana Hill is the best! O my friends, this hill supplies Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, along with Their calves, cows and cowherd friends, with all kinds of necessities—water for drinking, very soft grass, caves, fruits, flowers and vegetables. In this way the hill offers respects to the Lord. Being touched by the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, Govardhana Hill appears very jubilant.” (Bhāg. 10.21.18)**

The gopīs thus meditate on Girirāja as the best servant of Kṛṣṇa—hari-dāsa-varyo. Girirāja is the Lord’s manifestation both as the greatest servant of Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇa Himself. He assumed this form of Govardhana Hill to accept the offerings of all the residents of Vṛndāvana. After assuming this wonderful form, the Lord also simultaneously offered worship to that form.

Lord Caitanya worshipped Govardhana as nondifferent from Kṛṣṇa. For three continuous years, Lord Caitanya carried a Govardhana śilā and guñjā-mālā with Him, which were given to Him from a devotee named Śaṅkarānanda Sarasvatī. He would often put the śilā to His head, embrace it to His heart, and bathe it with His tears. Lord Caitanya thus worshipped Girirāja as nondifferent from Kṛṣṇa. After keeping this śilā and guñjā-mālā for three years, greatly satisfied by the behavior of Raghunātha dāsa Gosvāmī, Lord Caitanya gave them to him to worship. Lord Caitanya told him to very carefully worship this śilā by offering water and tulasī. By so doing, an intense love and greed for Kṛṣṇa would awaken within the heart.

Although Girirāja is nondifferent from the Supreme Lord, we should want to see Him specifically for the sake of developing our internal devotion—as Hari-dāsa-varyo, the servant of the Lord. We should want to follow the principle that if we want the fulfillment of our desires, then we must worship the great devotee of the Lord and render service unto him. This verse from the Bhāgavatam thus describes how Girirāja is actually rendering service to the Lord by assisting Him in His pastimes.

Just as the Lord’s internal potencies assist and serve the Lord in the facilitation of His desires to enjoy with His devotees, similarly Girirāja assists the Lord to facilitate His desire to reciprocate with His devotees. Girirāja serves the Lord, His devotees, the cowherd boys, and the cows and calves who are all very dear to Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, Girirāja is providing so much opulence of Vṛndāvana for the service of the Supreme Lord. Although we think of opulence as that which is very great, wonderful, and rich, the opulence of Vṛndāvana is that which actually satisfies the Lord and His devotees in His pastimes.

The opulence that Govardhana provides for the service of the Lord includes fragrant, cool, and fresh water (pānīya) for the Lord for drinking, bathing, and for washing His mouth after eating prasādam with His cowherd boyfriends. Girirāja also provides very soft grasses (sūyavasa) for Kṛṣṇa’s cows. This grass is a very special, aromatic grass that is very pleasing and attractive to the cows. Another quality of the grass that grows on Govardhana Hill is that it is very nourishing to Kṛṣṇa’s cows. The cows actually never feel any hunger, disease or fatigue. The grass is also so soft that even in the summer when there is no rain, when the cows are grazing on Govardhana Hill, they never pierce their cheeks, lips or tongues by chewing on the grass. The result from eating this grass is that the cows provide very nourishing milk.

Mother Yaśodā was very eager to personally take the milk that was produced by cows that had eaten special aromatic grass. Although she was the queen of Vṛndāvana and she could have arranged for anybody to prepare this butter for Kṛṣṇa, she wanted to do it herself. She was thinking that they would not do it right. She therefore personally selected these cows that had eaten this exceptionally aromatic grass. She prepared nice yogurt and butter for Kṛṣṇa so that He would stop stealing it from all the neighboring houses.

In addition to providing very nice grass, Girirāja also provides very nice caves (kandara) for Kṛṣṇa and His cowherd boyfriends to take shelter from the hot summer sun, and from the rain on other occasions. The same caves were also very wonderful places for Kṛṣṇa when He goes to meet with the gopīs. They would see how Girirāja is a very intimate and confidential associate of Kṛṣṇa, and they were very much eager to get Kṛṣṇa’s association. Girirāja also provides very nice fruits and wonderful types of beverages such as honey, mango juice and pīlu juice. Girirāja also features soft roots for eating, jewels for ornamenting the body, flat places for sitting, lamps and mirrors in the form of smooth stones, glistening water and other natural substances. Such is the opulence that Girirāja is offering as a service for the Supreme Lord.

Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura gives us a very wonderful explanation of how the gopīs are thinking in relation to Girirāja. They said, “We have heard from Gārgī, who was the daughter of Garga Muni that without rendering service to a devotee, one cannot get the fulfillment of one’s desire. Therefore, because Govardhana Hill is the best of all devotees, we should go to that place. Let us go and take our bath there in Mānasī Gaṅgā and then take darśana of Harideva.”

The Harideva Deity manifested there because of the intense desire and feelings of separation the gopīs have for Kṛṣṇa. One day, they were feeling a very intense separation from Kṛṣṇa and they were standing at Mānasī Gaṅgā, calling out: “Harideva! Harideva! Harideva!” By their intense desire to see Kṛṣṇa, a Deity manifested there in the form of the Harideva. From that day on, the gopīs would go there daily and worship that Deity. Thus they were saying, “Let us go and take bath in Mānasī Gaṅgā and take darśana of Harideva. Certainly, our elders will have no objection to this. How can they possibly complain if we go there and simply take darśana of Harideva?”

The gopīs were always very much concerned about what their elders were thinking in terms of their association with Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, they thought that while they were there to have darśana of Harideva, they would also get the opportunity to see Kṛṣṇa, who is there with the cowherd boys on the slopes of Govardhana. Having decided upon this plan, the gopīs glorified Govardhana, as He fulfills the desires of Kṛṣṇa, His companions, and hopefully also their own desire to meet Kṛṣṇa. Such is the intense desire and meditation that they always carry within their hearts. Because Girirāja facilitates all the pastimes of the Lord, the gopīs see Him as the best devotee of the Lord.

Girirāja also served the Lord by manifesting Himself as an umbrella to protect His devotees in Vṛndāvana who had been inundated by the torrential rains of Indra. In this way, Girirāja facilitated the most wonderful pastime of the Lord, bringing all the devotees together in one place to be with Kṛṣṇa. The most unique quality of that pastime is that all the devotees who had particular relationships with Kṛṣṇa were all in one place at the same time.

Mother Yaśodā had her vātsalya-prema for Kṛṣṇa, and she was always thinking of everything in terms of Kṛṣṇa as her son. When Kṛṣṇa would be in bed in the morning and mother Yaśodā would come and see scratches all over His body, she would think that these scratches were coming because Kṛṣṇa was not careful when He was going out. She would think that He was running into thorns and branches in the forest, and His body was being cut. Her vātsalya-prema was never disturbed in her observation of the behavior of her son. She would see Kṛṣṇa at home, and then she would also see Kṛṣṇa when He was leaving to go off to the pasturing grounds in the morning. She would want to go with Him when He was going off to the pasturing grounds, but Kṛṣṇa would not let her. However, in govardhana-līlā, Girirāja facilitated such a wonderful pastime that all the devotees were all together in the same place for seven days continuously.

Girirāja is therefore a very great devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa. We should also understand this principle that if we ever want to participate in the Lord’s pastimes and want to be in the association of the Lord, then we must obtain the mercy of the devotee of the Lord. We can never obtain devotional service to the Lord without obtaining the mercy of Kṛṣṇa’s devotees. By remembering Girirāja and His role as the greatest servant of Lord Kṛṣṇa, we can learn a little bit about devotion to Lord Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, certainly if we worship and serve Girirāja, we can also have hope within our hearts that we may also attain the association of Kṛṣṇa and His pastimes.

## Chapter 11 – Āśramas

## Brahmacārī-āśrama

The following is Śrīla Prabhupāda’s summary of the Seventh Canto, Twelfth Chapter of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam—The Perfect Society: Four Spiritual Classes.

This chapter particularly describes the brahmacārī and the person in the vānaprastha stage, and it also gives a general description of the four āśramas—brahmacarya, gṛhastha, vānaprastha and sannyāsa. In the previous chapter, the great saint Nārada Muni has described the varṇa institution of society, and now, in this chapter, he will describe the stages of spiritual advancement in the four āśramas, which are known as brahmacarya, gṛhastha, vānaprastha and sannyāsa.

The brahmacārī should live under the care of the true spiritual master, giving him sincere respect and obeisances, acting as his menial servant, and always carrying out his order. The brahmacārī should engage himself in spiritual activities and study the Vedic literature under the direction of the spiritual master. According to the brahmacarya system, he should dress with a belt, deerskin, and matted hair and should bear a daṇḍa, water pot and sacred thread. He should collect alms daily in the morning, and in the evening whatever alms he has collected he should offer to the spiritual master. A brahmacārī should accept prasāda upon the order of the spiritual master, and if the spiritual master sometimes forgets to order the disciple to eat, the disciple should not take prasāda on his own initiative; rather, he should fast. The brahmacārī should be trained to be satisfied with eating what is absolutely necessary, he should be very expert in executing responsibilities, he should be faithful, and he should control his senses and try to avoid the association of women as far as possible. A brahmacārī should very strictly abstain from living with women and should not meet with gṛhastha and those too addicted to women. Nor should a brahmacārī speak in a lonely place with a woman.

After completing one’s education as a brahmacārī in this way, one should give dakṣiṇā, an offering of gratitude, to one’s guru, and then one may leave for home and accept the next āśrama—the gṛhastha-āśrama—or else one may continue in the brahmacarya-āśrama without adulteration. The duties for the gṛhastha-āśrama and brahmacarya-āśrama, as well as the duties for sannyāsīs, are prescribed in the śāstras. A gṛhastha is not meant to enjoy sex life without restriction. Indeed, the whole purpose of Vedic life is to become free from sexual indulgence. All the āśramas are recognized for spiritual progress, and therefore although the gṛhastha-āśrama gives a kind of license for sex life for a certain time, it does not allow unrestricted sex life. Therefore, in gṛhastha life also, there is no illicit sex. A gṛhastha should not accept a woman for sexual enjoyment. Wasting semen is also illicit sex.

After the gṛhastha-āśrama is another āśrama, known as vānaprastha, which is midway between gṛhastha and sannyāsa. A person in the vānaprastha order is restricted in eating food grains and forbidden to eat fruits that have not ripened on the tree. Nor should he cook food with fire, although he is allowed to eat caru, grains that have been offered in a sacrificial fire. He may also eat fruits and grains that have grown naturally. Living in a thatched cottage, the vānaprastha should endure all kinds of heat and cold. He should not cut his nails or hair, and he should give up cleaning his body and teeth. He should wear tree bark, accept a daṇḍa, and practice life in the forest, taking a vow to live there for twelve years, eight years, four years, two years or at least one year. At last, when because of old age he can no longer perform the activities of a vānaprastha, he should gradually stop everything and in this way give up his body. (Summary of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Seventh Canto, Twelfth Chapter, The Perfect Society: Four Spiritual Classes)

There are many good instructions contained herein for the brahmacarya-āśrama. Especially if one does not take sannyāsa, he should continue as a brahmacārī without adulteration. Without adulteration means that he continues to accept the same sacrifices and austerities that he did when he first began practices of brahmacarya. He should not become a Kali-yuga brahmacārī, which is described in the śāstras as one who stays brahmacārī simply because householder life is too difficult. A brahmacārī must fully accept responsibility.

**Question: What is the main goal of the brahmacārī-āśrama?**

Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam states that the code of the brahmacārī-āśrama is to become learned in the scriptures; to renounce and become detached; to become fully dependent upon the instructions of the spiritual master, so much so that if the spiritual master does not call the disciple to eat, he fasts that day; to be expert in executing responsibilities; to be faithful; to be able to control the senses; and to avoid the association of women.

**Question: Sometime the brahmacārī leader in the temple is seen as not being loving and is too demanding, expecting too much discipline. There are no informal, warm relationships between the brahmacārīs and devotees. Is that the way the āśrama in the temple should be managed?**

In a relationship, there are at least two persons; not just one. It is very easy to put all the responsibility on the authority to be the person to initiate the relationship. However, if one really wants a relationship with someone, then according to our Vaiṣṇava philosophy, the method of having a relationship with somebody is to consider all the responsibilities that that person has, and without even asking, you should look for opportunities to do something that will help him. In other words, you serve him. By so doing, you will get his attention, and he will reciprocate. That is the Vaiṣṇava standard. Furthermore, if you really want attention, then serve him without any expectation of something in return. That is a foundational principle of love, and how we have reciprocal relationships according to Vaiṣṇava philosophy. However, if everything is motivated to get something in return, then nobody wants to extend an opportunity to serve, as they know that it is motivated by the desire for something in return. The nature of loving relationships is that you do something for somebody but do not expect anything in return. Simply try to please him. This will allow for loving relationships to develop.

The authority should not be blamed, thinking that it is his responsibility to have a relationship with you. That is what kaniṣṭha-adhikārīs and prākṛta-bhaktas do. However, there is a higher standard of devotional service than to be a materialistic devotee who is self-centered, sectarian, and thinking that his service is the most important service, and that everyone else is meant to facilitate his service. Such persons will only have relationships with people with the same mentality, and those are not real relationships or friendships.

In an āśrama, there must be rules. Dharmaṁ tu sākṣād bhagavat-praṇītam (Bhāg. 6.3.19)—Prabhupāda explains that the principles of religion are enunciated by the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Wherever you see laws, there is always a lawmaker. It may appear that there may be some disparity in the application of such rules, but in order for there to be organization, there must be rules. Thus, to live as a brahmacārī, the first principle is to accept that there will be rules. If one wants to make his own rules, then he has to take responsibility for having a place to make his own rules. It is that simple.

If you do not want to follow the rules, then you can become the lord of your own flat and make your own rules. However, if you want to stay in the brahmacārī-āśrama, then understand that you are a servant. Do not blame the people who have to make the rules. That creates anarchy. There have to be some rules for everyone to follow. For instance, one rule is to not bring prasādam into the brahmacārī āśrama. The reason behind it is to not attract cockroaches. Thus the rule must be accepted and followed.

Unfortunately, the brahmacārīs do not even want to follow such simple rules. However, if you want to stay in the āśrama, then follow the rules. That should be understood from the first day that one walks into the āśrama. If one does not want to follow the rules, then he should stay outside of the āśrama and visit the temple and hear Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. Nobody is banned from coming to the temple to hear Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and to take part in kīrtana. Kṛṣṇa consciousness is for everybody. However, if one wants to live in the brahmacārī āśrama, then he has to follow the rules, and somebody has to enforce them. No one is forced to stay in the āśrama. If someone decides to live in the āśrama, then it means that he has voluntarily agreed to submit himself to an authority.

**Question: Are the temple authorities allowed to tell a brahmacārī to move out of the āśrama?**

Generally, one comes to the āśrama on a trial basis. He is to be re-evaluated after some time to determine if he is qualified to live in the āśrama. Generally those who move into the āśrama should be people who come to the temple for a significant amount of time, and know the difference between what it means to live outside the temple and what it means to live inside the temple. It should be made clear what standards are expected from those living inside the temple before they are accepted in the āśrama.

When somebody moves into the āśrama, the temple is not bound to keep him there. The āśrama is meant for training. Training means to focus on something in particular, and then repeatedly one has to be reminded of what needs to be done. In training, one hears a certain set of rules, and then follows them. If there are any discrepancies or deviations from the rules, then one is reminded that he must adhere to the rules. In this way, he becomes trained.

Rules are not only those which prohibit activities. Training in spiritual life means that in the beginning there are some restrictions or prohibitions, but there are also positive activities. Of course, when you are trained to rise early in the morning, to participate in kīrtana with devotees, and to deeply study the philosophy of Kṛṣṇa consciousness in the association of devotees, it is supposed to awaken the taste within the heart for something higher—not simply to train the physical body.

We are spirit souls, and we need nourishment. If we do not get that nourishment from spiritual activities, then we start looking for other ways to gratify our senses. Training therefore also means to stay focused on the most essential practices of spiritual life. It means to learn how to avoid those activities which are detrimental for one’s spiritual life. Such is brahmacārī life—it requires training.

After a brahmacārī has undergone the training, he is allowed to enter the gṛhastha-āśrama. If he does not enter the gṛhastha-āśrama, then he remains as a brahmacārī without any adulteration. It does not mean that because he has been around for a long time that he can be more independent. One can be independent, but he has to always feel himself dependent on the training that he got throughout his brahmacārī life, and therefore he continues to follow the rules, to rise early, to chant attentively in the morning, to study śāstra, to hear śāstra in the association of devotees, and to preach Kṛṣṇa consciousness. By so doing, he is safe as a brahmacārī. Because he follows all the simple, basic practices of brahmacārī life in a devotional mood, he feels nourishment and is happy to continue with brahmacārī life.

Nobody will stay happy in spiritual life if he thinks his happiness is to avoid responsibility. The mind and senses will not cooperate. The heart will become filled with lusty desires, one will contemplate the objects of the senses, his determination for spiritual life will become weaker and weaker, and he will have to start adjusting everything according to his weaknesses in spiritual life. There are certainly opportunities for concessions for devotees who may have physical frailties or other problems. Although there will always be exceptions, the rules are as previously mentioned.

**Question: Are the āśrama standards too high?**

The standards are very high. However, if high standards are not maintained, one will obtain diminished results. If you keep lowering the bar, then what you get is something that is watered down. Thus we have to keep the standards high. Sometimes certain concessions can be made for valid reasons. However, everyone should not be checking to see what concessions everyone else may have received. Concessions should not be given because you want them. There has to be a valid reason for it. If there is no valid reason, there should be no concession. If the valid reason is that one does not have enough determination to live as a brahmacārī, then the concession for that is also given in the scriptures—to live as a gṛhastha.

**Question: How should a brahmacārī be engaged in service if he lacks certain external qualifications and abilities?**

This question does not apply only to the brahmacārī-āśrama. If there is no community, then there is no facility for the devotees who cannot simply follow the strict brahmacarya practices in the āśrama to remain serving in the society of devotees. There needs to be community leaders; not just brahmacārī leaders. Not everybody who is living in the brahmacārī-āśrama is going to stay under the authority of a brahmacārī leader. However, the brahmacārī leader has to recognize those devotees in a very personal and instructive way. Those devotees who cannot live as brahmacārīs still need to be engaged in other ways within the community of devotees, where there are other services available so that they can continue to serve within the community of Vaiṣṇavas. That is what the counselor system is supposed to do—create counselors who can help devotees who are in transition, and give them a way to continue serving within their particular capacity to serve. All the varieties and opportunities for service are not available in the brahmacārī-āśrama.

It is not the responsibility of the brahmacārī leader to start dreaming up different varieties of services to keep everyone engaged according to their particular nature. Rather, it is the duty of other leaders in the community to provide transitional-position services for devotees, in addition to counseling and encouraging them.

When there are community leaders, and when the community has been developed, there is a net. Not everybody will be able to conform to strict brahmacārī life. Thus a variety of services is needed, or for one to become specialized in a particular field of service. A developed community is like having a net that is ready to catch the devotees so that they do not fall out, to keep them engaged within the community, and to give them direction and proper training. Within ISKCON, it is more developed in some places than in others.

**Question: To what extent should brahmacārīs participate in activities like nāma-haṭṭas, preaching and book distribution, and dealing with the guests? In addition, what should be done if they do not feel like participating in the temple preaching programs?**

They have to have some service. The services mentioned are the main services for brahmacārīs.
